Marianne is devastated by news of Willoughby's imminent marriage to wealthy Miss Grey; Elinor manages Mrs. Jennings's well-meaning but clumsy sympathy, then learns from Colonel Brandon—who overheard the news in a shop—that Willoughby's engagement is confirmed, and the two discuss Willoughby's deceit and Marianne's suffering.

Colonel Brandon visits Elinor and reveals Willoughby's past seduction and abandonment of his ward Eliza Williams, including a duel with Willoughby, exposing Willoughby's true dissolute character to give Marianne perspective on her own heartbreak.

Elinor delivers news of Willoughby's marriage to a devastated Marianne, while Mrs. Dashwood urges the sisters to remain in London; the Steele sisters then reappear, with Lucy resuming veiled provocations at Elinor.

Elinor and Marianne encounter their half-brother John Dashwood in a jeweller's shop, and he reveals his mercenary priorities by urging Elinor to pursue Colonel Brandon for his fortune, hinting at Edward Ferrars's planned marriage to the wealthy Miss Morton, and calculating potential inheritances from Mrs. Jennings, all while complaining of his own expenses.

At the Harley Street dinner Mrs. Ferrars coldly snubs Elinor while warmly favouring Lucy Steele — unaware Lucy is secretly engaged to her son Edward — until Marianne, outraged by the slight, defends her sister aloud and collapses in tears, prompting Colonel Brandon's visible concern.

Lucy visits Elinor to gloat over Mrs. Ferrars's apparent approval, Edward arrives unexpectedly creating an excruciating three-way scene, and Elinor maintains heroic composure while Marianne inadvertently praises Edward's conscience, all three trapped by the secret Lucy and Elinor share.

Elinor and Marianne are pushed into daily visits at the Middletons' alongside Lucy Steele; at a musical party Elinor meets the conceited Robert Ferrars; Fanny Dashwood, to dodge hosting her sisters-in-law, invites the Miss Steeles to Harley Street instead, unwittingly advancing Lucy's scheme to be near Edward.

Mrs. Jennings brings news that Edward Ferrars's secret engagement to Lucy Steele has been exposed at the Dashwood house; Elinor reveals to a horrified Marianne that she has borne this knowledge for four months, and John Dashwood reports that Edward refused to break the engagement despite Mrs. Ferrars's threats and has been disinherited in favour of his brother Robert.

Anne Steele reveals to Elinor (via eavesdropped conversation) that Edward stood firm by Lucy despite disinheritance, plans to take orders, and Lucy then writes Elinor a letter confirming the engagement holds and soliciting help securing a living.
Colonel Brandon offers Edward Ferrars the living at Delaford through Elinor, while Mrs. Jennings comically misreads their window conversation as a marriage proposal to Elinor.

Colonel Brandon offers Edward Ferrars the living of Delaford through Elinor, who delivers the news to Edward in person amid mutual embarrassment, while Mrs. Jennings comically misreads the situation as a marriage proposal to Elinor before the confusion is cleared up.

Elinor visits John Dashwood, who marvels at Colonel Brandon's gift of the Delaford living to Edward; Robert Ferrars then ridicules Edward's clerical fate and his engagement to Lucy, exposing the Ferrars family's hypocrisy and class prejudice.

The Dashwood sisters leave London and arrive at Cleveland, where Marianne's obsessive grief over Willoughby drives her to reckless wet-weather rambles that bring on a violent cold, while Colonel Brandon briefs Elinor on Edward Ferrars's parsonage at Delaford and reveals his unspoken devotion to Marianne through anxious looks.

Marianne's illness deteriorates into near-fatal crisis at Cleveland; Elinor nurses her through a terrifying night while Colonel Brandon rides to fetch their mother; Marianne recovers, but the chapter ends with the shock entrance of Willoughby instead of Mrs. Dashwood.

Willoughby arrives at Cleveland to confess to Elinor his selfish motives for courting Marianne, explaining how financial necessity and vanity led him to abandon her and marry Miss Grey, and begging Elinor to relay his remorse and penitence to her sister.

After Willoughby departs, Elinor processes complex pity for him while Mrs. Dashwood arrives with Colonel Brandon and privately reveals to Elinor that Colonel Brandon has declared his love for Marianne, urging hope for their eventual marriage.

Recovering from illness, Marianne returns home with Elinor, confronts memories of Willoughby at the spot where they met, delivers a heartfelt confession of past selfishness and vows moral reformation, then learns Willoughby's apology from Elinor and weeps in private grief.

After Marianne reaches painful closure on Willoughby's selfishness through Elinor's cool analysis, a servant's report that Edward Ferrars has married Lucy Steele shocks the household and forces Mrs. Dashwood to recognize how much she has overlooked Elinor's silent, long-suppressed grief.

Edward Ferrars arrives unexpectedly at Barton Cottage and reveals that Lucy Steele married his brother Robert instead of him, releasing Elinor from her long-suppressed anguish and sending her from the room in tears of joy.

Edward Ferrars, freed from his engagement to Lucy Steele (who secretly married his brother Robert), arrives at Barton Cottage and proposes to Elinor Dashwood, who joyfully accepts, while Colonel Brandon also visits and the two men bond as the newly engaged couple plans reconciliation with Mrs. Ferrars.

The final chapter resolves all fates: Edward and Elinor marry and settle at Delaford parsonage with Colonel Brandon's help; Marianne overcomes her romantic idealism and marries Colonel Brandon; Lucy Steele's calculated flattery wins Mrs. Ferrars's favour over Edward; and Willoughby lives comfortably but always regards Marianne as his secret standard of perfection.

testi/bronte/atomized/agnes_grey/chapter.plot: Agnes recounts her family's modest parsonage life, their financial collapse after a merchant investment fails, her campaign to become a governess despite parental resistance, and her tearful departure to serve the Bloomfield family.

Agnes arrives at Wellwood, endures a frigid welcome from Mrs Bloomfield, and spends her first afternoon with pupil Tom Bloomfield, whose domineering manner and casual cruelty to trapped birds reveal how far reality falls short of his mother's flattering portrait.

Agnes endures her first weeks as governess at the Bloomfields', battling Tom's physical defiance and Mary Ann's stubborn obstinacy while suffering dismissive blame from parents who attribute the children's deteriorating behaviour to her, and resolves to persist through patience alone.

Agnes returns to the Bloomfield household and endures relentless chaos from her unruly pupils, while Mr. Bloomfield blames her for disorder she cannot control, the duplicitous grandmother undermines her behind her back, and Mrs. Bloomfield sides with Tom against Agnes's attempts at discipline.
Agnes kills nestlings to spare them Tom's torture, clashes with Mrs Bloomfield who defends her son, and is ultimately dismissed for allegedly failing to improve the children's conduct.

Agnes returns home after Wellwood failure, recovers health amid family's worries over father's decline and poverty, then advertises for a new governess post and secures a position with the Murray family at Horton Lodge.

Agnes arrives at Horton Lodge through a blizzard to begin her second governess post and spends her first year enduring the Murray family's indifference and their spoiled, unteachable children, while Mrs Murray makes clear that superficial polish, not genuine learning, is all she expects.

Rosalie Murray, excited about her debut ball, interrupts Agnes reading a letter from home and mocks her sister's modest engagement to a country vicar, revealing the gulf between their values and social expectations.

Rosalie Murray monopolizes Agnes on her return to recount her ball triumphs, cataloguing her admirers and conquests while cynically dismissing marriage—briefly introducing the new curate Weston by name only as an "ugly beast."

Agnes attends church twice, favourably contrasting new curate Weston's earnest sincere preaching against vain Mr. Hatfield's performative sermons, while Rosalie and Matilda Murray bicker over Harry Meltham's attentions and Agnes is ignored by all gentry present.

Agnes visits cottagers in her free time, hears Nancy Brown recount how Mr. Weston's compassionate pastoral care restored her spiritual peace (contrasted with Rector Hatfield's cold dismissiveness), and reflects on her own loneliness and growing admiration for Weston as a moral beacon.
Agnes visits widow Nancy Brown, where a rain shower detains Mr. Weston long enough for a brief, charged exchange; on return, Miss Matilda scolds Agnes for her absence.

Walking behind her pupils, Agnes encounters Mr. Weston who gathers primroses for her; they share a brief intimate conversation about home and resilience before parting, and when Rosalie mockingly notices, Agnes retreats to pray privately for Weston's happiness.

Mrs. Murray sends Agnes to chaperon Rosalie, who Agnes finds lingering with the Rector Mr. Hatfield; Rosalie dismisses the encounter as calculated amusement, confessing she intends to marry for wealth (Ashby Park) not love, while Agnes's warnings go unheeded.

Agnes briefly encounters Mr. Weston on the road, then endures Rosalie Murray's gleeful account of coldly rejecting Mr. Hatfield's marriage proposal, prompting Agnes's silent disgust at Rosalie's heartless vanity and casual dishonesty.

Agnes walks to the village with Rosalie Murray, briefly enjoys an intimate conversation with Mr. Weston, but Rosalie intercepts him, flirtatiously monopolizes his attention, and then boasts she has "fixed" him, leaving Agnes privately heartbroken and suppressing her tears.

Agnes accompanies Rosalie to church where she secretly admires Weston; Rosalie then intercepts him at the porch and engineers a contrived road meeting the next day, scheming to add him to her list of admirers before an expected marriage proposal.

Newly engaged Rosalie Murray deliberately excludes Agnes from all contact with Mr. Weston while relentlessly pursuing him herself out of vanity, leaving Agnes to suffer in silent jealousy and find outlet only in private poetry.

Rosalie Murray marries Sir Thomas Ashby and departs; Agnes quietly yearns for Weston and briefly meets him during a country walk; news of her father's mortal illness sends her racing home, where she arrives to learn he has died.

After her father's death Agnes and her mother resolve to open a school rather than accept charity, then receive and defiantly reject a letter from the estranged grandfather who offers reconciliation only if the mother renounces her marriage.

Agnes spends her final six weeks at Horton Lodge before departing to help her widowed mother start a school; she has one brief meeting with Weston in a field and, on her last Sunday, he bids her goodbye with a veiled hint they may meet again, leaving her struggling to contain her tears.

Agnes co-runs a school with her mother, silently pines for Weston while receiving no word, disciplines herself through faith to accept her lot, then gets a letter from the now-married Rosalie (Lady Ashby) begging her to visit Ashby Park.

Agnes visits Rosalie (now Lady Ashby) at Ashby Park, witnesses her friend's visibly faded happiness and oppressive marriage, and learns that Weston has left Horton a month prior, dimming Agnes's last hope of ever seeing him again.

Agnes visits the now-married Lady Ashby (Rosalie Murray), who bitterly confesses misery in her loveless marriage to Sir Thomas Ashby, and Agnes offers moral counsel on duty and endurance before departing.

Agnes takes a solitary early-morning walk on the beach where she unexpectedly meets Mr. Weston (who returns her dog Snap), and they walk back through town together as he hints at wanting a life companion and promises to visit her mother.
Weston proposes to Agnes on an evening walk, having already secured her mother's blessing, and the chapter closes with their marriage and a brief account of their contented family life.

testi/bronte/atomized/jane_eyre/chapter_.plot: Jane, excluded by Mrs Reed from family warmth, retreats to a window-seat with a book until John Reed discovers her, strikes her, and has her locked in the red-room as punishment for fighting back.

Jane is forcibly locked in the red-room by Mrs Reed as punishment for fighting back against John Reed, and alone in the death-haunted chamber she panics at a mysterious light she takes for a ghost, screams for release, but Mrs Reed returns only to lock her in again until she loses consciousness.

After collapsing from the red-room ordeal, Jane is tended by apothecary Mr. Lloyd, who questions her misery and ultimately recommends she be sent to school, while Jane learns for the first time the story of her parents' deaths.

Jane endures months of exclusion at Gateshead before Mrs Reed arranges her admission to Lowood school via Mr Brocklehurst, who brands her deceitful; Jane then confronts Mrs Reed directly, declaring her hatred and accusing her of cruelty, winning a first moral victory before learning she will soon leave for school.

Jane departs Gateshead alone by coach and arrives at Lowood Institution, where she endures harsh conditions (burnt porridge, bitter cold, scanty food) and first encounters an unnamed girl (Helen Burns) reading Rasselas in the garden.
Jane observes Helen Burns flogged by Miss Scatcherd, then converses with her about endurance, forgiveness, and faith — contrasting Helen's Christian stoicism with Jane's instinct to resist injustice.
Brocklehurst visits Lowood, publicly denounces Jane as a liar before the whole school and forces her to stand on a stool, but Helen Burns's silent smile gives Jane the courage to endure the ordeal.

After Brocklehurst publicly brands Jane a liar, Helen Burns comforts her with spiritual counsel, Miss Temple invites both girls to her room for tea and hears Jane's defence, and — once Mr Lloyd's letter confirms Jane's account — Miss Temple publicly clears Jane's name before the whole school.
Typhus epidemic sweeps Lowood giving Jane unexpected freedom, but Helen Burns dies of consumption in Jane's arms after a secret night visit and a final conversation about faith and heaven.

After 8 years at Lowood, Miss Temple's departure awakens Jane's restlessness; she advertises for a governess post, receives an offer from Mrs. Fairfax of Thornfield, and leaves Lowood — with a parting visit from Bessie who brings news of the Reed family and hints of a mysterious uncle Eyre bound for Madeira.

Jane arrives at Thornfield Hall, meets the warm housekeeper Mrs Fairfax, discovers her pupil Adele Varens is ward of the absent Mr Rochester, tours the grand but eerie house, and hears a mysterious laugh from the attic corridor.
Jane, restless at Thornfield, walks to Hay and helps a thrown horseman who turns out to be Mr Rochester, her employer, newly arrived at the hall.

Jane and Adele join Mr Rochester for tea; he interrogates Jane about her background and art, scrutinises her visionary watercolours, while Mrs Fairfax later hints that Rochester's troubled past and family mysteries explain his abrupt, unsettled temperament.

Rochester summons Jane and Adèle to the dining room for an evening together, where he engages Jane in a frank, probing dialogue about his right to command her, his morally compromised past, and his cryptic desire for redemption, hinting at a hidden secret burden.
Rochester confides to Jane his history with Céline Varens—her betrayal, a duel, and his charity toward Adèle—then Jane saves him from a mysterious bedroom fire, deepening their emotional bond.

Jane confronts the imperturbable Grace Poole, learns Rochester has left for a party where the beautiful Blanche Ingram is present, and forces herself into self-discipline by resolving to paint contrasting portraits of herself and Blanche to quash her romantic illusions.

Mr Rochester returns to Thornfield with a party of aristocratic guests including the admired Blanche Ingram; Jane watches from the margins, silently acknowledges her love for Rochester despite their social gulf, and endures a cutting conversation about governesses before a brief private exchange with Rochester at the chapter's end.

During a festive house party at Thornfield, guests perform charades spelling "Bride-well" with Rochester and Miss Ingram acting a mock marriage, Jane silently endures her unrequited love while observing their loveless courtship, a mysterious stranger named Mason arrives from Jamaica, and a gypsy fortune-teller reads the young ladies' futures—leaving Jane summoned last.

Rochester disguises himself as a gipsy fortune-teller to probe Jane's feelings and thoughts, then reveals himself; Jane then shocks him with news that a man named Mason has arrived from the West Indies.

After a midnight shriek wakes Thornfield Hall, Rochester secretly summons Jane to tend the bleeding Mason, who has been bitten by Bertha, then smuggles Mason out at dawn before confiding in Jane about his entrapment by past error and his need for redemption.

Jane is summoned to Gateshead where dying Mrs Reed, after years of hostility, confesses she lied to Jane's uncle John Eyre that Jane was dead to prevent her inheriting, then dies unreconciled despite Jane's offered forgiveness.

Jane returns to Thornfield after prolonged stay at Gateshead following Mrs Reed's death, meets Rochester unexpectedly on the road, blurts out that wherever he is is her only home, and—back at the hall with Mrs Fairfax and Adèle—quietly nurtures forbidden hope that his engagement to Miss Ingram may yet collapse.

On a Midsummer eve in the orchard at Thornfield, Rochester tells Jane she must leave to find new employment, prompting her passionate declaration of equality and love, after which he proposes and she accepts, while a storm splits the chestnut tree as an ominous portent.

Morning after Rochester's proposal: Jane resists being lavished with gifts and maintains governess duties, Mrs Fairfax warns of the age/class gap, Rochester confesses he feigned courtship of Miss Ingram to provoke Jane's jealousy, and Jane deliberately keeps Rochester at arm's length through the engagement month to preserve her independence.

On the eve of her wedding, Jane recounts to Rochester two ominous dreams and a terrifying nocturnal visit from a mysterious dark-haired woman who tried on her veil then tore it in two; Rochester dismisses the intruder as Grace Poole and sends Jane to sleep beside Adèle, but Jane lies awake all night, unsettled.

Jane and Rochester's wedding is halted mid-ceremony when solicitor Briggs and Richard Mason reveal Rochester's living mad wife Bertha Mason; Rochester confirms the secret, leads all to witness Bertha confined at Thornfield, and Jane is left alone in stunned desolation.

After the aborted wedding, Rochester confesses the history of his forced marriage to Bertha Mason and begs Jane to stay as his mistress; Jane, torn between love and moral principle, refuses and secretly flees Thornfield at dawn.

Penniless and abandoned on the moor after fleeing Thornfield, Jane wanders for days begging food and shelter, reaching near-death collapse on the doorstep of Moor House before St John Rivers admits her and his sisters nurse her back.

Jane recovers from near-death exhaustion at Moor House, reconciles with servant Hannah, then partially discloses her history to St John Rivers and his sisters — orphan, former governess, fled in secrecy — and secures their promise to help her find honest work.

Jane, recovered at Moor House, bonds with Diana and Mary Rivers, accepts St John's offer of schoolmistress post at Morton, then learns uncle John has died leaving his fortune to a distant relation rather than the Rivers siblings.

Jane reflects on her first day as village schoolmistress—torn between moral pride in leaving Rochester and feelings of degradation—while St John Rivers visits, coldly resists Rosamond Oliver's advances, and reveals his resolve to abandon her for missionary work.

Jane settles into village schoolteaching and finds quiet fulfillment, yet dreams nightly of Rochester; St John Rivers visits and Jane draws out his confession of love for Rosamond Oliver, only for him to renounce her for his missionary calling, before he spots something on Jane's drawing paper, secretly tears off a slip, and departs without explanation.

St John Rivers visits Jane during a snowstorm, reveals her true identity as Jane Eyre (using her own handwriting as proof), informs her she has inherited £20,000 from her late uncle, and discloses that he and his sisters Diana and Mary are her cousins; Jane insists on dividing the fortune equally among the four of them.

St John Rivers formally proposes Jane join him in India as his missionary wife; Jane refuses the loveless marriage but offers to go as fellow-worker, and the chapter closes in cold, unresolved impasse between them.

Jane endures St John's cold emotional punishment and refuses his marriage proposal again, then hears Rochester's voice supernaturally calling her name, which breaks St John's hold over her and resolves her to return to Rochester.

Jane departs from Moor House toward Thornfield, finds it a burnt ruin, learns from an innkeeper that Bertha Mason set the fire and died leaping from the roof, and that Rochester survived but was left blind and maimed, then sets off immediately to find him at Ferndean.

Jane returns to the blinded and maimed Rochester at Ferndean, they reunite and he proposes; she accepts, and he recounts a mystical summons he heard at midnight that matched Jane's own experience of the call.

Jane marries Rochester, briefly summarizes their ten years of happy marriage including his partial recovery of sight and the birth of their son, updates reader on Adele's schooling, and closes with St John Rivers's devoted missionary life in India approaching death.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_01.plot: Three quarrelsome curates dine at Whinbury lodgings until their rector Mr. Helstone arrives, rebukes their idleness, and dispatches Malone to stand guard at Robert Moore's mill, which faces a potential Luddite attack the same night.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_02.plot: Curate Malone visits Robert Moore at Hollow's Mill while Moore waits for wagons of new machinery; the wagons return empty with a threatening note revealing frame-breakers smashed the machinery on Stilbro' Moor, and Moore rides out with Mr. Helstone to rescue his bound workers.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_03.plot: Riding back from the mill after the frame-breaker threat, Helstone and Moore bicker over Napoleon versus Wellington until they meet Mr. Yorke, who rescued Joe Scott from a ditch, and adjourn to Yorke's parlour where the political sparring continues and Yorke challenges Moore's cold alienation from the Yorkshire community.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_04.plot: Chapter continues the detailed psychological portrait of Mr. Yorke — his radicalism, pride, and old rivalry with Helstone over Mary Cave — then depicts a sharp political and religious argument between Yorke and Helstone, with Moore as wry mediator, until Yorke abruptly ejects both guests at midnight.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_05.plot: After the Luddite frame-breaking raid, Robert Moore returns to Hollow's Cottage where his Belgian sister Hortense teaches Caroline Helstone French; Robert and Caroline discuss worker hostility, her wish for independent occupation, and his emotional coldness toward employees, before he departs for market having lingered to give her flowers and invite her to spend the day.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_06.plot: Caroline spends the day under Hortense's instruction at Hollow's Cottage; Robert returns unexpectedly from market and the cousins share an intimate evening reading Shakespeare's Coriolanus aloud, during which Caroline uses the play to warn Robert against arrogance toward his workers, and he walks her home before privately confessing to himself that his growing feelings for her are a dangerous weakness he must suppress.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_07.plot: Caroline endures Robert Moore's cold morning withdrawal of warmth, suffers an unwanted tea gathering of curates and the Sykes family at the rectory, then meets Robert privately in the dining room where he shares news of identifying a frame-breaker and gently signals she must regard him only as a cousin before slipping away through the window.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_08.plot: Moore has Luddite ringleader Moses Barraclough arrested when a workers' deputation arrives at the mill, then refuses all compromise with honest worker William Farren, who returns home to find his family destitute and is helped by compassionate vicar Mr Hall with a small loan.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_09.plot: Robert Moore visits the Yorke family at Briarmains, where the children Rose and Jessy reveal that Caroline Helstone had publicly defended his character; he then privately persuades Yorke to employ the destitute workman William Farren, while confiding that his mill is on the brink of collapse and that he regards love and marriage as luxuries beyond his means.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_10.plot: Mr. Helstone bans Caroline from visiting the Moores after his political rupture with Robert; isolated and lovesick, Caroline broods on her likely fate as an old maid, then visits Miss Mann and Miss Ainley, finding hidden virtue in their solitary lives and resolving to occupy herself with charitable work, though she continues to waste away pining for Robert.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_11.plot: Caroline, pining secretly for Robert Moore and briefly glimpsing him unseen near Fieldhead, is taken by her uncle to meet Shirley Keeldar—the newly arrived heiress—who warmly welcomes her while Helstone and Shirley spar over Robert Moore's politics and Shirley's unconventional self-image as a landowner.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_12.plot: Shirley and Caroline deepen their friendship on a walk across Nunnely Common and in an evening at Fieldhead, frankly discussing men, marriage, and poetry while Mrs Pryor also cultivates Caroline's acquaintance; the chapter closes with a note from Robert Moore delivered to Shirley.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_13.plot: Caroline silently suffers watching Robert Moore walk intimately with Shirley by moonlight; the next evening Robert visits Fieldhead to report his military preparations against Luddite reprisals, then walks Caroline home and lingers with tender familiarity before hiding behind a monument to evade Mr Helstone.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_14.plot: Caroline privately agonises over her jealousy of Shirley's perceived hold on Robert Moore, then Shirley visits and the two women reaffirm their sisterly bond before Shirley, driven by conscience about the local poor, organises a charitable relief scheme with Miss Ainley and the three rectors at Fieldhead.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_15.plot: Curates Malone and Donne visit Fieldhead and are routed by Shirley's dog Tartar; the more welcome Mr. Hall and Sweeting join them for an outdoor lunch, during which Donne's arrogant demands for charity and contemptuous mockery of Yorkshire's people provoke Shirley to expel him from her property.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_16.plot: On Whit-Tuesday, Caroline and Shirley lead the Briarfield school procession together — Caroline emboldened by Shirley's presence — while Moore privately warns Shirley that the charitable fund cannot pacify the workers and that violent unrest is only delayed, not averted.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_17.plot: At the Briarfield school feast, Helstone leads the Anglican procession in routing a Dissenting group from Royd Lane; at the subsequent tea Shirley maneuvers to keep a seat for Robert Moore, who attends briefly then departs to join a secretive council of local men, leaving Caroline silently pining over his farewell and Shirley vexed at being kept from his plans.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_18.plot: Shirley and Caroline skip church to linger in the sunset churchyard, where Shirley delivers a visionary feminist reimagining of Eve as a titan-goddess of Nature, then both engage working-class gardener Farren and Robert Moore's overlooker Joe Scott in sharp debates over class pride, labor discontent, and women's right to political and scriptural opinion.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_19.plot: After Mr Helstone leaves them armed and alone at the rectory overnight, Shirley and Caroline overhear a Luddite mob marching on Moore's mill, race across the fields too late to warn him, and witness the rioters' attack and Robert Moore's successful armed defense from hiding, while Caroline must suppress her desperate urge to run to the slightly wounded Robert.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_20.plot: After the night attack on Moore's mill, Shirley and Caroline return to Fieldhead where Shirley forcefully organizes provisions for soldiers and wounded rioters, while Robert Moore arrives to scale back her excessive generosity and the two spar over men's inability to read women's minds and actions.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_21.plot: After Shirley reconciles with Mrs. Pryor following a quarrel, visitors debate the mill riot and Moore's character, while Caroline and Mrs. Pryor walk together and share a fraught conversation about the dangers of marriage and governess life, ending with Mrs. Pryor making an emotional offer to share her home and fortune with Caroline.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_22.plot: Chapter "Two Lives" contrasts Robert Moore's relentless hunt of riot leaders with parallel portraits of Shirley's cheerful active life at Fieldhead (soon disrupted by Sympson relatives' arrival) and Caroline's lonely, melancholy confinement at the rectory, where she meditates bitterly on society's denial of meaningful occupation to single women.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_23.plot: Caroline visits Hortense Moore's cottage, endures Mrs. Yorke's cutting insinuations about her feelings for Robert, debates women's freedom with Rose Yorke, then is startled by Robert's unexpected return from market accompanied by his previously unknown brother Louis, whose arrival briefly rekindles her hope before a hint of Robert's interest in Shirley Keeldar extinguishes it.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_24.plot: Caroline Helstone falls dangerously ill with fever while secretly longing for Robert Moore, and her devoted nurse Mrs Pryor reveals herself to be Caroline's long-estranged mother, giving the dying girl a reason to live.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_25.plot: Caroline slowly recovers from dangerous illness under Mrs Pryor's devoted nursing, while their newly revealed mother-daughter bond deepens through tender domestic intimacy at the rectory.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_26.plot: Caroline, recovered from illness, visits Fieldhead where old French exercise-books surface revealing that Louis Moore was once Shirley's tutor, exposing a suppressed prior connection both hide behind mutual pride and social distance.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_27.plot: Shirley defiantly refuses all suitors pressed by her uncle while Sir Philip Nunnely courts her with growing earnestness; she slips away from a dinner party to visit the feverish Louis Moore, and later their resumed French lesson in the schoolroom — including Louis's recitation of Shirley's old "Première Femme Savante" devoir — rekindles the old teacher-pupil intimacy and exposes the charged, unspoken feeling between them.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_28.plot: Shirley finally confesses to Louis Moore that weeks of secret anxiety stem from being bitten by a dog she feared was rabid; Moore reassures her, extracts her full testament-related disclosures from Henry, and promises to protect her in any extremity, while their intimate exchange of guardianship and mutual dependence thinly veils unspoken romantic feeling constrained by class difference.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_29.plot: Louis Moore, left alone at Fieldhead while Shirley and the Sympsons visit Nunnely, wanders her rooms, handles her belongings, and writes a private journal confessing his obsessive love for Shirley—comparing her unfavourably with the faultless Caroline Helstone—then deliberately pockets Shirley's keys to engineer a future pretext for closeness.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_30.plot: Riding home from Stilbro', Robert Moore confesses to Mr. Yorke that he proposed to Shirley Keeldar in a coldly mercenary fashion, was indignantly rejected, and has since resolved never to court a woman without true love; the chapter ends with an unknown assailant shooting at Robert from behind a wall, avenging the convicted Luddite ringleaders.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_31.plot: Shirley confronts her guardian Mr. Sympson, defiantly revealing she refused Sir Philip Nunnely's proposal and asserting sole right over her own hand; the chapter closes when Louis Moore arrives to report that his brother Robert has been shot, and Shirley comforts him and agrees to inform Caroline Helstone.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_32.plot: Robert Moore lies gravely wounded at Briarmains under the iron rule of nurse Mrs Horsfall while Caroline Helstone, wandering a moonlit wood, meets young Martin Yorke, who first falsely tells her Moore is dying then retracts, inadvertently exposing her hidden love for Moore to the perceptive boy, who promises to smuggle her news of the patient.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_33.plot: Martin Yorke schemes to clear the house and secretly escorts Caroline Helstone upstairs to visit the convalescing Robert Moore, where the two share a tender reunion, confessing mutual longing and illness during their long forced separation.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_34.plot: Martin Yorke defies his mother to attend Sunday church in a snowstorm hoping to encounter Caroline Helstone; after the service Caroline intercepts him in the snowy fields to obtain news of the confined Robert Moore and to beg Martin's help smuggling in a visit, which Martin teases and withholds.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_35.plot: Recovering Robert Moore returns to Hollow's Cottage and invites Caroline Helstone to tea, where they discuss Shirley Keeldar's undisclosed love while exchanging veiled, charged hints of their own mutual feeling.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_36.plot: Louis Moore, writing in his private journal, engineers a private interview with Shirley Keeldar, declares his love and extracts her reciprocation, then physically expels the furious Mr. Sympson from Fieldhead after the engagement is revealed, though in the days that follow Shirley remains elusive and Louis is left in aching suspense awaiting a marriage date.

testi/bronte/atomized/shirley/chapter_37.plot: The final chapter wraps up secondary characters' fates, then the repeal of the Orders in Council rescues Robert Moore from bankruptcy, prompting him to propose to Caroline who accepts, while Louis Moore overcomes Shirley Keeldar's delays; both couples marry on the same August day in Briarfield church.

testi/bronte/atomized/the_professor/chap.plot: Currer Bell's preface explains her commitment to realism over romantic fantasy for her hero, followed by A.B. Nicholls's posthumous note authorizing publication of the manuscript Charlotte had set aside after repeated rejections.

William Crimsworth, in a letter to a school friend, recounts rejecting his aristocratic uncles' offers of a living and a cousin-bride, declaring himself a tradesman to honor his disgraced father's memory, and traveling north to seek employment from his rich but cold brother Edward at Crimsworth Hall.
William visits Edward's mill in X----, accepts a clerk post managing foreign correspondence at £90/year, and resolves to endure his brother's contemptuous authority through patient self-control.

William endures his clerkship under Edward's surveillance and petty mockery, suffers deliberate social isolation at Edward's birthday party, then has a blunt first real conversation with Yorke Hunsden, who openly challenges William's subordinate position and questions whether he belongs in trade at all.

William, miserable under Edward's tyranny at the counting-house, encounters Hunsden on an evening walk, accepts his invitation inside, and endures pointed taunts that he will never succeed as a tradesman, leaving in suppressed fury and sleepless agitation.

William Crimsworth, exhausted by degrading servitude, confronts his brother Edward during a violent altercation in which Edward brandishes a whip and accuses William of slandering him via Hunsden; William defies him, breaks the whip, and quits the mill, walking away feeling liberated.

Hunsden visits William at his lodgings after the dismissal, defends his interference as principled anti-tyranny, and persuades William to seek work on the Continent, pressing a letter of introduction to Brussels into his hands.

William Crimsworth arrives in Brussels, uses Hunsden's letter to secure a teaching post with Monsieur Pelet, successfully asserts authority over his Belgian pupils in his first class, and moves into lodgings where a boarded window faces the girls' school of Mademoiselle Zoraide Reuter.

William reflects on Pelet's smooth but morally flawed character and his contempt for Flemish ushers, then is summoned to tea by Madame Pelet, where Madame Reuter (Zoraide's mother) conspiratorially proposes that William take a teaching post at Zoraide's adjoining girls' school.

William Crimsworth visits Mademoiselle Reuter's pensionnat to arrange terms for teaching her female pupils, finds her unexpectedly young and charming rather than the elderly spinster he imagined, and they negotiate a salary of five hundred francs per annum while he grows pleasantly attracted to her.

William Crimsworth gives his first lesson at Mademoiselle Reuter's girls' school, quells flirtatious disruption by shaming ringleader Eulalie, then endures a subtle psychological duel with Reuter herself, each probing the other for weakness and neither gaining advantage.

William returns late from Mlle. Reuter's school and M. Pelet draws him into a fireside coffee conversation, dissecting Reuter's scheming character and then tempting William to pursue the wealthy female pupils instead.

William Crimsworth catalogs the moral failings of his female pupils, begins falling for directress Zoraide Reuter after a tender garden encounter, then overhears from his window at night that she is secretly engaged to M. Pelet, extinguishing his nascent love.

Having discovered Pelet and Reuter's treachery, Crimsworth coldly masters his emotions at breakfast and in class, rebuffs Reuter's attempts to regain his approval, and dismisses the newly arrived Frances Henri before she can take her first English lesson.

William Crimsworth observes the new pupil Frances Henri for the first time in Mlle. Reuter's school, watching her struggle through but persevere at his English dictation exercise, and rewards her partial effort with a passing mark.

Crimsworth first hears Frances Henri read English with flawless accent, then is cornered by Directress Reuter who flatters him extravagantly and asks him to mentor Henri, while Crimsworth privately dissects Reuter's manipulative, power-worshipping character.

Crimsworth reads Frances Henri's remarkable devoir—a creative retelling of Alfred the Great's exile—then keeps her after class to correct its faults and acknowledge her literary gifts, while Mlle. Reuter silently observes the private exchange.

Crimsworth holds a series of private end-of-lesson conversations with Frances Henri, discovering her Swiss-English origins, her resourceful self-education funded by lace-mending, and her determined plan to emigrate to England, while Mme Reuter twice intervenes to cut the exchanges short.

Crimsworth watches Frances Henri flourish as student and teacher, then discovers Reuter has quietly forced her out of the school; Reuter confesses her method of removing inconvenient staff through indirect pressure, refuses to give Frances's address, and Crimsworth vows to find his best pupil regardless.

William Crimsworth, after a month fruitlessly searching Brussels for his dismissed pupil Frances Henri, discovers her mourning at her aunt's fresh grave in the Protestant Cemetery, escorts her home through a storm, shares tea in her spartan lodgings, and privately resolves to win her as his wife.

William Crimsworth, disgusted by Pelet's drunken jealousy and the impending marriage of Pelet and Zoraide Reuter, resigns his position on moral grounds, choosing destitution over the temptation of remaining under the same roof as a woman still infatuated with him.

William receives two letters—Frances Henri's joyful news of a new teaching post and Hunsden's mocking announcement of his Brussels visit—and, agonized that his own dismissal and poverty bar him from proposing to Frances, resolves to seek a job recommendation from M. Vandenhuten (whose son he once rescued from drowning), only to find the family absent from town.

Having quit Pelet's pensionnat after Zoraide's marriage, William suppresses his longing for Frances, endures Hunsden's mocking visit and learns of Edward's financial ruin and sale of Crimsworth Hall, then discovers Hunsden secretly sent him his mother's portrait rescued from the auction, and finally secures a Brussels college professorship through Vandenhuten's recommendation.

William visits Frances, reads her revealing love poetry, impulsively proposes marriage which she accepts on condition she keeps her teaching post, then returns home and suffers nine days of hypochondria.

William Crimsworth brings Yorke Hunsden to meet Frances Henri; Hunsden—shocked William would marry a mere lace-mender—spars with her in a heated debate on English and Swiss national character before departing grudgingly impressed by her spirit and intelligence.

William and Frances marry, build a thriving school in Brussels over ten years, then retire to an English country home near Hunsden's estate, where their domestic happiness, Frances's dual role as wife and school directress, and the upbringing of their intense son Victor are described in the novel's closing retrospect.

testi/bronte/atomized/the_tenant_of_wild.plot: Gilbert Markham, narrator and gentleman farmer, introduces his family and local society, then recounts neighborhood excitement over the mysterious Mrs. Graham who has taken up solitary residence at ruined Wildfell Hall, culminating in Gilbert's first charged glimpse of her at church.

Gilbert Markham, hunting on the moors, catches Mrs. Graham's young son who falls from Wildfell Hall's garden wall; she reacts with alarmed suspicion before recognising him, then coldly dismisses him, and he retreats to Eliza Millward's company to soothe his wounded pride.

Mrs. Graham (Helen Huntingdon) pays her first call at Linden-Car, where she clashes sharply with Gilbert Markham and his mother over child-rearing: she defends shielding young Arthur from vice while Gilbert argues virtue requires exposure to temptation, and Helen exposes the hypocrisy of applying different moral standards to boys and girls.

At the Markham family's November 5th party — from which Mrs. Graham (Helen) is conspicuously absent — neighbors gossip about her unconventional method of teaching her son to despise alcohol; Mr. Lawrence defends her approach in a debate with the vicar; and Gilbert's mother reprimands him for flirting with Eliza Millward.

Gilbert and Rose visit Helen's studio at Wildfell Hall, where Helen paints under a false name to hide her whereabouts, a mysterious man briefly appears at the window, and Gilbert discovers a face-down hidden portrait that Helen sharply reclaims before they part on uneasy but cordial terms.

Over several months Gilbert repeatedly seeks out Mrs. Graham on the moors, befriends her son Arthur, and finds himself increasingly drawn to her; after a charged encounter by the brook and a sparring exchange with Lawrence about his interest, he returns home to a domestic debate with his mother and Rose on marriage and gender duty.

Gilbert Markham joins neighbors visiting Wildfell Hall, then accompanies Mrs. Graham (Helen) and a mixed party on a coastal picnic excursion to the cliffs, during which his attraction to her deepens as he seeks her company and sketches beside her, while neglecting Eliza Millward.

Gilbert Markham visits Wildfell Hall with a copy of "Marmion" as a gift for Mrs. Graham, who refuses it to avoid obligation, sparking a tense exchange that ends with her accepting the book on her own terms and their friendship cautiously reaffirmed.

At a neighbourhood party, Gilbert witnesses guests spreading slander about Mrs. Graham's character and suspected connection to Mr. Lawrence; he defends her silently, steals a private garden conversation with her and her son Arthur, then ends the evening in furious hostility toward Lawrence, whom he now suspects of concealed designs on her.

Gilbert visits Wildfell Hall, shares a near-romantic garden encounter with Helen who firmly confines him to friendship and hints at a secret vow, then confronts Lawrence on the lane, accusing him of duplicity toward her.

Gilbert defends his friendship with Helen (Mrs. Graham) against his sister Rose's warnings about village gossip, then the vicar arrives to report he has formally rebuked Helen for scandalous conduct, enraging Gilbert who storms out and heads to Wildfell Hall.

Gilbert visits Helen at Wildfell Hall, confesses love and urges her to clear her name by uniting with him, but she defers her secret confession to the next day; when Gilbert lingers and spies through the garden wall he sees Helen walking intimately with Mr. Lawrence, plunging him into a paroxysm of jealous despair.

Gilbert, brooding and ill-tempered after his disillusionment about Mrs. Graham, forces himself to tend to farm business at Ryecote Farm, endures spiteful mockery from Eliza and Miss Wilson, then deliberately turns away to avoid a chance hillside encounter with Mrs. Graham and her son, leaving him doubly miserable.

Gilbert, consumed by jealous rage, strikes Lawrence with a whip-handle during a chance road encounter, leaves him injured on the ground, then discovers Lawrence chooses not to report the assault — apparently to protect Mrs. Graham's reputation.
Gilbert confronts Helen in a tense standoff over what he overheard; she refuses to explain but finally thrusts her private diary into his hands to read as her defense.

Young Helen, back from her first London season, recounts her aunt's warnings about imprudent marriage, her charming first encounter with Huntingdon at a ball, and her firm rejection of the tedious suitor Boarham's proposal.

At a dinner party Helen watches Huntingdon flirt with Annabella, is rescued by him from an unwanted suitor, nearly hears his declaration before her aunt intervenes, then endures a long lecture warning her against a man of poor character — but she resolves to love and reform him regardless.

Huntingdon arrives for a shooting party at Helen's uncle's estate, discovers her secret portrait sketches of him, provokes her into burning the miniature in anger, then coldly redirects his flirtations to Annabella Wilmot while playing both her and Lord Lowborough, leaving Helen consumed by jealousy and regret.

Stung by Huntingdon's public slight in favour of Annabella's singing, Helen weeps alone in the library; Huntingdon follows, declares his love, and proposes; her aunt interrupts and defers approval to the next day.

Young Helen accepts Arthur Huntingdon's marriage proposal through her uncle while sparring with her aunt over Arthur's character and engaging in a scriptural debate on universal salvation versus eternal damnation.

Helen's engagement to Huntingdon is fixed for Christmas; Milicent and Annabella respond with doubt and veiled rivalry, while Huntingdon relays his bachelor friends' bitter complaints that the marriage will end their dissolute brotherhood.

During a riding party, Huntingdon recounts Lowborough's ruin through gambling and drink and casually reveals that Annabella (Miss Wilmot) privately confessed to despising Lowborough while courting him for his title; Annabella then announces her engagement to Helen, and Helen weeps over Huntingdon's moral callousness rather than the deceived lord.

Eight weeks into marriage, Helen confides in her diary that Arthur is selfish and superficial — he rushed their honeymoon and now demands she subordinate her religious devotion to him — while she argues back that true love of God deepens rather than diminishes earthly love.
Helen and Arthur quarrel after he boasts of past affairs; she maintains cold reserve for two days until his contrition breaks the standoff and they reconcile, agreeing to travel to London together.

Helen records months of anxious solitude at Grassdale after Arthur sends her home from London under pretense of business, learns Milicent Hargrave has been coerced into marrying Hattersley, and finally receives Arthur back debauched and exhausted—then nurses him to health while he plans a shooting party including Lord Lowborough, Annabella, and Walter Hargrave.

Helen suppresses jealousy as Annabella and Huntingdon openly flirt while Lord Lowborough suffers visibly; the party then visits the Grove where Helen silently condemns Mrs. Hargrave's social-climbing hypocrisy and its toll on her daughters.

Helen catches Arthur openly flirting with Annabella, confronts him that night and extracts a half-hearted promise to stop, then endures Annabella's cold taunting during a private exchange the next morning.

Helen's diary entries spanning two Christmases record her deepening disillusionment with Arthur's self-indulgent character, his refusal to take her to London, his months-long absence, and her bitter conclusion that she can never trust his word.

During Arthur's prolonged dissipated absence in London, Walter Hargrave returns to the neighbourhood and makes repeated sympathetic visits to Helen, who holds him at a guarded distance while learning from him that Arthur has been deliberately deceiving her about his planned return date.

Helen endures Arthur's debauched return home, restrains his drinking with Hargrave's covert help, watches him depart to Scotland and return briefly improved, yet dreads the approaching spring and his likely relapse.

Helen records a series of disgraceful autumn house-party evenings in which Arthur and his companions drink themselves into chaos, Hattersley physically brutalises Lord Lowborough and Milicent, Annabella shows cold contempt for her husband, and Helen endures it all in silent despair.

Helen and Milicent discuss Esther's future and their own unhappy marriages; Hattersley bluntly reveals his indifference to Milicent while praising Annabella; Helen confronts him about his cruelty; then Hargrave attempts to disclose an alarming secret about Huntingdon, which Helen refuses to hear.

Helen discovers Arthur's affair with Annabella by witnessing them together in the shrubbery, then confronts Arthur and declares their marriage a name-only arrangement after he refuses to let her leave with their child.

Helen confronts Annabella Lowborough privately about her affair with Huntingdon, refuses to expose her to Lord Lowborough or Milicent, and urges her to leave the house, while privately recording her hatred of her husband and wariness of Hargrave's calculated sympathy.

On the eve of the guests' departure, Helen endures Annabella's provocations and Arthur's open flirtation, repels Hargrave's advances in the library, and disciplines her fury through forced composure until the party leaves the next morning.

Helen records the cold, hostile coexistence with Arthur over three years of marriage: he drinks, mocks her, flaunts Annabella's love letter, and undermines her authority over their son, leaving Helen resolved to endure through faith alone.

Helen's diary recounts Walter Hargrave's persistent, escalating attempts to seduce her during Arthur's absences; she rejects him each time with moral firmness, ultimately giving him an ultimatum to stay silent or leave, and he departs for Paris.

Lord Lowborough discovers his wife Annabella's two-year affair with Huntingdon, confronts Helen for concealing it, refuses Hattersley's offer to arrange a duel, spends a near-suicidal night resisting self-destruction, then departs with Annabella at dawn while Huntingdon jeers.

Helen resolves to flee Grassdale with her son to escape Huntingdon's debauchery, secretly paints to raise funds; Hargrave makes a forced declaration which she rejects, then Huntingdon publicly accuses her of infidelity, and she compels Hargrave to clear her name before the men.

Arthur Huntingdon reads Helen's secret diary, discovers her escape plan, destroys her painting materials, confiscates her money and valuables, and reduces her to a small allowance, leaving her feeling utterly imprisoned and despairing of rescuing her son.

With her husband temporarily absent, Helen systematically conditions young Arthur against alcohol, negotiates a secret refuge plan with her brother Frederick, and counsels Esther Hargrave to resist a coerced marriage.

Helen shows Hattersley his wife Milicent's anguished letters to shame him into reforming his dissolute ways; he vows amendment and reconciles emotionally with Milicent, while Arthur Huntingdon remains absent and unreformed.

Helen, having discovered Huntingdon's governess Miss Myers is his mistress, secretly prepares flight with son Arthur and faithful servant Rachel, writes farewell letters to friends and family, and on the eve of departure records her final night at Grassdale before escaping under the alias Mrs. Graham.

Helen's diary records her predawn flight from Grassdale with son Arthur and Rachel to Wildfell Hall, where brother Frederick shelters her; Huntingdon hunts for her and bargains for the child's return; the chapter closes with Gilbert Markham as frame narrator noting the diary pages are torn where Helen was about to describe him.

Gilbert finishes reading Helen's diary, visits her at Wildfell Hall where they exchange forgiveness but she insists on permanent separation; he then goes to apologise to her brother Frederick Lawrence for a previous assault and they reconcile.

Gilbert waits out Helen's remaining months at Wildfell Hall while befriending her brother Lawrence, then warns Lawrence off a match with the malicious Jane Wilson, steering him away from the unsuitable alliance.

Gilbert Markham hears rumours Helen has reconciled with her husband, rides to Woodford, learns the truth from Lawrence, and reads Helen's letter describing her voluntary return to Grassdale to nurse the gravely ill Huntingdon while securing a written custody promise for their son.

Gilbert reads Helen's letter describing her exhausting nursing of the ailing Arthur Huntingdon and their cold exchange about forgiveness and the future, then uses the revelations to clear Helen's name in the neighbourhood, with digressions on the eventual fates of the Millward and Wilson families.

Gilbert reads Helen's letters describing Arthur Huntingdon's agonizing deathbed — relapse from drink, paralysing fear of damnation, desperate clinging to Helen — culminating in his death as she holds his hand.

After Huntingdon's death, Markham endures months of anxious waiting, unable to contact Helen due to pride and class concerns while Lawrence withholds news; the chapter then dispatches secondary characters — Lady Lowborough's ruin and death, Lord Lowborough's redemptive remarriage, and Hattersley's reform.

Alarmed by Eliza Millward's rumour that Helen is marrying Hargrave, Gilbert races through snow to Grassdale church, only to discover the bride is Esther Hargrave and the groom his friend Frederick Lawrence.

Gilbert travels to Grassdale then Staningley seeking Helen, but on learning she has inherited a vast fortune he halts at her gates and resolves to retreat, deeming the class gulf now unbridgeable and his pursuit an imposition on her.

Gilbert Markham unexpectedly encounters the newly wealthy Helen at Staningley, suppresses his feelings due to her inheritance, but Helen signals her love through a Christmas rose and they become engaged, closing the novel with their happy marriage.

testi/bronte/atomized/villette/chapter_0.plot: Lucy Snowe, visiting her godmother Mrs Bretton, witnesses the arrival of small, grieving Polly Home, a child placed temporarily in Mrs Bretton's care after her mother's death and her father's illness-forced travels.

Polly Home, pining miserably for her absent father, is suddenly reunited with Mr. Home on an unexpected visit; later that evening Graham Bretton returns and engages Polly in a comically formal yet sparring exchange, with Lucy Snowe observing both reunions with cool detachment.

After her father's departure, Polly forms an intense, devotional bond with young Graham at the Bretton house—marked by playful skirmishes, tender Sunday readings, and a brief rupture—until a letter summons her to join her father abroad, leaving her sleepless and heartbroken the night before she departs.

Lucy Snowe, adrift after personal losses, becomes live-in companion to the crippled Miss Marchmont, who confides the tragic death of her fiancé Frank on Christmas Eve thirty years past, then dies peacefully that same night after a final lucid conversation.
After her employer Miss Marchmont dies, Lucy travels alone to London seeking new employment, arriving bewildered and penniless at night yet resolving to press forward rather than retreat.

Lucy spends an exhilarating day exploring London alone, then boards a night vessel to the continent, meets the frivolous and selfish Ginevra Fanshawe during a rough Channel crossing, and arrives penniless and friendless at a foreign port with no plan beyond survival.

Lucy Snowe, stranded alone in Villette at night without luggage or contacts, wanders the dark city guided briefly by a kind English stranger, and by apparent fate stumbles upon Madame Beck's pensionnat, where Paul Emanuel reads her character and Madame Beck hires her on the spot.

Lucy Snowe arrives at Madame Beck's pensionnat, is covertly inspected during the night, witnesses Madame summarily dismiss the drunken nursemaid Mrs. Sweeny, and is then pushed by Madame to take over an unruly class of sixty pupils, succeeding by locking the ringleader in a closet and thereby earning a promotion from nursery governess to English teacher.

Lucy settles into teaching at Madame Beck's school while Ginevra Fanshawe confesses she has been accepting costly gifts from a lovesick suitor she calls "Isidore," whom she openly scorns, preferring instead a dashing officer named Colonel de Hamal.

testi/bronte/atomized/villette/chapter_1.plot: A young English doctor introduced as Dr. John sets Fifine's broken arm and becomes a regular visitor at the pensionnat through Désirée's feigned illness, while the overlooked Lucy recognizes him as the stranger who aided her on her arrival in Villette.

Lucy observes Dr. John emerge shaken from a secret encounter with flirtatious portress Rosine, while Madame Beck, who harbors romantic designs on the doctor, manages parental scandal over his school presence with shrewd diplomacy and then privately confronts her own bitter disappointment when she sees his indifference to her.

Lucy finds a love-note casket dropped into the forbidden garden alley, Dr. John (Graham Bretton) slips in at night to retrieve it and begs her silence, while Madame Beck covertly watches and later plays innocent to mask her suspicion.

Lucy catches Madame Beck secretly searching her belongings, then witnesses a second billet dropped from the neighboring house during Dr. John's visit to Georgette, after which Dr. John asks Lucy to act as guardian for a mysterious woman he admires—only for Madame Beck to interrupt the disclosure with an inadvertent sneeze while eavesdropping at the keyhole.

At Madame Beck's school fête, Paul Emanuel drafts Lucy Snowe into a last-minute male role in the vaudeville; she performs it with unexpected relish while Ginevra Fanshawe openly flirts with Graham Bretton (Dr. John) from the stage, and the night ends with Lucy confronting Ginevra about her callous treatment of Dr. John's devotion.

Left alone at the school during the long vacation while all others depart, Lucy Snowe descends into severe psychological and physical collapse, enduring weeks of desolation and feverish nightmares before wandering into a Catholic church to confess to a priest, then collapsing unconscious in the storm.

Lucy Snowe wakes from her breakdown in a room whose furnishings she gradually recognises as from her godmother's old home at Bretton, learns she has been taken in by Mrs Bretton, and reunites with Graham Bretton (Dr John), revealing that she had long known who he was while he had never recognised her.

Lucy Snowe, recuperating at La Terrasse under Mrs. Bretton's care, learns from Dr. Graham Bretton how he and a priest rescued her after she collapsed following a desperate visit to confession, and spends two tranquil evenings with the Brettons while silently observing Graham's unspoken longing for Ginevra Fanshawe.

Lucy loses patience and scolds Graham for his blind infatuation with the mercenary Ginevra Fanshawe; they quarrel, then reconcile that evening, after which Graham resumes confiding his lovesick obsession to a privately skeptical Lucy.

During her extended recovery at La Terrasse, Lucy visits galleries with Dr. John and encounters the Cleopatra painting, where Paul Emanuel forcibly redirects her to duller canvases on grounds of feminine propriety, then Dr. John rejoins her and dismisses Cleopatra by comparing her unfavourably to Ginevra.

testi/bronte/atomized/villette/chapter_2.plot: Lucy accompanies Mrs. Bretton and Graham to a grand royal concert in Villette where, after Ginevra Fanshawe mockingly ridicules Graham and his mother, Graham's infatuation with Ginevra collapses and he declares his mother worth more than any beauty.

Lucy returns to the pensionnat after vacation, wages an internal battle between personified Reason and Hope over Graham's promised letter, receives that letter delivered by the intrusive M. Paul, and defuses his furious classroom outburst while secretly hoarding the unopened letter as a private treasure.

Lucy steals away to read Dr. John's letter in the school garret, encounters a ghostly nun-figure that terrifies her, flees to Madame Beck's salon where Graham Bretton happens to be present, recovers her stolen letter from him, and hears his diagnosis that the apparition was a spectral illusion born of nervous strain.

Graham takes Lucy to see the actress Vashti perform, whose demonic intensity overwhelms Lucy while Graham watches with cold curiosity; a fire panics the theatre crowd and Graham rescues an injured young girl, then escorts her to her hotel where he treats her injuries.

After seven weeks of agonizing silence, Lucy receives a letter from Mrs. Bretton inviting her to La Terrasse, where she discovers that the injured girl she met weeks ago is Paulina Mary Home de Bassompierre — little Polly, now grown — who remembers Lucy and their shared Bretton past with vivid precision.

Lucy and Paulina (Polly) spend a snowbound day at La Terrasse with Mrs. Bretton, the Count de Bassompierre, and Graham, during which Lucy's status as a working teacher is revealed, the Count proposes enrolling Polly at Madame Beck's school, and Graham and Paulina begin a tentative, charged reacquaintance that hints at mutual attraction.

Lucy observes Paulina (Polly) silently and tenderly revisiting Graham's childhood books at Mrs Bretton's house, then anxiously waiting for her father and Graham to return from town, revealing her deep but wordless attachments to both.

Lucy ritually buries Graham's letters in the garden pear-tree as symbolic interment of her dead hope, sees the veiled nun apparition again, declines Paulina's offer to live with her family, endures Paul Emanuel's jealous surveillance of her outings, and learns from Paulina that Ginevra's boastful tales of Graham as her devoted suitor have made Paulina awkward and cold towards him.

At a Labassecour civic ceremony Paul Emanuel delivers a fiery political oration, then at the Hôtel Crécy evening gathering Graham openly pursues Paulina while Lucy endures his condescension and Paul's stinging insult, before Paul and Lucy quietly reconcile in the vestibule.

Lucy braves Paul Emanuel's furious classroom to deliver an urgent summons, accidentally shatters his spectacles which paradoxically softens him; that evening he returns, seats himself beside Lucy (then exiles himself to the far end of the bench in a fit of pique), reads Shakespeare aloud, then privately lectures her on her supposedly worldly dress and ribbon while she stitches him a silk watchguard, and they part on unexpectedly warm terms.

testi/bronte/atomized/villette/chapter_3.plot: On M. Paul's fête day Lucy crafts him a beaded guard but withholds it out of spite, clashes with him during his xenophobic tirade against England, then catches him secretly rifling through her desk.

Lucy catches Paul Emanuel secretly depositing books at her desk on his fête-day; after a tense confrontation over her deliberate refusal to bring him flowers, she presents him with a handmade silk chain, they reconcile, and the evening closes in warm, wordless companionship.

Lucy Snowe recounts M. Paul Emanuel's jealous, domineering pedagogy — his suspicions about her hidden classical learning, his contempt for "women of intellect," and their escalating battle over his demand that she perform an improvised public composition — ending with Lucy escaping while he fetches her water.

Lucy falls asleep in the classroom and wakes covered by shawls; Paul Emanuel reveals he secretly watches everyone through a rented window and a hidden garden key, and their twilight conversation about supernatural impressions ends when the ghostly nun sweeps violently past both of them in the garden.

Polly Home confides to Lucy Snowe that Graham Bretton secretly wrote her a love letter during her travels; she responds with careful restraint, and the two women discuss whether her father will ever sanction the match.

Paul Emanuel leads students on a country breakfast excursion, sharing moments of tender intimacy with Lucy and hinting at departure; that evening he urgently seeks her out, but Lucy panics and flees, Madame Beck intercepts and dismisses him, leaving Lucy in regret and suspense.

Lucy is sent by Madame Beck to deliver fruit to the monstrous Madame Walravens; sheltering from a storm, she is guided by Père Silas — her former confessor — who reveals that Paul Emanuel has devoted his income and celibacy to supporting Walravens's household out of undying love for the long-dead Justine Marie.

Lucy is dragged before two sneering college professors who doubt M. Paul's claim that her essay is her own; she vindicates him with a scathing impromptu piece on "Human Justice," then in a subsequent garden conversation M. Paul confesses his austere solitary life and proposes a deep brother-sister friendship, which Lucy accepts with quiet joy.

Lucy discovers Paul Emanuel's cold withdrawal was engineered by confessor Père Silas, who planted a Catholic conversion tract in her desk; Paul visits and they hold a frank interfaith dialogue that ends in unexpected spiritual accord, while Père Silas then visits Madame Beck to arrange his control of Lucy's religious direction.

Lucy acts as confidante and mediator as Graham Bretton seeks M. de Bassompierre's blessing to marry Paulina (Polly); the reluctant father relents, the couple weds and prospers, while Lucy remains a solitary, excluded observer.

testi/bronte/atomized/villette/chapter_4.plot: Madame Beck announces Paul Emanuel's departure for Guadeloupe and maneuvers to block Lucy from a farewell; after being given an opiate that backfires into feverish excitement, Lucy slips out at midnight into an illuminated festival park where she covertly observes the Bretton–Bassompierre party and uncovers Madame Beck's conspiratorial circle, receiving only a note from Paul promising one last private meeting before he sails.

Lucy covertly watches Paul Emanuel at the night festival, learns he delayed his voyage and seems devoted to his ward Justine Marie, then returns to the dormitory to find the phantom nun exposed as a stuffed dummy with a mocking farewell note.

Ginevra Fanshawe elopes overnight with Alfred de Hamal — revealed via her letter to Lucy as the man behind the "nun" disguise — and Lucy recounts Ginevra's breezy, self-satisfied married life in the years that follow.

Paul Emanuel secretly prepares a house and schoolroom in Faubourg Clotilde for Lucy, defies Madame Beck's interference, declares his love and proposes she run her own school during his three-year absence in Guadaloupe, then sails away the next day.

During Paul Emanuel's three-year absence Lucy runs a thriving school sustained by his faithful letters, but as his return approaches a catastrophic storm strikes — implying he is lost at sea — while the narrator withholds the ending and closes the novel.

testi/bronte/atomized/wuthering_heights/.plot: Lockwood visits his reclusive landlord Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, is met with cold reserve and aggressive dogs, yet is fascinated enough to resolve on a return visit.

Lockwood visits Wuthering Heights a second time, is met with cold hostility from the young Mrs. Heathcliff (Cathy Linton) and the rough Hareton Earnshaw, is attacked by dogs when trying to leave, and is compelled to spend the night after Zillah intervenes.

themes: the past intruding on the present
testi/bronte/atomized/wuthering_heights/.plot: Lockwood, sleeping in a forbidden chamber, discovers Catherine's childhood diary scrawled on the windowsill and suffers two nightmares—the second conjuring her ghost begging entry—before witnessing Heathcliff's desperate, tearful call for Catherine's spirit at the open casement at dawn.

Lockwood asks Nelly Dean about his neighbours' history; she begins her retrospective account of how old Mr Earnshaw brought the foundling Heathcliff home from Liverpool, sparking immediate resentment from Hindley while young Cathy accepted him, with Heathcliff already showing cold cunning in exploiting his hold over the master.
Old Mr. Earnshaw declines and dies in his fireside chair while Catherine and Heathcliff sit beside him; the two children comfort each other in grief as Nelly and Joseph react to the loss.

Hindley returns with a wife and degrades Heathcliff to a farm labourer; Heathcliff and Catherine sneak to Thrushcross Grange to spy on the pampered Linton children, Catherine is seized by the guard-dog and kept inside by the Lintons while Heathcliff is driven off, leaving her stranded among the gentry and widening the gulf between them.

Catherine returns from Thrushcross Grange transformed into a refined lady; her changed appearance humiliates the neglected Heathcliff, who is mocked and banished by Hindley during the Christmas visit of the Lintons, sparking Heathcliff's first vow of revenge.

Frances dies shortly after bearing Hareton, driving Hindley into reckless dissolution; Catherine maintains a double character between Heathcliff and Edgar Linton, and after a violent outburst during Edgar's visit the two confess their love.

Catherine confesses to Nelly that she accepted Edgar Linton's proposal for social reasons yet declares Heathcliff her true self ("I am Heathcliff"); Heathcliff overhears enough to flee into the storm, Catherine's anguish triggers a dangerous fever, and—after her recovery—she eventually marries Edgar while Heathcliff remains absent.

Heathcliff returns after three years transformed into a wealthy gentleman, is joyfully received by Catherine at Thrushcross Grange while Edgar remains coldly suspicious, and reveals he has lodged himself at Wuthering Heights with Hindley — all while Isabella develops an infatuation with him that Heathcliff privately notes with calculating interest.

Nelly finds Hareton feral and corrupted by Heathcliff at the Heights; back at Thrushcross Grange she catches Heathcliff embracing Isabella, triggering a violent three-way confrontation with Edgar Linton that ends with Heathcliff driven out and Catherine locking herself away in a hysterical fit, threatening to destroy herself if forced to choose between husband and friend.

Catherine collapses into feverish delirium after days of self-starvation, raving about Heathcliff and Wuthering Heights while Edgar stands helpless; Nelly fetches the doctor and discovers Isabella has eloped with Heathcliff.

Isabella writes Nelly from Wuthering Heights describing her grim arrival as Heathcliff's new wife—Hindley pacing with a knife-pistol and murderous intent toward Heathcliff, Joseph and young Hareton hostile, no proper room provided—while back at the Grange Catherine slowly recovers from brain fever under Edgar's devoted care.

Nelly visits Wuthering Heights to relay Edgar's cold refusal of contact with Isabella; Heathcliff then coerces Nelly into agreeing to smuggle him into Thrushcross Grange for a secret meeting with the ailing Catherine.

Heathcliff secretly visits the gravely ill Catherine at Thrushcross Grange; they share a desperate final embrace filled with anguished recriminations and declarations of love before Edgar returns from church and Nelly urges Heathcliff to leave.

Catherine Earnshaw dies hours after giving birth to infant Cathy; Nelly tells Heathcliff, who erupts in violent grief and begs Catherine's ghost to haunt him, secretly visits the corpse to exchange hair locks, then Catherine is buried on a plain slope at the edge of the moor.

Isabella flees Wuthering Heights and recounts Heathcliff's savage beating of Hindley the night before; Hindley soon dies drunk and in debt, leaving Heathcliff as mortgagee and de facto master of Wuthering Heights with Hareton wholly in his power.

During Edgar's absence, thirteen-year-old Cathy Linton secretly rides to Wuthering Heights, meets Hareton Earnshaw, and is shocked to discover he is her cousin and that Heathcliff has deliberately kept him illiterate and brutish.

Linton Heathcliff arrives at Thrushcross Grange after Isabella's death, briefly welcomed by Cathy and Edgar, but Heathcliff's servant Joseph immediately demands the boy back, forcing Edgar to concede Linton will be sent to Wuthering Heights the next morning.

Nelly delivers Linton Heathcliff to Wuthering Heights; Heathcliff receives his frail son with contempt and discloses his plan to use the boy to seize the Linton estates, keeping him alive only as an instrument of revenge.

Heathcliff engineers a meeting between Cathy Linton and Linton Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, reveals his scheme to unite them in marriage to secure the Grange property, and weeks of secret love letters between the cousins follow until Nelly discovers and burns them.

themes: parental illness and fear of loss
testi/bronte/atomized/wuthering_heights/.plot: Nelly accompanies a grieving Cathy on a walk where Heathcliff intercepts them and manipulates Cathy into believing Linton Heathcliff is dying for love of her, prompting Nelly to reluctantly escort Cathy to Wuthering Heights the next day.

Cathy and Nelly visit a sickly, peevish Linton Heathcliff at Wuthering Heights, where a quarrel over their parents' histories ends with Cathy accidentally triggering his coughing fit; Nelly falls ill afterward and, during her three-week convalescence, suspects Cathy is secretly returning to the Heights each evening.

Nelly discovers Cathy has been making secret nightly visits to Wuthering Heights to see the ailing Linton Heathcliff; Cathy recounts their bittersweet meetings and a violent confrontation with Hareton that left Linton coughing blood; Nelly then betrays the secret to Edgar, who forbids further visits.

Dying Edgar agonizes over Cathy's future and Linton Heathcliff's worthiness, eventually permitting supervised moor meetings, while Heathcliff secretly controls Linton's letters and both men decline toward death.

Cathy and Nelly meet a visibly failing Linton Heathcliff near Wuthering Heights, where his terrified deference to his absent father and his obvious deterioration alarm them, though they conceal the truth from Edgar on their return.

Heathcliff uses Linton Heathcliff's terror as bait to lure Cathy Linton and Nelly Dean into Wuthering Heights, locks them in, physically strikes Cathy when she tries to seize the key, and reveals his plan to force her to marry Linton before Edgar Linton dies, keeping them imprisoned overnight.

Nelly escapes Wuthering Heights, returns to dying Edgar at Thrushcross Grange and learns from Linton Heathcliff that Heathcliff struck Cathy; Linton secretly lets Cathy out, she reaches the Grange in time to be with Edgar as he dies peacefully, after which Heathcliff's bribed lawyer Green arrives to seize control of the estate.

Heathcliff arrives at Thrushcross Grange the evening after Edgar's funeral to claim Cathy Linton and take her to Wuthering Heights, then reveals to Nelly that he has opened Catherine Earnshaw's grave and been haunted by her ghost for eighteen years.

Nelly relays Zillah's account of Linton Heathcliff's death and Cathy's isolation at the Heights, Heathcliff's seizure of the inheritance through Linton's will, and Cathy's grudging descent into the household where her first cold encounters with Hareton hint at a future bond; Lockwood then announces he is recovering and plans to quit Thrushcross Grange.

Lockwood visits Wuthering Heights, delivers Nelly's note to Cathy, and witnesses a bitter clash between Cathy and Hareton over his secret hoard of books — ending with him striking her and burning the books — before Heathcliff arrives and mutters that he can barely look at Hareton because he sees Catherine Earnshaw's face in him; Lockwood then announces he is quitting Thrushcross Grange.
Lockwood returns to the neighbourhood after months away, witnesses Cathy and Hareton's tender literacy lessons and growing bond, and learns from Nelly that Heathcliff died three months earlier.

Cathy and Hareton's budding friendship provokes Heathcliff's fury, but when he glimpses Catherine Earnshaw's eyes in their faces he confesses to Nelly his loss of will to revenge himself and his all-consuming obsession with Catherine's ghost, sensing an approaching and undefined change.

Heathcliff, consumed by a mysterious ecstatic vision he cannot eat or sleep through, wastes away over several days and is found dead in the panelled room; Hareton grieves deeply, he is buried without ceremony, and rumors of his ghost walking the moors and Heights persist.

testi/chesterton/atomized/alarms_and_dis.plot: A priest of a simple island republic builds a three-walled tower of lilies, crystal, and pure water crowned by a diamond, striving to create something worthy of the Sun-god.
