Esther, Ada, and Richard arrive at Bleak House and are warmly welcomed by Jarndyce; they meet the charming, debt-ridden Harold Skimpole, who is arrested and whose bill Esther and Richard quietly pay, provoking Jarndyce's fond exasperation when he learns of it.

At rain-soaked Chesney Wold, housekeeper Mrs. Rouncewell hosts grandson Watt and two London lawyers (Guppy), who tour the house; Guppy is inexplicably transfixed by Lady Dedlock's portrait, and Mrs. Rouncewell narrates the Ghost's Walk legend—a wronged Dedlock ancestress who vowed to haunt the terrace whenever disgrace or calamity threatens the family.

Esther settles into Bleak House, hears Jarndyce explain the ruinous Chancery suit and Richard's uncertain future, then joins the overbearing Mrs Pardiggle on a visit to a brickmaker's hovel where a baby dies, throwing the contrast between mechanical charity and genuine compassion into sharp relief.

Esther observes Richard and Ada falling quietly in love at Bleak House while old friend Boythorn arrives raging against Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right-of-way dispute; solicitor's clerk Guppy then makes an awkward marriage proposal to Esther, which she firmly rejects.

Tulkinghorn traces the anonymous law-writer "Nemo" via law-stationer Snagsby to a foul garret at Krook's rag-and-bottle shop, where he discovers the man apparently dead or insensible on a bed amid opium fumes.

Mr Tulkinghorn and Krook discover the law-writer Nemo dead of an opium overdose; a coroner's inquest at the Sol's Arms rejects Jo the crossing-sweeper as a witness for ignorance, and Nemo is buried in a pestilential pauper's churchyard that Jo silently sweeps clean at night.

Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock return from Paris to Chesney Wold for a fashionable winter gathering; Mr Tulkinghorn finally arrives and privately reveals to Lady Dedlock that the mysterious law-writer whose handwriting had stirred her curiosity has been found dead in poverty, leaving both characters watching each other with mutual suspicion.

Richard chooses surgery as his profession and is placed with Mr. Bayham Badger in London, while Ada confesses her love for Richard to Esther, and John Jarndyce gives the young couple his cautious blessing.

Richard departs for his new career while Esther escorts Caddy Jellyby to the Turveydrop dancing academy—where the vain, idle elder Turveydrop exploits his hardworking son—before the group visits Miss Flite, whose landlord Krook ominously names her caged birds (Hope, Ruin, Death, Madness, and more) and shadows Mr. Jarndyce with watchful unease.

Jarndyce, Esther, Ada, and Skimpole visit the Bell Yard lodgings of the recently dead debt-collector Neckett, discovering his three orphaned children kept by thirteen-year-old Charley through washing work, and encounter the furious Gridley, the ruined "man from Shropshire," who denounces the Court of Chancery for destroying his life.

Lady Dedlock, veiled and disguised as a servant, seeks out Jo the crossing-sweeper and pays him to guide her to the places associated with the dead Nemo—his lodgings at Krook's and his pauper grave—while Mr Tulkinghorn broods in his chambers and Sir Leicester languishes with gout at Chesney Wold.

Richard abandons his medical training to pursue law (hoping to watch over the Chancery suit), Jarndyce privately discloses to Esther the scant facts of her birth and unknown aunt, and Allan Woodcourt departs on a long sea voyage leaving flowers anonymously for Esther.

Esther's party travels to Boythorn's Lincolnshire estate; at Sunday church in Chesney Wold park Esther is struck by an inexplicable, unsettling sense of recognition when Lady Dedlock's eyes meet hers, and the feeling recurs when Lady Dedlock unexpectedly takes shelter with them in a keeper's lodge during a storm, ending with Mademoiselle Hortense walking barefoot through wet grass in wounded pride.

Jo the crossing-sweeper is arrested for refusing to "move on" and brought to Snagsby's shop, where his account of a veiled lady who paid him to show her Nemo's haunts is interrogated by Guppy during a tea gathering with the pompous preacher Chadband, culminating in Mrs. Chadband's revelation that she once had charge of Esther Summerson.

Guppy arranges for his financially ruined friend Jobling, under the false name Weevle, to lodge secretly at Krook's rag-and-bottle shop, with the covert aim of investigating the enigmatic old landlord.

Trooper Mr. George visits the miserly Smallweed family to pay two months' interest on a loan, reveals he once knew the missing Captain Hawdon (whom he believes drowned), then returns to his shooting gallery where he sleeps alongside his scarred assistant Phil.

Tulkinghorn dispatches Inspector Bucket and Snagsby to the slum Tom-all-Alone's to retrieve Jo, who is then brought to Tulkinghorn's chambers and asked to identify a veiled woman; Jo confirms the dress matches the mysterious lady but not the hands or voice, revealing the figure is Hortense impersonating Lady Dedlock.

Esther holds a frank London conversation with the debt-ridden, Chancery-obsessed Richard who resolves to join the army instead of finishing his legal articles; then accompanies Caddy to secure old Mr Turveydrop's theatrical blessing and Mrs Jellyby's placid indifference to the engagement; and returns to Bleak House to find John Jarndyce has given her the orphan girl Charley as a personal maid.

Richard obtains his army commission and Jarndyce dissolves his informal engagement to Ada before departure; Richard and Esther then witness the absurd Chancery proceedings and follow Mr George to his shooting gallery, where Inspector Bucket—disguised as a physician—reveals himself to arrest the fugitive Gridley, who dies on the spot.

Tormented by guilt over his secret involvement with Jo and Mr. Bucket, Mr. Snagsby endures his jealous wife's surveillance and a hypocritical sermon by Chadband — who uses Jo as preaching fodder — while Mrs. Snagsby has a hysterical fit convinced Jo is her husband's illegitimate son; Snagsby slips Jo money and urges him to stay silent about "the lady."

Grandfather Smallweed visits Mr. George's shooting gallery and, after much evasion, pressures him to produce a handwriting sample of the deceased Captain Hawdon for a mysterious lawyer's inquiry; George reluctantly agrees to accompany Smallweed to meet the lawyer, taking a paper from his cupboard.

Smallweed brings trooper Mr. George to Tulkinghorn, who tries to obtain a specimen of dead Captain Hawdon's handwriting; George refuses, consults the sensible Mrs. Bagnet, then returns to confirm his refusal, and Tulkinghorn dismisses him angrily, branding him associate of the dangerous Gridley.

Ironmaster Rouncewell visits Chesney Wold to propose that his son court Rosa (Lady Dedlock's protégée) on condition she leave service there, sparking a sharp clash between Sir Leicester's aristocratic pride and the industrialist's self-made values, while Lady Dedlock privately reveals a tender, melancholy attachment to the girl.

Guppy visits Lady Dedlock to reveal he has uncovered Esther Summerson's real name is Hawdon, that a dead law-writer named Hawdon visited Lady Dedlock's past, and that a disguised noblewoman visited Hawdon's grave—evidence pointing to Esther as Lady Dedlock's secret daughter, leaving Lady Dedlock shattered and crying "O my child!"

Esther hosts the scheming Mrs Woodcourt, who subtly steers her away from any hope regarding Allan Woodcourt, then Esther helps Caddy Jellyby prepare her trousseau and witnesses Caddy's wedding to Prince Turveydrop, while Mrs Jellyby remains indifferent to her own daughter's marriage.

Esther finds the gravely ill Jo at a brickmaker's cottage and brings him to Bleak House over Skimpole's callous objections; after Jo vanishes in the night, Charley falls ill with his fever, Esther nurses her back from near-death while keeping Ada away, then contracts the illness herself and ends the chapter blind.
Weevle and Guppy meet at midnight to retrieve Hawdon's letters from Krook, but descend to find only greasy ash where the old man stood — Krook has been destroyed by spontaneous combustion.

After Krook's death by spontaneous combustion the Smallweed family descends to claim his estate as next of kin with Tulkinghorn as solicitor, shutting out Guppy who had hoped to seize Krook's papers; Guppy then visits Lady Dedlock to report the letters implicating her are destroyed, and Tulkinghorn witnesses the meeting.

Smallweed calls in a debt that threatens to ruin George's guarantor Bagnet; George and Bagnet are ejected by Smallweed and then negotiate with Tulkinghorn, who agrees to shield Bagnet legally only after George surrenders a private letter Tulkinghorn has long wanted.

Esther convalesces from a disfiguring illness, keeping Ada at bay; Jarndyce visits and laments Richard's Chancery-warped estrangement; eccentric Miss Flite dines with Esther, recounts Chancery's destruction of her own family, and reveals Woodcourt's heroism in a shipwreck—prompting Esther to silently release any hope of his love.

Esther, convalescing at Chesney Wold, confronts her scarred face in the mirror and accepts her changed appearance; Lady Dedlock then seeks her out in the park woods and reveals herself as Esther's mother, demanding they never meet again and confessing dread of Tulkinghorn's suspicions, before Ada arrives and reunites with Esther in tearful joy.

Richard secretly visits Esther and Ada at Boythorn's estate with Skimpole in tow, insists Jarndyce is an interested party in the suit and refuses all counsel to abandon it, then abruptly departs with his new solicitor Vholes when Jarndyce and Jarndyce is called into the Chancellor's paper.

Esther, restored to health, visits Caddy Jellyby's busy dancing household in London and then calls on Mr. Guppy to formally persuade him to abandon any inquiry into her origins, extracting his sworn promise to leave the matter alone.

Richard Carstone, financially and morally eroding, meets with his parasitic lawyer Vholes after another fruitless Chancery session and deepens his resentment of Jarndyce, while Guppy and Weevle retrieve belongings from Krook's former shop and encounter Tulkinghorn, who obliquely hints he knows of Guppy's secret connection to Lady Dedlock.

Tulkinghorn arrives at Chesney Wold during election season, reports Sir Leicester's political losses including Rouncewell's damaging opposition, then tells a thinly veiled allegorical story of a great lady who concealed an illegitimate child — a clear covert threat aimed at Lady Dedlock, who listens in rigid, silent terror.

Lady Dedlock confronts Tulkinghorn in his turret room demanding to know who he has told her secret, then attempts to flee Chesney Wold; Tulkinghorn stops her by threatening to raise the alarm, and forces her to maintain her public façade while he decides what to do, leaving her trapped under his absolute control.
Mademoiselle Hortense confronts Tulkinghorn in his chambers demanding employment or revenge against Lady Dedlock; he threatens her with imprisonment and orders her never to return.

Jarndyce takes Esther and Ada to Skimpole's dilapidated Somers Town home to caution him against draining Richard's money; Sir Leicester Dedlock then pays an unexpected visit to Bleak House, which finally compels Esther to confess to Jarndyce that Lady Dedlock is her mother.

Jarndyce writes Esther a marriage proposal letter asking her to become mistress of Bleak House; after a week of reflection, burning keepsake flowers, and tearful self-examination, Esther accepts him in person.

Esther travels to Deal after Vholes warns Jarndyce of Richard's debts; she delivers Ada's letter offering her inheritance to save him, but Richard—selling his army commission to fund the Chancery suit—refuses all dissuasion, and on leaving Esther unexpectedly meets Allan Woodcourt and enlists him as Richard's friend and guardian.

At dawn in Tom-all-Alone's, Allan Woodcourt treats a brickmaker's wife's injury, then chases down the fugitive Jo and learns that Jo was forcibly removed from Esther's house by a mysterious powerful man—having unknowingly infected her—and now drifts toward death.
Allan Woodcourt shelters the gravely ill Jo at Mr. George's shooting gallery, where Jo makes his dying "will" asking forgiveness and burial beside Nemo, then dies reciting the Lord's Prayer.

Lady Dedlock dismisses her maid Rosa to protect her from the shame of her own secret, but Tulkinghorn declares their non-disclosure agreement void and threatens imminent exposure of Lady Dedlock to Sir Leicester — and is found shot dead in his chambers before morning.

Inspector Bucket attends the Bagnet family's birthday celebration under a pretence of sociability, then manoeuvres trooper George alone and arrests him as a suspect in the murder of Mr. Tulkinghorn, for which Sir Leicester Dedlock has posted a reward.

Esther nurses the ailing Caddy Jellyby in London while confiding her engagement to Jarndyce, but notices Ada growing quietly sorrowful and self-deceivingly concludes Ada grieves for her sake, missing whatever Ada truly conceals.

Esther visits Richard at Symond's Inn, where Ada reveals she has secretly married Richard and will not return home; Richard's haggard decline under the Chancery suit is starkly visible, and John Jarndyce receives the news with sorrowful blessing.

Esther, Jarndyce, and Woodcourt visit imprisoned Mr. George — accused of murdering Tulkinghorn — who stubbornly refuses legal counsel, while George's mention of a cloaked figure at the murder scene shocks Esther into suspecting her mother Lady Dedlock, and Mrs. Bagnet sets off for Lincolnshire to fetch George's long-lost mother as potential leverage.

Inspector Bucket attends Tulkinghorn's elaborate funeral in disguise, collects multiple anonymous letters naming Lady Dedlock, reports cryptically to Sir Leicester that the case is nearly complete, and covertly confirms from a footman that Lady Dedlock was walking outside alone on the night of the murder — closing the net around her as prime suspect.

Inspector Bucket discloses Lady Dedlock's secret past to a devastated Sir Leicester, neutralizes a gang of blackmailers (Smallweed, Chadband, Mrs. Snagsby), then arrests Mademoiselle Hortense for the murder of Tulkinghorn, producing pistol and forged letters as proof gathered through his wife's covert surveillance.

Mrs. Rouncewell and Mrs. Bagnet travel to London to reunite Mrs. Rouncewell with her imprisoned son George (accused of Tulkinghorn's murder); Mrs. Rouncewell then confronts Lady Dedlock with a letter branding her "murderess," Guppy warns Lady Dedlock her compromising secrets are exposed, and Lady Dedlock writes a farewell to Sir Leicester declaring innocence of the murder and flees.

Sir Leicester suffers a paralytic stroke on learning Lady Dedlock has fled; Inspector Bucket is commissioned to find her, searches her rooms, discovers Esther Summerson's handkerchief, then enlists Esther—waking John Jarndyce—to accompany him on the urgent nighttime pursuit.

Inspector Bucket and Esther race through a winter night searching for the fugitive Lady Dedlock, gathering clues from brickmakers and roadside informants—while Bucket exposes Skimpole's paid betrayal of Jo—before reversing course back toward London when Bucket deduces Lady Dedlock has swapped identities with Jenny the brickmaker's wife.

Gravely ill Sir Leicester Dedlock waits through a wintry day and night for the absent Lady Dedlock to return, while London gossip swirls around her disgrace; attended by the newly returned George Rouncewell, he formally declares before witnesses his unaltered love and forgiveness toward her, but she does not come.

Esther Summerson and Inspector Bucket race through pre-dawn London, recover Lady Dedlock's farewell letter from the Snagsbys' epileptic servant Guster, and follow her trail to a squalid burial ground where Esther lifts the face of the woman lying dead at the iron gate and recognises her own mother.

Recovered Esther resumes her place beside guardian Jarndyce, who plans a Yorkshire medical post for Woodcourt; she visits Richard and Ada daily, watching Richard waste away under Vholes and Chancery's grip, until Ada confesses her steadfast love and reveals she is pregnant, fearing Richard may not live to see the child.

Esther confronts Skimpole to stop visiting the ailing Richard and Ada; he agrees for purely selfish reasons and shamelessly justifies accepting Bucket's bribe to betray Jo; that same evening Woodcourt confesses his love to Esther, who gently refuses him as already committed, yet is deeply moved and resolves to be worthier of his devotion.

Inspector Bucket brings moneylender Smallweed to Bleak House to surrender a newly discovered Jarndyce will (found in Krook's papers); Jarndyce and Esther deliver it to solicitor Kenge, who reveals it materially advances Richard Carstone and Ada Clare's interests — all while Jarndyce and Esther have privately agreed she will become mistress of Bleak House next month.

George the trooper travels to his ironmaster brother Rouncewell's factory in the industrial north, where the two reconcile joyfully; George declines to join the business, choosing instead to return and serve the ailing Sir Leicester Dedlock at Chesney Wold, and sends a formal letter to Esther Summerson clarifying his past role in delivering a letter on instructions from abroad.

Jarndyce brings Esther to a cottage he has secretly prepared and named Bleak House as a gift for Woodcourt, releases her from their engagement so she may marry Woodcourt instead, and then Guppy arrives to comically renew his marriage proposal, which Jarndyce firmly rejects on Esther's behalf.
The Jarndyce and Jarndyce suit ends having consumed the entire estate in costs, and the news breaks Richard Carstone, who dies reconciled with John Jarndyce and cradled in Ada's arms.
After Lady Dedlock's death, Chesney Wold falls into gloomy emptiness while the aged, near-blind Sir Leicester silently pays tribute at her mausoleum and the estate decays around him.

Seven years on, Esther closes her narrative by recounting the peaceful domestic life she, husband Allan, guardian Jarndyce, and Ada with her infant son Richard now share, marking full recovery from sorrow and the resolution of all major relationships.

testi/dickens/atomized/david_copperfield.plot: David narrates his own birth on a Friday night at Blunderstone, introducing his posthumous existence as son of a dead father and a fragile young widow, while the domineering great-aunt Betsey Trotwood arrives expecting a girl to champion, then storms out in contempt upon learning the newborn is a boy.

Young David recalls earliest memories of home with his mother and Peggotty, while the dark Mr. Murdstone begins courting the widowed Mrs. Copperfield, stirring in David instinctive jealousy and dread, before Peggotty arranges a trip to Yarmouth.

David travels to Yarmouth with Peggotty, stays in Mr Peggotty's converted boat-house, bonds with Little Em'ly in a childhood idyll, then returns home to learn his mother has secretly married Mr Murdstone.

After Miss Murdstone arrives and seizes control of the household, David fails his lessons under the Murdstones' oppressive watch, bites Murdstone's hand during a brutal beating, is locked in his room for five days, and is finally sent away to boarding school.

David is sent off alone by carrier and coach to Salem House school near London, enduring a tearful farewell from Peggotty, a comic exploitative waiter, a lonely wait unclaimed at the inn, and finally arrives with Mr Mell to the shut-up, holiday-emptied school where he is forced to wear a placard reading "Take care of him. He bites."

David, still wearing his humiliating placard at Salem House, is summoned by the bullying headmaster Creakle and then taken under the wing of the dominant older boy Steerforth, who appropriates David's money to host a clandestine midnight feast and appoints himself David's protector.

themes: cruelty of schoolmaster and corporal punishment
hero-worship and blind loyalty to Steerforth
storytelling as escape and currency of friendship
loyalty and betrayal (Traddles vs Mr Mell)
testi/dickens/atomized/david_copperfield.plot: David describes Mr Creakle's brutal reign at Salem House, his bond with Steerforth (who has David retell novels at night in exchange for protection and Peggotty's cake/wine), Steerforth's cruel goading that gets the kindly poor teacher Mr Mell dismissed for having a mother in an almshouse, and a visit from Mr Peggotty and Ham bringing seafood and news of home (including little Em'ly), ending with the long-awaited approach of the holidays and David's journey home.

David returns home for school holidays, shares one tender fireside evening with his mother and Peggotty (revealing Barkis's courtship of Peggotty), then suffers weeks of suffocating constraint under the Murdstones before departing with a haunting final image of his fragile mother holding his infant brother at the garden gate.
David learns on his birthday that his mother has died, returns home from Salem House for the funeral, and hears Peggotty recount his mother's final days and dying words.

After his mother's death David is coldly neglected by the Murdstones; he accompanies Peggotty to Yarmouth where she secretly marries Mr. Barkis, then returns home only to be dispatched by Murdstone to earn his keep at the Murdstone and Grinby warehouse in London.

Ten-year-old David begins labouring at Murdstone and Grinby's warehouse and lodges with the perpetually insolvent Micawber family, enduring secret misery while Micawber is arrested for debt and imprisoned, yet David persists alone in his degrading existence without revealing his suffering to anyone.

After Micawber is discharged from debtor's prison and the family departs for Plymouth, David—facing renewed isolation at Murdstone and Grinby's—resolves to run away to his aunt Betsey Trotwood near Dover, but a dishonest carter steals his half-guinea and luggage, leaving him penniless and alone on the road to Greenwich.

Penniless David walks six days from London to Dover, selling clothes to survive and enduring trampers and a mad shopkeeper, until he reaches Aunt Betsey Trotwood's cottage, reveals himself as her nephew, breaks down weeping, and is taken in, bathed, and put to bed.

Betsey Trotwood deliberates David's fate, then fiercely confronts Murdstone when he arrives to reclaim the boy, rejects his authority, and resolves to keep David as her ward under the new name Trotwood Copperfield.

Betsey Trotwood drives David to Canterbury to find him a school, visits lawyer Wickfield who offers to board David in his house, and David meets the unsettling Uriah Heep and the serene Agnes Wickfield for the first time.

David enrolls at Doctor Strong's school and settles into the Wickfield household, has his first extended encounter with the obsequiously "umble" Uriah Heep, and witnesses Jack Maldon's India farewell party, where Annie Strong's swoon and anguished expression hint at a secret attachment to her departing cousin.

David, settled at Doctor Strong's, exchanges letters with Peggotty and hosts Mr. Dick's Wednesday visits; during tea at the Heep household Uriah and his mother worm confidences about Wickfield and Agnes out of him, then Micawber unexpectedly walks in, befriends Uriah, and departs Canterbury with a melodramatic debt-confession letter after a jovial farewell dinner.

David retrospectively surveys his Canterbury school years through two failed crushes (Miss Shepherd and Miss Larkins) and a losing fight with a butcher, tracing his gradual growth from boy to head-boy while Agnes serves as steady companion and confidante.

David leaves school, bids farewell to Agnes and the Wickfields in Canterbury (where he notices Wickfield's dark suspicion about Annie Strong and the returning Jack Maldon), then travels to London and unexpectedly reunites with his old idol Steerforth at the Golden Cross hotel.

David breakfasts with Steerforth in London, spends the day sightseeing with him, then travels to Steerforth's mother's house at Highgate, where he meets the doting Mrs Steerforth and the sharp-tongued Miss Dartle, learns Steerforth scarred her lip with a hammer as a boy, hears Steerforth speak contemptuously of "that sort of people" like Mr Peggotty's family (whom David hopes Steerforth will visit with him in Yarmouth, mentioning Little Emily), and retires uneasy after seeing a portrait of Miss Dartle.

David and Steerforth travel to Yarmouth, where David joyfully reunites with Peggotty and Mr Barkis, then surprises Mr Peggotty's household to discover that Em'ly and Ham have just announced their engagement, while Steerforth's charismatic ease with the fishing family hints at the predatory interest he is concealing.

David and Steerforth linger near Yarmouth—David revisiting Blunderstone graves while Steerforth buys a boat renamed "Little Em'ly" and suffers a dark crisis of conscience—then the chapter closes with fallen woman Martha Endell appealing to Emily for money to flee to London, leaving Emily in guilty tears in Peggotty's arms.

David returns from Yarmouth with Steerforth, consults him about becoming a proctor at Doctors' Commons, reunites with Aunt Betsey who pays off a mysterious threatening stranger, then visits Spenlow and Jorkins to arrange his articles and secures his first independent chambers in the Adelphi.

David hosts a raucous dinner party in his new bachelor rooms with Steerforth and two Oxford friends, drinks to excess, stumbles to the theatre where he humiliatingly encounters Agnes, and wakes the next day consumed by remorse and shame.

Agnes warns David that Steerforth is his "bad angel" and that Uriah has gained coercive power over her father; at a Waterbrook dinner party obsessed with aristocratic "Blood," David encounters Uriah again, who later confesses his calculated scheme to exploit Mr. Wickfield's weakness and win Agnes as his wife.

David, troubled by fears for Agnes under Uriah Heep's shadow, accompanies Mr. Spenlow to his Norwood home where he instantly and helplessly falls in love with Dora Spenlow, while Miss Murdstone—Dora's unwelcome companion—resurfaces from David's childhood.

David visits old schoolfellow Traddles in his cramped Camden Town room, learns of his legal struggles and long engagement, and discovers the perpetually debt-ridden Micawbers are Traddles's landlords.

David hosts a chaotic dinner for the Micawbers and Traddles; Mrs. Micawber urges Micawber to "throw down the gauntlet" to society via newspaper advertisement, but a post-party letter reveals he is crushed by debt and has already signed Traddles's name to a bill; Steerforth then arrives unexpectedly bearing a letter from Peggotty reporting that Barkis is dying, and persuades David to delay a Yarmouth visit by one day.

David visits Steerforth at his Highgate home, where Rosa Dartle's jealous surveillance and cryptic interrogation expose her obsessive feelings for Steerforth; after dinner she plays harp under his persuasion but violently rejects his embrace, and the chapter closes with a tender, ominous farewell between David and Steerforth as the narrator laments they will never again meet in friendship.

David arrives in Yarmouth, learns Barkis is dying; after a conversation with Mr. Omer about Emily's unsettled attachment to her uncle, he joins Peggotty and Mr. Peggotty at the deathbed, where Barkis revives briefly to say "Barkis is willin'" and dies with the ebbing tide.
After settling Barkis's will and attending his funeral, David learns at the Peggotty boathouse that Little Emily has eloped with Steerforth, shattering Mr. Peggotty and Ham.

After Little Emily's elopement with Steerforth, Mr Peggotty resolves to search the world for her; he and David travel to London, confront a cold Mrs Steerforth who refuses any marriage, while Miss Mowcher visits David to confess her unwitting complicity, and the chapter closes with Mr Peggotty departing alone on his open-ended quest.

David escorts Peggotty through her legal affairs (where Murdstone briefly appears collecting a marriage licence), then attends Dora's birthday picnic, declares his love, and the two become secretly engaged through the mediation of Miss Mills.

Betsey Trotwood arrives unannounced at David's London chambers with all her belongings and announces she is completely ruined, urging David to face misfortune with courage; meanwhile Traddles recounts Micawber's debt troubles and enlists Peggotty to recover Sophy's flower-pot from a broker's shop.

After Betsey Trotwood's ruin forces David to confront poverty and a failed attempt to cancel his legal articles, Agnes Wickfield arrives in London, secures him a secretarial post with Doctor Strong, and exposes Uriah Heep's suffocating grip over her father—while David's anxious obsession with Dora colours his every despairing thought.

Spurred by financial ruin into furious industry, David secures extra work assisting Dr. Strong's dictionary, resolves to master shorthand, arranges copying employment for the troubled Mr. Dick, and learns from the departing Micawbers that Micawber has taken a clerical post under Uriah Heep in Canterbury.

David, resolved to be practical after losing his fortune, visits Dora at Miss Mills's, confesses he is now poor and urges her to prepare for a frugal life (accounts, housekeeping, a cookery book), which terrifies and upsets her until Miss Mills soothes her and gently declines the suggestion as unsuited to Dora's nature, while Peggotty departs for home and Aunt Betsey meanwhile routs the housekeeper Mrs. Crupp at Buckingham Street.

Miss Murdstone discovers David's love letters to Dora and exposes the secret courtship to Mr. Spenlow, who confronts David and orders the romance abandoned; days later Spenlow dies suddenly in his carriage, leaving his affairs in chaos and Dora penniless, while David suffers helpless anguish as she mourns her father.

David visits Canterbury, finds Micawber clerking for Heep, confides in Agnes about Dora, then witnesses Uriah's suffocating surveillance of the household, his brazen declaration of intent to marry Agnes, and Mr. Wickfield's anguished breakdown revealing how Heep has systematically destroyed him.

On a snowy London night David encounters Mr Peggotty, who recounts his months-long quest across France, Italy, and Switzerland for Little Emily, shares her remorseful letters begging forgiveness, and resolves to set out again at dawn following a postal clue to the Upper Rhine.

David and Traddles visit Dora's maiden aunts (the Misses Spenlow) to seek formal permission to court Dora; the aunts grant conditional visiting rights under strict terms, and David is briefly reunited with Dora, who is treated as a charming plaything by everyone around her, including David himself.

Uriah Heep forces a confrontation in which he and Mr. Wickfield expose Doctor Strong to long-suppressed suspicions about his young wife Annie's attachment to Jack Maldon, wounding the Doctor deeply; meanwhile Agnes visits and immediately bonds with Dora, and a letter from Mrs. Micawber alerts David that Micawber has become disturbingly secretive under Uriah's employ.

David, now 21 and earning income as parliamentary reporter and writer, marries Dora Spenlow in a dreamlike ceremony attended by Betsey Trotwood, Agnes Wickfield, and Peggotty, while Mr Peggotty is glimpsed haunting dark streets in search of Emily.

Newly married David and Dora bungle housekeeping and cycle through incompetent servants; Betsey Trotwood counsels patience and refuses to interfere; Dora asks David to always think of her as his "child-wife," accepting her limitations.

Mr. Dick engineers a meeting that prompts Annie Strong to kneel before her husband and deliver a full confession of her suppressed secret—Maldon's dishonorable conduct and her own silence—restoring trust and reconciling the estranged couple, while David finally reveals what he witnessed that earlier night.

David is summoned by Miss Dartle, who has Littimer recount how Steerforth abandoned Emily in Italy and she escaped; David then brings the news to the grieving Mr Peggotty, and together they set out through London to find Martha, hoping she can lead them to the missing Emily.

David and Mr. Peggotty intercept Martha on the Thames riverbank as she contemplates suicide, persuade her to search for Little Emily instead, and on returning home David discovers Betsey Trotwood secretly paying off her estranged, still-living husband.

David narrates domestic chaos with a thieving page, his failed project to "form" Dora's mind, his resignation to loving her as she is, and the ominous onset of Dora's physical decline as Betsey Trotwood nurses her.

Micawber sends David a cryptic letter arranging a secret meeting near the King's Bench Prison, then at Betsey Trotwood's Highgate house breaks down and dramatically reveals that his employer Uriah Heep is a villain guilty of fraud and deception, vowing to expose him at a Canterbury gathering the following week.

Martha leads David to a London lodging house where Rosa Dartle savagely confronts and humiliates the fallen Emily, but Mr Peggotty arrives in time, and carries his unconscious niece away, his long dream of finding her at last fulfilled.

Mr Peggotty tells David and Betsey Trotwood the full story of Emily's flight, fever, and rescue by Martha; they then travel to Yarmouth for farewell, where Ham asks David to carry a message of forgiveness to Emily, and Mrs Gummidge unexpectedly begs to join the Australia emigration, winning Mr Peggotty's consent.

Micawber confronts Uriah Heep at the Wickfield office, reading aloud a letter that catalogues Heep's years of forgery and fraud against Mr. Wickfield, forcing Heep to surrender incriminating documents; the chapter ends with Betsey Trotwood proposing that the Micawbers emigrate to Australia as reward for their service.

David keeps vigil at dying Dora's bedside through three remembered scenes; Dora confesses she was too young for marriage and asks to see Agnes alone, then Jip dies at David's feet and Agnes's mute, upraised gesture signals Dora has also died.

In the aftermath of Uriah Heep's exposure, Traddles reports that Betsey Trotwood's embezzled money is recovered, Mr. Wickfield's accounts are cleared, and the Micawber family are financed to emigrate; meanwhile Betsey reveals her estranged husband has died in hospital, closing that long-hidden wound.

David travels to Yarmouth during a catastrophic storm to deliver Emily's farewell letter to Ham; Ham dies heroically trying to swim out to a wrecked ship, and Steerforth's body washes ashore as the sole casualty from the wreck.

David brings Steerforth's drowned corpse to his mother's house at Highgate, where Rosa Dartle erupts in a frenzied tirade blaming Mrs. Steerforth for her son's ruinous upbringing and confessing her own obsessive love for him, while the mother sits rigid and speechless with shock.

David conceals a recent catastrophe from Mr Peggotty and sees the emigrant party — the Micawbers, Mr Peggotty, Little Emily, and Martha — off to Australia, with Micawber arrested twice and released before the ship sails at sunset.

David wanders Europe for three years after Dora's death, descending into despair, until Agnes's letter reaches him in Switzerland and reignites his will to work — while he silently realises he loves her but resolves the feeling is too late and must be renounced.

David returns to England after years abroad, joyfully reunites with the newly married Traddles in Gray's Inn, learns from Dr. Chillip that Murdstone's religious tyranny has broken his new wife, then travels to Dover where Betsey Trotwood, Peggotty, and Mr. Dick welcome him with open arms.

David returns to Canterbury and reunites with Agnes, who calms his lingering grief; her father reveals the tragic story of Agnes's mother, while David wrestles silently with his suppressed love for Agnes, vowing to revere her as his lifelong spiritual guide.

David and Traddles visit Creakle's model prison and discover that the celebrated model penitents Numbers Twenty Seven and Twenty Eight are the unreformed villains Uriah Heep and Littimer, whose pious performances David sees through as cynical self-interest.

David rides to Canterbury, confesses his long-suppressed love to Agnes, discovers she has loved him all her life, and they marry within a fortnight; Agnes then reveals that Dora herself, on her deathbed, had asked Agnes to take her place.

Mr. Peggotty visits David and Agnes in London after years in Australia, recounting Emily's quiet redemption, Martha's marriage, Micawber's triumph as a colonial magistrate, and closing with a visit to Ham's grave to gather earth for Emily.

In this closing retrospect David surveys the faces of his past — Agnes at his side, Aunt Betsey and Peggotty in old age, Micawber still whimsically hopeful, Traddles prosperously settled — before dismissing all shadows and ending his written story with a rapturous apostrophe to Agnes as his guiding, heavenly presence.

themes: social class disparity in domestic service
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Mrs Chick and Miss Tox procure the Toodle family as candidates, and Mr Dombey coldly hires Polly Toodle (renaming her "Richards") as wet-nurse for his motherless infant son, negotiating terms with her and her husband while privately wrestling with grief, wounded pride, and fears about being dependent on a lowly hired woman.

After Mrs Dombey's funeral, wet-nurse Polly Richards, isolated with infant Paul in the gloomy Dombey house, befriends grieving little Florence (comforting her about her dead mother despite the jealous supervision of nursemaid Susan Nipper), then persuades the icy, self-absorbed Mr Dombey to let Florence spend time with her and Paul, though his brief, awkward attempt at fatherly contact with Florence only leaves her feeling unwanted.

At the Wooden Midshipman shop, old Solomon Gills waits for his nephew Walter Gay, who arrives from his first day's work at Dombey and Son; over dinner and a bottle of old Madeira, Sol laments his shop's decline and urges Walter toward a steady career rather than the sea, they swap sea-disaster stories, Captain Cuttle joins them with toasts and talk of instruments and fate, and Walter mentions office gossip that Mr Dombey has a neglected daughter and dotes on his infant son, prompting a toast "to Dombey—and Son—and Daughter."

Mr Dombey, pressed by his sister Mrs Chick, agrees to make Miss Tox godmother to baby Paul, then broods alone over a letter of his dead wife's before the cold, joyless christening ceremony proceeds at a dismal church and a chilly dinner afterward, during which he rewards the nurse Richards by enrolling her son in the Charitable Grinders school, all while Florence's aching love for her baby brother goes largely unnoticed except by Susan Nipper and Richards.

themes: loss and vulnerability of a lost child
exploitation of the poor by the poor (Mrs Brown)
class contrast between the Toodles and the Dombeys
cold paternal authority vs maternal warmth
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Polly (Richards) and Susan Nipper take baby Paul and Florence to visit Polly's family in Staggs's Gardens amid railway construction; on the way back Florence gets separated, is lured away and stripped/disguised by the old ragwoman "Good Mrs Brown," then wanders lost until Walter Gay finds her and takes her to his uncle Solomon Gills's shop before Walter races to inform Mr Dombey, and when Florence is finally brought home, Mr Dombey discharges Polly for having taken Paul to Staggs's Gardens.

themes: faded hopes projected onto an infant
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Major Bagstock, living opposite Miss Tox in shabby-genteel Princess's Place, notices she has grown cold toward him and instead lavishes all her attention and hopes on baby Paul Dombey, whom Mrs Chick brings to visit.

themes: mortality and the limits of money
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: As sickly little Paul Dombey grows older under Mrs Chick and Miss Tox's care and his father's cold, ambition-driven detachment, he startles Mr Dombey with questions about what money can do and why it could not save his mother, is then sent with Florence to Mrs Pipchin's severe seaside boarding-house at Brighton to recover his health, where he forms an odd fascination with the old woman and spends his days by the sea musing on death, distance, and what the waves are saying.

Walter cherishes boyish, idealized feelings for Florence and occasionally meets her in the street, but then discovers his uncle Solomon Gills is in debt and the broker Brogley has taken possession of the Wooden Midshipman shop, so Walter fetches Captain Cuttle, who resolves to seek a loan from Mr Dombey using the shop's stock as security, and finding Dombey away in Brighton, sets off with Walter to follow him there.

Major Bagstock schemes his way into Mr Dombey's acquaintance through Paul and becomes his intimate friend, feasting on Dombey's hospitality while nursing rivalry over Miss Tox; then Walter Gay, backed by Captain Cuttle, comes to beg Dombey's help for his Uncle Sol's debts, and Dombey coldly grants the loan only by making it nominally a gift from little Paul, leaving Walter grateful but humbled.

Mr Dombey visits Mrs Pipchin to arrange for Paul, now six, to leave her care and become a weekly boarder at Doctor Blimber's forcing-house school in Brighton, and after touring the establishment and meeting the Blimber family and pupil Toots, he takes his leave, kissing Paul goodbye while Paul, heartbroken at being parted from Florence, is left alone and desolate in the study.

Paul is inducted into Doctor Blimber's stifling school (meeting Miss/Mrs Blimber, Feeder, Toots, Briggs, and Tozer), grows more strange and solitary under the crushing weight of lessons, while Florence, aided by Susan Nipper who buys her his textbooks, secretly tutors him each Saturday out of love, and Paul, gazing from his window, sees Florence's nightly wave and speaks to Toots of a spectral boat and beckoning vision.

themes: hierarchy and servile deference in business
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: In Dombey's counting-house, Carker the Manager fawns over Dombey then abruptly gets Walter Gay appointed to a junior post in Barbados; afterward Carker berates his disgraced brother John Carker for associating with Walter, and John Carker reveals to Walter his past theft, ruin, and lifelong penance, leaving Walter shaken as news of his own posting spreads through the office.

As the Midsummer holidays near, ailing little Paul Dombey grows increasingly beloved and "privileged" at Doctor Blimber's school despite being deemed strangely "old-fashioned," receives his written character analysis, falls faint one night and is tended by doctor and Mrs Pipchin, then attends the school's farewell party where Florence dances and sings to great admiration, before a tearful, affectionate leave-taking and a coach journey home during which his declining health leaves him only confused memories, ending with his relief that his father did not weep to see him.

Walter enlists Captain Cuttle to break the news of his Barbados posting to Uncle Sol, but Cuttle instead resolves to plead Walter's case to Mr Dombey himself; afterward Walter, wandering near Dombey's house and musing on Florence, is swept up by a distraught Susan Nipper in a coach to find Polly Toodle in the transformed Staggs's Gardens, since little Paul, gravely ill, has asked for his old nurse.

themes: river as symbol of passing life
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Little Paul Dombey, bedridden and fading, drifts through visions of light, river, and night with Florence at his side, asks after his mother and old nurse, bids farewell to his father, his nurse, and Walter, and dies in Florence's arms as the golden light plays on the wall.

Captain Cuttle breaks the news to Solomon Gills that Walter must sail for the West Indies, then, convinced he can advance Walter's cause, visits Carker at Dombey's office and, misreading Carker's smiling silence as agreement, boasts of Walter's prospects and his supposed match with Florence, unaware of Carker's sinister, mocking manner.

After little Paul's death the household and office go through a hushed, ritualized mourning culminating in the funeral (where Carker seems quietly relieved and the inscription is corrected from "child" to "son"), Florence is comforted only by Susan Nipper and by Diogenes the dog (brought by Mr Toots) while she is shut out from her grieving, cold father, and when she finally creeps to his door one night and enters, he rebuffs her coldly before departing next morning to travel with the Major.

themes: class distance between master and employee
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: On the eve of his voyage to Barbados, Walter Gay bids farewell to his Uncle Solomon Gills and Captain Cuttle, is visited by Florence Dombey and Susan Nipper (Florence pledges to be Sol's friend and Walter's sister and gives Walter a purse for Paul), briefly parts with the melancholy John Carker the Junior, and is then escorted by his Uncle and Captain Cuttle to the ship Son and Heir, which sails away.

Mr Dombey breakfasts with Major Bagstock (who mocks Miss Tox's ambitions) before they journey by train to Leamington, during which a chance encounter with the stoker Toodle—whose educated son has gone bad and who wears mourning for a dead child—plunges Dombey into bitter brooding on his own dead son, resentment of Florence's love, and a vision of the train's journey as the relentless monster Death, before he and the Major settle into a companionable daily routine at Leamington.

Major Bagstock introduces Mr Dombey to the vain, affected Honourable Mrs Skewton (who poses as "Cleopatra") and her proud, widowed daughter Edith Granger at Leamington; after repeated chance meetings Dombey and the Major visit the ladies, where Dombey learns of Edith's late husband and drowned child and watches her play harp and sing, while the narrator mourns that none of this stirs him to think of his own neglected daughter Florence.

Carker sorts letters and coldly rebuffs his brother John's plea to visit their sister Harriet, reads a letter from Dombey mentioning Walter Gay and Captain Cuttle, then intimidates and recruits the boy Rob Toodle as a spy to report on Solomon Gills and any visitors (especially Florence) while placing him in Gills's shop, and finally rides to Dombey's house where he witnesses Mr Toots's bungled attempt to court Susan Nipper end in a dog attack by Diogenes.

Florence lives alone in her father's gloomy, decaying house nursing her secret hope of winning his love, then, worried over the long-overdue ship carrying Walter, she and Susan Nipper visit Uncle Sol and enlist Captain Cuttle and the oracular Captain Bunsby for reassurance, before finding Uncle Sol strangely unsettled and evasive when they return to him.

Staying at the Skettles' villa, Florence studies other children's easy affection for their parents in hopes of learning how to win her father's love, overhears a lady tell an orphan girl the painful truth of Mr Dombey's coldness toward her, befriends a poor waterman devoted to his sickly daughter Martha, and is finally accosted on a walk by the sinister, smiling Carker, who is riding to see her father and cryptically tells her there is no news of the ship.

themes: loyalty and duty to a friend
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Captain Cuttle learns from Rob the Grinder that Solomon Gills has vanished overnight leaving keys, his will, and a letter asking Cuttle to keep the shop for Walter's sake; after a fruitless search fearing Gills has drowned himself or died, Cuttle resolves to take over the instrument shop himself and stealthily flees his landlady Mrs MacStinger's lodgings at midnight to move in permanently with Rob.

themes: scheming and manipulation behind false friendship
testi/dickens/atomized/dombey_and_son/ch.plot: Carker arrives at Leamington and, under cover of flattery toward Major Bagstock and feigned devotion to Dombey, needles Dombey about Florence while the Major separately visits Mrs Skewton and Edith, delivers Dombey's invitation to a Warwick/Kenilworth excursion, and openly schemes to marry Edith to Dombey, before an evening dinner where Carker's games mastery and a glimpse in his mirror hint at his hidden, predatory designs.

Carker, after a morning encounter with Edith and a fortune-telling beggar woman in a grove, joins Dombey's party at breakfast where he is introduced to Mrs Skewton and Edith (whom he recognizes), then accompanies them on a day trip to Warwick Castle and Kenilworth (sketching, sightseeing) and an evening of music, all while covertly observing the cold, transactional courtship between Dombey and Edith; that night Edith bitterly denounces her mother for selling her into marriage to Dombey like merchandise, admitting she has no love for him and never had a real childhood.

Florence, discussing Mr Carker's mysterious influence over her father with Susan Nipper and bidding an awkward farewell to Mr Toots, returns to the Dombey house to find it under extensive renovation and is introduced by her father to Edith Granger, who is to become her new stepmother.
Paul Dombey Sr. exults over the birth of his long-awaited male heir while his wife Fanny, too weak to rally, dies as Florence clings to her.

After his wife Fanny's death, the coldly proud Mr. Dombey hires working-class Polly Toodle as wet nurse for infant Paul, renames her "Richards," and insists the arrangement be purely transactional with no emotional bond formed.

After Mrs. Dombey's funeral, wet-nurse Polly Richards comforts the grieving Florence and, despite Susan Nipper's orders to keep them apart, wins Mr. Dombey's cold permission for Florence to visit baby Paul — exposing Dombey's emotional distance from his daughter.

Walter Gay returns home after his first day at Dombey and Son's firm; uncle Solomon Gills and Captain Cuttle celebrate with the prized Madeira wine, share seafaring tales, and Sol urges Walter to embrace commerce over the sea while hinting at Walter's future prospects tied to the Dombey house.

Little Paul is christened with Miss Tox as godmother in a bleak, cheerless ceremony that mirrors Mr. Dombey's icy pride, while Florence is marginalized by her father's indifference and finds solace only by creeping beside her infant brother, as Susan Nipper secretly plans to escort Richards to see her own child.

Florence is separated from her nurses during street chaos, abducted and stripped of her clothes by the sinister "Good Mrs Brown," then found by Walter Gay who brings her safely to his uncle Solomon Gills's shop before Walter fetches Susan Nipper to return her home to a cold, indifferent Mr Dombey — who dismisses nurse Polly Richards for the unauthorized visit to Staggs's Gardens.

Miss Tox snubs Major Bagstock and lavishes obsessive attention on baby Paul Dombey, nursing secret matrimonial ambitions toward Mr. Dombey while the Major watches from across Princess's Place in bewildered jealousy.

Sickly young Paul Dombey grows up under his cold father's impatient ambition, questions whether money can save lives, is sent to Brighton under the harsh Mrs Pipchin, and begins listening mystically to the sea while clinging to Florence for comfort.

Walter Gay, nursing romantic daydreams about Florence, discovers Uncle Solomon Gills is under a broker's execution for a £370 bond debt, rushes to Captain Cuttle for help, and the two set off for Brighton to petition Mr Dombey for a loan.

Major Bagstock engineers a friendship with Mr Dombey at Brighton, while Walter Gay and Captain Cuttle plead for rescue of Solomon Gills from debt, which Dombey grants by letting young Paul symbolically "lend" the money.

Mr. Dombey enrolls six-year-old Paul at Dr. Blimber's relentlessly rigorous boarding school, where Paul weeps at parting from Florence and is left isolated in the cold, mechanically learned establishment.

Paul Dombey arrives at Doctor Blimber's hothouse school and endures relentless academic grinding, finding his only relief when Florence secretly masters his textbooks and tutors him on Saturday visits, their bond deepening as Paul grows solitary and morbidly contemplative.

Mr Dombey, prompted by Carker the Manager, appoints Walter Gay to a junior post in Barbados; afterward Carker the Junior privately confesses his past embezzlement and social death to Walter, urging him to keep his integrity.

Ailing little Paul Dombey is released from studies at Doctor Blimber's, attends the school's end-of-term party where Florence's singing moves him to tears, bids emotional farewells to all, and is carried home in a feverish and confused state that signals his approaching death.
Walter Gay enlists Captain Cuttle to break news of his forced Barbados posting to Uncle Sol, then encounters Susan Nipper searching for Paul Dombey's old nurse as the dying child asks to see her.

Young Paul Dombey lies dying, comforted ceaselessly by sister Florence, bids farewell to Walter Gay and his grief-stricken father, then slips away peacefully in a vision of a river bearing him to the sea where he glimpses his dead mother.

Captain Cuttle visits Carker at Dombey's offices to sound out Walter Gay's prospects, and is duped by Carker's sly smiling into believing Walter is headed for fortune and romance with Florence, while the narrator flags Carker's cat-like treachery.

After little Paul's funeral, Florence mourns alone while Mr. Dombey shuts himself away; Mr. Toots brings her Paul's dog Diogenes as a keepsake; Florence's nightly vigil at her father's door finally leads to a confrontation in which he coldly repels her, extinguishing her last hope for his affection.

On the eve of Walter Gay's voyage to Barbados, Florence Dombey and Susan Nipper visit Sol Gills's shop to say goodbye; Florence pledges to befriend the lonely old man in Walter's absence, asks Walter to be her brother in memory of dead Paul, and the next morning Captain Cuttle escorts Walter and Sol to the Son and Heir, which then sails away.

Mr. Dombey and Major Bagstock travel by train from London to Leamington; a chance encounter with stoker Toodle (wearing mourning crape for his own dead son) sharpens Dombey's jealous grief over little Paul, while the train journey becomes a sustained meditation on death and Dombey's bitter resentment that Florence survived instead of his son.

At Leamington, Major Bagstock introduces Mr Dombey to the vain Mrs Skewton and her proud widowed daughter Edith Granger; repeated encounters lead to an evening visit where Dombey grows visibly drawn to Edith's beauty and accomplishments.

Carker the Manager recruits the wayward Rob Toodle as a spy to be placed in Sol Gills's shop and report on all visitors—especially a young lady—while coldly dismissing his brother John's plea for reconciliation with their sister Harriet.

Florence, living alone in the desolate Dombey house and longing for her father's love, visits Captain Cuttle and drags him to consult the oracle Bunsby about Walter's overdue ship, while Uncle Sol behaves with unsettling urgency and secrecy that troubles them all.

Florence, staying with the Skettles family at Fulham, obsessively studies children with loving fathers to learn how to win her own father's love, overhears a stranger pity her as a child outcast from a living parent, and ends the chapter with an unsettling roadside encounter with Carker, who offers to carry her message to Mr. Dombey at Leamington and leaves her trembling.

Captain Cuttle discovers Solomon Gills has vanished overnight, leaving him the shop keys and a letter asking him to keep a home for Walter; after a fruitless week searching for the old man's body, Cuttle secretly flees his landlady Mrs MacStinger and installs himself at the Instrument-maker's to await news.

Carker arrives at Leamington and insinuates himself into Major Bagstock's and Dombey's confidence, while Bagstock conspires with Mrs Skewton to push Dombey's courtship of Edith Granger forward; the evening's dinner reveals Carker's hidden predatory ambitions beneath a facade of servility.

Carker joins Dombey, Major Bagstock, Mrs Skewton, and Edith on a day excursion to Warwick Castle, where he covertly observes the cold transactional courtship; that night Edith erupts to her mother in bitter shame, declaring she knows Dombey is buying her but has refused to actively lure him.

Florence returns from the Skettles villa to find the Dombey house gutted by workmen, and her cold father introduces her to Edith — his future wife — who silently embraces Florence and privately begs her to begin by thinking well of her.
Mrs Chick visits Miss Tox to announce Paul Dombey's engagement to Edith, and upon realizing Miss Tox has nursed secret romantic hopes for Dombey herself, furiously severs their long friendship.

In the week before her wedding to Mr. Dombey, Edith brings Florence to stay with her and Mrs. Skewton; Florence endures an awkward dinner reunion with her cold father; and on the wedding eve Edith, consumed by guilt over the mercenary match, orders Florence home to protect her innocence, then breaks down weeping over the sleeping girl.

Mr. Dombey weds Edith Granger in a grand church ceremony attended by Major Bagstock, Carker, Florence, and Captain Cuttle, while Edith's cold compliance and Carker's ominous attentions cast a dark shadow over the union.

Captain Cuttle, sheltering at the Wooden Midshipman, receives confirmation via Mr Toots that Walter Gay's ship the Son and Heir is wrecked and all aboard perished; he grieves, confronts Carker at Dombey's office only to be contemptuously dismissed, then returns to don mourning clothes and privately read the Burial Service for Walter.

Chapter contrasts Carker the Manager's opulent Norwood cottage—where he broods over a portrait resembling Edith—with the poor home of his disgraced siblings Harriet and John Carker, where Harriet receives a mysterious elderly benefactor and then shelters a destitute ex-convict woman with quiet compassion.

Alice Marwood returns from transportation to her squalid mother Good Mrs Brown, bitterly indicts her ruined childhood and unjust conviction, learns her mother has spied on the Dombey household, then discovers she unwittingly accepted charity from Harriet Carker—sister of the man she despises—and flings the money back with violent curses before the chapter closes with a pointed parallel to Edith Dombey and her own scheming mother.

testi/dickens/atomized/great_expectation.plot: Young orphan Pip, visiting his family's graves on the Kent marshes, is seized by an escaped convict who threatens him into promising to bring food and a file by morning.

Pip, tormented by guilt over his promise to the convict, hides food down his trousers at tea, suffers Mrs Joe's abuse and tar-water punishment, learns about prison hulks, and at dawn secretly steals food and a file from the forge before fleeing to the marshes.

Pip delivers stolen food and a file to the convict on the marshes, accidentally encounters a second escaped convict, and reports this to the first convict, who frantically files his leg-iron to pursue the other man.

On Christmas Day Pip endures a dinner of moral lectures from Mrs Joe, Pumblechook, Wopsle, and the Hubbles while concealing his theft from the pantry; Pumblechook accidentally drinks tar-water Pip substituted for brandy; just as the missing pork pie is about to be discovered, soldiers appear at the door bearing handcuffs.

Soldiers arrive at Joe's forge to repair handcuffs, then Joe and Pip join the marsh hunt and witness Magwitch recaptured after he deliberately drags down the other convict; Magwitch confesses to stealing Joe's food, and Joe responds with unsentimental compassion before Magwitch is rowed back to the prison hulk.

Pip, carried home by Joe after the convict episode, silently resolves not to confess his theft to Joe, fearing loss of Joe's good opinion, while the household invents wild theories about how the convict entered the pantry.

Pip shows Joe a crudely written letter, Joe confesses his own illiteracy and recounts his abusive childhood, then Mrs Joe returns with Uncle Pumblechook announcing Miss Havisham has summoned Pip to her house to play.

Pip is escorted to Satis House where he meets the eerily time-frozen Miss Havisham in her yellowed bridal dress, then plays cards with the scornful Estella, who humiliates him over his coarse hands and common origins, leaving him weeping in the brewery yard and newly ashamed of his social station.
Pip fabricates wild lies about Miss Havisham's to satisfy Mrs. Joe and Pumblechook, then privately confesses the truth to Joe and reveals his shame at being called "common" by Estella.

Pip asks Biddy to teach him, then at the pub encounters a mysterious stranger who secretly shows him a file linked to Magwitch and slips him money, leaving Pip haunted by guilt over his convict connection.

Pip returns to Satis House, is made to walk a morbid Miss Havisham around her cobwebbed wedding-feast room on her forbidden birthday while sycophantic relatives visit, meets a burly stranger on the stairs (Jaggers, unnamed), fights a pale young gentleman (Herbert Pocket, unnamed) in the overgrown garden, and receives a contemptuous kiss from Estella as reward.

Over eight to ten months Pip regularly visits Miss Havisham, pushing her wheelchair and singing for her while Estella remains coldly capricious; the period ends when Miss Havisham tells Pip to bring Joe Gargery so he can be formally apprenticed.

Joe and Pip visit Miss Havisham to sign Pip's indentures; she pays 25 guineas as apprenticeship premium, and Pip is formally bound to Joe's forge trade — leaving him secretly wretched and disillusioned while Pumblechook falsely claims credit at a celebratory dinner.

Pip reflects on his shame of home and forge apprenticeship, contrasting his former innocent belief in both with his current sense of coarseness, haunted by fear Estella will see him at his grimiest and despise him, while crediting Joe's faithfulness alone for keeping him from abandoning his indentures.

Pip takes a half-holiday to visit a cold, dismissive Miss Havisham and learns Estella is abroad beyond his reach; meanwhile Orlick's quarrel with Mrs Joe and his subsequent brawl with Joe foreshadow the chapter's dark close, when Mrs Joe is found savagely struck down by an unknown hand.

Mrs Joe is found brutally attacked with a convict's filed leg-iron; she survives but is left brain-damaged and mute, Biddy joins the household to care for her, and Pip suspects Orlick or the stranger with the file—a suspicion reinforced when Mrs Joe's slate-drawings repeatedly summon Orlick, toward whom she shows fearful submission.
Pip confides to Biddy his obsession with Estella and desire to become a gentleman; Biddy wisely challenges his motives; on the walk home Orlick lurks menacingly behind them.

Lawyer Mr Jaggers arrives at the forge to announce Pip has "great expectations" from a secret patron, cancels his apprenticeship to Joe, and instructs him to come to London to be educated as a gentleman.

Pip burns his apprenticeship indentures, quarrels with Biddy over Joe's manners, shops for gentleman's clothes while discovering money's social power, visits Miss Havisham to say goodbye, and finally departs for London in tears, closing the first stage of his expectations.

Pip arrives in London, wanders near Newgate Prison, waits in Jaggers's grim office, witnesses Jaggers bully clients and expose a witness-tampering attempt, receives his financial arrangements, and is escorted by Wemmick toward Barnard's Inn.

Wemmick escorts Pip to the grim, dilapidated Barnard's Inn, where Pip waits for Herbert Pocket, who arrives late with fruit and they instantly recognise each other as the "prowling boy" and "pale young gentleman" from their childhood fight at Miss Havisham's.

Pip and Herbert Pocket recognize each other as old sparring partners, bond over dinner at Barnard's Inn where Herbert reveals Miss Havisham's backstory — jilted at the altar by a scheming swindler who conspired with her half-brother — and then escorts Pip to the chaotic Pocket household in Hammersmith.

Pip settles into the Pocket household, meeting Mr. Pocket and fellow lodgers Drummle and Startop, and observes the chaotic domestic life where servants wield real authority while Mrs. Pocket neglects her children in favour of obsessing over aristocratic titles.

Pip arranges his studies under Mr. Pocket, visits Jaggers's office to secure twenty pounds for furnishings, and Wemmick shows him the grim death-cast trophies and Jaggers's courtroom dominance, hinting at the lawyer's terrifying power over all around him.

Pip visits Wemmick's eccentric Walworth home — a miniature castle with drawbridge, cannon, and the Aged Parent — and learns that Wemmick keeps his private life rigorously separate from his professional identity at Jaggers's office.

Pip and his companions dine at Mr Jaggers's gloomy Gerrard Street house, where Jaggers manipulates his guests, singles out the brutish Drummle with cryptic approval, and forces his housekeeper Molly to display her scarred, powerful wrists before dismissing her.

Joe visits Pip in London, awkward and out of place; Pip feels ashamed of him; Joe delivers Miss Havisham's message that Estella has come home, then departs with quiet dignity, telling Pip they belong in different worlds.

Pip travels by coach to his hometown, seated beside a convict he recognises from childhood who unknowingly reveals he once delivered Magwitch's two-pound-note gift to Pip; arriving shaken, Pip finds a local newspaper falsely crediting Pumblechook as his earliest patron.

Pip visits Satis House, finds the transformed adult Estella returned from France, walks with her in the ruined garden while she coolly declares she has no heart, dines alongside Mr Jaggers and Miss Havisham, and ends the night haunted by Miss Havisham's frenzied command to love Estella unconditionally.

Back in London, Pip confesses his hopeless adoration of Estella to Herbert, who warns she may bring misery given Miss Havisham's influence, then Herbert reveals his own secret engagement to Clara; the chapter also shows Pip's humiliation by Trabb's boy and his report of Orlick to Jaggers.

Pip and Herbert attend a rowdy, mockery-filled performance of Hamlet starring their acquaintance Wopsle, visit him backstage out of pity, take him to supper, and Pip goes to bed miserably dreaming of Estella and Miss Havisham.
Pip accompanies Wemmick on a visit to Newgate Prison while anxiously awaiting Estella's arrival in London, then feels morally contaminated by the prison atmosphere just as her coach appears.

Pip escorts Estella by carriage from an inn to her new lodgings in Richmond, during which Estella reveals she is being deployed by Miss Havisham to enter society, warns Pip that the Pocket relatives slander him to Miss Havisham, and Pip suffers the ache of knowing Estella attracts him deliberately yet feels nothing for him.
Pip reflects on how his great expectations have corrupted him and Herbert through lavish spending and mounting debt at Barnard's Inn, while the chapter closes with news of Mrs. Joe Gargery's death.

Pip returns to the forge for Mrs Joe's funeral, observes its comic-grotesque ceremony, buries his sister near his parents' graves, then walks with Biddy who gently exposes his hollow promise to visit Joe often, leaving Pip to depart knowing she is right.
On Pip's 21st birthday, Mr Jaggers grants him £500/year from his unnamed benefactor while refusing to reveal the patron's identity, and Wemmick bluntly advises Pip never to invest money in a friend.
Pip visits Wemmick at Walworth Castle, secures his help to secretly fund Herbert Pocket's entry into a shipping partnership via Clarriker, then mentions Estella as the next chapter's subject.

Pip escorts Estella to Satis House where she and Miss Havisham clash bitterly over Estella's trained inability to love; back in London, Pip is tormented by Estella's deliberate encouragement of the brutish Bentley Drummle.

On a stormy night Magwitch, the convict from Pip's childhood, arrives at Pip's London rooms and reveals he is the secret source of Pip's fortune and gentleman status, destroying Pip's illusions about Miss Havisham and leaving him stunned with abhorrence and guilt.

Pip hides Magwitch in his chambers, confirms from Jaggers that Magwitch is his true benefactor, arranges lodgings and a disguise for the fugitive, and swears Herbert Pocket to secrecy upon his return.

Pip reveals Magwitch's identity to Herbert; horrified and indebted, they agree Magwitch must be smuggled out of England before Pip can break free of him, and resolve to ask Magwitch about his past history at breakfast the next morning.

Magwitch recounts his life story to Pip and Herbert — childhood destitution, partnership with swindler Compeyson (including Arthur's dying hallucination of a woman in white), and the trial where class prejudice gave Compeyson a lighter sentence — ending when Herbert silently passes Pip a note identifying Compeyson as Miss Havisham's false lover.

Pip, tormented by shame over harboring Magwitch and jealousy about Estella, travels to find her already gone to Satis House, then endures a bristling confrontation with rival Bentley Drummle at the Blue Boar inn before pressing on to Miss Havisham's.

Pip confronts Miss Havisham about letting him believe she was his benefactor, then declares his love to Estella who coldly announces she will marry Drummle; walking back to London in anguish, Pip receives Wemmick's urgent note warning him not to go home.

After a sleepless night at a Covent Garden inn following Wemmick's warning note, Pip visits Wemmick at Walworth, where Wemmick reveals that Magwitch is being watched and that Herbert has already secretly relocated him to a safer riverside lodging near Limehouse.

Pip navigates to Magwitch's secret riverside lodging at Mill Pond Bank, meets Herbert's sweetheart Clara, relays Wemmick's warnings about being watched, and the three devise a boat-on-Thames scheme to smuggle Magwitch out of England when the moment comes.

Pip, burdened by debt and anxiety over Magwitch's hiding, visits a theatre where Mr. Wopsle reveals he spotted Compeyson sitting directly behind Pip, confirming the enemy is dangerously close and prompting Pip and Herbert to redouble their caution.

Pip dines with Jaggers and Wemmick, recognizes Jaggers's housekeeper Molly as Estella's mother by her distinctive hands and eyes, then Wemmick reveals Molly was acquitted of murder decades earlier through Jaggers's brilliant legal defense.

Pip returns to Satis House, secures £900 from Miss Havisham for Herbert's partnership, learns that Mr Jaggers brought infant Estella to her as an orphan, exchanges mutual forgiveness with a broken Miss Havisham, then saves her when her rotting bridal dress catches fire, burning his own hands in the struggle.

While Herbert tends Pip's fire-injuries, he relays Magwitch's dark past—a jealous woman tried for murder, defended by Jaggers, who then destroyed their child and vanished—leading Pip to the sudden revelation that Magwitch is Estella's father.

Pip confronts Mr Jaggers and Wemmick with the truth of Estella's parentage—Magwitch as father, Molly as mother—and Jaggers, speaking in elaborate hypotheticals while admitting nothing, counsels that the secret must stay buried for everyone's sake.

Pip receives Wemmick's coded letter signalling the time to act, finalises the river-escape plan for Magwitch with Herbert and Startop, then impulsively races alone to the marshes after an anonymous letter threatens to reveal information about "Provis."

Orlick lures Pip to a remote marsh sluice-house, binds him at gunpoint, confesses to attacking Mrs Joe and to spying on Magwitch, and is about to murder him when Herbert Pocket and Startop burst in and drive Orlick off.

Pip, Herbert, and Magwitch row Magwitch down the Thames toward a Hamburg steamer to smuggle him out of England, but a police galley intercepts them; Compeyson is unmasked among the pursuers, both convicts go overboard in a violent struggle, Compeyson drowns, and the badly injured Magwitch is recaptured and manacled—while Pip, whose inherited fortune is now forfeit, resolves to stay at Magwitch's side until death.

While Magwitch is formally committed for trial and Pip's forfeited inheritance proves unrecoverable, Herbert departs for Cairo after offering Pip a clerk's post, and Wemmick secretly marries Miss Skiffins with Pip as best man.

Magwitch lies dying in prison after his death sentence; Pip attends him daily and, at the last moment, reveals that Estella—Magwitch's lost daughter—is alive and beautiful, whereupon Magwitch dies peacefully.

Gravely ill and arrested for debt after Magwitch's death, Pip is nursed back to health by Joe Gargery, who quietly pays off the debt and slips away; recovering, Pip resolves to go to the forge and propose to Biddy.

Ruined Pip returns to his hometown, suffers Pumblechook's smug moralising, discovers Joe and Biddy have just married, begs their forgiveness, then departs abroad to pay his debts and build an honest career with Herbert's trading firm.

Pip returns to England after eleven years, visits Joe and Biddy at the forge, then walks alone to the ruins of Satis House where he unexpectedly meets Estella, and they part as friends, suggesting a hopeful reunion rather than final separation.

testi/dickens/atomized/hard_times/chapte.plot: Thomas Gradgrind harangues a classroom of children, insisting that facts are the one thing needful and that nothing else has any place in education.

Gradgrind and Bounderby observe a schoolroom drill where Sissy Jupe cannot define a horse by rote facts while Bitzer recites the mechanistic definition perfectly, dramatising the system's crushing of imagination.
Gradgrind and Bounderby catch Louisa and Tom secretly peeping at the circus through a wall gap, exposing the failure of rigid fact-based upbringing to extinguish the children's natural curiosity.
Thomas Gradgrind introduces Sissy Jupe to the boastful self-made banker Josiah Bounderby, who relentlessly brags about his wretched origins while Louisa and Tom look on.

Dickens describes the grim industrial landscape of Coketown and introduces Stephen Blackpool as one of its factory "Hands," contrasting the workers' bleak existence with the wealth of mill-owner Bounderby.

Gradgrind and Bounderby arrive at Sleary's circus, catch Louisa and Tom sneaking a look at the show, then learn that Sissy Jupe's father has vanished and Gradgrind resolves to take Sissy into his household to be educated on Fact.

Mrs Sparsit, formerly of aristocratic Powler lineage but now reduced to keeping house for Bounderby, is introduced as a proud, sharp-eyed dependent who privately looks down on her loud, self-made employer while relying on his patronage.
Gradgrind and Bounderby assess Sissy Jupe's failure to absorb fact-based schooling, illustrating how the utilitarian system systematically extinguishes children's natural capacity for wonder.

Gradgrind reviews Sissy's dismal progress under the Fact-based curriculum, learns she still mourns her missing father, and decides to keep her in the household despite her failure to absorb utilitarian doctrine.
Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask about divorcing his drunken wife and is told that divorce, easily obtained by the rich, is wholly inaccessible to a man of his station.

Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask how a working man might escape a ruinous marriage, but Bounderby and Mrs Sparsit make clear that divorce law is the privilege of the wealthy, leaving Stephen with no way out.
An enigmatic old woman (Mrs. Pegler) encounters Stephen Blackpool near Coketown and questions him admiringly about Bounderby, hinting at a hidden connection to him.

Stephen Blackpool endures a night at home with his drunken estranged wife while Rachael nurses her, and narrowly averts disaster when the wife nearly drinks poison, laying bare his trapped domestic condition and his moral bond with Rachael.
Time passes over two years; Bounderby proposes to Louisa, Thomas Gradgrind presents the match as cold fact, Tom selfishly urges acceptance, and Louisa consents with joyless resignation.
Louisa confronts her father Thomas Gradgrind, blaming his cold utilitarian upbringing for leaving her emotionally stunted and driving her to the edge of ruin.
Gradgrind presents Bounderby's marriage proposal to Louisa, who accepts with chilling passivity, unable to express desire or preference after her fact-based upbringing stripped her of feeling.
Chapter 17 ("Effects in the Bank") contains only its heading and page marker in this file — no narrative prose is present, indicating a stub or extraction artifact.

James Harthouse arrives in Coketown, introduced as a cynical gentleman of leisure who takes up the political cause of Gradgrindism purely out of boredom, positioning himself as a dangerous influence in the Bounderby circle.
Harthouse cultivates a cynical friendship with Tom Gradgrind, flattering the selfish young man into drunkenly revealing details about Louisa, whom Harthouse uses Tom to pursue.
Stephen Blackpool refuses to join the workers' union combination, is publicly denounced by orator Slackbridge, and is shunned and isolated by his fellow workers as a result.
Bounderby dismisses Stephen Blackpool after Stephen refuses to join the union and is shunned by his fellow workers, while Harthouse observes the stark divide between masters and men.
Chapter unit contains no narrative body; only the title "Fading Away" is present with no prose, characters, or events.
During a thunderstorm Mrs Sparsit secretly trails Louisa and witnesses her clandestine meeting with Harthouse, watching as Louisa teeters on the brink of moral ruin.
Unit contains only the chapter title "Explosion" with no narrative body; no characters or events are rendered in this fragment.

Mrs. Sparsit, drenched from following Louisa, rushes to Bounderby with news of supposed elopement, but when they confront the matter at Gradgrind's house Louisa is found safely with her father, leaving Mrs. Sparsit exposed and Bounderby furious.

Mrs. Sparsit envisions a metaphorical staircase descending into ruin and watches with obsessive satisfaction as Louisa, drawn ever closer to Harthouse, appears to her to be stepping down it toward disgrace.
Mrs. Sparsit pursues Louisa through a violent storm, convinced she is witnessing Louisa's final descent down the imagined fatal staircase toward elopement with Harthouse.
Louisa flees to her father in the storm and, in a desperate confrontation, indicts his Fact-based system for destroying her capacity for feeling before collapsing broken at his feet.

James Harthouse arrives in Coketown with a letter of introduction to Bounderby, presenting himself as a fashionable idler who adopts the Fact philosophy out of bored cynicism, and is introduced to Louisa.

Sissy Jupe visits James Harthouse at his lodgings and, with quiet but unyielding resolve, demands he leave Coketown forever and relinquish all claim on Louisa; Harthouse, disarmed by her plain earnestness, capitulates and departs.
Chapter file contains only the heading "Very Decided" with no narrative text; no events or characters are rendered in this unit.
