Chapter titled "Lost" contains no narrative body in this atomized file — only the chapter heading and title are present, indicating a unit stub with no extractable plot content.
Sissy Jupe confronts James Harthouse at his lodgings and, through quiet moral earnestness, persuades him to abandon his pursuit of Louisa and leave Coketown permanently.
Unit contains only the chapter title "The Starlight" with no narrative prose — file is a stub header with no plot content.
Tom Gradgrind (the "Whelp"), hiding in disguise at the circus, is tracked down and confronted, while Thomas Gradgrind faces the ruin of his system as Sissy Jupe's loyalty helps secure Tom's escape.
Chapter VIII presents no narrative prose; the unit contains only the heading and subtitle "Philosophical," offering no depicted events or characters.

Unit is a list of illustrations only, naming key scenes: Harthouse dining at the Bounderbys', Harthouse conspiring with Tom Gradgrind in the garden, and Stephen Blackpool recovered from the Old Hell Shaft.
Unit contains no narrative content — it is a bare section-title page marking the start of Book the First ("Sowing") with no characters, dialogue, or events.
Thomas Gradgrind delivers his rigid utilitarian creed — Facts above all else — while surveying a bare schoolroom full of children ready to be filled with them.

In Gradgrind's school, a government inspector and Gradgrind interrogate Sissy Jupe about horses and flowers, forbidding all fancy, then introduce teacher M'Choakumchild to begin drilling pupils with pure facts.

Gradgrind catches Louisa and Tom secretly peeping at Sleary's circus and marches them home, repeatedly invoking Bounderby's opinion as moral authority while Louisa confesses she is tired of everything.

Bounderby boasts of his wretched origins to Mrs. Gradgrind on his birthday; when Gradgrind returns with Louisa and Tom caught peeping at the circus, the two men blame idle imagination and resolve to expel Sissy Jupe from the school.

Gradgrind and Bounderby walk through industrial Coketown (depicted as a monotonous triumph of fact suppressing all fancy), encounter Sissy Jupe being chased by Bitzer, and accompany her to her injured father's lodgings.
Gradgrind and Bounderby visit the circus to dismiss Sissy from school, discover her father has already fled, and Gradgrind offers to take Sissy in; she tearfully accepts.

Bounderby breakfasts with Mrs Sparsit and boasts of her aristocratic connections; Gradgrind arrives with Louisa and resolves to take Sissy Jupe into his household at Stone Lodge for strict rational education, silencing her talk of fairy tales.

Louisa and Tom share a twilight fireside talk lamenting their joyless Gradgrind upbringing; Tom reveals he plans to exploit Louisa's influence over Bounderby, while Mrs. Gradgrind interrupts to forbid Louisa from "wondering," embodying the chapter's theme of Never Wonder.

Sissy confides to Louisa about her failures under M'Choakumchild's fact-based schooling and her father's mysterious disappearance, revealing an instinctive empathy that defies utilitarian logic, while Louisa listens with quiet compassion and Tom interrupts only to summon her for Bounderby.

Stephen Blackpool walks home through Coketown after the factory bells ring, briefly accompanies Rachael (keeping cautious distance), then arrives at his lodging to find his estranged drunken wife collapsed on the floor of his room.

Stephen Blackpool visits Bounderby to ask how he can legally divorce his drunken wife and remarry, but Bounderby informs him that divorce is only accessible to the wealthy, leaving Stephen trapped with no way out.

Stephen Blackpool meets a mysterious old woman who makes an annual 40-mile pilgrimage just to glimpse Bounderby, then broods on his own wrecked life — bound to a drunken wife, unable to marry Rachael.

Stephen returns home to find Rachael tending his degraded wife; while he sleeps in tormented dreams, his wife seizes a poison bottle but Rachael wakes in time to wrest it away, and Stephen kneels before Rachael calling her his angel and sole hope.

Time passes in Coketown as Gradgrind dismisses Sissy from school for failing at facts, Tom enters Bounderby's bank, and Tom cryptically hints to Louisa that their father is arranging her marriage to Bounderby.

Thomas Gradgrind presents Bounderby's marriage proposal to Louisa, who accepts with cold resignation after her father reframes love as mere statistical fact, revealing how her utilitarian upbringing has extinguished all emotional life; Sissy watches in silent grief.

Bounderby tells Mrs. Sparsit he is marrying Louisa Gradgrind; she responds with condescending pity and accepts relocation to the Bank, after which the cold, fact-dominated wedding takes place and Book One ends.
This unit is a stub containing only the Book the Second title and subtitle "Reaping," with no narrative content or character action.

James Harthouse, a bored gentleman bearing a letter of introduction to Bounderby from Gradgrind, wanders into the Coketown Bank where Mrs Sparsit—after gossiping with Bitzer about Tom Gradgrind's dissipation—receives him and unwittingly reveals Louisa's youth and Bounderby's address.

James Harthouse, a bored gentleman of no real convictions, arrives in Coketown bearing Thomas Gradgrind's letter of introduction, is received by Bounderby who introduces him to Louisa, and Harthouse—observing her cold reserve crack only at Tom's arrival—silently identifies her brotherly attachment as a lever for future influence.

Harthouse plies Tom with drink and flattery at his hotel, extracting Tom's cynical confession that he pressured Louisa into marrying Bounderby purely to secure his own comfort, revealing Tom's selfishness while Harthouse covertly gathers intelligence about the Bounderby household.

At a Coketown union meeting, orator Slackbridge denounces Stephen Blackpool for refusing to join the workers' association; despite crowd sympathy Stephen stands firm and is collectively shunned, enduring four days of total social isolation before being summoned to Bounderby's house.

Summoned before Bounderby and Harthouse, Stephen Blackpool defends striking workers' integrity despite their ostracism of him, diagnoses the industrial "muddle" as a systemic failure no repression can fix, and is dismissed from his job by Bounderby.

Stephen Blackpool, blacklisted by Bounderby and shunned by fellow workers, receives money from Louisa and a suspicious private instruction from Tom to linger nightly outside the Bank before departing Coketown at dawn — unknowingly being set up as a scapegoat.

Harthouse systematically wins Louisa's trust by feigning concern for Tom's debts and gambling losses, extracts her financial secrets, and simultaneously manipulates Tom into being kinder to his sister — all as calculated steps in his cynical campaign to seduce her.

After Bounderby announces the bank robbery and accuses Stephen Blackpool, Mrs Sparsit installs herself at the house while Harthouse courts Louisa in the garden; that night Louisa goes to Tom's room and begs him to confess, but he stays doggedly silent and, once she leaves, collapses in guilty anguish.

Mrs Sparsit's scheming widens the rift between Louisa and Bounderby while pushing Louisa closer to Harthouse, then Louisa is called to Stone Lodge where she watches her mother die murmuring that something vital—unnamed, not an Ology—was missing from the Gradgrind upbringing.

Mrs Sparsit, lodging at Bounderby's retreat, constructs an allegorical staircase in her mind and obsessively watches Louisa descend it step by step toward ruin as Louisa grows ever closer to Harthouse in secret garden trysts.

Mrs Sparsit covertly trails Louisa, witnesses her secret woodland meeting with Harthouse, then pursues her by train through a thunderstorm back to Coketown, only to lose her in the chaos and cry "I have lost her!"

Louisa returns to her father during a storm and delivers a devastating reckoning: Gradgrind's cold rationalist system robbed her of feeling, forced her into a marriage she never loved, and has now left her on the verge of adultery with Harthouse — she collapses at his feet demanding he save her by means other than his philosophy.
Unit is the title page for Book the Third ("Garnering"), containing no narrative content beyond the book heading.

Louisa wakes bedridden in her childhood room; her remorseful father confesses his utilitarian system has failed and questions head-over-heart wisdom, then Sissy Jupe offers unconditional love and Louisa collapses into her arms begging forgiveness.

Sissy Jupe visits James Harthouse at his hotel and, acting alone on moral conviction, informs him Louisa will never see him again and demands he leave Coketown permanently—which he ultimately agrees to and does.

Bounderby storms Stone Lodge with an ailing Mrs Sparsit, confronts Thomas Gradgrind over Louisa's flight, rejects Gradgrind's plea for patience and reconciliation, and delivers an ultimatum that if Louisa does not return by noon the next day he will send her belongings and resume a bachelor life — which he immediately does.

Bounderby posts a public wanted placard naming Stephen Blackpool as suspected bank robber; Rachael confronts Louisa and Bounderby demanding Stephen be cleared, promises he will return within two days to vindicate himself, but Stephen never appears — having fled after receiving her warning letter — while Tom skulks guiltily at Bounderby's side throughout.

Sissy and Louisa travel secretly to Sleary's circus where Sleary reveals Tom is hidden disguised as a blackface servant in the show, then Gradgrind arrives, confronts Tom about the robbery he coldly confesses to, arranges his disguised escape to Liverpool for shipment abroad, but as the family says goodbye Bitzer bursts in and seizes Tom by the collar.

Sissy and Rachael find Stephen Blackpool's hat near the abandoned Old Hell Shaft, organize a rescue, and bring him up mortally injured; Stephen delivers a dying speech condemning industrial negligence and the "muddle" of society, forgives those who wronged him, and asks Gradgrind to clear his name before dying.

After Stephen Blackpool's death exposes Tom as the real bank thief, Sissy secretly engineers Tom's escape to Sleary's circus while Gradgrind, shattered, tells Bounderby the truth and vindicates Stephen's memory.

testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: This unit is the table of contents for Book the First: Poverty, listing all 36 chapter titles of that book, from "Sun and Shadow" through "The Marshalsea becomes an Orphan," including chapters naming Mr Merdle's Complaint and Mr Pancks.

Unit presents Book Two's chapter list and Dickens' 1857 preface, in which he defends his satirical inventions—especially Mr Merdle as stand-in for real financial fraudsters—and describes revisiting the physical ruins of the Marshalsea Prison where Little Dorrit was born.

In a stifling, sun-baked Marseilles, two prisoners, Rigaud and his cellmate John Baptist Cavalletto, are fed by the jailer and his small daughter, after which Rigaud boastfully recounts to Cavalletto his self-justifying version of his wife's death before being led out under guard to face trial amid a hostile crowd.

Released from quarantine at Marseilles, the Meagles family (with daughter Pet and her maid Tattycoram), Arthur Clennam, the aloof Miss Wade, and other travellers breakfast together and part ways, with Mr Meagles recounting Tattycoram's foundling origins and Clennam his bleak childhood, while Miss Wade gives ominous farewells and Tattycoram is later overheard raging with resentment at her position before being calmed by Miss Wade.

Arthur Clennam returns to London on a bleak Sunday, goes to his old family house where he coldly reunites with his rigid, bedridden mother Mrs Clennam, learns from the Flintwinches about their marriage and glimpses Little Dorrit in his mother's room, before retiring upstairs to muse on childhood and lost love.

Affery Flintwinch, in what seems a vivid dream, gets up at night and finds her husband Jeremiah awake watching an identical double of himself asleep in a hidden room, sees the double roused, given wine, and sent off with an iron box, then is caught by Jeremiah on the staircase and shaken by the throat, after which he tells her she was only sleepwalking and dreaming.

Arthur Clennam tells his mother he is giving up the family business and asks whether his late father may have wronged someone requiring reparation, provoking her furious, self-righteous denial and threat to disown him, after which Flintwinch is confirmed as her partner, Arthur takes lodgings elsewhere while keeping daily business hours at the house, and he grows increasingly curious about the mysterious seamstress Little Dorrit.

themes: birth and death within the prison walls
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: A shy, helpless debtor is committed to the Marshalsea with his pregnant wife and two children, has a daughter born there attended by the drunken jail doctor Haggage and charwoman Mrs Bangham, loses his wife years later, and gradually settles into prison life so completely that on the old turnkey's death he inherits the title "Father of the Marshalsea," growing proud of it and ritually receiving parting tributes from departing debtors.

The chapter traces Amy Dorrit's growth from infancy in the Marshalsea (befriended by turnkey Bob) into the self-sacrificing "Child of the Marshalsea," who after her mother's death cares for her broken father, educates herself and gets her sister taught dancing and herself needlework, repeatedly tries to rescue her wastrel brother Tip (sending him to Canada, then covering for his return as a debtor), and preserves her father's genteel fiction until, at twenty-two, she is glimpsed by Arthur Clennam returning home to the prison one September evening.

Arthur Clennam is led by Frederick Dorrit into the Marshalsea prison, where he meets William Dorrit ("Father of the Marshalsea"), watches Amy quietly serve and support her father, gets locked in overnight after a private word with Amy, and lies awake in the Snuggery brooding over whether his mother's secret dealings with Mrs Clennam connect to William Dorrit's long imprisonment.

themes: budding sympathy between Arthur and Amy
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Waiting outside the Marshalsea, Arthur Clennam seeks out Amy Dorrit at her uncle's lodging, then walks her to the Iron Bridge and back, asking about her father's creditors and his link to Mrs Clennam while Amy passionately defends her father's dignity and weeps over his imprisonment, and on the way they encounter the devoted simple-minded Maggy before Arthur leaves Amy at the prison gate.

themes: satire of bureaucratic obstruction ("How not to do it")
futility of individual effort against institutions
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Arthur Clennam, trying to learn the nature of a Crown claim against the imprisoned debtor Dorrit, is shunted between Barnacle Junior, Mr Tite Barnacle, and various clerks at the evasive Circumlocution Office, then afterward runs into Mr Meagles, who introduces him to the engineer Daniel Doyce, whose useful invention the same Office has spent years stalling and shelving.

themes: chance reunion with a past accomplice
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Rigaud, travelling under the alias Lagnier, arrives footsore at a French inn where locals discuss him as a notorious wife-murderer acquitted at trial, then discovers his old prison comrade Cavalletto asleep in the same room, forces him under threat to accept the alias and join him in going to Paris and England, before Cavalletto secretly flees at dawn.

Clennam and Doyce visit Bleeding Heart Yard to find the plasterer Plornish, whose wife recounts how Little Dorrit came to work for Mrs Clennam through the landlord Casby and his rent-collector Pancks; Clennam then engages Plornish, in secret, to negotiate with the horse-dealer Captain Maroon and pay off Tip Dorrit's debt to secure his release from custody without revealing his own role as benefactor.

themes: loneliness and regret over a barren past
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Arthur Clennam calls on Christopher Casby, meets rent-collector Pancks and is crushingly disillusioned to find his boyhood love Flora now a garrulous widow (Mrs Finching) burdened with the eccentric "Mr F.'s Aunt"; after dinner he walks off with Pancks discussing money and rents, then helps a foreign traveller injured by a mail-coach get treated at St Bartholomew's, and back at his lodging broods bitterly over his bleak past until a voice announces "Little Dorrit."

themes: protective devotion to a flawed father
night wandering and homelessness in London
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Little Dorrit visits Clennam late at night to thank the unknown benefactor who freed her brother, warn him that Mrs Clennam may have learned her secret via Flintwinch's watching, and beg him never to lend money to her father; then, locked out of the Marshalsea, she and Maggy wander the streets till dawn, encounter a fallen woman who mistakes Amy for a child, and finally rest by a vestry fire before Amy's exhausted return home at daybreak.

In a dream, Mistress Affery overhears Mr Flintwinch and Mrs Clennam quarrel over old grievances and secrets (including Arthur's father and Little Dorrit's unknown address), then wakes to find it was real tea-time, growing more haunted and fearful of the house as Little Dorrit and Arthur Clennam arrive.

themes: class/age difference as barrier to affection
honest inventive labour vs bureaucratic obstruction
resignation to a settled, monotonous fate
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Clennam walks to Twickenham, falls in with Daniel Doyce (who needs a business partner for his engineering works), and they arrive at the Meagles cottage, where after a warm family evening—marked by Tattycoram's tense exchange about Miss Wade—Clennam privately resolves not to fall in love with Pet, reasons himself into and out of that resolve, arranges to be considered as Doyce's business partner via Meagles, and ends the night troubled by a nameless unhappiness he insists is "nobody's weakness."

themes: art as dilettantism vs true vocation
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Arthur Clennam, visiting the Meagles' house, meets and grows to dislike Pet's suitor Henry Gowan, endures a dinner dominated by Mr Meagles's fawning over the visiting Barnacle relative and the tongue-tied Young Barnacle, then learns from Doyce that Mr Meagles disapproves of Gowan as a match for his daughter yet has failed to prevent their attachment, leaving Clennam privately miserable though outwardly resolved against loving Pet himself.

Young John Chivery, the turnkey's son long smitten with Amy Dorrit, calls on her father with his usual gift of cigars, then finds Amy alone on the Iron Bridge and stammeringly tries to declare his love, but she gently and firmly refuses him, asks him never to seek her out there again and to think of her only as unprotected and ordinary, and sends him away heartbroken.

William Dorrit, as "Father of the Marshalsea," parades his brother Frederick then holds court in the Lodge before retreating to his room where, upset over a slight from turnkey Chivery, he alternates between grandiose self-pity and boasting about his lost prosperity, until Amy comforts and soothes him to sleep, then watches dawn over the prison yard and grieves that she has never truly seen the father he once was.

themes: money as means of dismissing a scandal
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Amy Dorrit visits her sister Fanny backstage at the theatre and their clarionet-playing uncle, then accompanies Fanny to call on Mrs Merdle, who recounts how Fanny rejected the advances of Mrs Merdle's son and was paid off with a bracelet and money to end the acquaintance, after which Fanny berates Amy for disapproving before the sisters reconcile.

themes: psychosomatic illness with no physical cause
contrast between Merdle's opulence and the Marshalsea's shadow
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: At a lavish Harley Street dinner, magnates (Bar, Bishop, Treasury, a physician, etc.) fawn over the immensely rich but taciturn Mr Merdle and his bosom-displaying wife, urging him toward more public/philanthropic ventures, while Merdle privately confesses to feeling unwell though the physician can find nothing wrong with him — his vague "complaint" going unnoticed by all, even as, elsewhere, Amy Dorrit stitches her father William Dorrit's shirts under the real shadow of the Marshalsea.

themes: prison's grip on identity and duty
secrecy and gossip among the poor
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Mrs Chivery tells Clennam that her son John is heartbroken over Little Dorrit's rejection and begs him to intervene, then Clennam meets Little Dorrit on the Iron Bridge, intercepts begging letters from her father and brother via Maggy, and Little Dorrit, distressed, insists on hurrying back to the Marshalsea, which she calls home.

Meagles brokers Clennam's partnership with the honourable Daniel Doyce (forming Doyce and Clennam), after which Flora Finching and Mr F.'s Aunt pay a comic, rambling visit to the counting-house followed by Mr Casby and Pancks, and Pancks then presses Clennam for information about the Dorrit family (striking a bargain of mutual disclosure) before storming off to harass Bleeding Heart Yard tenants, including inquiring about a lame foreigner Clennam has vouched for, over unpaid rents.

Little Dorrit, engaged by Flora Finching (who reminisces at length about her old romance with Arthur Clennam) to work as a companion, is then cryptically approached by Mr Pancks, who reads her palm, warns her to pretend not to know him outside Mr Casby's house, and thereafter mysteriously pervades her daily life, all while she avoids seeing Clennam when he calls and instead tells Maggy a veiled fairy-tale about a princess and a tiny woman guarding a secret shadow.

Mr Pancks, lodging with the Ruggs in Pentonville, hosts Young John Chivery (who loves Miss Dorrit) at a dinner where the three secretly divide up detective "cases" (churchyards, enquiries, records) like a card game to fund Pancks's covert investigation, while separately Pancks grows fond of the lame Italian exile Mr Baptist (Cavalletto), whom the prejudiced but kind-hearted Bleeding Heart Yard residents and Mrs Plornish have been teaching broken English, and whom Arthur Clennam has helped find carving work.

themes: hollow gentility of the leisured class
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Having resolved to suppress his love for Pet Meagles, Clennam discusses Henry Gowan with Doyce, then endures a visit to Gowan's mother at Hampton Court, where the snobbish Mrs Gowan and her aristocratic circle disparage the Meagles family while wrongly accusing them of scheming to trap Henry, leaving Clennam uneasy and troubled on the drive home.

Clennam broods over Pancks's mysterious interest in the Dorrit family, then learns from Mr Meagles that Tattycoram has stormed off after refusing to "count five-and-twenty," and accompanies him to Miss Wade's lodgings, where Tattycoram, now sheltered by Miss Wade, defiantly rejects every plea to return.

themes: failed attempts to reclaim a runaway
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Mr Meagles's efforts (letters, personal visits, newspaper advertisements) to recover the vanished Tattycoram all fail and only attract impostors and beggars, while Arthur Clennam walks to the Meagles' Twickenham cottage and Pet (Minnie) meets him alone to confide that she is to marry Henry Gowan, asking Clennam to comfort her father, reconcile him to Gowan, and watch over her parents; Clennam, finally giving up his own secret hope for her, later walks alone by the river and casts her farewell roses into the water.

Mrs Clennam questions Little Dorrit about Pancks after his visit, then kisses her and sends her home; outside, Affery locks herself out and a mysterious foreign traveler (asking after the name Clennam) breaks in through a window to help her, just as Flintwinch returns and Mrs Clennam is heard calling out to know who is there.

A stranger calling himself Blandois — who strikingly resembles Rigaud and unnerves Affery — arrives at the Clennam house with a letter of credit, is lodged nearby by Flintwinch, then dines with Mrs Clennam, questions her closely about the cryptic "D. N. F." (Do Not Forget) watch and the family's secrets, tours the old house with Flintwinch needling him with veiled insinuations, drinks with him afterward, and then abruptly departs for the Continent, vowing they will meet again.

Little Dorrit escorts Mrs Plornish's elderly workhouse father, Old Nandy, into the Marshalsea on his birthday outing, provoking Fanny's furious shame and William Dorrit's wounded sense of "Spirit" at seeing his daughter arm-in-arm with a pauper, until he calms himself, lavishly patronizes Nandy at tea before Arthur Clennam, then clashes with his son Tip over a refused loan and inflated notions of gentlemanly "spirit," before being called away to preside over the Collegians, leaving Clennam finally able to speak with Amy alone.

Arthur Clennam visits Little Dorrit in the Marshalsea, notices her distress, confesses he once mistakenly fancied himself in love (not with Flora) but now considers himself too old for such things, and presses her to trust him with any secret (which she denies having), before an ecstatic, half-drunk Mr Pancks bursts in with Mr Rugg to reveal that they have all but completed a discovery proving William Dorrit is heir to a fortune.

Mrs Gowan visits Mrs Merdle to rehearse and get validation for the face-saving fiction that she reluctantly consented to her son Henry's marriage to Minnie Meagles despite the match being beneath the Gowans, after which Mr Merdle arrives home and Mrs Merdle (backed by her son Edmund Sparkler) complains that he fails to hide his business preoccupations and thus damages his fitness for Society, leaving Mr Merdle to wander his house alone and dejected.

themes: loss of a child through marriage
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: On Pet Meagles's wedding day to Henry Gowan, swarms of the aristocratic, do-nothing Barnacle family (including Lord Decimus Tite Barnacle and William Barnacle) descend on the Twickenham cottage to lend the marriage borrowed lustre, while Gowan confides to Clennam his cynical sense of being a disappointed man selling out his art, and after the ceremony Pet departs for Dover leaving Mr Meagles, Mrs Meagles, and Clennam desolate.

Mr Pancks tells Clennam how he secretly traced and proved that William Dorrit is heir to a great fortune, after which Clennam breaks the news to Amy (Little Dorrit) at Flora Finching's house and they rush to the Marshalsea to tell her father, who alternates between shock, tears, and feverish plans to reward everyone and show himself to the cheering prisoners, while Amy, resting beside him, confides to Clennam her uneasy feeling that it seems hard he must pay both in suffering and in money.

Mr Dorrit and family, amid farewell festivities, speeches, and gifts to the Collegians, finally depart the Marshalsea prison forever, but in the commotion Amy is forgotten and found fainted in her room, then carried out and revived by Arthur Clennam as the carriage drives off.

At a convent atop the Great Saint Bernard Pass, three parties of travellers — including the now-wealthy Dorrit family, the newlywed Gowans, and a smooth-talking stranger who signs the register as "Blandois" — take shelter for the night, and after Mrs Gowan faints and is put to bed, Amy Dorrit secretly visits her to deliver a hidden letter before the sinister traveller trails her back downstairs.

Chapter narrates Mrs General's backstory (widowed by a commissary who hid his wealth, then forming young ladies' minds and manners for hire) and how Mr Dorrit, newly rich, negotiates delicately over payment and secures her as chaperone-companion for his two daughters, followed by a description of her cold, "varnished," opinion-suppressing character.

themes: unreality of new wealth vs memory of prison
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Descending from the Great St Bernard, the Dorrit family bickers over Amy's tending to sick Mrs Gowan and her past association with Clennam, Mr Dorrit lectures Amy on maintaining rank, they travel on through the Alps and Italy with Blandois/Rigaud lurking ominously, a hotel dispute with Mrs Merdle and her son Sparkler is smoothed over, and the procession continues to Venice where Amy, feeling her old life is more real than her new grand one, spends solitary evenings on her balcony recalling the Marshalsea.

themes: homesickness and nostalgia for past poverty
discomfort with new wealth and status
loyalty and gratitude to old friends
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Writing to Clennam from Venice, Little Dorrit relays news of Mrs Gowan, expresses longing for old friends (Maggy, the Plornishes, Mr Nandy), confesses she cannot adjust to her family's new fortune and still feels haunted by memories of the Marshalsea and her father's imprisonment, and closes by begging Clennam never to think of her as anything other than the poor girl he once protected.

In Venice, Mr Dorrit enlists Mrs General to reform Amy's demeanor, then rebukes Amy himself for not "blotting out" their Marshalsea past as her siblings have, until Amy's tender touch reduces him to tears; later at breakfast, talk of visiting the Gowans and their connection to the great Mr Merdle wins Dorrit's approval for Amy, but Uncle Frederick erupts in a rare passionate protest against Fanny's disrespect toward Amy.

Amy and Fanny Dorrit visit Mrs Gowan in Venice where they meet the sinister Blandois posing as a model for Henry Gowan's painting, witness Gowan's dog Lion violently attack Blandois and get beaten for it, are pursued by the smitten Mr Sparkler (whom Fanny plans to enslave as revenge on Mrs Merdle), have Mr Dorrit entertain Sparkler and consider commissioning Gowan's portrait, and finally, at the opera, learn from Blandois that Lion has been poisoned and is dead.

In Venice, Mrs General polishes the Dorrit family's manners while Fanny confides to Amy her suspicion that Mrs General has designs on their father, Blandois (Rigaud) arranges for Gowan to paint Mr Dorrit's portrait and shows a sinister private power over both Amy and Mrs Gowan (who confides he killed her dog), and, once the family relocates to Rome, Mrs Merdle visits and Mr Dorrit expresses his eagerness to become known to the great Mr Merdle.

themes: bureaucratic obstruction and satire of the Circumlocution Office
resigned, melancholy longing across social barriers
family pride and awkward in-law relations
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Clennam persuades a reluctant Doyce to let him renew the fight for recognition of Doyce's invention at the Circumlocution Office, then, while missing the now-distant Little Dorrit, visits the Meagles at Twickenham where the Dowager Mrs Gowan pays a call and, after sparring with Mr Meagles over blame for her son Henry's marriage to Pet, disclaims all responsibility and departs declaring that such mismatched unions "never do."

Mr and Mrs Meagles decide to leave for Italy to see Pet, leaving Arthur to look after their cottage, where Mrs Tickit reports a fleeting glimpse of Tattycoram; soon after, Arthur spots Tattycoram in London with a mysterious foreign stranger, secretly follows them to a riverside meeting with Miss Wade where money is discussed, trails the trio to Mr Casby's house, visits Flora (whose rambling talk delays him) and questions Casby, who refuses to give Miss Wade's address, and afterward learns from Pancks that Miss Wade is of unknown parentage, volatile, and receives money from Casby that she came to collect that night.

Walking to his mother's house brooding on secrets, Arthur Clennam again encounters the foreign stranger (Blandois) from his earlier sighting with Miss Wade, who forces his way in demanding Flintwinch and audience with "my lady," and despite Arthur's angry objections Mrs Clennam receives the man calmly as a known business acquaintance while Flintwinch returns and greets him with false bonhomie, Blandois then taunts Flintwinch with veiled threats about not trusting people who might want him "under the ground" before Arthur is dismissed and leaves troubled, with Affery, terrified, telling him she has been "in a dream" and to ask nothing and go away.

Writing from Rome to Arthur Clennam, Little Dorrit describes the Gowans' lodging and Mr Gowan's neglectful, restless treatment of his lonely wife Minnie, reports family news (Fanny's suitor, the Meagles' new grandson), confesses her homesickness and childhood dreams of her old poverty, and closes asking Clennam to remember Minnie kindly and send her regards to Mr Pancks.

themes: worship of wealth as false idol
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Mr Merdle hosts a grand dinner for Bishop, Bar, Lord Decimus, Mr Tite Barnacle and other Barnacles so that he and Lord Decimus can privately arrange a political appointment for Edmund Sparkler, during which talk turns to the debt case and inheritance of "Mr Dorrit" (William Dorrit), and the visit ends with Sparkler's appointment to the Circumlocution Office being announced.

themes: gullibility of the poor toward wealth
duty to profit for others' sake
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Merdle-mania spreads like a disease through Bleeding Heart Yard and beyond, infecting even the skeptical Pancks, who visits the Plornishes (where a terrified Mr Baptist has just fled a dreaded stranger), then goes home with Clennam, confides his own investment in Merdle's enterprises, and urges Clennam—torn over his mother's troubling secret and Doyce's finances—to invest too and "go in and win."

themes: social status anxiety of newcomers to fashion
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Fanny Dorrit, agitated after a Merdle ball, confides in her sister Amy her contempt for their precarious social position and her plan to marry the foolish Mr Sparkler chiefly to spite and outrank his mother Mrs Merdle, and weeks later she and Sparkler announce their engagement to Amy, who is distressed but offers her congratulations.

themes: ruins and nostalgia for lost past
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Mr Dorrit negotiates and settles Fanny's marriage to Mr Sparkler (leveraging correspondence with Mr Merdle for social gain), the wedding is celebrated with great pomp in Rome, and afterward, with Fanny departed for Florence/England, Mr Dorrit tells Amy he now wishes to see her married off too, leaving her lonely under Mrs General's care to wander reflectively among Rome's ruins.

Newly wealthy Mr Dorrit and his daughter (now Mrs Sparkler) are absorbed into fawning London high society; Mr Merdle pays a call, vaguely offers Dorrit financial advice and a share of favor in his ventures, escorts him into the City amid public adulation, and Dorrit basks in reflected glory at dinners and invitations, troubled only by the Chief Butler's unsettling scrutinizing stare.

Flora Finching visits Mr Dorrit in his hotel and, in rambling talk, shows him a handbill about the mysterious disappearance of Monsieur Blandois (an acquaintance of Henry Gowan), prompting Mr Dorrit to skip the Merdle dinner and instead visit Clennam and Co. that night, where he questions the stern Mrs Clennam and Jeremiah Flintwinch (watched by the fearful Affery) without learning anything, and returns home haunted by the eerie house and imagined fate of the missing man.

After a grand farewell at the Merdles', Mr Dorrit is confronted at his hotel by John Chivery bearing cigars and news of the Marshalsea, reacts with rage and shame at the reminder of his past, then gives him a large cheque and swears him to secrecy before touring through France toward Rome absorbed in elaborate daydreams (his "castle in the air") and buying gifts for a lady in Paris.

themes: pride and social ambition ('castle in air')
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Returning to Rome, Mr Dorrit grows increasingly confused and unwell over several days, then publicly breaks down at Mrs Merdle's dinner—mentally reverting to his old identity as the Father of the Marshalsea—after which Amy gets him home, where his mind remains trapped in the prison past until, tended devotedly by her, he dies with his brother Frederick, who dies of grief soon after.

themes: dependency and power over a subordinate
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: In Calais, Arthur Clennam visits Miss Wade seeking news of the vanished Blandois (Rigaud), gets only bitter, evasive answers and her confession of hiring him plus her venomous hatred of Gowan and his wife, witnesses her cruel clash with the dependent Harriet (Tattycoram) over the girl's secret visit to the Meagles' cottage, and departs empty-handed except for a manuscript Miss Wade gives him recounting her own life.

themes: rescuing a kindred spirit from bondage
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Miss Wade narrates her own life story of perceiving insult and patronage everywhere -- from a schoolgirl "friend," through governess posts marred by a jealous nurse and a condescending mistress, to a broken engagement undermined by the mocking Mr Gowan -- ending with her taking in a girl (Tattycoram) whose situation mirrors her own.

Doyce settles accounts with Clennam and departs abroad for an engineering commission after Clennam refuses to abandon pursuing his invention, and then Cavalletto, recognizing the wanted man on a handbill as the assassin Rigaud (alias Lagnier/Blandois) he once knew in Marseilles and Chalons, vows to secretly help Clennam find news of him.

themes: secrecy and power within the household
fear and intimidation of a servant
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Troubled by news that Blandois (Rigaud) was once imprisoned in France on a murder charge, Arthur tells his mother, who coldly refuses concern or aid and forbids him to repeat it, then, using Flora Finching's contrived tour of the house as cover, presses the terrified Affery for the truth about the house's noises and Flintwinch's suspicious conduct the night Blandois vanished, but Affery, cowed by her husband, will only promise to "tell her dreams" if Arthur ever gets the better of "them two clever ones."

themes: boredom and vanity of high society marriage
public adulation of Merdle's wealth and fame
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Fanny and Edmund Sparkler while away a tedious, stifling summer evening bickering and discussing family matters (Amy's expected arrival, brother Edward's illness, and papa's unsettled estate), until Mr Merdle pays a strangely listless, aimless visit, borrows a penknife, and departs, leaving Fanny convinced it was the longest, most wearisome day ever.

themes: public rumor and reversal of fame
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Physician is summoned to the warm-baths where Mr Merdle has cut his throat and died, leaving a confessional letter; he and Bar break the news to the household (whose Chief Butler resigns rather than serve on), and by day's end London learns Merdle's "complaint" was really forgery and robbery, turning him from celebrated financier into reviled fraud.

themes: loyalty and reparation to a partner
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: After the exposure of the great financial swindle ruins Clennam and Doyce's firm, Pancks and Clennam grieve together over the loss, Clennam resolves through his lawyer Mr Rugg to publicly clear Doyce of blame and surrender his own property to creditors, and is then arrested on a debt writ and taken to the Marshalsea prison, where alone in a room prepared for him he weeps for the absent Little Dorrit.

themes: memory and reflection on the past
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: Imprisoned again in the Marshalsea, Arthur Clennam broods on Little Dorrit until Young John Chivery brings him his belongings and tea, then reveals — to Clennam's stunned disbelief — that Amy Dorrit has long loved him, after which the Plornishes visit to console him.

In the Marshalsea, Clennam, increasingly isolated by imprisonment, is visited first by Ferdinand Barnacle who cynically defends the Circumlocution Office and confirms Merdle's fraud ruined him, then by Mr Rugg who urges him to move to the Bench for the sake of public opinion, before Rigaud (Blandois), tracked down by Cavalletto and Pancks, bursts in drunk and boastful, admits he faked his disappearance to extort Mrs Clennam over a secret, dictates a threatening letter demanding her answer within a week, and is then confronted by Flintwinch, who delivers Mrs Clennam's terse reply agreeing to the appointment, before Rigaud departs taking Cavalletto into his service and leaving Clennam alone again.

Clennam, sick and despairing in the Marshalsea, is visited by Amy Dorrit (now wealthy, returned from abroad), who tends him, offers him her whole fortune, which he refuses out of pride and shame, sends him away with her love, and John Chivery reports having seen her safely to her hotel and delivered her message of undying love.

Rigaud, with Mr Pancks and Mr Baptist in tow, arrives at Mrs Clennam's house and, after Pancks leaves (hinting Affery should "tell her dreams"), extorts Mrs Clennam by threatening to reveal a suppressed codicil and the true story of Arthur's parentage, forcing her and Flintwinch (aided by Affery's interjected "dreams") to narrate the hidden family history of the marriage, the mistress, and the concealed paper, until Rigaud reveals he has left a duplicate packet at the Marshalsea for Little Dorrit to open if not bought off by nightfall, prompting Mrs Clennam to rush out of the house.

Mrs Clennam, briefly able to walk again, goes to the Marshalsea to reclaim the incriminating packet from Little Dorrit, confesses her long concealment and harsh treatment of Arthur, begs Little Dorrit to keep the secret from him until her death, and then they hurry back together just as the old Clennam house collapses in a sudden roar, killing the blackmailing foreigner while Flintwinch escapes with the firm's money, after which Mrs Clennam collapses paralyzed and mute for the rest of her life.

Tormented by guilt over Arthur's imprisonment and financial ruin caused by the Merdle collapse, Pancks quits Casby's service and publicly denounces him in Bleeding Heart Yard as a hypocritical exploiter, then cuts off his long hair and shears his hat before fleeing amid the crowd's laughter.

themes: social climbing and hypocrisy after scandal
testi/dickens/atomized/little_dorrit/cha.plot: While Arthur lies ill and Little Dorrit tends both him and her fractious family amid the fallout of Merdle's death, Mr Meagles fruitlessly hunts across Europe (including confronting Miss Wade) for Rigaud's papers, until Tattycoram, having secretly taken the box, brings it back and begs forgiveness, after which Meagles resolves to fetch Doyce home.

Recovering in the Marshalsea, Arthur learns from Little Dorrit that both her family's and her own fortune are gone and that she has nothing, and they declare their love and become engaged; Flora tearfully bids farewell to any hope of Arthur while Mr F.'s Aunt causes a scene; Doyce returns from abroad with Mr Meagles bringing news of restored business success and no debt to Arthur; and the next morning Arthur and Little Dorrit burn a paper together, leave the prison, and are married at St George's Church with Doyce, Flora, Pancks, and Maggy present, before going out into a life of quiet usefulness.

testi/dickens/atomized/martin_chuzzlewit.plot: The narrator mock-seriously traces the Chuzzlewit family's fictional ancient lineage, satirizing aristocratic pride, dubious genealogical claims, and the vanity of noble descent.

Seth Pecksniff, a fraudulently pious architect, is introduced with his daughters; his former pupil John Westlock departs after exposing Pecksniff's financial swindles, while loyal Tom Pinch — whom Westlock reveals is systematically exploited — defends Pecksniff to the last and bids his friend farewell.

Old Martin Chuzzlewit falls ill at the Blue Dragon inn where his young companion Mary Graham nurses him; landlady Mrs Lupin summons Pecksniff, who recognises his wealthy cousin and listens to a bitter confession that riches corrupt all who surround him, then departs after urging Martin to remember his grandson in his will.

Pecksniff meets the shabby swindler Montague Tigg (proxy for cousin Chevy Slyme) while eavesdropping on Old Martin at the Blue Dragon; the entire Chuzzlewit clan descends to scheme over the old man's will, convenes in chaotic council at Pecksniff's house, erupts in mutual recrimination, and is humiliated when Old Martin quietly slips away during the meeting.

Tom Pinch drives to Salisbury to collect Pecksniff's new pupil, meets Mark Tapley on the road debating trades that would test his cheerfulness, finds Martin Chuzzlewit waiting at a tavern, and returns with him to Pecksniff's house where Pecksniff stages an effusive welcome feast for the new arrival.

Pecksniff departs for London leaving Martin and Tom Pinch alone, whereupon Martin confides his disinheritance by his grandfather and his secret love for a dependent young woman, revealing she is the mysterious church visitor Tom had mentioned the night before.

Montague Tigg arrives at Pecksniff's to extract payment for his stranded companion Chevy Slyme's inn bill; Martin and Tom guarantee the debt and are introduced to the drunken, boastful Slyme; Tigg then swindles Tom's last coin as a personal loan; meanwhile Mark Tapley bids farewell to Mrs Lupin and the Blue Dragon and sets off for London.

Pecksniff travels by night coach to London with his daughters, shares the journey with Anthony Chuzzlewit and Jonas (who trade barbs on hypocrisy and money-grubbing), and on arrival in foggy London installs the family at Mrs Todgers's dingy commercial boarding house.

Pecksniff and his daughters stay at Todgers's London boarding house, pay a patronising visit to Tom Pinch's sister Ruth (a governess), are ejected from her employer's grand house, then attend a boisterous Sunday dinner at Todgers's where Pecksniff becomes helplessly drunk and must be locked in his room.

Old Martin Chuzzlewit arrives secretly at Todgers's to forge an alliance with Pecksniff, revealing that young Martin has concealed a secret engagement, and orders Pecksniff to expel him while hinting at rewarding Pecksniff's loyalty.

Jonas Chuzzlewit courts Charity Pecksniff during a visit to Anthony's grim counting-house, while Anthony and Pecksniff tacitly broker the match; the chapter closes with the Pecksniff family departing Todgers's amid a mournful commercial-boarders serenade.

Tom Pinch and Martin dine with former pupil John Westlock in Salisbury, who praises Tom, condemns Pecksniff, and returns Tigg's borrowed money; on their return Pecksniff coldly snubs Martin and formally expels him, whereupon Martin resolves to emigrate to America.

Expelled from Pecksniff's, Martin walks penniless to London, spends five weeks in deepening poverty pawning possessions and fruitlessly seeking passage to America (encountering Tigg at the pawnbroker), receives a mysterious anonymous £20 note, and is then found by Mark Tapley, who volunteers to emigrate with him and reveals that Mary Graham and Old Martin are staying in London.

Martin and Mary Graham meet secretly at dawn in St. James's Park for a clandestine farewell before Martin and Mark Tapley sail to America, during which Martin reads aloud a letter entrusting Tom Pinch with Mary's welfare, while the narrator quietly exposes Martin's fundamental egotism.

Martin and Mark Tapley endure the Atlantic crossing in steerage aboard the ship Screw — Mark cheerfully helps fellow poor emigrants while Martin sulks in his berth hiding class shame — until they arrive at New York.

Martin arrives in New York aboard the Screw, is taken up by Colonel Diver (editor of the Rowdy Journal) and his war correspondent Jefferson Brick, dines at the Pawkins boarding house among a company of hollow American boosters, and is ultimately offered a rare candid critique of American society by an honest fellow guest.

In New York, Martin and Mark are befriended by the candid Mr. Bevan, who takes them to visit the respectable Norris family, where Martin is socially humiliated when General Fladdock reveals he crossed in steerage, exposing the Norrises' shallow class pretensions and their hollow abolitionism, leaving Martin despondent about his prospects in America.

Anthony Chuzzlewit collapses in a fit while Jonas secretly reads the will confirming himself sole heir; Pecksniff, summoned to London by Anthony's cryptic letter about the Jonas–Mercy match, stays as witness through the night as the old miser hovers between life and death.

Pecksniff fetches nurse-and-layer-out Mrs Gamp on Jonas's orders; Anthony Chuzzlewit's lavish funeral proceeds with Jonas, Pecksniff, the undertaker Mould, and the doctor all performing grief cynically for profit or reputation, while only old clerk Chuffey mourns with genuine anguish.

Jonas Chuzzlewit negotiates a dowry with Pecksniff during their coach journey home, then shocks everyone by proposing to younger daughter Merry instead of Cherry, throwing the household into uproar at the very moment Tom Pinch announces the unannounced arrival of Old Martin Chuzzlewit and Mary Graham at the door.

Martin and Mark Tapley travel by train through America, where Martin buys a lot in the sham Eden settlement from the shifty agent Scadder (with Mark as new business partner), then witnesses the Watertoast Sympathisers' meeting collapse in fury when they discover their Irish hero advocates abolition.

After buying land in Eden, Martin is mobbed as a celebrity "lion" by the Watertoast community, endures a chaotic public reception and the insufferable Mrs Hominy, and boards a steamboat for Eden—just as Mark learns from Captain Kedgick that no one who goes to Eden ever returns alive.

Martin and Mark arrive at Eden to find a disease-ridden, desolate swamp utterly unlike what was promised; Martin collapses in despair and falls ill while Mark, with desperate cheerfulness, makes the wretched cabin habitable and resolves to hold firm.

Old Martin visits Pecksniff's house with Mary Graham, Jonas confronts Tom Pinch on the road and is struck down in a scuffle, Charity secretly thanks Tom for it, and old Martin questions Merry about her joyless engagement to Jonas while Jonas privately vows revenge after marriage.

Mrs Gamp negotiates with undertaker Mould to take a night-nursing job at a Holborn inn, then spends the night beside a delirious fever patient who cries out the name of Jonas Chuzzlewit in his ravings.

Poll Sweedlepipe and the precocious Bailey escort Mrs Gamp to Jonas Chuzzlewit's house to collect her belongings after being replaced by his new bride Merry, whose arrival is greeted by old Chuffey's ominous cry of woe upon the wicked house.

Montague Tigg, now grandly styled Tigg Montague and chairing the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee Disinterested Loan and Life Assurance Company, lures Jonas Chuzzlewit into becoming a complicit investor by openly boasting of its swindling mechanics, then secretly commissions the spy Nadgett to dig up information on Jonas.

Jonas dines at Montague Tigg's opulent Pall Mall lodgings, is flattered and drawn deeper into the fraudulent insurance scheme, then is brought home drunk by Bailey and physically strikes his wife Merry.

Sairey Gamp visits Poll Sweedlepipe's barber shop then helps transport the gravely ill Lewsome to a country-bound coach; Lewsome cryptically hints to John Westlock of a dreadful secret he helped perpetrate, while undertaker Mould gleefully eyes the wasted man as a future client.

Pecksniff negotiates Charity's departure to Mrs Todgers's, manoeuvres Old Martin into moving into his house, then corners Mary Graham alone and proposes marriage while threatening that refusal will ruin young Martin's prospects.

Pecksniff eavesdrops from a church pew as Mary Graham reveals his coercive marriage proposal to Tom Pinch, then dismisses Tom on a fabricated charge of making improper advances to Mary, with Old Martin as unwitting witness to the deception.

Charity Pecksniff returns to Todgers's boarding house and, coaching herself on Mrs Todgers's advice, deliberately maneuvers the lovesick Moddle—who has been pining for her married sister Merry—into a tearful betrothal with herself.

Martin and Mark Tapley both nearly die of fever in the wretched Eden settlement; nursing each other through illness, Martin undergoes a moral reckoning with his own selfishness, and they eventually receive money from Mr Bevan and escape Eden to return to England.

Martin and Mark, sailing home from Eden, meet pompous Congressman Elijah Pogram on the steamboat, endure his jingoistic rhetoric and a levee at the National Hotel, then secure return passage to England through Mark's ingenuity as ship's cook, funded by their generous friend Mr Bevan.
Martin and Mark return to England penniless and witness a public stone-laying ceremony where Pecksniff receives civic honours for a grammar-school design Martin recognises as his own stolen work.

Dismissed by Pecksniff, Tom Pinch coaches to London, reunites with John Westlock, confronts his sister Ruth's condescending employer and extracts her from service, then the two siblings find cheap lodgings in Islington to start life afresh together.

Tom Pinch wanders lost in London, stumbles on Charity Pecksniff near the Monument, is brought to Todgers's where he has a tearful reconciliation with the unhappy Mercy (now Jonass wife), promises to relay her penitent message to old Mr Chuzzlewit, then reunites briefly with John Westlock before returning to his sister at Islington.

Nadgett delivers his secret dossier on Jonas Chuzzlewit to Montague Tigg, who uses the damning intelligence to blackmail Jonas into compliance and strong-arm him into recruiting Pecksniff into the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee scheme.

Tom Pinch and sister Ruth enjoy cheerful London domesticity while John Westlock brings word of a mysterious offer: an unnamed employer, acting through the enigmatic Mr Fips, installs Tom as secretary-librarian in dusty Temple chambers to catalogue a vast collection of books, the patron's identity kept wholly secret.

Tom Pinch, at a steamboat wharf, unwittingly delivers a mysterious letter to Jonas Chuzzlewit that aborts Jonas's planned escape abroad; Montague Tigg then appears and leads Jonas away, exposing Jonas as a man trapped under his control, while Mrs Gamp and a distraught Merry are also swept up in the scene.

Trapped by Montague Tigg's knowledge of a damning secret and unable to flee, Jonas capitulates and agrees to travel with Tigg that night to lure Pecksniff into investing in the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee company; a dark interlude with a doctor and a lancet foreshadows murderous intent.

Jonas and Montague travel by carriage through a violent storm toward Pecksniff's, during which Jonas nearly kills Montague when rampaging horses throw their carriage and young Bailey is mortally injured; at the Salisbury inn Montague is tormented by a nightmare of Jonas as murderous threat, then wakes to find Jonas standing over him through a door left suspiciously open.

Martin and Mark return to England from America, reunite with Mrs Lupin at the Blue Dragon, then confront Old Martin at Pecksniff's house where Martin seeks forgiveness, but Pecksniff intercepts every appeal and manipulates the feeble old man into rejecting his grandson, while Martin manages a brief whispered reunion with Mary before being expelled.

Jonas brings Pecksniff to dine with Montague Tigg, who persuades Pecksniff to invest nearly his entire savings in the fraudulent Anglo-Bengalee Assurance company, after which Tigg notes he can now manage Pecksniff alone.

Tom Pinch and his sister Ruth spend a cheerful afternoon with John Westlock — dining at his Temple chambers, enjoying music and easy company — while Tom recounts the mysterious wharf errand involving Mrs. Gamp, prompting John to suspect dark dealings and urge Tom to distance himself from the affair.

Tom Pinch and Ruth visit the battered Merry at Jonas's house where Chuffey's senile mutterings about "foul play" and death unsettle the gathering; Jonas returns and violently drives Tom out before he can reveal Nadgett's name, then enlists Mrs Gamp to silence Chuffey and slips out in secret disguise at night to commit a murder.

Jonas Chuzzlewit ambushes and murders Montague Tigg in a secluded wood after Tigg parts from Pecksniff at a country stile, then flees back to London and slips home, gripped by paranoid dread but utterly without remorse.

Martin Chuzzlewit and Mark Tapley return to London and reunite with Tom Pinch; at John Westlock's rooms they hear Lewsome confess he supplied drugs to Jonas Chuzzlewit to poison old Anthony, and the group resolves to reach the clerk Chuffey through Sairey Gamp to build a case against Jonas.

Mrs Gamp hosts Betsey Prig for tea to discuss nursing old Chuffey, but the evening explodes in a furious quarrel when Betsey denies Mrs Harris exists, inadvertently revealing to the watching Martin Chuzzlewit and John Westlock that Chuffey holds dangerous secrets about Jonas Chuzzlewit.

Martin Chuzzlewit confronts Tom Pinch with an accusation of betrayal and leaves without hearing Tom's defense; afterward Ruth reveals she has discovered Tom's secret unrequited love, and the two siblings share a tender, honest conversation in which Tom accepts his hopeless attachment with dignified calm.

Jonas, wracked with guilty terror while keeping the old clerk Chuffey confined and awaiting news of the body's discovery, is confronted by Old Martin Chuzzlewit, Chuffey, Lewsome and Mark Tapley, whereupon Chuffey first reveals Anthony's old poison plot before Nadgett exposes proof that Jonas murdered Montague Tigg, leading to Jonas's arrest and, after bribing Slyme for a few private minutes, his fatal self-poisoning in the coach.

Old Martin gathers everyone at the Temple, strikes down Pecksniff when he approaches with false unctuousness, publicly exposes Pecksniff's hypocrisy and his own past schemes and mistrust, reconciles with young Martin and blesses his marriage to Mary, praises Tom Pinch's honesty, dismisses the crushed and impoverished Pecksniff, then fends off the comic intrusions of Poll Sweedlepipe, Bailey, and Mrs Gamp (whom he pays off and rebukes) before all part to dine together.

John Westlock proposes to Ruth Pinch by the Temple Fountain and she accepts, they tell Tom who reacts with overjoyed emotion, and the day closes with a festive dinner hosted by Mark Tapley (with Old Martin Chuzzlewit, young Martin, Mary, and old Fips present) at which Old Martin gives Ruth jewels and John promises Tom he will always have a home with them.

themes: hollow family loyalty vs true kindness
testi/dickens/atomized/martin_chuzzlewit.plot: On the morning of Cherry Pecksniff's wedding, old Martin Chuzzlewit visits Todger's, forgives and rescues the grieving widowed Merry from her sister's neglect, reunites joyfully with Mark Tapley's old Eden neighbours, then the wedding party assembles at Todger's only for Augustus to jilt Cherry at the altar via a rambling farewell letter announcing his flight to Van Dieman's Land, closing with a lyrical coda showing Tom Pinch living tranquilly, playing the organ, supporting a now-destitute Pecksniff, and surrounded by his sister Ruth and loved ones.

testi/dickens/atomized/nicholas_nickleby.plot: Chapter 1 narrates the Nickleby family backstory: grandfather Godfrey inherits a modest fortune, his elder son Ralph becomes a ruthless London moneylender obsessed with wealth, while younger son Nicholas (the protagonist's father) squanders the family farm on a stock speculation, loses everything, and dies broken, leaving his widow and two young children destitute.

Ralph Nickleby, a cold-eyed moneylender who exploits his destitute clerk Newman Noggs for pittance wages, attends a farcical public meeting for the fraudulent United Metropolitan Improved Hot Muffin and Crumpet Baking Company, where manipulative speeches drive the crowd to inflate worthless shares.

Ralph Nickleby learns of his brother's death from Newman Noggs, visits the destitute widow and children in London, treats them with cold contempt, and maneuvers Nicholas into accepting a poorly-paid teaching post at Squeers's Yorkshire school by promising to support the family in his absence.

Ralph Nickleby brings Nicholas to the Saracen's Head Inn to meet Yorkshire schoolmaster Wackford Squeers, whose cruelty to pupils is laid bare, and negotiates Nicholas's appointment as assistant master at Dotheboys Hall, after which Nicholas delivers papers to Ralph's eccentric clerk Newman Noggs.

Nicholas tearfully leaves his mother and Kate, joins Squeers and his starved pupils on the Yorkshire coach, receives a secret letter from Newman Noggs as Ralph looks on, and endures a brutal winter journey that ends when the coach overturns on the road.

After a coach overturn strands Nicholas, Squeers, and passengers at a roadside inn, two gentlemen trade embedded tales — the elegiac "Five Sisters of York" (sisters resist monastic pressure; youngest Alice dies young, memorialized in stained glass) and the darkly comic "Baron of Grogzwig" (a despairing baron is talked out of suicide by the Genius of Despair) — before the journey resumes to Greta Bridge.
Nicholas arrives at the squalid Dotheboys Hall, meets Mrs. Squeers and the wretched Smike, and discovers a secret letter of warning and friendship from Newman Noggs.

Nicholas witnesses Dotheboys Hall's brutal daily routine—medicinal fraud, starvation meals, sham lessons, corporal punishment—then has a compassionate exchange with the broken Smike, who despairs of hope or home.

Miss Squeers develops a one-sided infatuation with Nicholas after a brief schoolroom encounter, arranges a tea party to pursue him, but the evening collapses into rivalry and tears between her and her friend Miss Price, while Nicholas retreats to his dismal dormitory reflecting bitterly on his captivity at Dotheboys Hall.

Ralph Nickleby arranges Kate's employment at Madame Mantalini's dressmaking establishment and promises her rent-free lodging in his own property, providing for his niece with calculated coldness rather than genuine warmth.

Newman Noggs escorts Kate Nickleby and her mother to their bleak new lodgings in Thames Street—a gloomy, decaying house arranged by Ralph Nickleby—where Newman has secretly furnished basic comforts without taking any credit.

Fanny Squeers reconciles with Matilda Price after their quarrel and learns of Matilda's coming marriage, then engineers a meeting with Nicholas who bluntly rejects her romantic delusions; humiliated, Fanny redirects her spite onto Smike, who meanwhile clings to Nicholas as his sole protector and begs him not to leave Dotheboys Hall.

Smike flees Dotheboys Hall but is recaptured; when Squeers attempts a public flogging, Nicholas intervenes, beats Squeers unconscious, and quits the school—with Smike secretly following him on the road to London.

Newman Noggs attends the Kenwigs family's wedding anniversary party, where lower-class neighbors gather around the esteemed water-rate collector uncle Lillyvick, until Newman is abruptly summoned away by two mysterious mud-soaked visitors.

Nicholas and Smike arrive exhausted at Newman Noggs's London garret; Newman reads aloud Fanny Squeers's accusatory letter about the Dotheboys Hall assault; Nicholas resolves to confront Ralph Nickleby but is persuaded to wait; he incidentally rescues the Kenwigs baby from a nursemaid's fire, winning the admiration of the party downstairs.

Nicholas searches London for work, witnesses a satirical parliamentary confrontation at corrupt MP Gregsbury's lodging before declining his inadequate secretary post, then accepts Newman Noggs's arranged French-tutoring job for the Kenwigs family as his only available income.

Kate Nickleby endures her first day at Madame Mantalini's millinery, suffering condescension from Miss Knag and open insolence from a wealthy customer, then walks home to her daydreaming mother while privately mourning and clinging to Nicholas's letter as consolation.

Miss Knag at Madame Mantalini's millinery feigns sisterly affection for Kate for three days, but when aristocratic customers single out Kate's beauty and dismiss Miss Knag from the showroom, her friendship instantly turns to furious hatred and public denunciation.

Ralph Nickleby uses Kate as social bait at a dinner for his dissolute business clients, where Sir Mulberry Hawk harasses her shamelessly while Ralph looks on, and Kate flees in tears; Ralph then reveals—when confronted—that he brought her deliberately as a lure for Lord Frederick Verisopht, though Kate's distress momentarily pierces even his mercenary shell.
Nicholas returns to London, confronts Ralph at his mother's house, refutes the theft and assault charges, then leaves his family in Ralph's hands while pledging to journey on together with Smike.

Bailiffs arrive at Mantalini's millinery with a writ of execution, Mantalini stages a farcical fake suicide, the business collapses into bankruptcy, Kate is dismissed, and Ralph (who secretly engineered the failure) steers her toward a companion post with the affected socialite Mrs. Wititterly of Cadogan Place.

Nicholas and Smike depart London penniless for Portsmouth seeking work, bid farewell to Newman Noggs on the road, and at a roadside inn meet theatrical manager Vincent Crummles, who recruits them both to join his travelling theatre company.

Nicholas and Smike arrive in Portsmouth with the Crummles troupe, are introduced to the eccentric theatrical company and Mrs. Crummles, witness a rehearsal of the Indian Savage ballet (including the famously age-frozen "infant phenomenon"), and Nicholas is pressed to translate a French play and take on multiple acting roles by Monday.

Nicholas helps Miss Snevellicci canvass local patrons for her bespeak benefit night, then makes a triumphant first stage appearance in his own adapted piece, winning thunderous audience applause alongside the Crummles company.

Miss Petowker arrives to join the Crummles company and secretly marries the elderly Mr. Lillyvick in a farcically theatrical wedding ceremony, while Nicholas patiently coaches Smike for his stage debut as the Apothecary in Romeo and Juliet.

Sir Mulberry Hawk and Lord Verisopht pressure Ralph Nickleby into revealing Kate's address so they can pursue her, while Mrs. Nickleby's chance visit to Ralph's house lets the two rakes extract even more information about Kate under the guise of flattery.

Sir Mulberry Hawk's toadies Pyke and Pluck flatter Mrs. Nickleby into attending the theatre, where Hawk maneuvers to isolate Kate and harass her, while her oblivious mother mistakes Kate's distress for signs of love.

Kate Nickleby, relentlessly persecuted by Sir Mulberry Hawk during his visits to the Wititterly household, finally confronts Ralph Nickleby and begs him to intervene, but Ralph coldly refuses on business grounds, leaving Kate to depart in tears while Newman Noggs offers silent sympathy.

Nicholas earns twenty pounds from a benefit performance, sends money to Kate via Newman Noggs, defends himself against a theatrical rival (Lenville) who challenges him to a humiliating confrontation, knocks Lenville down and forces an apology, then receives a cryptic warning letter from Newman hinting that Kate may soon need her brother's protection.

Nicholas bids farewell to the Crummles troupe with staged "last appearances" and a rowdy supper party, then abruptly quits Portsmouth with Smike after an urgent letter from Newman Noggs summons him back to London.

Newman Noggs, after spying on Ralph and running an errand, visits Miss La Creevy to reveal Ralph's mistreatment of Kate and plan how to carefully break the news to the returning Nicholas without provoking reckless violence.

Nicholas returns to London with Smike, discovers Kate's situation is alarming, overhears Sir Mulberry Hawk and companions mock Kate at a hotel, confronts Hawk demanding his name, and the standoff erupts into a violent carriage struggle in which Nicholas wounds Hawk with a whip handle before being flung to the ground.

After fighting Sir Mulberry Hawk, Nicholas rescues Kate from the Wititterly household, evacuates his mother from Ralph's lodgings, and delivers a letter to Ralph severing all family ties in condemnation of his villainy.

Ralph Nickleby meets Mantalini to discount bills and witnesses his comic marital skirmish, then receives Squeers who reports Nicholas's attack on Sir Mulberry Hawk, prompting Ralph and Squeers to conspire against Nicholas by using the abandoned boy (Smike) as a weapon.

Nicholas introduces Smike to his mother and Kate, then encounters the philanthropic Cheeryble Brothers at a register office, who immediately hire him as a clerk and arrange cheap lodgings, restoring the Nickleby family to modest happiness.

Nicholas visits the Kenwigs household during Mrs. Kenwigs's confinement and delivers the devastating news that Mr. Lillyvick has married Miss Petowker, destroying the family's hopes of inheriting his fortune.

Nicholas wins Tim Linkinwater's approval as a clerk at Cheeryble Brothers and attends their annual birthday dinner, then returns home where Mrs. Nickleby confides that their eccentric next-door neighbour has been tossing vegetables over the garden wall as love-tokens and has proposed marriage to her.

Smike is ambushed and seized on the London streets by Squeers and his son and locked up at Snawley's lodgings, while Ralph Nickleby visits the bedridden Sir Mulberry Hawk and deliberately fans his rage for revenge against Nicholas.

John Browdie, visiting London with his new wife and Fanny Squeers, learns that Squeers has recaptured Smike; he feigns illness to get upstairs unattended, then frees Smike from the locked room and sends him running home before Squeers can notice.

Smike flees Squeers and is sheltered by Newman Noggs before being reunited with Nicholas and Kate; meanwhile Nicholas becomes obsessively infatuated with a mysterious young woman glimpsed at the Cheeryble brothers' office, enlists Newman as go-between, and the clandestine meeting ends in farce when Newman has followed the wrong servant to entirely the wrong girl.

Mrs. Nickleby and Kate are pelted with vegetables and propositioned by their eccentric mad neighbor who scales the garden wall; Kate is alarmed, but Mrs. Nickleby, flattered, half-believes his extravagant declarations are genuine courtship until his keeper drags him down and reveals him as a long-mad, wicked old man.

Nicholas dines with John and Tilly Browdie, who recount how John helped Smike escape from Squeers, until Squeers and his daughter Fanny burst in and berate the Browdies and Nicholas before storming out in theatrical fury.

Nicholas meets Frank Cheeryble by chance at an inn after a brawl, they are formally introduced at the counting-house next morning, and Frank accompanies his uncle Charles on a warm visit to the Nickleby cottage — ending with Smike collapsing alone in silent bitter grief.

Ralph coldly rebuffs his returned-convict former clerk Brooker who claims a secret hold over him, then witnesses Madame Mantalini publicly renounce her husband and cede the business to Miss Knag, before departing covertly with Squeers and an unknown third man—an exit that alarms Newman Noggs.

Ralph Nickleby arrives at the Nickleby cottage with Squeers and Snawley, who presents documents claiming to be Smike's father and demands his return, but Nicholas refuses to surrender Smike despite the seemingly valid legal claim, and Ralph departs with threats of legal ruin.

Cheeryble Brothers commission Nicholas to secretly support Madeline Bray by posing as an art buyer, and on his first visit he silently falls in love with her while enduring her father's petulant pride — all while Ralph Nickleby's earlier attempt to poison the brothers against Nicholas is rebuffed.

Ralph Nickleby and elderly moneylender Arthur Gride secretly conspire to coerce imprisoned debtor Walter Bray into pressuring his daughter Madeline into marriage with Gride, while Newman Noggs eavesdrops from a closet and is horrified by the scheme.

Nicholas, brooding over his hopeless love for Madeline Bray, stumbles upon a playbill announcing Vincent Crummles's last London appearance, reunites with the troupe, attends their farewell supper, and debates the ethics of dramatic adaptation before bidding the Crummles family goodbye as they depart for America.

While Smike's health visibly deteriorates and Kate's feelings for Frank Cheeryble grow, the Nickleby household is comically disrupted when the mad neighbor in small-clothes descends the chimney, convinced Miss La Creevy is his beloved.

At a Hampton race-course gambling den, Sir Mulberry Hawk and Lord Frederick Verisopht quarrel over Sir Mulberry's vowed revenge against Nicholas (aided by Ralph Nickleby's intelligence), come to blows, fight a pistol duel at dawn, and Lord Frederick is shot dead while Sir Mulberry flees to France.

Newman Noggs, carrying a letter between Ralph Nickleby and miser Arthur Gride, secretly reads it and discovers the imminent plot to marry Madeline Bray to Gride, then urgently reveals the scheme to Nicholas, who storms off in fury to stop it.

Nicholas despairs over Madeline Bray's imminent forced marriage but, rallied by Newman Noggs, resolves to appeal to her directly; meanwhile Newman escorts young Morleena Kenwigs to a barber, where they encounter the humbled Mr. Lillyvick, who reveals his wife eloped with a captain and, reconciled with the Kenwigs family, pledges to settle his fortune on their children.
Nicholas makes a desperate last appeal to Madeline to postpone her marriage to Gride, then confronts Gride directly, but both efforts fail and the wedding remains set for the following morning.

On Madeline Bray's wedding morning, Nicholas and Kate burst in to offer her refuge; Bray dies suddenly before the ceremony can proceed, and Nicholas seizes the moment to carry the unconscious Madeline away, defeating Ralph and Gride's scheme.

While Madeline Bray recovers from dangerous illness under Kate's nursing and Mrs. Nickleby schemes around Frank Cheeryble's suspected love for Kate, Nicholas firmly rejects any encouragement of the match out of honour toward the brothers; Smike's consumption then worsens critically and Nicholas departs with him to Devonshire, parting from Kate in a sorrowful farewell.

Ralph Nickleby, seething after Nicholas foiled Gride's marriage scheme and learning of a financial ruin, dismisses Newman Noggs and recruits Squeers to steal a deed proving Madeline's inheritance, planning to destroy it and defeat Nicholas.

Squeers, operating as Ralph Nickleby's agent, plies the deaf housekeeper Peg Sliderskew with drink to examine stolen documents she took from Arthur Gride, pockets a deed naming Madeline Bray, then is knocked senseless by Newman Noggs while Frank Cheeryble looks on.

Nicholas tends the dying Smike at their childhood home, where Smike sees a terrifying vision of the man who first brought him to Dotheboys Hall, then peacefully dies after confessing his secret love for Kate Nickleby.

Ralph Nickleby, sleepless and increasingly paranoid, discovers his co-conspirators Snawley and Squeers have been arrested or turned against him, and is finally confronted at the Cheeryble Brothers' office by Newman Noggs—who reveals he exposed the plot—and by the brothers themselves, who lay out the full evidence of Ralph's scheme against Smike and warn him to flee before justice falls.

Brooker confesses to the Cheeryble Brothers that Smike — whom Ralph persecuted to death — was Ralph's own secret son, placed at Dotheboys Hall under a false name; Ralph, shattered by the revelation, flees into the night.

Nicholas returns home after Smike's death, confesses his secret love for Madeline to Kate (who has likewise refused Frank Cheeryble's proposal out of duty), then visits brother Charles to disclose his feelings and beg that Madeline be removed from his household, learning that a meeting with Ralph Nickleby has been arranged.
Ralph Nickleby, broken by the revelation that Smike was his own son and that all his schemes have collapsed, returns home in anguish and hangs himself in the garret.

The Cheeryble Brothers reveal Madeline's rightful inheritance has been recovered and orchestrate betrothals — Nicholas to Madeline, Frank to Kate — while Tim Linkinwater proposes to Miss La Creevy and a transformed Newman Noggs reappears, all celebrated at a triumphant dinner.

Nicholas travels to Yorkshire to share his good fortune with John Browdie, stumbles upon the degraded Mantalini grinding a mangle in a London cellar, then witnesses news of Squeers's transportation trigger a full pupil revolt at Dotheboys Hall, which empties and closes forever.

The concluding chapter resolves all fates: Nicholas weds Madeline and joins the Cheeryble firm, Kate marries Frank Cheeryble, the villains (Ralph, Squeers, Hawk, Gride) meet ruin or death, Newman Noggs retires contentedly near Nicholas's household, and Smike's grave is tended by Nicholas's children.

testi/dickens/atomized/oliver_twist/chap.plot: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse to an unknown woman who dies moments after childbirth, leaving him a nameless pauper orphan with no known origin.

On Oliver's ninth birthday Mr. Bumble collects him from Mrs. Mann's farm and delivers him to the workhouse board, where a starvation regime finally drives Oliver to ask for more gruel, earning him confinement and an offer of five pounds to any master willing to take him as apprentice.

After a week in solitary confinement, Oliver is nearly apprenticed to Gamfield, a brutal chimney-sweep, but a magistrate notices Oliver's terror and refuses to sign the indentures, returning him to the workhouse.
The parish board apprentices Oliver to undertaker Sowerberry; Mr Bumble delivers him there, where he is fed dog scraps and bedded among coffins.

Oliver, apprenticed to undertaker Sowerberry, endures bullying from charity-boy Noah Claypole, then accompanies his master and Mr Bumble to a pauper's funeral where he witnesses a starved woman's hasty, perfunctory burial and the grief of her destitute family.

Goaded past endurance when Noah Claypole slanders his dead mother, Oliver violently attacks him, is subdued and locked in the dust-cellar by the Sowerberry household, and Noah is dispatched to fetch Mr. Bumble.

After Noah's false complaint brings Mr Bumble, Oliver defiantly refuses to be cowed, endures beating and confinement, then at dawn escapes the undertaker's and bids farewell to his dying workhouse friend Dick before fleeing into the open road.
After a week-long starving journey on foot, Oliver reaches Barnet where he meets the Artful Dodger, who leads him into London's slums and delivers him to Fagin's criminal den.
Oliver wakes in Fagin's den, secretly watches Fagin gloat over hidden stolen jewels, then witnesses and is taught pickpocketing tricks by the Dodger and Charley Bates while Nancy briefly visits.
