Oliver accompanies the Dodger and Charley Bates on their first "job," witnesses them pick Mr Brownlow's pocket, flees in panic, and is seized by the crowd and a police officer as the presumed thief.

Oliver is dragged before the bullying magistrate Mr. Fang, nearly condemned despite Mr. Brownlow's doubts, then discharged when a bookseller witness proves his innocence; fainting from illness, Oliver is carried away in a coach by Mr. Brownlow.

Oliver convalesces at Mr Brownlow's house under Mrs Bedwin's care until Brownlow notices Oliver's face exactly matches a mysterious portrait on the wall, while the Artful Dodger and Charley Bates flee back to Fagin after abandoning Oliver during the pickpocketing arrest.

Fagin and Bill Sikes learn Oliver has been taken away by a benefactor after being cleared of theft; they coerce Nancy into infiltrating the police office to locate him, and she discovers Oliver is gone to Pentonville, prompting Fagin to order the gang to find and recapture him.

Oliver recuperates at Mr Brownlow's house, enjoys kindness and new clothes, then is sent on an errand to return books and pay a debt — an act Mr Grimwig bets he will never complete — and fails to return as darkness falls.

Nancy, coordinating with Fagin, intercepts Oliver on the street and—with Sikes's physical force—drags him back into the criminal gang by falsely claiming him as her runaway brother before horrified bystanders.

Sikes and Nancy drag Oliver back to Fagin's den, where the gang mocks him, strips his gentleman's clothes, and Nancy violently defends Oliver against Fagin's beating before fainting, after which Oliver is locked in the dark.

Mr. Bumble travels to London on parish business, spots Mr. Brownlow's reward advertisement for Oliver, visits him and delivers a damning false account of Oliver's character, causing Brownlow to denounce the boy as an impostor.
Fagin uses threats, isolation, and the Dodger's persuasion to slowly wear down Oliver's resistance and groom him into accepting a life of crime.
Fagin visits Sikes and Nancy to plan the Chertsey burglary, and the three agree to use Oliver as the small boy needed to break in, with Nancy tasked to fetch him the next night.

Fagin warns Oliver to obey Bill Sikes without question, then Nancy delivers Oliver to Sikes, who loads a pistol and threatens to shoot him if he speaks, before leading him out on a criminal errand at dawn.

Sikes drags Oliver through pre-dawn London and Smithfield market, then by cart and foot across the countryside to a ruinous isolated house near Shepperton, where Oliver, terrified, suspects Sikes intends to murder him.
Sikes and Toby Crackit bring Oliver to Chertsey, force him through a small window to open a house for burglary, but are discovered, shots are fired, and Oliver is wounded as they flee.

Mr. Bumble visits workhouse matron Mrs. Corney, they share tea and flirt until he kisses her, whereupon they are interrupted by news that a dying pauper, Old Sally, insists on revealing a secret before she dies.
Dying workhouse inmate Old Sally confesses to matron Mrs. Corney that she stole a gold keepsake from Oliver's dying mother years ago, but expires before revealing what the object was.

Fagin and his gang idle in their den until Toby Crackit arrives haggard and alone, confessing the burglary failed, Oliver was shot and abandoned in a ditch, and Sikes is unaccounted for — sending Fagin fleeing the house in panic.

Fagin, agitated after the failed robbery, scours the criminal haunts of Saffron Hill seeking Monks, stops to check on a drunk and anguished Nancy at Sikes's lodgings, then holds a tense secret midnight meeting with Monks at his own den, where they argue over what to do with Oliver and are briefly terrified by the shadow of a figure on the wall.

Mr Bumble snoops through Mrs Corney's belongings, discovers her savings, proposes marriage and is accepted, then stops at the undertaker's to order a pauper coffin, before the narrator pivots to check on Oliver still lying wounded in a ditch.

After the failed burglary Sikes abandons wounded Oliver in a ditch and flees; Oliver regains consciousness, staggers back to the very house they tried to rob, collapses at the door, and is taken in — with the young lady (Rose Maylie) urging the servants to treat him kindly.

Doctor Losberne arrives at the Maylie household, examines the wounded intruder shot by Giles, discovers the "thief" is merely a boy (Oliver), and urges Mrs. Maylie and Rose to see the patient before any further action is taken.

Rose Maylie and Mrs. Maylie visit the wounded, sleeping Oliver and are struck by his innocence; the doctor manoeuvres to shield him from arrest by pressuring Giles and Brittles to doubt their identification, while Oliver recounts his history to the ladies—until the unexpected arrival of Bow Street officers threatens the plan.

Bow Street officers Blathers and Duff investigate the Maylie burglary; Dr. Losberne cleverly misdirects them by presenting the feverish Oliver as accidentally wounded by a spring-gun, the servants' contradictory testimony and the harmless pistol charge undermine any case against Oliver, and he is ultimately bailed into Mrs. Maylie's and Losberne's custody.

Oliver recovers from his wounds under the Maylies' care, travels with Dr. Losberne to find Mr. Brownlow but learns he has emigrated to the West Indies, then spends three blissful months in a country cottage where peaceful rural life, education, and the affection of Rose and Mrs. Maylie transform him into a happy, domesticated member of their household.

Rose Maylie falls suddenly into a dangerous fever; Oliver rushes to send for a doctor and on the errand collides with a mysterious hostile stranger who collapses in a fit upon seeing him; after days hovering near death, Rose at last shows signs of recovery.

Harry Maylie arrives at the cottage, learns Rose is recovering, and privately declares his love for Rose to his mother (who warns of Rose's uncertain birth); meanwhile Oliver dozes at a window and wakes to find Fagin and Monks peering in at him.

Oliver spots Fagin and Monks lurking at the cottage window but the search finds no trace of them; Harry Maylie then declares his love to Rose, who refuses him—insisting the stain on her unknown origins would blight his prospects—though she admits she returns his feelings.

Harry Maylie departs with Dr. Losberne, privately enlisting Oliver to send him fortnightly letters about Rose and the household without telling the ladies, while Rose watches the carriage vanish and weeps in silence behind the curtain.

Mr. Bumble, stripped of his beadle status and henpecked by his new wife, is approached in a pub by the mysterious Monks, who bribes him for information about the woman who knew Oliver Twist's mother, arranging a secret meeting for the following night.

Mr and Mrs Bumble meet Monks at a derelict riverside building at night, sell him the locket and wedding ring stolen from Oliver's dead mother, and watch him destroy the evidence by dropping it through a trap-door into the river.

Nancy, nursing the ill and abusive Sikes, secretly eavesdrops on a private meeting between Fagin and Monks at Fagin's den, then drugs Sikes with laudanum and races across London to seek out Rose Maylie at her hotel.

Nancy secretly meets Rose Maylie and reveals that Monks has conspired with Fagin to corrupt Oliver and suppress proof of his true identity, then refuses rescue and agrees to meet Rose on London Bridge every Sunday night.

Rose Maylie, wrestling with keeping Nancy's secret, brings Oliver to Craven Street where he is joyfully reunited with Mr Brownlow, and the assembled group resolves to unmask Monks through private stratagem rather than legal prosecution in order to recover Oliver's stolen inheritance.

Noah Claypole and Charlotte arrive in London fleeing their stolen money, stumble into the Three Cripples tavern, where Fagin secretly observes them, then recruits Noah into his criminal gang under threat of exposure, assigning him to the "kinchin lay" — robbing small children of their errand money.

Fagin recruits Noah Claypole (Bolter) into his gang and sends him to spy on the Artful Dodger's court hearing, where the Dodger defies the magistrates with comic bravado before being committed for transportation.

Nancy fails her appointed midnight meeting with Rose Maylie because Sikes physically detains her past the hour, while Fagin, suspecting her of secret dealings, begins scheming to use blackmail and the threat of Sikes's violence to bring her under his full control.
Fagin recruits Noah Claypole as a spy to tail Nancy, suspecting she has contacted outsiders; after six nights' wait, on a Sunday he sends Noah to follow her as she slips out alone at night.

At midnight on London Bridge, Nancy secretly meets Mr Brownlow and Rose Maylie, gives them details to identify and trap Monks, refuses to betray Fagin or accept rescue for herself, and is covertly watched throughout by Noah Claypole, who immediately rushes to report to Fagin.
Fagin uses Noah Claypole's eyewitness account to inflame Bill Sikes with news of Nancy's secret meetings with gentlefolk, and Sikes rushes home and beats Nancy to death as she pleads for mercy.

After murdering Nancy, Bill Sikes flees London and wanders the countryside haunted by visions of her corpse, unable to escape his guilt, before resolving to return to London and seek refuge through Fagin.

Mr Brownlow forces Monks into a private confrontation, reveals knowledge of the destroyed will and Oliver's true parentage as Leeford's illegitimate son, and extracts a sworn promise of full confession and restitution, while news arrives that the murderer (Sikes) is about to be caught and Fagin seized.

Sikes, hunted by an enormous mob at Jacob's Island after Nancy's murder, attempts rope-escape from the rooftop but, hallucinating Nancy's eyes, loses his balance and accidentally hangs himself; his dog leaps after him and dies too, while Fagin is noted to have been captured the same day.

Mr Brownlow compels Monks to publicly confess Oliver's true parentage and the destroyed will; the Bumbles are disgraced over the stolen locket; Rose Maylie is revealed as Agnes Fleming's sister and therefore Oliver's aunt; and Harry Maylie proposes marriage to Rose, who accepts now that her illegitimate stigma is lifted — the chapter ends with the death of Dick.

Fagin is convicted and sentenced to hang; on his final night in Newgate, Mr Brownlow and Oliver visit him in the condemned cell, where Fagin—deranged with terror—reveals the location of Monks's hidden papers before being dragged away screaming by guards.

The final chapter dispenses the fates of all characters: Oliver is adopted by Mr Brownlow, Rose Maylie marries Harry, Monks squanders his inheritance and dies in prison, the Bumbles sink into workhouse poverty, and the novel closes on Agnes's nameless memorial tablet.

testi/dickens/atomized/our_mutual_friend.plot: Book 1 table of contents lists 17 chapter titles that trace the introduction of the Wilfer family, Boffin's Bower, Silas Wegg's self-interest, a marriage contract, "Podsnappery" satire, and the tracking and downfall of a bird of prey.

themes: structure and organization of the novel
categorization of people ('birds of a feather')
testi/dickens/atomized/our_mutual_friend.plot: This unit is simply the table of contents for Book the Second, "Birds of a Feather," listing its sixteen chapter titles (from "Of an Educational Character" through "An Anniversary Occasion") with no narrative prose.

Book 3 ("A Long Lane") charts Nicodemus Boffin's progressive moral deterioration as he falls into bad company, while Silas Wegg and Mr Venus (the "Friendly Move") tighten their scheme to use documents found in the dust heaps to extort him, culminating in Wegg preparing his figurative grindstone for Boffin's nose.

Book 4 table of contents lists 17 episodes tracing Boffin's feigned miserliness, Bella and John Harmon's secret elopement, Bradley Headstone's near-fatal attack on Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie's rescue, Jenny Wren's pivotal discovery, and the final checkmate of Silas Wegg's extortion scheme.

themes: scavenging death from river for profit
testi/dickens/atomized/our_mutual_friend.plot: Gaffer Hexam and his daughter Lizzie row a boat on the Thames at dusk searching the water, pull a corpse and money from it, then Gaffer rebuffs another waterman's offer of partnership over a past accusation of robbing a living man, all while towing the body behind the boat.

Gaffer Hexam and daughter Lizzie dredge the Thames at night, hauling a drowned body in tow while Gaffer repudiates his former partner for robbing the living — a sin he considers far worse than plundering the dead.

At a glittering Veneering dinner party Mortimer narrates the life of John Harmon—son of a dust-contractor, exiled after pleading for his sister, recalled to inherit a vast fortune on condition he marry a specified girl—and the chapter ends when a note arrives mid-story announcing that Harmon has drowned.

Mortimer Lightwood and Eugene Wrayburn follow Gaffer Hexam's son to the riverside hovel, view the drowned body of John Harmon at the police station alongside a mysterious agitated stranger who signs himself "Julius Handford," while at home Lizzie Hexam confides to Charley her vision of his rise through education and her own self-sacrifice; the inquest returns an open verdict on the suspicious "Harmon Murder," which then drifts into public notoriety.

The impoverished Wilfer family is introduced, with Bella bitterly lamenting her fate as a "kind of widow" jilted by the Harmon will, while a mysterious, reserved lodger signs the lease under the name John Rokesmith—hinted at the chapter's close to be the same man as Julius Handford and, by extension, John Harmon himself in disguise.

Illiterate but newly wealthy Nicodemus Boffin hires one-legged street vendor Silas Wegg to read Gibbon's Decline and Fall aloud at Boffin's Bower, while Wegg privately schemes to exploit the arrangement for as much profit as possible.

Miss Abbey Potterson warns Lizzie Hexam that her father Gaffer is suspected of murder, urges her to leave him; Lizzie refuses, instead sends brother Charley away to school for a better future, then returns home to face Gaffer with news of Charley's departure while he is himself shunned by the riverside community.

Silas Wegg visits Mr Venus's dim bone-and-taxidermy shop, learns Venus still holds his amputated leg unsold and cannot fit it into any "miscellaneous" skeleton, hears Venus's melancholy complaint that his beloved rejects him because of his grisly profession, and picks up a rumour that hidden wealth may lie in the Harmon dust mounds before stumping away to the Bower.

Boffin formally inherits the Harmon fortune at Lightwood's office, instructs a £10,000 murder reward and a will leaving all to Mrs. Boffin, briefly meets Eugene Wrayburn, then is followed on Fleet Street by a mysterious stranger who names himself Rokesmith—Harmon in disguise—and proposes to serve as his secretary.

Newly rich Mr and Mrs Boffin plan fashionable life, consult Rev. Milvey about adopting an orphan to bear John Harmon's name, then visit the Wilfers to invite Bella into their household, where she notices lodger Mr Rokesmith react with uncanny alarm at mention of the dead Harmon boy.

Alfred Lammle and Sophronia Akershem marry at the Veneering house, but on their Isle of Wight honeymoon discover each deceived the other about having property, and they forge a cynical pact to collude as adventurers against the world.

At Podsnap's birthday dinner for his daughter Georgiana, Mr Podsnap performs English self-satisfaction for a foreign guest and silences talk of street starvation, while the Lammles cynically cultivate shy Georgiana's friendship, privately scheming to exploit her for money.

Roger Riderhood visits Lightwood's office and, lured by the reward money, accuses his former partner Gaffer Hexam of the Harmon murder, claiming Hexam confessed; Lightwood, Wrayburn, and the police inspector then move to apprehend Hexam at the Six Jolly Fellowships.

Eugene Wrayburn, Lightwood, and Mr Inspector spend a night staking out Gaffer Hexam's riverside dwelling—during which Eugene secretly watches a weeping, solitary Lizzie through her window—until Riderhood returns from the river to report Gaffer's boat found empty and adrift.

Gaffer Hexam's drowned corpse is hauled from the Thames, entangled in his own rope, and Mr Inspector methodically reconstructs how Gaffer fell overboard in a squall and accidentally strangled himself while trying to loot a floating body.

Boffin hires John Rokesmith (the disguised John Harmon) as his secretary, installs Wegg as caretaker of the Bower, then is alarmed when Mrs Boffin is visited by ghostly visions of the old miser's face and the dead children throughout the house.

John Harmon (as Secretary Rokesmith) settles into Boffin's affairs, avoids Lightwood, accompanies Mrs Boffin to Brentford to assess orphan Johnny at Betty Higden's home, then encounters Bella Wilfer in the fields and reveals his secretarial role while hinting at her prospects with the Boffins.

Boffins settle into their aristocratic mansion and are besieged by social climbers and beggars of every stripe seeking their fortune, Bella Wilfer moves in as their guest, while Wegg secretly prowls the old house probing dust-mounds in search of something hidden.

Schoolmaster Bradley Headstone walks with his pupil-teacher Charley Hexam past Miss Peecher's school to visit Charley's sister Lizzie at her lodging (shared with the doll's dressmaker Jenny Wren), where Charley presses Lizzie to abandon her old life and not hinder his advancement, Headstone probes Charley about Lizzie's lack of education and about Eugene Wrayburn (spotted on the street), and hints he may himself consider marrying Lizzie once such an "inequality" were overcome.

Bradley Headstone, the rigidly self-made schoolmaster, accompanies Charley Hexam to visit his sister Lizzie, where they encounter Eugene Wrayburn, igniting Bradley's jealous fixation on Lizzie and establishing the central rivalry between the two men.

themes: satire of electioneering and empty political ambition
testi/dickens/atomized/our_mutual_friend.plot: Veneering, bribing his way into a rotten borough seat, enlists Twemlow, Podsnap, Lady Tippins, Boots and Brewer to noisily "rally round" and "work" for his election, and after empty speechifying at Pocket-Breaches he is duly brought in as MP, leaving Twemlow exhausted and dismayed at ever having befriended him.

Eugene Wrayburn visits Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren, persuades Lizzie to overcome her pride and accept his offer of funded education lessons; afterward Jenny's drunken father staggers home and she scolds him with stern maternal authority, enacting a stark parent-child role reversal.

Veneering buys a parliamentary seat at Pocket-Breaches by mobilizing his social network (Twemlow, Podsnap, Lady Tippins, Boots, Brewer) in a frantic day of performative "work," and is duly elected despite knowing none of his constituents.

The Lammles cultivate Georgiana Podsnap's friendship and then orchestrate a dinner and opera outing to engineer a match between her and the awkward Fledgeby, while privately revealing their scheme is driven by Georgiana's money.

Fledgeby breakfasts with Lammle, agreeing to pursue Georgiana Podsnap through their scheming compact, then visits his secret moneylending front (run by the Jewish elder Riah under the name Pubsey & Co.), where he finds Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren resting on the rooftop, and Jenny delivers her otherworldly vision of peace in imagined death.

Charley Hexam and Bradley Headstone confront Eugene Wrayburn at his chambers, demanding he cease his secret visits and tutoring of Lizzie Hexam; Eugene deflects with languid contempt while Bradley's anguished jealousy erupts, and Eugene afterwards admits to Mortimer he cannot explain his own intentions toward Lizzie.

Silas Wegg enlists Mr Venus into a secret "friendly move" — a pact to secretly search Boffin's dust mounds for hidden money or wills — before John Harmon (as Rokesmith) appears at the window to deliver a message, unsettling the conspirators.

Bella visits her irritable family, then escapes with her father for a joyful Greenwich dinner funded by a Boffin gift, confessing she intends to marry for money while wishing the late John Harmon had lived to marry her.

Rokesmith (secretly John Harmon) and Mrs Boffin, with Bella, transport the gravely ill orphan Johnny to a children's hospital after overcoming Betty Higden's terror of institutional charity; the doctor privately declares it too late, and Johnny dies peacefully bequeathing his toys and asking for a kiss for "the boofer lady."

After the death of young Johnny, the Boffins resolve not to revive the name "John Harmon" and, prompted by Mrs Boffin's desire for unselfish charity, choose ungainly Sloppy — who insists on still caring for Betty Higden — as their new ward.

Bradley Headstone visits Jenny Wren's home to confront Lizzie Hexam and demand she reject Eugene Wrayburn's help in favor of her brother's plans, but Lizzie refuses him calmly, and afterward she secretly confesses her love for Wrayburn to Jenny through a fantasy of a wealthy lady.

John Harmon, disguised as a sailor carrying George Radfoot's knife and coat, confronts Rogue Riderhood at his Limehouse pawnshop, exposes his false testimony against Gaffer Hexam, and compels him to agree to sign a written retraction to clear the Hexam family name.

John Harmon, living as secretary John Rokesmith, wanders Limehouse reliving the night he was drugged and nearly drowned, resolves in an extended interior monologue to keep his true identity buried forever, then returns to the Boffin house where Bella Wilfer angrily rejects his declaration of love.

Rokesmith (the disguised John Harmon) resolves to keep his buried identity, dispatches Riderhood's exonerating recantation to Lizzie Hexam by post, hires Bradley Headstone as tutor for Sloppy—uncovering Headstone's fierce jealousy of Eugene Wrayburn—and bids farewell to the proudly independent Betty Higden as she departs to earn her own keep on the road.

Bradley Headstone makes a desperate marriage proposal to Lizzie Hexam in a churchyard; she firmly refuses him, her brother Charley furiously disowns her for it, and as she weeps alone an elderly Riah comforts her before Eugene Wrayburn appears, exposing himself as Headstone's unnamed rival and the true reason behind Lizzie's rejection.

At the Lammles' hollow first-anniversary breakfast, Mortimer Lightwood reveals that Lizzie Hexam has mysteriously vanished, while Mrs Lammle secretly confesses to Twemlow that she and her husband are conspiring to marry Georgiana to Fledgeby for money, imploring him to warn the girl's father.

Riderhood, run down by a steamer and believed drowned, is carried to Miss Abbey's and revived through the efforts of a doctor and bystanders, while his daughter Pleasant hopes the brush with death has reformed him, but once he regains full consciousness his old sullen, malevolent character returns and everyone's interest turns to dislike.

Fledgeby reviews accounts with Riah (whom he uses as a front for his moneylending), receives Lammle's news that the Podsnap scheme has collapsed, then interrogates Riah until he learns that Riah helped Lizzie Hexam flee to safety and that her dangerous pursuer is Wrayburn.

Jenny Wren and Riah visit Miss Abbey Potterson at the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters to present a document vindicating Lizzie Hexam's father, and the visit ends when a foggy river collision brings in a recovered body revealed to be Riderhood.

Rogue Riderhood is dragged from the river after being struck by a steamer and brought to Miss Abbey's pub, where bystanders labor to revive him; hope briefly flickers that near-death will reform him, but he regains consciousness as sullen and irredeemable as before.

Bella joins her family for the Wilfer wedding anniversary, plays cook amid Mrs Wilfer's martyrdom, then confides to her father four secrets: Rokesmith (John Harmon) proposed and was refused, Lightwood would propose, the Boffins plan to portion her on marriage, and Mr Boffin is visibly being corrupted and hardened by his new prosperity.

Bella watches Boffin grow miserly and tyrannical toward his secretary (Rokesmith/Harmon) — humiliating him over wages, obsessively hoarding books about misers, and preaching money-worship — while Mrs Lammle cultivates a treacherous friendship with Bella and coaxes out the secret of Rokesmith's declaration.

Wegg and Venus conspire at the Bower while Boffin arrives with miser biographies for Wegg to read aloud; afterward Boffin secretly digs up a bottle buried atop the mound, Wegg and Venus spy on him, and Wegg—maddened by greed—tries to seize Boffin by force but is wrestled down by Venus as Boffin escapes.

Wegg reveals to Venus that he found a hidden cash-box containing John Harmon's earlier will (which largely benefits the Crown over Boffin), and the two conspirators argue over custody of the document before agreeing to lie in wait and eventually extort Boffin for half his fortune, with Venus taking physical possession of the will as leverage over both Boffin and his own partner.

Old Betty Higden, dying after a long flight from parish charity, collapses near a mill where Lizzie Hexam finds her, receives the letter for the Boffins, and promises never to surrender Betty to the parish — Betty dies in her arms.

At Betty Higden's riverside burial, Bella Wilfer and John Harmon (disguised as Secretary Rokesmith) travel to the paper-mill village where Lizzie Hexam is hiding; Bella and Lizzie form an intimate friendship, and Lizzie reveals she fled a violent suitor (Headstone) while carrying a secret, selfless love for a gentleman far above her station (Wrayburn).

Eugene Wrayburn visits Jenny Wren, then uses her drunken father Mr Dolls as a paid informant to locate Lizzie Hexam, before leading Bradley Headstone—who has been shadowing him—on an exhausting nocturnal chase across London.

Bradley Headstone, driven by murderous jealousy, stalks Eugene Wrayburn through the night and encounters Rogue Riderhood outside the Temple, recruiting him as a paid informant to track Wrayburn's movements and locate Lizzie Hexam.

The Lammles, bankrupt swindlers, devise a scheme to manipulate Mr Boffin by falsely denouncing his Secretary's mercenary motives, while Sophronia also flatters Fledgeby into supposedly interceding with moneylender Riah — though Fledgeby in fact orders Riah to seize the Lammles' furniture.

Fledgeby uses Riah as a scapegoat front-man, performing false generosity toward Twemlow while secretly directing Riah to press him for full repayment of an old debt; Jenny Wren, watching, denounces Riah as the wolf who will one day sell and betray Lizzie.

Mr Venus secretly warns Boffin about Wegg's blackmail scheme over a discovered will, lets Boffin hide to overhear Wegg's boastful threats, and the two agree to coordinate their response before Mrs Lammle intercepts Boffin with further alarming news.

Boffin publicly humiliates and dismisses Rokesmith (John Harmon) for allegedly courting Bella for money; Bella, appalled, defends him, denounces Boffin as corrupted by wealth, and leaves the house for good.

Bella visits her father R. Wilfer at his Mincing Lane office, where John Rokesmith (John Harmon) follows and proposes; she accepts, renouncing the Boffin household for poverty and love, and the three then walk home to face the Wilfer family together.

As the Lammles face bankruptcy, Mrs Lammle visits Twemlow to enforce his silence and reveals Riah is merely Fledgeby's mask; meanwhile at the Veneerings' wondering dinner Eugene Wrayburn quietly receives Lizzie Hexam's whereabouts from Mr Dolls and slips away.

Bella secretly leaves home with her father Pa, is married to John Rokesmith at Greenwich church (watched over by the one-legged pensioner Gruff and Glum), sends a letter home confessing the marriage, and then celebrates with a wedding breakfast and dinner at Greenwich before Pa affectionately returns home to Holloway.

Bradley Headstone, disguised in Riderhood's clothes, stalks Eugene Wrayburn upriver past Plashwater Weir Lock, bribes lock-keeper Riderhood for intelligence, returns blood-spitting and exhausted after confirming Eugene has met Lizzie, then collapses in Riderhood's hut while Riderhood—suspicious the disguise implicates him—secretly unbuttons Bradley's coat to find a counterfeit red neckerchief matching his own, setting up a mutual trap.

Mr Boffin pays off the scheming Lammles £100 for a past service, firmly dismisses them from his household, then intercepts the naive Georgiana Podsnap's cash and necklace offered to help the very people who exploited her friendship.

Silas Wegg, backed by a reluctant Mr Venus, confronts Nicodemus Boffin at the Bower and extorts him into surrendering two-thirds of the Harmon estate under threat of exposing a will, then escorts him home in gleeful contempt.

Bella Wilfer secretly elopes with John Rokesmith (Harmon) at Greenwich church, with only her father Pa as witness, then celebrates the wedding with breakfast and dinner before Pa returns to London, leaving the newlyweds at their Blackheath cottage.

After news of Bella's elopement with John Rokesmith shocks the Wilfer household, Bella's joyful visit disarms her mother's hostility; the chapter then follows the couple's contented Blackheath domestic life — Bella learning housekeeping, mentioning Lizzie Hexam, and finally hinting to John that she is expecting a child.

Eugene meets Lizzie by the river where she pleads with him to leave due to their insurmountable class difference; after she departs, he is ambushed and beaten nearly to death by an unseen assailant, falls into the river, and Lizzie—hearing the attack—rows out alone to pull his broken body from the water and carry him to safety.

After attacking Eugene Wrayburn and throwing him in the river, Bradley Headstone shelters at Riderhood's lock-house and disposes of his bloody clothes, while Riderhood secretly tails him to gather blackmail leverage, and Charley Hexam renounces Headstone entirely for endangering his own social respectability.

Jenny Wren deflects Fledgeby's attempts to extract Lizzie Hexam's whereabouts, then arrives at his Albany chambers to find him thrashed by Lammle; she tends his wounds while secretly sprinkling pepper into the vinegar-and-brown-paper plasters as covert revenge for his tricks.

Jenny Wren visits Riah at Pubsey & Co., confirms Fledgeby's identity and wins Riah his freedom; her drunken father Mr Dolls collapses and dies in the street; Mortimer Lightwood then arrives to escort Jenny to the bedside of the dying Eugene Wrayburn.

Dying Eugene, nursed by Jenny Wren and Mortimer Lightwood, begs Mortimer to let Bradley Headstone go unpunished so Lizzie's reputation is spared, then—after Jenny whispers the key word—asks Mortimer to fetch Lizzie and arrange their deathbed marriage as his final act of reparation.

Bella (as Mrs Rokesmith) travels with Lightwood and the Milveys to witness Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie Hexam's bedside wedding; at the station Bradley Headstone overhears of the marriage and collapses in a fit, while Eugene and Lizzie exchange vows at dawn, Eugene confessing doubt he deserves to live.

Bella's husband John Rokesmith—suspected as Julius Handford in the Harmon murder—is confronted by Lightwood and escorted by Mr Inspector through a police-station identification scene, while Bella trusts him absolutely; the chapter closes with Mr and Mrs Boffin welcoming them to their new home, signalling the imminent disclosure of John's true identity as John Harmon.

Mrs Boffin reveals to Bella that her husband Rokesmith is truly John Harmon, and Mr Boffin confesses that his miser act was a deliberate scheme to test and correct Bella's greedy tendencies, ending in joyful reunion of the whole household.

testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The author reflects that the Sketches were written and published serially in his youth as his first attempts at authorship, admits their crudeness (especially the Tales), and explains he chose not to remodel or expunge them beyond minor wording changes since they were favorably received originally.

themes: satire of social vanity and fickle popularity
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Narrator surveys parish characters and institutions chapter by chapter — the pompous beadle Simmons, the tyrannical workhouse master and the broken-down pauper schoolmaster; a fashionable curate's rise and fall in popularity against a rival preacher; a kindly old lady and her mischievous half-pay-captain neighbour Purday; the four identical spinster Miss Willises and the mystery of which one married Mr. Robinson; a corrupt, bribery-ridden parish election in which Bung defeats Spruggins for the vacant beadleship; and closes by introducing Bung, now a broker's man, as source for further anecdotes.

Broker's man Mr. Bung recounts several distress-warrant jobs — a rich gentleman who disguises him as a servant, a destitute family in George's-yard whose members end up dead or in the workhouse, and a genteel family where the wife's hidden grief and self-sacrifice go unnoticed until she dies after the debt is paid — after which the narrative shifts to a satirical account of Our Parish's rival ladies' charitable societies (the Miss Browns' child's-examination society vs. Mrs. Johnson Parker's Bible-and-prayer-book distribution society) and closes with the story of the narrator's next-door neighbour's lodgers, ending in the death of a poor young copyist, William, who has worked himself to death to support his widowed mother.

themes: panorama of London street life from dawn to night
class contrast between poverty and gentility
satirical observation of institutions (Parliament, courts, charity dinners)
decay, change and the passage of time in the city
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: This unit is a sequence of loosely linked descriptive/satirical sketches (streets by morning and night, shops and their changing tenants, Scotland-Yard, Seven Dials, Monmouth-street's old-clothes trade, hackney-coach stands, Doctors' Commons, London recreations, the Thames, Astley's circus, Greenwich Fair, private theatres, Vauxhall Gardens, early coaches, omnibuses, a parliamentary debate night, public charity dinners, May Day chimney-sweeps, brokers'/marine-store shops, gin-shops, a pawnbroker's shop, the criminal courts, and a visit to Newgate) in which the narrator ("we") tours London's streets, trades, entertainments, and institutions, contrasting the bustle, comedy, and vice of city life with glimpses of poverty, crime, and suffering among its inhabitants.

themes: London social types and urban loneliness
poverty, crime and institutional misery (hospital, prison van)
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: A twelve-chapter gallery of London character sketches — from lonely clerks, misanthropic old men and boisterous apprentices, through a Christmas family reunion and New Year party, to comic misadventures of courtship and vanity (Samuel Wilkins and Jemima at the Eagle, John Dounce's oyster-shop infatuation, Amelia Martin's failed singing debut, Augustus Cooper's dancing-academy breach-of-promise scrape, and Potter and Smithers's drunken night out ending in police court) — closing on darker notes with a dying woman's deathbed testimony shielding her abuser and a crowd watching young female prisoners loaded into the Bow Street prisoners' van.
This unit contains only the section title "Tales" and the heading for Chapter I, "The Boarding-House," with no narrative prose.

Mrs. Tibbs runs a fussy, genteel boarding-house where widow Mrs. Maplesone and her two daughters join existing boarders Simpson, Hicks, and Calton, and after months of flirtation each of the three men secretly arranges marriage plans (Calton to the mother, Hicks and Simpson to the daughters) via the unwittingly duped Tibbs acting as father, only for the mutual deceptions to surface, the marriages to go badly (Hicks's wife leaves him, Simpson's wife elopes, Calton is sued and pays damages), and Mrs. Tibbs to lose all her boarders but her husband, whom she now confines to the kitchen.

themes: social pretension and snobbery among the newly moneyed middle class
comic mistaken identity and exposed deception
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: This unit bundles nine separate Dickens sketches back to back — a boarding-house farce in which gossip and a bungled midnight spying scheme expose Mrs. Tibbs's husband and break up several romances (ending the Tibbs marriage and Mrs. Bloss's remarriage to Gobler); the mishap-filled visit of bachelor Augustus Minns to his vulgar cousin Budden's house; the elopement of Lavinia Brook Dingwall with the pretentious Theodosius Butler from Miss Crumpton's finishing school; the Tuggs family's sudden inheritance and subsequent fleecing by swindling "Captain and Mrs. Waters" at Ramsgate; the unmasking of the mysterious "Horatio Sparkins" as a lowly draper's-shop assistant; a grim tale of a surgeon summoned by a veiled woman to the body of her hanged son; the disastrous river steamer pleasure excursion organized by Percy Noakes; the farcical mistaken-identity elopements and near-duel of Alexander Trott and Horace Hunter at Great Winglebury; and Mrs. Joseph Porter's mischievous sabotage of the Gattleton family's amateur theatrical production.

Timid, impecunious bachelor Mr. Watkins Tottle is talked by his blunt friend Gabriel Parsons into courting the wealthy, prim Miss Lillerton, and after an awkward dinner visit at the Parsons' house (enlivened by Parsons's comic tale of his own clandestine wedding-night misadventure hiding in a chimney) Tottle leaves encouraged about his prospects, with a trip to Beulah Spa planned for the following Saturday.

themes: social satire of manners and matchmaking
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: This file actually contains three separate Sketches by Boz tales run together: first, Watkins Tottle is bailed out of Solomon Jacobs's debtors' lock-up by his friend Gabriel Parsons and pushed into proposing marriage to Miss Lillerton, only to learn via the curate Mr. Timson that she is already engaged to him, a humiliation Tottle never recovers from, ending in his death (a body found in the canal); second, the perpetually gloomy bachelor Mr. Dumps reluctantly serves as godfather at his nephew Charles Kitterbell's chaotic christening party for baby Frederick in Bloomsbury; third, an unnamed drunkard named Warden alienates and loses his family, unknowingly helps have his fugitive son William arrested, is abandoned by his daughter Mary, and finally drowns himself in the Thames near Waterloo Bridge.

themes: parody and satire of literary rivals
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: A mock dedication addressed to the young ladies of the United Kingdom, in which the "Dedicator" denounces a rival book "Sketches of Young Ladies" (by "Quiz," illustrated by "Phiz") for insulting women, and offers his own "Sketches of Young Gentlemen" as the antidote to be read alongside it.

themes: courtship rituals and shyness with young ladies
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Narrator recounts a bashful young gentleman's mortifying conduct at a dinner party (random handshake, spilled bread landing in soup, spilled wine, leaving in the wrong coat and hat), then generalizes the type's characteristic bashful behavior when meeting young ladies in the street and at a quadrille dance (as Mr. Hopkins with Miss Lambert), concluding such men should be "cured, or avoided."

themes: contempt for family and domestic life
drunken revelry and eccentricity as excuse for vice
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The sketch satirizes the "out-and-out young gentleman" type — his rough, showy dress, his idleness at work, his loutish behavior in streets and theatres, his contemptuous treatment of mother and sisters, his forced attendance at a family party where he bonds with a fellow out-and-outer (the notorious Mr. Warmint Blake), and the pair's drunken, noisy conduct at supper — closing with a note on a poorer subclass of out-and-outers who sponge off the others.

themes: satire of dinner-party and social manners
vanity and self-regard masked as warmth
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The narrator satirically profiles "the very friendly young gentleman" through the example of Mr. Mincin, who at a dinner with old friend Capper and his wife, and later at an evening party among the Martins, Cappers, and Watsons, smothers everyone with exaggerated compliments, fussy attentions, and self-important anecdotes, exposing the hollow, self-serving nature of his relentless friendliness.

Boz satirizes the "military young gentleman" type — civilians obsessed with uniforms and soldiers who parade their swords and swagger — following one such figure from admiring sentries at Whitehall to strutting at the garrison theatre, where he and his companions are fawned over by a mamma eager to secure them for her daughters.

themes: politics intruding on courtship and society
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Boz satirizes the "political young gentleman" type, contrasting the blustering Conservative (obsessed with church, state, and "the people") with the theorizing Radical/utilitarian (full of doctrines and aphorisms, quoting Miss Martineau), showing how both bore dinner-tables and ladies with fruitless political disputes, and closes by advising ladies to discountenance such talkers.

Sketch profiles Felix Nixon, a fussy young bachelor bound tightly to his mother, recounting his inflated tales of past bravado (facing down a coachman, reading late at night) before an evening scene where he takes tea, plays flute, and escorts Miss Thompson home past the admiring Miss Greys, all watched over by his fond, garrulous mother.

Dickens satirizes the "censorious young gentleman" type through Mr. Fairfax, who cultivates a reputation for deep, critical judgment merely by sneering, repeating words, and giving evasive non-answers, fooling the admiring young ladies (Miss Greenwood, Miss Marshall, Mrs. Thompson, and others) into believing he harbors profound, damning opinions about people like Mrs. Barker.

themes: forced hilarity and social performance of wit
practical jokes and their unintended consequences
mockery of a stock social type
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: At a Christmas family party the narrator observes Mr. Griggins, the self-styled wit acclaimed by the company as a great joker, perform a string of pranks and puns—startling the room, singeing a young gentleman's hair while snuffing a candle (nearly causing a quarrel resolved by his betrothed's dramatic intervention and faint), stealing at cards, scaring a small child with a mask, and finally kissing the ladies under mistletoe—all met with uproarious laughter from most guests despite some grumbling, prompting the narrator's satirical remark that every social circle has its own "Griggins."

The sketch satirizes the "theatrical young gentleman" type, detailing his gossip about actors and plays (like Flimkins and Boozle's melodrama dispute), his pet nicknames for theatres, his reverence for backstage life, his credulous praise of overblown stage effects and melodramatic acting conventions, and his habit of lecturing ladies with dubious theatrical trivia.

themes: satire of empty superlatives and sentiment
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The sketch satirizes two young-gentleman types: the "poetical young gentleman," who affects melancholy, strikes brooding poses, admires a murderer as a "great spirit," and pens overwrought verse for ladies' albums, and the "throwing-off young gentleman" (exemplified by Mr. Caveton), a boastful impostor who invents rich Irish ancestry, feigned talents, and famous acquaintances to seduce credulous young ladies, ending with the narrator warning ladies against such swindling fools.

themes: satirical typology of the vain, flirtatious 'ladies' man'
courtship rituals and flirtation among young ladies and gentlemen
social performance at a group pleasure-excursion
comic mock-worship of a trivial social figure
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The narrator satirically profiles the type of the "young ladies' young gentleman" through the character of Mr. Balim, who arrives late (having overslept after a party) to a group excursion to Epping Forest, is fussed over and fed by admiring young ladies, flirts and plays games with them during the coach ride and dinner, and is later found in the woods being adorned with ribbons and flowers while singing to a group of reclining young ladies, prompting the narrator's amused, mocking retreat.

In this mock-serious conclusion, the narrator declines to recommend any single type of "young gentleman" from his prior sketches, advises young ladies instead to seek one combining all their best qualities, quotes Dean Swift's letter of marital advice on a wife retaining her husband's esteem, then jokingly hints he himself may be the eligible candidate and invites marriage offers to be sent via the publishers Chapman and Hall.

A mock-legal "remonstrance" from bachelors/widowers of England protests that Queen Victoria's announced engagement to Prince Albert, combined with Leap Year custom allowing women to propose marriage, has incited young ladies (citing cases like a Camberwell girl and Mr. Smith, and a Tottenham cousin John) into a supposed nationwide plot to force mass marriages, prompting a satirical call for a public meeting and dismissal of the Queen's Ministers.

themes: romantic idealization of marriage by onlookers
class contrast between servants and gentry
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: A housemaid and her friend Jane Adams sneak upstairs to admire bride Miss Emma Fielding before her wedding to Mr. Harvey, then witness the lavish breakfast, a flirtation with footman Mr. John, the wedding party's departure for church, the festive breakfast afterward, and finally the young couple's secretive but publicly cheered departure by carriage for the country.

Sketch profiling "the formal couple," who reduce every social act—condolence calls, funerals, child-rearing, theatre outings, a christening supper—to rigid, self-serving observance of form, illustrated by their outraged commentary on a funeral lacking feathers and port, and the formal lady's tearful exit from a christening after a godfather's risque toast.

Dickens satirizes Mr. and Mrs. Leaver, a couple whose theatrical shows of tenderness before company culminate in a Twickenham boating party where Mr. Leaver's clumsy "catching a crab" mishap and Mrs. Leaver's melodramatic fainting spell, all admired by the credulous widow Mrs. Starling, expose their affection as performance rather than genuine feeling.

themes: effect of parental conflict on children
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: A husband and wife, Edward and Charlotte, return home from a dinner party and fall into an escalating series of petty contradictions (over doors in a house, whether a guest was Jenkins or Morgan, his coat colour, Mrs. Parsons' height), a pattern that persists even in front of their children James and Charlotte, showing how such trifling disputes make up much of the couple's domestic life.

themes: self-love and egotism disguised as love
social tedium inflicted by boastful parents
domestic chaos of a large family
satire of Victorian bourgeois family pride
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The sketch satirizes Mr. and Mrs. Whiffler, a couple with eight (soon nine) children who date all events by their children's births and mishaps, bore their friend Saunders at dinner with anecdotes and a chaotic display of the children, and end the evening by asking him to be godfather to their expected ninth child.

Sketch portrays "the cool couple," Charles and Louisa, a husband and wife who feel nothing for each other, bicker over who neglects home life more, then part for separate evenings (his club, her outing with Mrs. Mortimer), later feigning warmth and good breeding in public while remaining privately distant, a pattern the narrator says can end in ruin though it looks trivial.

Boz satirically anatomizes "the plausible couple" — exemplified by Mr. and Mrs. Bobtail Widger — showing how, through affected mutual endearments, flattering third parties (like the Clickits) to win favor with those present, and backhanded depreciation of others (Slummery, Mrs. Tabblewick, Mrs. Finching) dressed as sympathy, they win universal social esteem and invitations.

themes: friendship and teasing between married and bachelor life
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Narrator describes Mr. and Mrs. Chirrup, an affectionate, well-matched little couple, praising Mrs. Chirrup's domestic virtues (especially her skill at carving a goose) and Mr. Chirrup's pride in her, then depicts a pleasant dinner visit with their bachelor friend followed by a round game and supper.

The narrator describes two types of egotistical couples: one who dominate a morning call by topping each other's and the hosts' claims of suffering, name-drop nobility while garbling a story's origin, and boast of tenuous personal connections to famous events; and Mr. and Mrs. Sliverstone, who instead lavish exaggerated public praise on each other's virtues and toils before any audience.

Sketch satirizes Mr. and Mrs. Merrywinkle and old Mrs. Chopper, who obsess over imaginary ailments, swaddle themselves against cold and damp, dose themselves with remedies, and structure their whole day around eating, dosing, and complaining, exemplifying couples who selfishly coddle themselves at others' expense.

themes: loss of children and loved ones to death
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The sketch portrays an aged couple on their eightieth birthday, reflecting through memory on their dead children, vanished friends (Lucy), and a loyal old servant Jane Adams, before celebrating with grandchildren, a barber's anecdote about Crofts, gifts, and a festive dinner where they feel young again amid their descendants.

themes: role of women/daughters in national character
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: The narrator closes the "Sketches of Young Couples" series by explaining the selection of twelve married-couple types, urging young men and women to seek happiness in home and domestic virtue rather than worldly splendor, and holding up the young queen's marriage as an example that true joy lies in nature and domestic worth over crown and throne.

Coal-dealer-turned-Mayor Nicholas Tulrumble, puffed up by London's Lord Mayor's show, stages a grand mock-procession (with drunken Ned Twigger humiliated in brass armour) and bans music at the Jolly Boatmen, alienating old friends until he repents and returns to his former haunts — after which the piece shifts into a burlesque newspaper report of the pompous, absurd first meeting of the "Mudfog Association for the Advancement of Everything," with its squabbling professors, a dog experimented on, and ridiculous papers on fleas, cauliflowers, learned pigs, and infinitesimal medicine doses.

This unit contains no prose narrative, only two truncated title/index fragments ("Ditto and Bean-stalk" and "Ditto and Eleven Brothers") with numeric markers, apparently remnants of a table of contents rather than story text.

Unit contains no prose narrative, only bare numerals ("2,845", "1,998"), the fragment "Ditto and Jill" (apparently a story title), and the word "Total" — resembling a stray index/count table rather than story text.

themes: mock-scientific pomposity and satire of learned societies
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Fake newspaper report of the Mudfog Association's meetings: statistics-section members present absurd figures (children's book-reading habits, dogs-meat skewers, chair legs), mechanical-science exhibitors show ridiculous inventions (personal railway, share-price machine, pickpocket machine, automaton police), a correspondent narrates a chaotic steamboat journey to the second meeting at Oldcastle including Professor Woodensconce and Grime's coin-toss and seasickness mishaps, a run-in with the beadle Sowster over policing boys, and further sections on zoology (lament for vanished dancing bears/monkeys), anatomy (a monomania cure and a homoeopathic misadventure), and statistics/"umbugology" (a one-eyed pony and a mistaken skull), ending with Professor Woodensconce's toast to the "spread of science."

themes: farewell to change / passing of an era
testi/dickens/atomized/sketches_by_boz/s.plot: Boz argues that everyday life mirrors stage pantomime (clowns, pantaloons, harlequins, swindlers like Captain Fitz-Whisker Fiercy and Do'em, and political "clowns" in Parliament), then illustrates the idea further with a sketch of a fawned-over literary "lion" at a party, a comic pub scene where Robert Bolton spins an exaggerated murder tale to his cronies at the Green Dragon, and closes with a farewell letter handing over "Bentley's Miscellany" (personified as a child) to Mr. Ainsworth.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_battle_of_lif.plot: On the ancient battle-ground estate of Doctor Jeddler, Alfred Heathfield formally receives his trust fund from the lawyers Snitchey and Craggs and bids farewell to the household—including his betrothed Marion and her devoted sister Grace—before departing on a three-year medical tour abroad, while philosophical debate about whether life is serious or mere farce runs through the breakfast gathering.

Michael Warden confesses his financial ruin and romantic designs on Marion to his lawyers, then secretly meets her at night with Clemency's reluctant help; on the very evening Alfred Heathfield joyfully returns home after years abroad, Marion is discovered to have fled, leaving only a note begging forgiveness.

Six years on, Michael Warden returns and is recognised by Clemency at the Nutmeg-Grater inn; that same evening Marion reappears on her birthday to confess she voluntarily fled so that Grace could marry Alfred, and the whole family is joyfully reunited.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_chimes/chapte.plot: Elderly ticket-porter Trotty Veck, sustained by his devotion to the church Chimes, shares a meal with daughter Meg who reveals Richard's New Year's Day marriage proposal, but Alderman Cute and Mr. Filer mock and belittle the poor couple's plans with callous condescension, crushing their joy and driving Trotty into despair over whether the poor have any right to exist.

Trotty delivers Alderman Cute's letter to Sir Joseph Bowley, who hypocritically condemns Will Fern as a vagabond; Trotty then meets Will Fern and his niece Lilian on the street, warns them, shelters them in his home, and finally—driven by the haunting chimes—climbs the church tower alone and collapses in a swoon.

Trotty's ghost, guided by the spirit-child, witnesses visions of future suffering: the Bells arraign him for despair toward the poor; Will Fern delivers an impassioned indictment of class injustice at Bowley Hall while Alderman Cute smirks; Meg toils in grinding poverty as Richard degrades into drunkenness; and Lilian, fallen and broken, returns to die repentant in Meg's arms.

Trotty witnesses in his vision Meg's descent into destitution after her husband's death, nearly drowning her infant before Trotty's anguished plea saves her; he then awakens to find it was a nightmare and Meg, Richard, Will Fern, and little Lilian are joyfully celebrating the New Year and Meg's impending wedding.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_cricket_on_th.plot: Critic George Alfred Williams contextualizes The Cricket on the Hearth within Dickens's Christmas Books series, ranking it second in popularity after A Christmas Carol, and argues that Dickens's genius for humanizing characters — not caricature — drives the story's emotional power.

Front-matter page listing three Chirps and illustration captions that preview Bertha's lament over her blindness, John's wordplay pun on Dot's name while holding the baby, Tilly Slowboy's presence, and the cricket's first chirp as the hearth fire blazes to life.
Unit is a title-page stub containing only the heading "THE CRICKET ON THE HEARTH" with no narrative content or character action.

themes: domestic warmth and the hearth as symbol of home
cynicism and mockery of domestic happiness
testi/dickens/atomized/the_cricket_on_th.plot: On a stormy evening the kettle and cricket sing a competing welcome song as carrier John Peerybingle comes home to his young wife Dot, their baby, and nursemaid Tilly Slowboy, bringing a deaf old Stranger he found on the road and a wedding-cake for Tackleton, the sour toy-merchant soon to marry young May Fielding, who visits with dozy toymaker Caleb Plummer, needles John about his marriage, provokes an inexplicable shock and fit of weeping/laughing in Dot at the sight of the Stranger, and departs, leaving John uneasy and the Stranger lodged for the night, while the chapter closes on the Cricket's fireside vision of John's happy domestic life shadowed by an unnamed young man's ghostly lament of "Married! and not to me!"

themes: loving deception to shield the blind
testi/dickens/atomized/the_cricket_on_th.plot: Blind Bertha lives happily unaware her father Caleb has hidden their poverty and disguised the cold Tackleton as a kind benefactor, and after Tackleton announces his engagement to May Fielding and Bertha confesses her heartbreak to May, the Peerybingles' picnic visit ends with Tackleton showing John, through a lit window, Dot secretly embracing the disguised old stranger, shattering John's trust in his wife.

John Peerybingle, tormented by jealous suspicion of Dot and nearly moved to kill the disguised Stranger, is stayed by the Cricket's chirp and a night-long vision of her goodness, so that by morning he resolves to free her rather than blame her; Tackleton discovers the Stranger gone, Caleb confesses to Bertha that he has long disguised harsh reality (including Tackleton's true nature) to spare her feelings, and the Stranger is revealed as Edward Plummer, Caleb's son thought dead, returned to marry his true love May Fielding instead of Tackleton, whereupon Dot explains her innocent role in the secret, John and Dot are reconciled, a chastened Tackleton joins the wedding celebrations, and the day ends in a joyful family dance and feast.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_haunted_man_a.plot: Redlaw, a tormented chemist haunted by grief over betrayal and loss, is confronted by a spectral double that offers to erase his painful memories; he accepts the bargain, only to learn the gift will involuntarily strip memory and its emotional bonds from every person he approaches.

Redlaw wanders through the Tetterby household and a sick student's room spreading his curse of memory-erasure, then guides a feral boy to a squalid lodging house where he watches Philip Swidger and William Swidger lose all filial feeling for dying George Swidger under his influence, before fleeing back to his chamber while Milly Swidger pounds on the door begging him to reverse the harm he has wrought.

Redlaw confronts the Phantom at dawn, learns only Milly can undo the harm of his curse, and through her intercession — reconciling the Tetterbys, aiding the fallen Longford, and hearing her testament of lost-child love — has his memory fully restored and leads the assembled Swidger clan in a Christmas feast under the motto "Lord keep my memory green."

testi/dickens/atomized/the_mystery_of_ed.plot: John Jasper wakes in a London opium den after smoking through the night, surveys his debased surroundings with cold contempt, pays the haggard hostess, and hastens to Cloisterham Cathedral to take his place in the vesper choir.

After evensong, Mr Crisparkle checks on the ailing Jasper at the Cathedral gatehouse; Edwin Drood arrives for dinner and the two men talk intimately — Edwin complaining about his pre-arranged betrothal to Rosa Bud while Jasper confesses his crushing monotony and reveals he takes opium, all while casting a covertly hungry, watchful gaze on his nephew.

Edwin Drood visits Rosa Bud at the Nuns' House seminary in Cloisterham, and their bickering, affection-less exchange lays bare that their willed betrothal breeds mutual resignation rather than love, though a fleeting moment of honest compassion briefly disarms them both.

Edwin and Rosa walk near the Cathedral, hear the organ (Edwin thinks he detects Jack's voice), then part at the Nuns' House gate with a playful but hollow farewell, neither glimpsing a happy present or future.

Jasper visits the pompous auctioneer Sapsea, who brags of worldly knowledge and recites the absurdly self-glorifying epitaph he wrote for his dead wife; stonemason Durdles arrives to collect the monument key, and Jasper lingers over examining his keys before the evening ends in backgammon and cold beef.

Jasper stops a street boy named Deputy from pelting the drunken stonemason Durdles, walks him home through Cloisterham's churchyard while Durdles demonstrates his uncanny ability to locate entombed remains by tapping walls, then returns alone to his gatehouse where he fills a pipe with opium and stands in silence over his sleeping nephew Edwin.

Mr Crisparkle arranges to receive Neville and Helena Landless as wards placed by their bullying guardian Honeythunder; the two arrive in Cloisterham, are welcomed at a dinner that Honeythunder's overbearing harangues reduce to misery, and he is finally hustled away.

Neville confides his abusive past to Mr Crisparkle; that evening Rosa breaks down singing under Jasper's controlling gaze, and later Helena privately draws from Rosa her terrified confession of Jasper's silent, obsessive hold over her.

Neville Landless and Edwin Drood trade insults after dinner; Jasper intervenes and draws both to his rooms where wine inflames the quarrel until Neville flings his goblet at Edwin and storms out, whereupon Jasper visits Crisparkle to brand Neville as murderous and dangerous.

Mr Grewgious visits Rosa to clarify her betrothal is non-binding and review her finances, then meets Jasper outside the Cathedral where Jasper's ominous slip — "God save them" versus Grewgious's "God bless them" — hints at dark intent toward the engaged couple.

Mr Crisparkle walks with the Landless siblings, extracts Neville's secret love for Rosa Bud and his pledge to keep peace, then visits Jasper to secure Edwin Drood's agreement to make the first advance, which Drood does via letter inviting Neville to Christmas Eve dinner.

Edwin Drood visits Mr Grewgious at Staple Inn, dines with him, and receives Rosa's mother's diamond-and-ruby ring to place on Rosa's finger as a solemn seal of fidelity; alone afterward, Grewgious broods over his own long-suppressed love for Rosa's mother.

Jasper takes Durdles on a moonlit night expedition through Cloisterham's cathedral crypt and tower, deliberately plies him with drink, covertly spies on Neville Landless from the shadows with predatory intensity, and while Durdles sleeps appears to handle the crypt key — suggesting sinister premeditation.

Rosa Bud and Edwin Drood mutually and tenderly dissolve their childhood betrothal during a riverside walk, agreeing to become brother and sister instead of spouses, while John Jasper watches them unseen from under the cathedral trees.

On Christmas Eve in Cloisterham, Neville prepares a solitary walking departure, Edwin wanders the town and receives a cryptic warning from an opium woman that the name "Ned" is dangerous, Jasper hosts both at the gatehouse with an unsettlingly composed manner, and on Christmas morning Edwin is discovered missing — last seen going to the river with Neville in the storm.

Neville is hunted down and dragged back to Cloisterham under suspicion of murdering the vanished Edwin Drood; Jasper orchestrates his impeachment before Mayor Sapsea while Grewgious then shatters Jasper by revealing that Edwin and Rosa had already broken off their engagement before Edwin disappeared.

Mr Crisparkle dives into Cloisterham Weir and recovers Edwin Drood's monogrammed watch and shirt-pin; the evidence triggers Neville Landless's arrest and eventual forced expulsion from town under murder suspicion, while Jasper privately records a sworn oath to hunt down and destroy the murderer.

Mr Crisparkle confronts the bullying philanthropist Honeythunder then visits Neville's bleak London garret to offer support, calls briefly on Mr Grewgious who spots Jasper lurking and spying on the lodgings, and at midnight Neville meets his cheerful ex-naval neighbor Tartar on the staircase.

Mysterious stranger Dick Datchery arrives in Cloisterham, takes lodgings next to Jasper's gatehouse, flatters Mayor Sapsea into confirming suspicions about Edwin Drood's fate, and meets Durdles and Deputy while covertly positioning himself to investigate Jasper.

Jasper corners Rosa alone in the Nuns' House garden, confesses his mad obsessive love, and threatens to destroy Neville Landless with fabricated evidence unless she yields to him; Rosa, paralysed by terror, cannot flee and faints after he departs.
Terrified by Jasper's declaration of love and fearing his power over Neville, Rosa flees Cloisterham alone to London and takes refuge with her guardian Grewgious, who vows fierce protection.

Rosa Bud, sheltered at Mr Grewgious's lodgings, is joined by Mr Crisparkle; sailor Mr Tartar arrives and is recognised as Crisparkle's old school rescuer, then Grewgious devises a scheme to use Tartar's adjacent Staple Inn chambers as a covert rendezvous so Rosa can pass news of Jasper's threat to Helena Landless without Jasper's spies detecting the contact.

Rosa Bud, sheltered in Mr Tartar's nautical chambers, reunites across rooftop gardens with Helena Landless; consulting Mr Crisparkle and Mr Grewgious — who names John Jasper a brigand — they devise a plan for Tartar to visit Neville openly and thus expose any covert campaign by Jasper to isolate him.

Rosa bids farewell to Helena (confessing she could not avoid provoking Jasper's malice), then Mr Grewgious secures London lodgings at Mrs. Billickin's, a boat trip with Mr. Tartar offers brief pastoral relief, and Rosa settles into a restless, gritty London existence as Miss Twinkleton arrives and immediately clashes with the landlady.

Jasper visits a London opium den and in drug-induced visions reveals he mentally rehearsed "the journey" (Edwin's murder) countless times; the opium-woman (Princess Puffer) secretly follows him back to Cloisterham to track him, while the mysterious Mr. Datchery covertly observes both Jasper in the Cathedral choir and Puffer's hostile reaction, recording progress with a chalk mark in his cupboard.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_old_curiosity.plot: An elderly narrator finds Little Nell lost in the city at night, escorts her to the old curiosity shop, meets her grandfather and the comic errand-boy Kit, then lingers outside in unease after the grandfather departs on a suspicious nightly errand, leaving Nell alone among the dark antiques.

Nell's dissolute brother Fred intrudes on the grandfather's curiosity shop, bringing the drunk Dick Swiveller, demanding money and access to Nell, while the grandfather protests poverty; the chapter ends with Nell herself appearing at the door.

Quilp visits the curiosity shop alongside Nell's estranged brother Fred and Dick Swiveller, delivers gold to the grandfather while probing his secret dealings, and the grandfather privately reveals to the narrator his obsessive gamble to win a fortune for Nell's future.

Quilp's wife and her female neighbors gossip about resisting male tyranny, but Quilp returns home unexpectedly, disperses the women with sarcastic mockery, bullies Mrs Quilp and her mother into submission, then spends the night smoking and drinking while keeping his wife captive in silent torment.

Quilp torments his wife and mother-in-law through the night and at breakfast, then travels to his wharf where he physically bullies his boy, and is interrupted from a nap by Little Nell arriving with a letter.

Quilp reads a mysterious letter from Nell's grandfather, proposes grotesquely to Nell, forces her to his home where he uses Mrs Quilp to spy on Nell's confidences, extracting the secret of the grandfather's nightly absences and desperate state, while Kit escorts Nell and Mrs Quilp is left remorseful.

Fred Trent persuades Dick Swiveller to agree to a scheme for Dick to marry young Nell and thereby inherit the grandfather's fortune, which they plan to share; the chapter ends with a letter from Dick's current romantic interest Sophy Wackles complicating matters.

Dick Swiveller dines on credit, attends the Wackles' seminary party intending to feign jealousy but ends up genuinely wounded when Sophia encourages market-gardener Cheggs, storms out in dudgeon, and resolves at home to commit fully to Fred's scheme to marry little Nelly for her fortune.

Quilp confronts the grandfather, revealing he knows all loans were squandered at the gaming table; the grandfather begs for more money to win back Nell's future, Quilp refuses, then falsely names Kit as the informant to cover his own tracks.

Kit keeps secret nightly watch over Nell's window; grandfather falls ill in a fit and Nell comes to Kit's home to dismiss him, claiming the grandfather blames Kit for his misery, leaving Kit and his mother stunned.

Quilp seizes legal possession of the curiosity shop while Nell's grandfather lies delirious with fever, installs himself and lawyer Sampson Brass in the house, and Kit secretly appears beneath Nell's window to offer his mother's home as a refuge.

After grandfather slowly recovers from illness with a weakened mind, Quilp pressures them to vacate the shop; grandfather regains sudden clarity and resolves to flee with Nell; at dawn Nell secretly retrieves the locked door key from Quilp's bedroom, and the two slip out of the city into the open road.

Quilp and Brass wake to find Nell and her grandfather have secretly fled; Dick Swiveller arrives hoping to court Nell as part of a scheme with Frederick Trent, discovers them gone; Quilp oversees removal of the shop's goods; Kit Nubbles fights Quilp's wharf-boy to rescue Nell's pet linnet.

Kit roams London streets seeking odd jobs to support his family, pauses to mourn the abandoned curiosity shop, then earns a shilling minding the Garlands' pony while Abel Garland is formally articled to notary Witherden, and returns home hopeful that Nell and her grandfather may yet reappear.

Nell and her grandfather slip out of London at dawn, pass through its poverty-stricken fringes into open countryside, receive charity from a cottager family who tend Nell's blistered foot, and hitch a ride on a cart to reach a country town by nightfall.

Nell and her grandfather stumble upon two Punch-and-Judy showmen repairing puppets in a churchyard, join them at a nearby inn where they watch the show, and Nell secretly sews their last gold coin into her dress for a future emergency.

Nell wanders a churchyard at dawn and meets an elderly widow who has mourned her young husband for fifty-five years, then Nell and her grandfather join Punch-and-Judy men Codlin and Short on the dusty road toward the races, briefly encountering another traveling troupe before stopping for the night.

At the Jolly Sandboys inn, Nell and her grandfather sleep exhausted by the fire while showmen Codlin and Short, over stew and ale, debate whether to detain the fugitive pair and claim a reward from their London friends.

Nell and her grandfather travel with showmen Codlin and Short toward a race-town; Codlin secretly warns Nell to trust him over Short (both men covertly watching the pair to prevent escape), until Nell seizes a distracted moment during a Punch performance to flee with her grandfather across the racecourse into open fields.

Kit daily hopes Nell and her grandfather will return, learns neighbours believe they have emigrated abroad to protect hidden savings from Quilp, then keeps his appointment at the notary's office where Mr. Garland approves of him and records his address for future employment.

Kit is hired by the Garlands as a domestic servant for six pounds a year; Quilp then arrives with Dick Swiveller to seek news of Nell and her grandfather, plies Dick with liquor to extract their secret marriage scheme, and privately exults at his plan to exploit it for revenge.

Kit Nubbles leaves his mother and siblings behind, walks to Finchley with his trunk, and arrives at the Garlands' charming cottage to begin his new service, where he is warmly received and meets the shy servant-girl Barbara.

Quilp extracts Trent's secret from a drunk Swiveller, then hosts both men to seal a covert alliance aimed at locating the fugitive Nell and her grandfather and engineering Nell's marriage to Dick for mutual profit and revenge.

Nell and her grandfather flee the race-ground and take shelter with a melancholy village schoolmaster who, unaware his favourite dying pupil is gravely ill, waits in vain for the boy and asks Nell to pray for him.

Nell and her grandfather rest at the schoolmaster's cottage; Nell observes a chaotic school day cut short by a half-holiday, then accompanies the schoolmaster to the bedside of his favourite dying pupil, who expires holding the schoolmaster's hand.
After leaving the schoolmaster grief-stricken by a pupil's death, Nell and her grandfather trudge wearily along the road until a stout lady in a painted caravan feeds them and takes them aboard.

Nell and her grandfather ride in Mrs Jarley's wax-work caravan, accept her offer of board and employment as guides to the exhibition, then that night Nell spots Quilp passing under the town gateway and hides in terror, spending the rest of the night in broken, nightmare-haunted sleep.

Nell and her grandfather help Mrs Jarley set up her travelling waxwork exhibition in a new town, Nell is trained as guide to narrate sensational histories of the figures, and a hack poet Slum sells advertising verses — Quilp only haunts Nell's fearful thoughts.

Sheltering from a violent storm at the Valiant Soldier inn, Nell's grandfather hears card-players and is seized by uncontrollable gambling fever, snatching Nell's purse and joining the game despite her desperate pleas to leave.

Nell and her grandfather spend the night at the Valiant Soldier inn after gambling drains their purse; Nell is paralysed with terror by a shadowy figure creeping through her room, only to discover it is her grandfather stealing the last gold coin she had hidden in her dress.

Nell discovers her grandfather stole her money at night for gambling, confronts him indirectly on the road, then visits Miss Monflathers's school to deliver wax-work handbills and is publicly humiliated by the governess for her low social station.

Nell's grandfather returns penniless from gambling and extorts money from her, while Nell silently endures her isolation by vicariously sharing in the joyful reunion of two sisters; Mrs Jarley meanwhile resorts to tricks to lure paying visitors back to her struggling waxwork exhibition.

Quilp delivers Dick Swiveller to Sampson Brass's squalid Bevis Marks office as an imposed clerk, while the formidable Sally Brass dominates her craven brother and Dick sits stupefied by his new monstrous colleague.

Dick Swiveller settles into his new clerkship at Brass's office, encounters the tiny unnamed servant girl (the future Marchioness), and admits a brusque mysterious single gentleman who pays two years' rent on the spot and immediately goes to bed.

Dick Swiveller, new clerk at Brass's law office, deals with Sampson and Sally Brass's scheming over the mysterious single gentleman lodger who sleeps 26 hours, then confronts the lodger directly and shares drinks with him, reporting back to the Brasses with embellished tales of the man's magical travelling trunk.

Dick Swiveller, having risen to informal influence at Brass's office through his odd friendship with Sally Brass, secretly follows her to the basement kitchen and witnesses her deliberately starving and beating the small servant (the Marchioness).

The single gentleman's mania for Punch shows repeatedly disrupts Sampson Brass's office until he finally identifies the puppet showmen Codlin and Short as former companions of Nell and her grandfather, pays them a sovereign each, and arranges for them to return the next day with a lead on the missing pair's whereabouts.

A mysterious gentleman lodging at Brass's interrogates Kit about Nell and her grandfather's disappearance; Dick Swiveller spots the pair together and privately resolves to keep his own counsel about the mounting mysteries at Brass's house.

Kit Nubbles collects his first quarter's wages and treats his mother, Barbara, Barbara's mother, and the younger children to an evening at Astley's circus-theatre followed by an oyster supper, ending in high spirits.

Kit refuses the single gentleman's offer to leave the Garlands' service, but agrees to help locate Nell and her grandfather by pledging to produce his mother—familiar to both fugitives—as a companion for the rescue journey that same night.
Kit retrieves his mother from a dissenting chapel where Quilp lurks watching, then sees her off in a post-chaise with a wealthy gentleman, bound to rescue Little Nell.

Nell secretly overhears gamblers Jowl and Isaac List manipulate her grandfather into agreeing to steal money for a gambling stake, then invents a prophetic dream to frighten him into immediate flight from the town.

Nell and her grandfather flee by foot through the night, then accept passage on a canal barge crewed by rough drunken boatmen; Nell keeps the men peaceful by singing through the night, and they arrive at a grim industrial town, lost and bewildered.

Nell and her Grandfather wander destitute and lost through a dark industrial city, are taken in for the night by a solitary furnace-worker who shelters them amid the roaring steel foundry, shares his scant breakfast, and presses two pennies into Nell's hand before directing them onward toward the countryside.

Nell and her grandfather drag themselves through a hellish industrial wasteland, begging for food and being turned away, as Nell grows visibly weaker and finally collapses at the feet of a mysterious traveler she seems to recognize.

The schoolmaster finds the collapsed Nell on the road, carries her to an inn where she recovers, then escorts her and her grandfather by wagon to his new village posting, arriving at an ancient churchyard where Nell waits pensively in the porch.

The Single Gentleman races by post-chaise with Kit's mother to find Nell, arrives at Mrs Jarley's wedding, and learns Nell and her grandfather vanished weeks ago — while unknowingly the pair sit alive in a church porch nearby.

Quilp, having extracted information from a drunk Swiveller about the single gentleman's search for Nell and her grandfather, trails the party to their destination, confronts the single gentleman at the inn, learns the search failed, sets spies, terrorises Kit's mother on the return journey, and vows to exploit the situation for profit while disposing of Kit.
Quilp, believed drowned, secretly returns home and spies on wife, mother-in-law, and Sampson Brass drinking and composing his death notice, then bursts in alive to terrorise them all.
