Quilp abandons his terrified wife to set up a grotesque bachelor lair at his wharf counting-house, then visits Dick Swiveller — who is nursing heartbreak over Sophy Cheggs — to probe news of Fred Trent's failed introduction to a mysterious stranger, resolving to keep Dick as an unwitting spy.

Quilp visits Bevis Marks, encounters the mysterious small servant (Marchioness), then hosts Sampson and Sally Brass at his decrepit riverside summerhouse where he torments Brass with wet miserable conditions before secretly proposing that the trio conspire to destroy Kit Nubbles.

The schoolmaster reveals he has secured an ancient house near the churchyard as home for Nell and her grandfather, who are appointed church-keepers; the benevolent Bachelor welcomes them, furnishes their rooms, and introduces the village schoolchildren to their new master.

Nell explores the ancient village church alone, converses with the aged sexton whose talk of graves and time ignores his own mortality, then returns repeatedly to sit among the tombs reading scripture, finding deep peace and rest there until dusk.

Nell and her grandfather settle into the village churchyard, where Nell learns its legends from the bachelor, discusses fading remembrance with the old sexton, receives the schoolmaster's consolation that the dead live on through good deeds, and begins tending graves with her grandfather as a shared garden.

Nell's grandfather awakens to selfless devotion as the village embraces the visibly fading child with tender compassion; a young boy friend pleads with Nell not to die and become an angel, while a visit to a grave-like crypt well deepens the foreshadowing of her imminent death.

Brass sends Swiveller away on an errand to clear the office, then flatters Kit and slips him coins from the single gentleman upstairs, while he and Sally Brass exchange conspiratorial smiles that signal a trap being laid.

Dick Swiveller discovers the half-starved servant girl spying through the keyhole, feeds her, teaches her cribbage, and dubs her "the Marchioness," while Sampson Brass manipulates Kit with false generosity and contrives to keep Swiveller away during Kit's visits.

Dick Swiveller shares purl and cards with the Marchioness, learns she eavesdrops on the Brasses to survive, then reports missing office money to Sally and Sampson Brass, who blame Kit Nubbles for the thefts while Sampson hotly defends him.

Sampson Brass plants a five-pound note in Kit Nubbles's hat, then with Dick Swiveller pursues and apprehends Kit on a theft charge, leading to a search that "discovers" the planted note and ends with Brass calling for a constable.

Kit Nubbles is arrested after a bank note planted in his hat by Sampson Brass is "discovered," Quilp gloats from a tavern window, and despite Kit's passionate protests of innocence before the Garlands and notary Witherden, he is committed to prison to await trial.
Kit Nubbles endures his first night in jail wrongfully accused, is visited by his mother and siblings who affirm his innocence, and receives a humorous note with daily beer from Dick Swiveller.

Quilp summons Sampson Brass to his wharf counting-house at night, reveals his scheme against Kit (beating a figurehead representing him) and the grandfather's party, orders Brass to dismiss Dick Swiveller once Kit's trial ends as he is no longer useful, and sadistically torments the drunken lawyer with scalding rum and extinguished lantern before letting him stumble home in the dark.

Kit Nubbles is tried and convicted of theft through the perjured testimony of Sampson and Sally Brass; Dick Swiveller, dismissed by Brass afterward, vows to help Kit's mother but is immediately struck down by raging fever.

Dick Swiveller wakes after three weeks of near-fatal fever to find the Marchioness has nursed him single-handedly; she reveals the Brass siblings' plot—at Quilp's instigation—to plant stolen money in Kit Nubbles's hat and frame him, prompting Dick to dispatch her to fetch the Garlands and expose the injustice.

Marchioness escapes Bevis Marks, pursues Mr Abel Garland after the notary's office by clambering into his phaeton, and brings him to Dick Swiveller's sickroom, where the recovering Dick has her repeat her testimony that can prove Kit's innocence and urges Abel to act at once.

Dick Swiveller convalesces with the Marchioness as nurse while Garland's party confronts Sally Brass about the plot against Kit; Sampson Brass then arrives uninvited and, to save himself, confesses everything against Quilp, securing his own detention, a warrant for Quilp's arrest, and Kit's imminent pardon—after which Dick learns he has inherited a small annuity.
Quilp receives Sally Brass's warning that Sampson has confessed and officers are coming; he sends away his wife and Tom Scott, attempts to flee through dense fog, falls into the river, and drowns.

Kit Nubbles is pardoned and released from prison, reunites tearfully with his family and shares a first kiss with Barbara, then learns from Mr. Garland that Little Nell's retreat has at last been discovered and they will journey to find her the next morning.

Kit and the Single Gentleman depart by carriage on a bitter winter journey to find Nell; Kit parts tenderly with Barbara, who betrays jealous feelings; the Single Gentleman narrates to Mr. Garland the full family backstory — the two rival brothers, Nell's grandfather's downfall, and the frantic search — ending with dread they may again arrive too late.

Kit and the Garland party travel through a snowstorm to reach a remote village at midnight, and Kit approaches a ruined building where a lone light burns and an unearthly sound issues from within, hinting at what awaits inside.

Kit Nubbles finds Nell's grandfather alone and deranged, rocking by the fire and refusing to accept Nell is dead; the schoolmaster, bachelor, and grandfather's long-lost brother arrive and attempt consolation, but all discover that Little Nell has died peacefully in the adjoining room.

Nell's death is recounted, her burial draws the whole village in mourning, and her grandfather—unable to accept the loss—sits daily at her grave whispering that she will return, until he is found dead there and laid beside her.

Epilogue chapter wraps all fates: Sampson Brass convicted and imprisoned, Sally Brass vanishes into destitution, Quilp's body found and buried as suicide, Dick Swiveller educates then marries the Marchioness, Kit Nubbles prospers and marries Barbara, and Nell's memory lives on through Kit's stories to his children.

testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: The text is the book's title page and full table of contents rather than narrative prose; the entry for Chapter LVI describes an important conference taking place between Mr. Pickwick and Samuel Weller, assisted by his father, during which an old gentleman in a snuff-coloured suit arrives unexpectedly.

Pickwick Club formally constitutes its Corresponding Society, appointing Pickwick, Tupman, Snodgrass, and Winkle as traveling members, then a verbal clash between Pickwick and Mr. Blotton is defused when both agree their insults were meant only in a "Pickwickian sense."

themes: decline through poverty, drink and disease
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: At the inn, Pickwick and friends meet the melancholy actor "Dismal Jemmy," who recounts the grim tale of a dissolute pantomime clown's death from drink and fever, after which Winkle's officer acquaintances arrive and nearly provoke a duel with Jingle (mistaken for Tupman's card-playing companion) over a borrowed coat, until Lieutenant Tappleton recognizes Jingle as a strolling actor and the officers depart, leaving Pickwick's anger soothed by brandy-and-water.

At a grand military review near Rochester, Pickwick and his companions are jostled and mock-charged by troops, Pickwick loses and chases his hat, and the group is spotted and welcomed by the jovial Mr Wardle and his family (including Tupman's new flirtation with spinster aunt Rachael), who invite them to Manor Farm, Dingley Dell; the following morning Pickwick meets a "dismal man" on Rochester Bridge who asks him to forward a manuscript, and then the four friends set off for Dingley Dell in a chaise and on horseback, suffering runaway horses and a wrecked carriage, being accused of horse theft by suspicious innkeepers, before finally arriving battered at Manor Farm to Wardle's welcome.

At Wardle's fireside party Pickwick and friends join a whist game and round-game amid the old lady, host, clergyman and guests, then after supper the clergyman recites his poem "The Ivy Green" and tells the tale of John Edmunds, a convict whose cruelty to his devoted mother, transportation, and return years later end in his accidentally causing the death of his estranged, unrecognizing father.

At Wardle's estate, Winkle's inept rook-shooting wounds Tupman (leading to the spinster aunt's hysterics and a budding flirtation), then the party attends the Dingley Dell vs. All-Muggleton cricket match, re-encounters the voluble stranger who introduces himself as Alfred Jingle, and joins a boisterous celebratory dinner full of toasts and tall tales.

Tupman woos and wins the spinster aunt Rachael in the garden arbour, but the fat boy Joe spies on them and tells the old lady, prompting Jingle to exploit the secret—first convincing Rachael to feign coldness toward Tupman by claiming he secretly loves Emily, then extracting Tupman's blessing and ten pounds under false pretenses while secretly becoming Rachael's accepted suitor himself; meanwhile Pickwick, Winkle, and Snodgrass return from a cricket dinner uproariously drunk.

Jingle elopes with spinster Rachael after swindling Tupman of ten pounds, prompting Wardle and Pickwick to chase the runaway pair by chaise through a stormy night, overturning their own carriage before Jingle mockingly outpaces them and escapes toward London to marry her.

At the White Hart Inn Sam Weller's chat unwittingly leads Wardle, Perker and Pickwick to Jingle just as he is about to marry Rachael, and after a shrieking scene Jingle is bought off with a cheque and abandons her; Pickwick, Winkle and Snodgrass then learn by letter that the heartbroken Tupman has fled to Cobham, find him there recovered, Pickwick unearths and buys an old inscribed stone as an antiquarian treasure, and that night he begins reading the clergyman's "Madman's Manuscript."

Mr Pickwick's innocent announcement that he intends to hire a manservant is misread by his landlady Mrs Bardell as a marriage proposal, leading her to faint in his arms just as Tupman, Winkle, and Snodgrass walk in on the compromising scene; once the confusion is smoothed over, Pickwick formally hires Sam Weller as his servant, fits him out with new livery, and Sam sets off with the party for Eatanswill.

Pickwick and his companions arrive at Eatanswill amid the fierce Blue-versus-Buff election contest, lodge with newspaper editor Mr. Pott (whose wife charms Winkle), hear Sam Weller recount tales of electoral bribery and trickery (including a comic anecdote about his father Tony Weller), and then witness the riotous nomination-day procession, hustings speeches, and scuffles that end with Samuel Slumkey being declared elected pending a poll, which he ultimately wins.

While Pickwick and Winkle are occupied elsewhere, Tupman and Snodgrass while away evenings in the Peacock's commercial room, where a one-eyed bagman tells "The Bagman's Story" about Tom Smart, who, sheltering at an inn during a storm, is visited by an old chair that comes alive as a ghostly gentleman, reveals that his rival Jinkins (the tall man courting the widowed landlady) is secretly already married, and thereby helps Tom win and marry the widow himself.

The chapter heading alone announces a portrait of two distinguished persons and a public breakfast at their house and grounds, which leads to the recognition of an old acquaintance and the start of another matter; no further body text is present in this unit.

Mr. Leo Hunter invites Pickwick to his wife's fancy-dress breakfast, Pickwick quarrels briefly with Tupman over his bandit costume before reconciling, the Pickwickians attend the absurd literary fete hosted by Mrs. Leo Hunter (meeting the pompous Count Smorltork), and the event is disrupted when Jingle appears disguised as "Charles Fitz-Marshall," prompting Pickwick to rush off with Sam Weller to pursue him to Bury St. Edmunds.

Travelling to Bury St Edmunds in pursuit of Jingle, Pickwick and Sam are tricked by Jingle's servant Job Trotter into a fake rescue plan, leading Pickwick to be caught trespassing at night in a girls' boarding-school garden during a thunderstorm and locked in a closet until Wardle and Trundle arrive to vouch for him, while Jingle escapes the ruse unscathed.

Laid up with rheumatism, Mr. Pickwick spends his convalescence writing up Sam Weller's tale, then reads to Wardle and Trundle "The Parish Clerk," the comic story of timid clerk Nathaniel Pipkin's doomed courtship of Maria Lobbs, his discovery hiding in a closet by her fierce father old Lobbs, and the reveal that Maria loves her cousin Henry, whom Pipkin nobly shields from blame before the pair are allowed to marry.

Mr. Pott accuses Winkle of an affair with Mrs. Pott based on a libellous newspaper verse, triggering Mrs. Pott's hysterics and Pott's abject climb-down, before Winkle and the others rejoin Pickwick at Bury (learning of Trundle's coming wedding to Bella and Rachael's departure) just as a letter from Dodson & Fogg arrives announcing Mrs. Bardell's breach-of-promise suit against Pickwick.

On a partridge shoot with Wardle's party, Winkle and Tupman blunder dangerously with their guns while Pickwick is wheeled along in a barrow by Sam Weller, and after a punch-fueled lunch Pickwick falls asleep and is discovered trespassing by the irate Captain Boldwig, who has him wheeled off and locked in the village pound until Wardle and Sam rescue him.

Pickwick and Sam visit attorneys Dodson and Fogg, who serve him with a writ for £1500 damages in Mrs Bardell's suit and needle him into calling them swindlers, after which Sam hustles him away; at a tavern they unexpectedly meet Sam's long-lost father Tony Weller, who reveals Jingle and Job Trotter are lodging in Ipswich, prompting Pickwick to resolve to follow them there; failing to find his absent solicitor Perker, Pickwick leaves the writ with Perker's clerk Lowten at the Magpie and Stump and joins the clerks' drinking party.

themes: ghost stories and old legal chambers
grief over loss of wife and child
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: At the Magpie and Stump, a little old man regales Mr. Pickwick and the company with ghost stories about old Inn chambers, then narrates "The Old Man's Tale About the Queer Client": Heyling, imprisoned in the Marshalsea with his wife and child who both die of poverty and grief, swears revenge on his wife's father who cast them out, and over years ruins him financially, lets his son die before his eyes at the seaside, and finally confronts and terrifies him to death before vanishing from the attorney's knowledge forever.

themes: father-son advice on marriage and family honor
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Tony Weller feasts and gives Sam rambling fatherly advice (mocking widows and warning against marriage) before departing for London, after which Sam encounters the disguised, grimacing Job Trotter near a green garden gate, forces him to drop the act, hears Trotter's tearful (and evidently false) tale about reforming and marrying a cook, and arranges to meet him that night at the Great White Horse as part of his scheme to catch Trotter and his master, which he then reports to Mr. Pickwick.

Pickwick coaches Peter Magnus on proposing to Miss Witherfield, but when Magnus successfully proposes and introduces her, Pickwick and the lady recognize each other from the previous night's bedroom mishap, sparking Magnus's jealous rage; the frightened lady reports a supposed duel to magistrate Nupkins, who issues warrants, and constable Grummer's men arrest Pickwick and Tupman, sparking a brawl with Sam Weller and a comic procession by sedan chair to the magistrate's house.

Pickwick and friends, hauled before the pompous magistrate Nupkins on suspicion of duelling and required to find bail, privately expose Jingle (posing as "Captain Fitz-Marshall") as an impostor to the horrified Nupkins family, leading to Jingle's and Job Trotter's ejection from the house, while Sam Weller taunts the constables below stairs and begins a flirtation with the housemaid Mary.

Pickwick returns to London and sends Sam Weller to settle his lodgings with Mrs Bardell, where Sam plies her gossiping friends Mrs Cluppins and Mrs Sanders with drink and learns the breach-of-promise trial (egged on by Dodson and Fogg) is set for February or March, leaving Pickwick to prepare for his Christmas visit under the shadow of the coming suit.

Sam Weller gets leave from Mr. Pickwick to visit his father at the Marquis of Granby in Dorking, where he meets his overbearing stepmother and the hypocritical, toast-and-rum-guzzling deputy-shepherd Mr. Stiggins, then later shares drinks and mocking commentary with his returned father about Stiggins and his mother-in-law's religious zeal before departing back to London the next morning.

themes: courtship and romantic teasing among young couples
festive games and traditions (mistletoe, blind-man's buff, snap-dragon, wassail)
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Pickwick and his friends travel by coach to Dingley Dell for Christmas, where they attend Bella and Trundle's wedding, enjoy a festive breakfast and dinner with toasts and dancing, and on Christmas Eve join the Wardle household's mistletoe games, blind-man's buff, snap-dragon, and wassail by the fire, ending with old Wardle beginning the tale of Gabriel Grub and the goblins.

Sexton Gabriel Grub, a sour misanthrope who mocks Christmas cheer and strikes a singing boy, is confronted in the churchyard by a goblin and a chorus of spirits who drag him underground, force him to drink fire, kick him, and show him visions of domestic joy, death, and endurance until he repents his sullenness; he vanishes for years, believed carried off by goblins, then returns a changed, humbled man who tells the true tale.

themes: vanity and embarrassment on the ice
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: On Christmas morning at Manor Farm the Pickwickians meet the boisterous medical students Bob Sawyer and Benjamin Allen, then join a skating party where Winkle's incompetence causes a collision and earns him Pickwick's rebuke, before Pickwick himself falls through the ice, is rescued unharmed, and the group warms him with punch before the party disperses and Bob Sawyer invites Pickwick to visit him in London.

Dodson & Fogg's clerk Jackson serves subpoenas on Pickwick, Snodgrass, Tupman, Winkle and Sam Weller for the upcoming Bardell breach-of-promise trial; Pickwick then consults his attorney Perker and insists on meeting the eminent Serjeant Snubbin to affirm his innocence, before the scene shifts to a raucous bachelor party at Bob Sawyer's lodgings (with Pickwick, Ben Allen, Jack Hopkins and others) that is repeatedly disrupted by Sawyer's furious unpaid landlady Mrs Raddle until the guests are driven out.

themes: comic exposure of a fraudulent preacher
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: While Pickwick frets over the next day's trial against Mrs. Bardell, Sam Weller writes a comic valentine to Mary with his father's help, then the two Wellers attend a temperance meeting where they expose and physically thrash the drunken, hypocritical Reverend Stiggins.

themes: social pretension and snobbery in Bath
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: At the Guildhall trial of Bardell v. Pickwick, Serjeant Buzfuz's inflammatory speech and the testimony of Mrs Cluppins, Winkle, Tupman, Snodgrass and Sam Weller lead the jury to award Mrs Bardell £750 damages, after which Pickwick vows never to pay and instead sets off with his friends for Bath, where they meet the blustering Mr Dowler and are introduced by Master of Ceremonies Angelo Bantam into Bath's card-playing and ball-going society.

Pickwick settles into Bath lodgings and takes up the water-drinking routine, then one night reads a manuscript legend of Prince Bladud (exiled for loving an Athenian maid against his father's wishes, who founds Bath's baths and dies in its waters), before the night ends in farce when Winkle is locked out in the wind, mistaken for absconding with Mrs. Dowler, and chased around the crescent by the enraged Mr. Dowler.

themes: class pretension and imitation among servants
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Sam Weller attends a footmen's "swarry" in Bath with John Smauker, where he mocks the servants' aped gentility amid comic incidents (Tuckle's bullying of the greengrocer, Whiffers' resignation speech over being made to eat cold meat), and the next morning Pickwick, learning Winkle has fled the house fearing violence from Dowler, sends Sam to track him down in Bristol and bring him back.

themes: sham appearances and deception (fake surgery/business tricks)
romantic anxiety over a rival's claim
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Fleeing Dowler's threat, Winkle escapes to Bristol where he stumbles on Bob Sawyer's sham "surgery," drinks and hears Ben Allen's maudlin talk of sister Arabella's supposed prior attachment, then unexpectedly meets and reconciles with the now-apologetic Dowler at the inn, before Sam Weller arrives on Pickwick's orders to lock him in his room pending word back from Pickwick.

themes: imprisonment for debt / satire of the legal system
prison life and its social inequities
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Sam Weller tracks down Arabella Allen through his sweetheart Mary and arranges a secret garden meeting where Winkle, chaperoned by Pickwick amid a comic dark-lantern mishap, declares his love to her, after which Pickwick is arrested by the sheriff's officer Namby for refusing to pay the Bardell damages and is committed to the Fleet Prison, where he spends an uneasy first night observing the debtors' squalor and meeting fellow prisoners Smangle and Mivins.

themes: charity and pity toward the destitute
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Pickwick wakes in the Fleet, is chummed with three rough roommates who try to extort payment to be left alone, rents a private room from Roker instead, tours the poor side where he finds the destitute, weeping Jingle and Job Trotter and secretly gives Jingle money, then tells Sam he must leave his service while Pickwick is imprisoned, prompting Sam to refuse and storm out.

At the Insolvent Court, Tony Weller and attorney Solomon Pell help discharge coachman George's debt case while comically reminiscing and drinking, then Sam finds his father, borrows money from him to stage a fake debt arrest so he can be committed to the Fleet prison and thereby stay with Mr. Pickwick, and after the mock legal proceedings and a rowdy send-off Sam is delivered to the prison and reveals to the astonished Pickwick that he has gotten himself arrested for debt in order to remain by his side.

In the Fleet, Sam Weller refuses to name his creditor and distracts Pickwick with a comic tale, then settles into lodgings with an old cobbler who recounts how Chancery litigation over an inheritance ruined and imprisoned him for years; the next day Pickwick's friends Tupman, Snodgrass and Winkle visit (Winkle behaving mysteriously about a secret errand and enlisting Sam's help), and that night the turnkey Roker tells Pickwick the cobbler is dying, leading Pickwick to the infirmary where he watches the old Chancery prisoner die.

themes: charity and redemption toward fallen enemies
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Sam Weller is visited in the Fleet by his father Tony, stepmother, and the drunken hypocrite Stiggins, whom Sam mocks; afterward Pickwick reconciles with the destitute, ailing Jingle and Job Trotter (whom he has been secretly feeding and housing), tours the squalid prison with Sam and Job (including a "whistling-shop" gin den and the corpse of a dead Chancery prisoner), and, sickened by what he has seen, resolves to shut himself in his room for three months.

Mrs. Bardell and her companions enjoy a comic outing to Hampstead until Mr. Jackson, sent by Dodson and Fogg, lures her away under pretext of urgent business and instead has her arrested on a cognovit for costs and delivered to the Fleet prison, where she is confronted by the imprisoned Mr. Pickwick and Sam Weller.

themes: legal costs and manipulation by attorneys
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Perker persuades imprisoned Pickwick to pay Mrs Bardell's legal costs (securing her release and a letter exonerating him from blame on Dodson and Fogg), after which Winkle and Arabella burst in newly married, Pickwick forgives them and agrees to help reconcile Arabella with her brother, then leaves the Fleet with Sam, delivers Jingle and Job to Perker for further help, and travels to Bristol where news of the marriage causes an uproar among Ben Allen, Bob Sawyer and Arabella's aunt until Pickwick calms them, ending at an inn where a one-eyed bagman begins telling a story.

themes: satire of provincial journalism and political rivalry
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: The bagman narrates his uncle's ghostly tale of boarding a phantom mail-coach in Edinburgh, rescuing a mysterious lady from villains, and waking to find it all vanished; then Mr. Pickwick, accompanied by Sam Weller, Bob Sawyer and Ben Allen, journeys to confront Mr. Winkle senior about his son's secret marriage (getting only a cold, businesslike rebuff), and en route the party's stay at Towcester is disrupted by a farcical brawl between rival newspaper editors Pott and Slurk, which Sam Weller breaks up.

Sam Weller gets word via a garbled letter that his stepmother has died, travels to Dorking where his father Tony Weller mourns her, fends off pursuing widows and a coaxing cook, explains his plan to become a coachman again and invest the inheritance for Sam, then violently ejects the hypocritical preacher Mr Stiggins by kicking him out of the inn and dunking his head in a horse-trough.

Pickwick settles accounts with Perker, sees off the reformed Jingle and Job Trotter to Demerara, angrily denounces the smug lawyers Dodson and Fogg, then joins Wardle who reveals Emily's secret engagement to Snodgrass, ending in a dinner where the fat boy's antics expose Snodgrass hiding in the bedroom and Wardle reconciles with the young lovers.

themes: settling an estate/inheritance through comic legal bureaucracy
loyalty and faithful service (Sam refusing wages/independence)
testi/dickens/atomized/the_pickwick_pape.plot: Tony Weller finds his late wife's will and, with Pell's help (and coachman "umpires"), gets probate and sells the stock via Wilkins Flasher, then entrusts the proceeds to Pickwick, who arranges Sam's future with Mary while Sam refuses to leave his master's service, Winkle's father arrives and forgives the marriage, and Pickwick dissolves the Pickwick Club, retires to Dulwich, hosts Snodgrass's wedding to Emily, and the narrator closes with brief fates of Tupman, Snodgrass, Winkle, Bardell, Jingle, Sam and Tony Weller, and Pickwick himself.

testi/poe/atomized/the_narrative_of_a_go.plot: Young Pym and his drunk friend Augustus take the sailboat Ariel out in a storm at night, nearly drown when Augustus collapses and their boat is run down by the whaling ship Penguin, and are both miraculously rescued — Pym found pinned to the ship's hull, Augustus kept afloat by a rope Pym had tied around him.

Pym and Augustus execute a stowaway plan aboard the whaling brig Grampus; Pym endures days locked in a secret box in the hold, suffers thirst, fever, and nightmarish visions, finds the escape trap sealed shut, and discovers a mysterious note tied to his dog Tiger.

Trapped in ship's hold without light or water, Pym struggles to read a warning note from Augustus using phosphorus matches, survives a frenzied attack by the maddened dog Tiger, and is finally rescued when Augustus reaches him with water and food.

Aboard the Grampus, the crew mutinies—massacring 22 loyal sailors and setting Captain Barnard adrift—while Augustus, trapped between the hidden Pym below and the murderous mutineers above, is eventually clapped in irons, with Dirk Peters introduced as the grotesque figure who repeatedly saves Augustus's life.

Augustus, held captive in the forecastle after the ship's mutiny, escapes his handcuffs, cuts through a bulkhead partition, and navigates the dark hold to reach the hidden Pym — sending him a blood-written note via the dog Tiger and finally locating him alive after near-giving-up in despair.

Pym and Augustus drag the recovering dog Tiger through the hold to a hiding spot near the bulkhead, narrowly avoid discovery by mutineers, gain an unexpected ally in Dirk Peters, and endure eight days of storms and internal mutineer conflict while plotting to retake the brig.

Pym, Augustus, and Peters plot to retake the Grampus from the mutinous mate during a gale, eliminate the watch (Allen), and execute their plan by disguising Pym as the ghastly corpse of poisoned crewman Rogers to exploit the mate's guilty conscience and superstitious terror.

Pym and Peters use a ghoulish disguise to terrify the mutineers, triggering a bloody cabin battle in which most rebels are killed or die of fright; the survivors then fight a severe storm that floods the brig and strips it of masts, rudder, and longboat, leaving the vessel a sinking hulk by midnight.

Pym and companions survive a hurricane lashed to the wrecked brig's windlass, tend to the injured Augustus and Peters after the storm passes, then exhaust multiple desperate diving attempts to reach submerged stores for food and water.
Survivors spot an approaching brig and feel ecstatic hope of rescue, only to discover the vessel is crewed entirely by putrefied corpses ravaged by disease, leaving them more desperate than before.

Stranded on capsized hulk for six days without food or water, the survivors recover only a bottle of wine (companions drink it and go delirious), fail to break into the storeroom, watch two passing ships sail away without rescuing them, and the chapter ends with Parker proposing that one of them be killed so the others may eat.

Stranded survivors draw lots; Parker loses and is killed and cannibalized; survivors then chop through deck to retrieve provisions, finding olives, ham, wine, and a Galapagos tortoise with fresh water, ending chapter with grim relief.

Adrift on a capsizing hulk, Pym and Peters endure worsening starvation, putrid water, and shark-besieged days while Augustus dies of his infected wound and his corpse is thrown overboard; the brig finally rolls keel-up stranding them until the British schooner Jane Guy spots and rescues them.

Rescued by the Jane Guy, Pym and Peters recover at sea while the schooner voyages south through a violent gale to Kerguelen's (Desolation) Island, where Pym records detailed natural-history observations of penguin-albatross rookeries and the crew conducts a largely unsuccessful seal hunt before departing.

Ship departs Christmas Harbour, surveys Tristan d'Acunha group (history, geography, thriving settlement under Glass), then sails south to locate the disputed Aurora Islands and after three weeks of systematic search finds no trace of them.
Narrator surveys prior Antarctic expeditions (Cook, Weddell, Morrell, Briscoe, and others) as context before Captain Guy resolves to push the Jane boldly southward beyond the Antarctic Circle.

The schooner crosses the Antarctic Circle southward through ice fields, loses a man overboard, encounters and kills a gigantic white bear, discovers Bennet's Islet at 82°50' S, and presses further south into warming open seas despite crew scurvy and fuel shortage.

Pym's schooner reaches islands near 84° S, makes first contact with islanders led by chief Too-wit who board the vessel in astonishment; the shore party then ventures inland and discovers utterly alien landscape including a multicolored, vein-streaked water unlike any natural liquid, marking the first link in a chain of inexplicable phenomena.

Pym's party marches to Too-wit's village, observes its crude dwellings and exotic fauna, endures a tense crowd-surrounded meeting in the chief's hut with diplomatic gift exchange and a revolting meal, then is guided to reefs teeming with biche de mer before returning to the schooner—unease lingering from the savages' systematic reinforcement of their escort along the route.
Crew trades goods with Tsalal islanders, negotiates biche-de-mer harvesting deal, then on a farewell visit is escorted through a narrow gorge where the natives spring a catastrophic ambush.

Pym and Peters claw free from a cave-in that buries companion Allen alive, climb a fissure to the surface, and discover the gorge landslide was engineered by the island's natives to massacre their entire thirty-two-man party, leaving the two men the only surviving whites on the island.

Pym and Peters, hiding in a hilltop chasm, watch helplessly as native islanders led by Too-wit overwhelm and massacre the Jane's skeleton crew, loot and burn the schooner, and are then devastated by the ship's powder-magazine explosion — after which the survivors flee in terror at the sight of the strange white-furred creature, crying "Tekeli-li!"

Pym and Peters, hiding on the hilltop after the massacre, exhaust their food and repeatedly attempt descent but are blocked by chasms and precipices; exploring a series of labyrinthine black-granite caverns they discover enigmatic wall indentures that Peters thinks are writing but Pym attributes to natural forces, and they return dejected, still fully trapped.

Pym and Peters descend a sheer soapstone cliff by carving pegs, Pym nearly falls into the abyss gripped by suicidal vertigo, Peters rescues him, and after reaching the bottom they fight off five ambushing savages, seize a canoe, destroy the second to prevent pursuit, and flee south by sea with a captive native.

Pym and Peters sail south through mounting Antarctic strangeness—milky warming seas, falling white ash, and a titanic vapor curtain—while their captive Nu-Nu dies of terror at any white object, until they plunge into a vast cataract where a colossal white shrouded figure rises before them.

testi/poe/atomized/the_narrative_of_arth.plot: Pym, consumed by longing for sea adventure, secretly stows away in a hidden box in the hold of the whaling brig Grampus with Augustus's help, and after days of growing thirst, fever, nightmares, and a blocked trapdoor, finds his dog Tiger has somehow appeared with a note tied to its body.

Pym, trapped in the ship's hold, feverish and dehydrated, deciphers a fragmented warning note from Augustus by phosphorus light, escapes a maddened Tiger, and is finally rescued by Augustus who brings water and food.

While Pym lies unconscious in the hold in a narcotic stupor, the first mate and cook lead a bloody mutiny aboard the Grampus—massacring twenty-two loyal sailors, setting Captain Barnard adrift, and leaving Augustus shackled below deck with Dirk Peters as his only protector.

Imprisoned below decks during a mutiny, Augustus escapes his handcuffs, cuts through a bulkhead, sends a blood-written note to Pym via the dog Tiger, then navigates the dark hold a second night and, despite near-despair, finally reaches Pym alive in his box.

Pym and Augustus drag the stuporous Tiger through the bulkhead to a safer hiding-spot; a long digression on improper cargo stowage illustrates maritime danger; the mutineers splinter and lose men overboard while Peters, feigning drunkenness, secretly forges an alliance with Augustus to retake the Grampus from the mate.

Pym, Peters, and Augustus secretly ally to retake the mutinied brig; after crew allegiances collapse and a gale strikes, Peters silently kills the watchman Allen, and Pym disguises himself as the disfigured corpse of the poisoned Rogers to exploit the mate's superstitious guilt.

Pym, disguised as the rotting corpse of Rogers, descends into the cabin and paralyzes the mutineers with supernatural terror; Peters, Augustus, and Tiger then kill or subdue all but one survivor, retaking the brig, before the victors spend a desperate night pumping floodwater and cutting away masts as the storm-ravaged vessel fills with seawater.

After a hurricane leaves the waterlogged brig adrift, Pym and companions endure lashed to the windlass through the night, revive the injured Augustus and Peters, then spend days starving and attempting increasingly desperate underwater dives into the flooded cabin to reach the locked storeroom.

Survivors spot an approaching brig and rejoice at rescue, but the vessel proves a ghost ship drifting with a cargo of putrefied corpses, shattering all hope and provoking horror and madness — with a dropped morsel of flesh momentarily tempting the narrator toward the unspeakable.

Stranded on waterlogged hulk, survivors dive repeatedly for provisions and find only a bottle of wine which sends companions into drunken delirium; two passing ships fail to rescue them, and Parker finally proposes that one must be killed so the others may survive.
Stranded survivors draw lots; Parker loses and is killed and consumed; survivors then recover food and a Galapagos tortoise from the flooded storeroom, restoring hope.

Pym and Peters endure days of worsening privation on the capsized hulk—Augustus dies from gangrene and starvation, all provisions are lost when the brig rolls over throwing them into shark-infested water, but they survive on barnacles and crabs until the schooner Jane Guy spots and rescues them.

Rescued by the Jane Guy schooner, Pym and Peters recover from their ordeal during a southward voyage that survives a violent gale near the Cape of Good Hope, then anchors at bleak Kerguelen's Island, where the narrator catalogs the island's sparse flora, elaborate penguin-albatross rookeries, and a largely fruitless seal hunt before the crew reunites with Captain Guy.

The Jane Guy sails from Christmas Harbour to Tristan d'Acunha — described in geographic and historical detail, including Glass's self-governed settlement — takes on supplies and trades for sealskins, then pushes south to search systematically for the disputed Aurora Islands, finding no trace of them after three weeks of careful navigation.

Pym surveys prior Antarctic expeditions (Cook, Weddell, Morrell, Briscoe) to establish how little of the southern ocean has been crossed, then reports Captain Guy's resolve to drive the Jane boldly toward the pole.

The schooner pushes deep into Antarctic waters past 82°S, losing a crewman to the ice, killing a monstrous white bear that nearly capsizes the boat, landing on desolate Bennet's Islet, and pressing still southward despite mounting scurvy and fuel shortages.

Pym's schooner reaches a southern island at 83° latitude, makes first contact with black-skinned islanders led by chief Too-wit who board the vessel in astonishment at mirrors and guns, then escorts a landing party inland where they find alien landscape and impossibly multicolored water that behaves like no natural liquid.

Pym's party follows chief Too-wit inland to village Klock-Klock, observes primitive dwellings and strange fauna, endures a tense confinement surrounded by dozens of armed savages in the chief's hut, declines a meal of raw entrails, then is shown abundant biche de mer reefs before returning to the schooner with a promise of trade goods.

Crew trades with islanders and strikes a biche-de-mer harvesting deal with Too-wit, then during a farewell march through a narrow ravine the savages spring a catastrophic ambush just as Pym and two companions duck into a rock fissure.

Pym and Peters claw free from a cave-in, find companion Allen dead beneath the rubble, climb out through a narrow rock fissure, then discover the gorge collapse was a deliberate savage trap—stakes and vine cords used to hurl the cliff face onto the party—leaving them the only two white men alive on the island.

Pym and Peters watch helplessly from their chasm hideout as a vast native force overwhelms and slaughters the Jane's crew, strips and burns the vessel until a powder explosion kills hundreds of savages, then scavenge food and water while the surviving natives flee in screaming terror at the white-furred animal carcass blown ashore, crying "Tekeli-li."

Stranded atop hill on hostile island, Pym and Peters exhaust food, fail every descent route blocked by chasms, then explore series of interconnected black-granite chasms where strange marl indentures—initially read as letters—are proved natural formations, leaving them still imprisoned with no escape.

Pym and Peters descend a sheer soapstone cliff using improvised pegs and rope — Pym nearly falls in a trance-like compulsion to leap — then survive an ambush by island savages, take a captive, disable a second canoe, and flee southward by sea as the pursuing native fleet abandons the chase.

Pym and Peters drift south through warming, milky Antarctic waters while captive Nu-Nu dies of terror at white objects, until they plunge into a vast luminous cataract and encounter a colossal shrouded white figure; an appended editor's note reports Pym's death, the loss of final chapters, and decodes the Tsalal chasm-figures as ancient words for darkness, whiteness, and "the region of the south."

testi/shakespeare/plays/alls_well_that_e.plot: The King of France discusses the Florentine-Sienese war with his lords, then warmly receives young Bertram at Paris, eulogizing his late father's honor and lamenting his own declining health.

Bertram woos Diana with false vows and surrenders his ancestral ring in exchange for a midnight assignation; Diana, already party to Helen's bed-trick scheme, agrees while privately vowing to cozen him without yielding her chastity.

testi/shakespeare/plays/antony_and_cleop.plot: Cleopatra, terrified of Antony's fury, flees to her monument and sends Mardian to falsely tell Antony she has killed herself.

testi/shakespeare/plays/as_you_like_it/a.plot: Duke Frederick threatens Oliver: find Orlando within a year or lose lands and be banished; Oliver admits he never loved his brother, which only enrages Frederick further.

Rosalind (disguised as Ganymede) interrupts Phoebe's cruel rejection of Silvius, rebukes Phoebe's pride, but inadvertently causes Phoebe to fall in love with "Ganymede," after which Phoebe resolves to send Silvius with a taunting letter to the disguised Rosalind.

Rosalind (disguised as Ganymede) exchanges barbs with Jaques on melancholy, then conducts a playful mock-wooing and mock-marriage ceremony with Orlando, warning him of love's transience before he departs to attend the Duke.

Oliver arrives in the forest to deliver Orlando's bloodied napkin to Rosalind and Celia, recounting how Orlando saved him from a snake and lioness, whereupon Rosalind faints at the news, nearly exposing her female identity beneath the Ganymede disguise.

Rosalind (as Ganymede) promises Orlando, Oliver, Phoebe, and Silvius that all shall be married tomorrow, orchestrating a fourfold resolution while Oliver announces he will wed Aliena and surrender his inheritance to Orlando.

testi/shakespeare/plays/coriolanus/act_1.plot: Defeated Aufidius, bloody after the fall of Corioli, vows to kill Coriolanus by any means — fair fight, treachery, or ambush — abandoning all scruple of honour or hospitality.

testi/shakespeare/plays/coriolanus/act_4.plot: Coriolanus bids farewell to his mother Volumnia, wife Virgilia, and friends Menenius and Cominius before departing into exile, urging them to suppress tears and promising to remain true to himself.

After Coriolanus's banishment, Volumnia and Virgilia confront the tribunes Sicinius and Brutus in the street, unleashing furious curses and reproaches before the tribunes retreat and the grieving women depart with Menenius.

testi/shakespeare/plays/coriolanus/act_5.plot: After Cominius reports that Coriolanus coldly refused to hear him or acknowledge his name, the tribunes persuade a reluctant Menenius to attempt his own appeal, while Cominius doubts it will succeed and pins last hope on Volumnia and Virgilia.

testi/shakespeare/plays/cymbeline/act_2/.plot: Posthumus rages in misogynistic soliloquy blaming Innogen and all women for vice after believing her unfaithful; then Cymbeline, the Queen, and Cloten jointly defy Rome's ambassador Lucius and refuse to pay Caesar's tribute, inviting war.

testi/shakespeare/plays/cymbeline/act_3/.plot: Belarius leads his adopted sons Guiderius and Arviragus from their cave for the hunt, praises wilderness over corrupt court life while they chafe at their ignorance of the world, then reveals in soliloquy that he kidnapped them as Cymbeline's heirs in revenge for his own unjust banishment.

Exhausted and starving, Innogen in male disguise stumbles into Belarius and his foster-sons' cave, is discovered taking food, and is welcomed as a companion named Fidele, unwittingly meeting her own lost brothers.

testi/shakespeare/plays/cymbeline/act_4/.plot: Cloten, wearing Posthumus' stolen garments, delivers a boastful soliloquy declaring himself Posthumus' superior in every way and vowing to kill Posthumus, rape Innogen, and return her to Cymbeline.
Belarius urges retreat to the mountains to avoid Roman forces, but Guiderius and Arviragus insist on joining the battle, shaming idleness in hiding; Belarius yields and all three march to fight.

testi/shakespeare/plays/hamlet/act_1/sce.plot: Laertes warns Ophelia not to trust Hamlet's love before departing; Polonius then interrogates Ophelia about Hamlet's courtship and commands her to refuse all further contact with him.

testi/shakespeare/plays/hamlet/act_3/sce.plot: Claudius and Polonius spy on Hamlet's encounter with Ophelia during which Hamlet delivers the "To be or not to be" soliloquy and then cruelly rejects Ophelia, sending her to a nunnery; Claudius concludes Hamlet's behavior is not love-madness and resolves to send him to England.

Claudius dispatches Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to escort Hamlet to England, then kneels alone in failed prayer over his brother's murder; Hamlet finds him praying but sheathes his sword, resolving to kill him in a damned state rather than send his soul to heaven.

Hamlet confronts Gertrude in her chamber, kills Polonius hiding behind the arras, forces Gertrude to face her moral corruption, and receives the Ghost's reminder to stay on course, before dragging Polonius's body away.

testi/shakespeare/plays/hamlet/act_4/sce.plot: Gertrude reports to Claudius that Hamlet in a mad fit has killed Polonius; Claudius sends Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to find Hamlet and retrieve the body, and resolves to ship Hamlet out of Denmark.
Hamlet, having hidden Polonius's body, mocks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern as royal sponges and refuses to reveal the body's location before running off with them in pursuit.
Claudius interrogates Hamlet about Polonius's body, then dispatches him to England with secret orders for his execution.

testi/shakespeare/plays/henry_v/act_2/sc.plot: Chorus narrates England's war fever as Henry readies to sail for France, then exposes a French-funded conspiracy by Cambridge, Scrope, and Grey to kill the king at Southampton before he can embark.

testi/shakespeare/plays/henry_v/act_3/sc.plot: Henry V delivers his famous "Once more unto the breach" speech, urging his troops to charge Harfleur's walls with fierce resolve and pride in their English heritage.

testi/shakespeare/plays/henry_v/act_4/sc.plot: Chorus describes the tense eve of Agincourt — overconfident French gambling while the weary English wait in dread — then celebrates Henry V's nocturnal walkabout among his troops as a source of morale and comfort.

testi/shakespeare/plays/henry_v/act_5/sc.plot: Chorus bridges narrative gap: describes Henry V's humble return from France to jubilant London crowds, his refusal to parade war trophies, then skips ahead past diplomatic negotiations to Harry's return to France.
Fluellen beats Pistol and forces him to eat the leek as payback for mocking Welsh customs; Pistol then learns his wife Nell is dead and vows to return to England as a petty thief.

testi/shakespeare/plays/julius_caesar/ac.plot: Brutus orders Messala to ride and signal his legions to attack at once, sensing weakness in Octavius's wing.

testi/shakespeare/plays/macbeth/act_1/sc.plot: Duncan praises Macbeth and Banquo, names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland, and plans to visit Macbeth's castle; in an aside Macbeth reveals his dark ambition to overcome Malcolm as an obstacle.

Macbeth soliloquizes doubts about killing Duncan, then Lady Macbeth enters and overrides his hesitation through taunts and a detailed drugging-the-chamberlains plan, ending with Macbeth resolved to proceed.

testi/shakespeare/plays/macbeth/act_2/sc.plot: Macbeth returns to Lady Macbeth immediately after killing Duncan; he is paralysed by guilt and unable to return the daggers, so Lady Macbeth does it herself, while Macbeth fears his bloodied hands can never be washed clean.

testi/shakespeare/plays/macbeth/act_5/sc.plot: Macbeth and Macduff fight; Macduff reveals he was born by caesarean section, shattering Macbeth's belief in his charmed life, yet Macbeth refuses to yield and is slain.
Macduff enters the battlefield seeking Macbeth alone, driven by guilt over his family's deaths, and refuses to fight lesser soldiers.

testi/shakespeare/plays/measure_for_meas.plot: Angelo and Escalus prepare for the Duke's return to the city, then Angelo alone confesses in soliloquy that he has deflowered (as he believes) Isabella and still had Claudio executed, and fears the consequences of his corruption.

testi/shakespeare/plays/much_ado_about_n.plot: Antonio reports to Leonato that a servant overheard Don Pedro confess love for Hero to Claudio and plan to declare it at the night's dance, so Leonato resolves to warn Hero to prepare her answer.

Don Pedro, Claudio, and Leonato mock Benedick's obvious lovesick change, while Don John arrives to plant doubt in Claudio and Don Pedro about Hero's fidelity, inviting them to spy on her chamber window the night before the wedding.
Claudio and Don Pedro, dressed in black, visit Leonato's monument at night, where Claudio reads an epitaph and sings a solemn hymn for Hero before departing at dawn to attend the planned wedding.

testi/shakespeare/plays/othello/act_3/sc.plot: Othello hands Iago letters to deliver to the pilot for the senate, then leads gentlemen to inspect the fortifications.

Iago plants seeds of jealousy in Othello's mind about Desdemona and Cassio, fabricates dream-evidence and the handkerchief as proof of adultery, and secures Othello's vow of revenge — ending with Othello ordering Cassio's death and promoting Iago to lieutenant.

testi/shakespeare/plays/othello/act_4/sc.plot: Othello publicly humiliates Desdemona by calling her a whore while Emilia and Iago witness her distress; Iago then manipulates the duped Roderigo into agreeing to murder Cassio so that Othello cannot leave Cyprus.

testi/shakespeare/plays/pericles/scenes/.plot: Gower narrates how Pericles receives news that Antiochus is dead and Tyre demands his return as king; he departs from Simonides' court with the pregnant Thaisa, and a violent storm at sea sends Thaisa into labor.
Pericles, departing Tarsus after his wife Thaisa's death at sea, entrusts his newborn daughter Marina to Cleon and Dionyza's care, vowing not to cut his hair until she is married.
Dionyza defends Marina's murder to a horrified Cleon, rationalizing it as done for their own daughter's benefit, and plans to deceive Pericles with a false monument and fabricated grief.

Gower narrates Pericles sailing to Tarsus to reclaim Marina; Cleon and Dionyza show him a tomb (dumb show), deceiving him into believing Marina dead, whereupon he departs in sackcloth and overwhelming grief while Gower reads Marina's false epitaph.

Gower narrates that Marina has escaped the brothel and thrives in an honest house through her arts of singing, dancing, and needlework, while Pericles' ship arrives at the very city where she dwells, setting the stage for their reunion.

testi/shakespeare/plays/richard_duke_of_.plot: After victory at Barnet, Edward IV and brothers Clarence and Richard learn Queen Margaret has landed from France with forces marching toward Tewkesbury, and Edward orders immediate pursuit.

Richard of Gloucester visits the imprisoned King Henry VI in the Tower, murders him twice with his dagger, then delivers a cold soliloquy proclaiming his plan to eliminate Clarence and all rivals until he alone holds power.

testi/shakespeare/plays/richard_ii/act_1.plot: Duchess of Gloucester urges John of Gaunt to avenge her husband's murder, but Gaunt refuses, arguing that since Richard II — God's anointed deputy — ordered the killing, only heaven can exact revenge.

testi/shakespeare/plays/romeo_and_juliet.plot: Capulet tells Paris to woo Juliet at his feast; Romeo and Benvolio chance upon the servant's invitation list and decide to attend, Romeo hoping to see Rosaline.
Lady Capulet and the Nurse summon Juliet and urge her to consider marrying the suitor Paris, who will attend the Capulet feast that night.

themes: transition from old to new desire
testi/shakespeare/plays/romeo_and_juliet.plot: The Chorus declares Romeo's old infatuation dead, replaced by mutual love with Juliet, and notes that though they are enemies barred from easy meeting, passion lends them the power and means to find each other.
Romeo secretly enters the Capulet orchard at night, overhears Juliet lamenting the barrier of his name, they declare mutual love, and Juliet proposes to arrange their marriage the following day.
Romeo visits Friar Laurence at dawn, declares his new love for Juliet and begs him to marry them that day; the Friar agrees, hoping the match will end the Capulet-Montague feud.
Juliet impatiently awaits the Nurse's return with Romeo's message; after prolonged teasing and complaint, the Nurse reveals Romeo waits at Friar Laurence's cell to make Juliet his wife.
Friar Laurence cautions Romeo against violent passion, Juliet arrives and the lovers exchange brief words of joy, then Friar leads them away to be married by the Church.

Juliet eagerly awaits Romeo's arrival, but the Nurse brings news of Tybalt's death at Romeo's hand and Romeo's banishment, plunging Juliet from joyful anticipation into anguish; torn between grief for her cousin and loyalty to her husband, she sends her ring to Romeo for a final farewell.

Romeo learns from Friar Laurence that the Prince has sentenced him to banishment rather than death; he collapses in despair, attempts self-stabbing, but is rebuked by the Friar and comforted by the Nurse bearing Juliet's ring, then is urged to spend the night with Juliet before fleeing to Mantua.
Capulet, citing Tybalt's recent death, abruptly decides to wed Juliet to Paris on Thursday and instructs his wife to inform her.

Romeo and Juliet part at dawn after their wedding night; Juliet is then told she must marry Paris on Thursday, her father Capulet rages violently when she refuses, her mother abandons her, and the Nurse betrays her by advising she comply — leaving Juliet alone, resolved to seek Friar Laurence's help or die.
Friar Laurence gives Juliet a sleeping potion to fake her death and avoid forced marriage to Paris, promising to alert Romeo so he can retrieve her from the Capulet tomb.

Juliet dismisses the Nurse and Lady Capulet, then alone delivers a fearful soliloquy weighing every danger of the potion—poison, premature waking in the tomb, Tybalt's ghost—before steeling herself and drinking it, collapsing onto her bed.

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_comedy_of_er.plot: Antipholus of Syracuse arrives in Ephesus, dispatches Dromio of Syracuse to the inn with gold, then is accosted by Dromio of Ephesus — his twin's servant — who knows nothing of the money but demands he come home to dinner; confusing the two Dromios, Antipholus beats him, then suspects theft and fears the city is full of sorcerers and cheats.

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_history_of_k.plot: Gloucester confides to Edmund his plan to secretly aid the banished King Lear despite Cornwall's prohibition, then Edmund immediately resolves to betray his father to the Duke to gain his inheritance.

Kent, disguised, tells a gentleman how Cordelia wept on reading letters about Lear's plight, explains that Lear's burning shame over his cruelty to her keeps him from reunion, and warns that Albany and Cornwall's armies are already moving.

Edmund forges a letter to frame Edgar as plotting against Gloucester, tricks their father into suspecting Edgar of parricide ambition, then manipulates Edgar into hiding — securing his own rise through calculated villainy.
After French forces are defeated and Lear and Cordelia are captured, Edgar urges the despairing blind Gloucester to flee with him, counseling that men must endure their fate — "ripeness is all."

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_tragedy_of_k.plot: Kent, disguised, meets a gentleman on the stormy heath: reveals Lear rages alone with the Fool, warns of Albany-Cornwall rift and French spies, and dispatches the gentleman to find Cordelia bearing a ring as proof of his identity.
After Lear and Cordelia's forces are defeated and taken prisoner, Edgar leads the blind Gloucester away from the field, urging him to endure with the maxim "ripeness is all."

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_two_gentleme.plot: Valentine departs for Milan while Proteus stays behind for love of Julia; Speed arrives and reveals Proteus's love letter to Julia got a cold reception, leaving Proteus resolved to send a better messenger.

Valentine, oblivious to his own lovesickness, writes a letter at Silvia's bidding to her "nameless friend," only to have Speed reveal that Silvia engineered the trick so Valentine unknowingly wrote a love letter to himself.

Proteus, alone, resolves to betray both Julia and Valentine — planning to inform Silvia's father of Valentine's secret elopement scheme so Valentine is banished and Proteus can pursue Silvia for himself.

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_two_noble_ki.plot: The three Queens process severally with their lords' hearses, sing a funeral dirge, exchange brief valedictions, and part — closing Act 1 on an image of death as the universal marketplace.

Palamon bursts from the bush still shackled, accuses Arcite of treachery for courting Emilia; Arcite denies dishonor and promises to secretly return with food, filed shackles, and weapons so they can fight a fair duel for Emilia's love.

Arcite secretly brings imprisoned Palamon food, wine, and files in the forest; they drink and reminisce warmly until Palamon accuses Arcite of sighing for Emilia, their fragile truce collapses into insults, and Arcite promises to return with sword and armour so they can duel properly.

Palamon and his knights kneel before Venus's altar; Palamon delivers an elaborate prayer proclaiming his lifelong fidelity to love and begging the goddess for victory in the coming combat, then receives a favorable omen of music and fluttering doves.

Emilia prays alone at Diana's altar to remain a virgin or have the worthier suitor win, then receives ambiguous divine signs — a rose blooms and falls — suggesting she will be taken as a bride against her will.

testi/shakespeare/plays/the_winters_tale.plot: Time as Chorus bridges a 16-year gap, noting Leontes remains shut up in grief while pivoting the action to Bohemia where Florizel and the now-grown Perdita will become the story's new focus.

Polixenes convinces Camillo to abandon plans to return to Sicilia and instead accompany him in disguise to a shepherd's cottage, where Florizel has been secretly spending time with a remarkable shepherd's daughter.

testi/shakespeare/plays/timon_of_athens/.plot: Despite having no money left, Timon orders Flavius to invite Lucius, Lucullus, and Sempronius to yet another feast, ignoring his steward's warnings about empty coffers.
Timon stands outside Athens walls, delivers furious curse calling for total societal breakdown, tears off clothes, and departs alone into the woods vowing hatred for all mankind.

testi/shakespeare/plays/troilus_and_cres.plot: Pandarus tells Cressida she must leave Troy and be exchanged for Antenor; Cressida refuses, swearing undying love for Troilus and vowing never to depart.
Troilus prepares to hand Cressida over to the Greeks for the prisoner exchange, likening himself to a priest sacrificing his own heart at an altar.
Achilles commands his Myrmidons to hold back their own blows and encircle Hector with weapons when found, declaring Hector's death decreed.
Hector, having just disarmed after battle, is surrounded by Achilles and his Myrmidons and murdered while defenseless; Achilles then orders the body dragged behind his horse.

testi/shakespeare/plays/twelfth_night/ac.plot: Orsino dispatches Viola (disguised as Cesario, having already won the Duke's trust in three days) to court Olivia on his behalf, while Viola privately reveals in an aside that she herself loves Orsino.
Sebastian parts from Antonio, reveals his twin sister drowned in the shipwreck and that he is bound for Orsino's court, while Antonio resolves to follow despite having enemies there.

Malvolio returns a ring to Viola (as Cesario) claiming Olivia sent it back, and Viola's soliloquy reveals she has no ring to return — deducing Olivia has fallen for her disguise, creating a hopeless love triangle.

Sebastian and Antonio arrive in Illyria; Antonio, fearing arrest for past offenses against the Count, gives Sebastian his purse and directs him to sightsee while he secures lodging at the Elephant inn.
Sebastian, bewildered by Olivia's gifts and unsure if he or she is mad, agrees to a secret betrothal ceremony with Olivia before a priest in a nearby chapel.

testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker recounts his origins in Paumanok and his wanderings across America's cities, plains, and wilderness, absorbing its nature and creatures, before declaring he rises to sing for a New World.

themes: cosmos, time, identity, faith as unifying forces
the poet as focal point for a vast interminable audience
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker surveys the globe's continents filling with peoples and institutions, then envisions successive generations of Americans marching on through time, each turning back to look at him.

themes: geography of the continent as subject
song/chant as vehicle for national spirit
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Speaker hails Americans and the marching century, then offers chants celebrating the prairies, the Mississippi down to the Mexican sea, and the states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, Wisconsin and Minnesota, radiating outward from Kansas like pulses of fire.

The poet urges his "leaves" (poems) to spread everywhere across America, then reflects that though he studied the old masters, he now wishes they could study him, and asks whether honoring America's newness means scorning antiquity, answering no since present things justify the old.

themes: reverence for dead poets, priests, and past civilizations
claiming one's own place in the present day
male and female as heirs of the world
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker honors and credits the legacy of past poets, priests, artists, and nations before declaring he takes his own place in the present, where male and female inherit the world and the soul arrives as its long-awaited satisfier.

themes: poetry of body, soul, and immortality
unity and comity among the States
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Speaker vows to write poems of soul, body and immortality, songs of the States' unity and of a fierce warlike nation, to acknowledge all lands and honor heroism from an American view, and to sing the song of companionship and comrades' love that only he can voice.

themes: self as embodiment of all peoples
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker declares himself embodiment of all peoples and both good and evil, claims to inaugurate a new religion, and asserts that true and lasting grandeur—of self, nation, earth and stars—depends on religion.

themes: the poet's inclusive acceptance of all pursuits
transience of mundane pursuits against spiritual/religious fire
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The poet addresses an unnamed young man, questioning his devotion to literature, science, art, love, politics, and ambition, and declares he does not condemn these but is their poet too, yet notes such pursuits quickly subside, consumed like fuel for religion's sake, since not all matter can feed the impalpable flame that is earth's essential life.

themes: search for something greater than love
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Speaker questions a pensive "camerado"/"dear son" whether what he seeks is love, then tells him (and America) that loving to excess is painful yet great, but something even greater and beyond materials coincides with and sustains everything.

themes: unseen mystical forces shaping the self
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Speaker sings to drop seeds of a "greater religion," addressing a comrade to share the combined greatness of love, democracy, and religion, then reflects on unseen spiritual forces and daily contacts (not mere childhood ties) that shape him, closing with praise of equality and the "divine average" as themes he takes up and passes forward.

themes: hidden meaning beyond the immediate audience
transmission of gift to future generations
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Walking in Alabama, the speaker watches a mocking-bird pair (hen nesting, male singing) and realizes the male's song carries a secret charge meant not just for mate or self but as a gift transmitted to those yet to be born.

The poet addresses Democracy and "Ma femme," vowing to sing bold new songs of passion, the body, sexuality, and the equality of the sexes, declaring death itself beautiful and affirming that every part of the universe and every poem must refer back to the soul.

themes: unity of body and soul as one meaning
kinship of self with nature (trees, rivers, rocks)
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: Speaker addresses reader directly, asserting body and soul cannot die or be truly buried, that the real body carries forward what it accrued from birth to death indifferent to death, and that body and soul are one, superb and divine.

themes: catalog of American lands and regions
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The poet addresses "whoever you are" and catalogs America's diverse lands and peoples (from Chesapeake to Colorado, Louisianian to Kanadian), declaring he includes and loves them all, roams among them as companion, and applies his "leaves" to unite new and old alike.

themes: rugged unadorned persona vs dainty refinement
life as hard-won prize through perseverance
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker urges the addressee to hold fast and adhere to him despite needing much persuasion (comparing this to how Nature too must be persuaded), then describes himself as no dainty, delicate figure but a bearded, sun-burnt, forbidding man who offers himself as a solid prize to be won only by those who persevere in wrestling with him.

themes: the vanished voice of Native Americans
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The poet pauses to hail America's present and future greatness, then honors the past by voicing the "red aborigines," whose vanished presence lingers only in the natural, bird- and wind-like sounds of the many native place-names now charging the land and water.

Speaker proclaims a swiftly expanding new world and race with new politics, arts, and religions, then declares he will sleep no more but rise, feeling the calm oceans within him stir into unprecedented waves and storms.

themes: poems as embodiment of the nation
progress and technology (railroad, telegraph, printing press)
testi/whitman/atomized/025_starting_from.plot: The speaker catalogs a sweeping panorama of America contained within his poems—steamers, immigrants, frontier scenes, both oceans, prairies and buffalo, cities, factories, telegraph and locomotive, workers and leaders—then presents himself as inseparable companion to the reader, urging them to hear his songs' echoes and grasp their meaning at last.
Speaker calls his "camerado" close for one final, ecstatic, wordless moment of shared triumph and love before they set off together.

testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Unit is bare section title "SPECIMEN DAYS" with no prose body — functions as header introducing Whitman's autobiographical prose collection of wartime memories and nature observations.

Whitman answers a friend's request for details of his early life, ancestry (especially the Dutch/Netherlands maternal line), and Brooklyn/New York years as background to "Leaves of Grass," agreeing to supply authentic, informally-told items he had already collated during a week's illness.

Whitman traces his maternal Van Velsor family's farm at Cold Spring, Long Island, and his paternal Whitman family's land at West Hills, Suffolk county, back through generations to John Whitman (born 1602 in England, emigrated 1640) and his brother Rev. Zechariah Whitman, whose descendants settled Huntington, Long Island, noting he wrote these notes during a visit to West Hills and his ancestors' burial grounds in his 63rd year.

Returning to Long Island after decades away, Whitman revisits the old Whitman family homestead and farm, then sits and reflects among the graves of generations of Whitmans on their burial hill (July 29), and the next day visits the more secluded, primitive Van Velsor family burial ground near Cold Spring where his maternal grandparents Cornelius and Amy (Naomi) are buried (July 30).

Whitman revisits the site of his mother's childhood home, the now-vanished Van Velsor homestead, and recalls its vanished buildings alongside memories of his grandmother Amy and grandfather Major Cornelius Van Velsor, and the family history of his mother Louisa Van Velsor and her Dutch and Quaker forebears.

themes: ancestral family life and slavery on Long Island
women of strong character in family lineage
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman quotes Burroughs's accounts of his slaveholding farm ancestors and strong-willed grandmothers, then describes his own birth and boyhood roaming Paumanok (Long Island) — eeling on the ice, gathering gull eggs, watching cattle and shipwrecks, and bathing at Coney Island.

themes: discovery of literature through library access
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman recalls his family's Brooklyn years, schooling, an office job where a library subscription opened him to voracious reading of the Arabian Nights and Walter Scott, and closes with a footnote by John Burroughs recounting how Lafayette, laying a library cornerstone in 1824, lifted and kissed the five-year-old Walt Whitman.

Whitman recalls learning the printing trade as a boy at S. E. Clements' Long Island Patriot and later Alden Spooner's Long Island Star, his friendship with old printer William Hartshorne, his large family of siblings, and (in a footnote) old rural Brooklyn of the 1830s-40s with its landmarks and notable citizens.

themes: teaching and early print trade work
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Narrator recounts his youth (1833-40): growing fast into a strong young man, moving with his family to the country while his mother recovered from illness, summers on Long Island, joining debating societies, devouring novels and theatre in New York, then working as a printing compositor, teaching country schools on Long Island while "boarding round," starting a weekly paper in Huntington, and finally returning to New York and Brooklyn to work as printer and writer.

themes: love of ferries and river scenery
sensory immersion in New York harbor life
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: The narrator recalls his years-long passion for riding the Fulton ferry across New York's harbor, savoring the ships, tides, and panorama, and fondly names the old pilot friends he knew there.

themes: memory and reminiscence of old New York
celebrity sightings on a public thoroughfare
the crowd and human flux of the city street
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman recalls decades of frequenting Broadway in New York, where he glimpsed politicians and celebrities, spoke briefly with Edgar A. Poe about a published piece, watched James Fenimore Cooper in a courtroom, and as a boy witnessed the aged John Jacob Astor being ceremoniously helped into a fur-lined sleigh.

themes: nostalgia for a vanished Broadway era
vitality and camaraderie of working men
influence of street life on poetic creation
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman recalls the now-vanished Broadway omnibus lines and fondly names and describes their drivers, robust, storytelling men he rode among for hours declaiming Shakespeare, crediting those jaunts with feeding into the making of "Leaves of Grass."

themes: nostalgic catalog of theatre and opera going in youth
celebrated actors, singers and Shakespearean performances in old New York
transatlantic careers of performers (Kemble, Italian opera troupes)
memory tied to specific theatres and places (Park, Bowery, Castle Garden)
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman recalls his youthful theatre- and opera-going in New York, listing the actors, singers, plays and operas he frequented at the old Park, Bowery, Chatham-square and Castle Garden venues, singling out Fanny Kemble, Booth, and the Havana musical troupe under Maretzek among many others.

Whitman recounts 1848-56: editing Brooklyn/New Orleans newspapers, an 8,000-mile journey with brother Jeff through the mid-South and around the Great Lakes back to Brooklyn, house-building, his father's death, and finally sending Leaves of Grass to press.

themes: Dutch maternal and English paternal lineage
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman traces his character to three sources—Dutch maternal stock, English paternal stubbornness, and his Long Island/Brooklyn upbringing plus Civil War experience—then notes that in 1862 news of his brother George being wounded at Fredericksburg sent him to the Virginia battlefield.

Narrator, walking down Broadway after the opera on the night of April 13 1861, learns from newsboys and a bought newspaper extra of the attack on Fort Sumter, then joins a silent crowd of thirty or forty gathered under the lamps at the Metropolitan Hotel to hear the telegram read aloud before dispersing.

themes: secession war as test of democracy
hidden national will surfacing in crisis
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman argues that the volcanic, spontaneous armed uprising of the North after the firing on the flag at Charleston settled the question of disunion and stands as democracy's grandest proof, matched at war's end by the equally remarkable peaceful, voluntary disbanding of the armies in summer 1865.

Whitman recalls how, even after Sumter, most Northerners contemptuously dismissed the secession as trivial and short-lived, illustrating this with the Brooklyn mayor's hope for a quick squelching of the "fire-eaters" and with Brooklyn militia companies who marched off carrying ropes to lead back Southern prisoners.

themes: chaos and panic of military defeat
political despair over the Union's survival
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes the defeated Union army's panicked, rain-soaked retreat into Washington after Bull Run, the citizens' mix of pity and mockery, the sleeping exhausted soldiers, the blustering officers at Willard's, and the capital's despairing talk of surrender and Lincoln's possible abdication.

themes: grief and memory of the war
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: After the Bull Run defeat, Lincoln recovers and reorganizes his forces while New York newspapers rally the despondent public with defiant editorials, and Whitman recalls that day of gloom in Brooklyn alongside the later day of Lincoln's assassination, both spent in near-silence with his mother.

Narrator visits a crowded, makeshift Union hospital in a mansion near Fredericksburg, describing piles of amputated limbs and fresh graves outside, then goes room to room among the badly wounded, talks with a wounded Confederate captain, writes letters home for dying men, and comforts a few who seem most in need.

themes: suffering and death of wounded soldiers
presence and small comfort to the dying
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Narrator describes visiting crowded, poorly-equipped division hospitals after the Battle of Fredericksburg, sitting with wounded and dying soldiers, then tours the camps at night talking with officers and men living in tents and log huts with meager rations.

The narrator travels by rail and steamer from Falmouth camp with wounded soldiers to Washington, then spends days visiting hospitals (Campbell, Armory-square) distributing food, money, writing paper, and letters home, noting particular cases like the sick D. F. Russell (who recovers) and the young amputee Charles Miller.

themes: suffering and endurance of the wounded
war's mix of cruelty and mercy
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: An unnamed Pennsylvania soldier, wounded at Fredericksburg and left lying helpless on the field for fifty hours, recounts to Whitman how passing rebels mostly taunted him but one middle-aged Confederate kindly bandaged his wounds and gave him biscuits and whiskey-and-water before he was finally retrieved under a flag of truce.

The narrator recounts hospital visits (Campbell and Armory-square) where he writes letters for wounded soldiers, distributes paper, envelopes, candy and small money, and observes scenes of surgery, a mother and a wife tending sick relatives, a nurse comforting a hemorrhaging patient, and a young New York soldier long suffering from a Bull Run bladder wound.

themes: makeshift institutional space repurposed for war
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: The narrator recalls visiting the crowded, makeshift hospital once housed in the Patent-Office's model-filled halls, describing the wounded and dying soldiers lying among the glass display cases before noting the hospital has since been cleared out.

themes: White House as symbol of nation
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: On a soft February night the narrator walks alone under the moon and gazes at the President's House, describing its white columns and moonlit, dreamlike splendor while armed sentries pace silently at the gates and portico.

themes: physical toll of war on young bodies
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes a visit to Ward 6 of Campbell hospital, depicting rows of sick and wounded young soldiers from many states lying quietly in pain, mostly without friends or familiar faces to comfort them.
