The narrator recounts befriending H. D. B., a sick young Connecticut soldier in bed 25, procuring him a home-made rice pudding (made by Mrs. O'C.) for his weak appetite, giving him a pipe as a keepsake, and later sharing dinner with him after he received a box from home.

Whitman visits two young Brooklyn men, members of the 51st New York whom he knew from home, in the hospital ward; one, J. L., recovers from an arm amputated after Fredericksburg, having borne it stoically, and still talks of encountering Confederate soldiers.

Whitman recounts a flag-presentation ceremony at the War department where a soldier named Gant presented a captured rebel battle-flag, and an officer told him it had been carried to the mouth of a Union cannon by a seventeen-year-old Confederate boy who was killed trying to stop the gun with fence-rails, the flag-staff itself severed by a Union shot.

themes: chaos and horror of night battle
inadequacy of words/art to capture war
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes wounded soldiers arriving by boat from Chancellorsville to a landing near Sixth Street, then recounts the furious night battle of May 2-3 near Chancellorsville and Fredericksburg (Hooker's forces vs. Stonewall Jackson's, Sedgwick's corps fighting on), where woods catch fire and burn wounded and dead, and hundreds lie suffering in field camps under a calm moon, closing with note that Berry, though not yet fallen, is marked for death.

themes: failure of history/art to record ordinary sacrifice
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman laments that the bravest soldiers of the Civil War go unnamed and unrecorded by history, poem, or report, imagining a typical unnamed soldier crawling off wounded to die alone and unburied in the underbrush after the battle sweeps past.

themes: small acts of comfort and compassion
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Narrator visits Civil War hospital wards, recording brief individual sketches of wounded and dying soldiers (Thomas Haley, W.H.E., J.G., J.T.L., Marcus Small, Thomas Lindly, Amer Moore and others), sitting with them, giving small comforts like tobacco, money, tea, apples, and writing letters home for them.

The narrator describes how, during the war, he prepared for his hospital visits by resting, bathing, dressing cleanly, eating well, and cultivating a cheerful manner, believing his personal presence and cheer helped patients more than medicine, delicacies, or money.

Whitman describes watching long, recurring processions of ambulance wagons carrying wounded soldiers through Washington streets (Fourteenth and Seventh streets) toward hospitals, a sight that had become common since the previous winter near Fredericksburg.

Whitman notes most soldiers arriving wounded from Chancellorsville are young, native-born Americans, describes the ward's burns, amputations, and probed wounds, and recounts a visitor fainting after glimpsing an awful wound.

themes: juxtaposition of glory and wounded aftermath
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: On June 29 and July 3, Whitman describes watching large cavalry forces, bugle bands, led horses, and baggage-wagons parade through Washington streets, calling it the most inspiriting of war's shows, then notes a string of ambulances bearing wounded men to hospital following right after.

themes: war news reaching the home front
contrast between patriotic celebration and hospital suffering
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: On July 4th in Washington, the narrator watches a small patrol/Fourth-of-July parade, reads a bulletin announcing Meade's victory over Lee at Gettysburg, then visits Armory hospital to tell wounded soldiers the news and serve them blackberry and cherry syrup with ice water as evening bells and firecrackers mark the holiday.

themes: close observation of Lincoln's daily habits
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes watching a cavalry camp opposite his window through summer weeks, recounts reading Scripture to dying soldier Oscar F. Wilber, describes a hymn-singing evening among wounded men in Armory-square hospital, and records his frequent sightings of President Lincoln riding with his cavalry escort to and from the Soldiers' Home.

themes: heat wave and human suffering in wartime Washington
war's armies circling but not touching the city
city's shift from anxiety to pride after Gettysburg
public health toll of extreme heat
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes an eleven-day heat wave in Washington causing sunstroke and horse deaths, contrasting it with the city's livelier, more confident mood now that the Fredericksburgh-to-Gettysburg campaign has passed it by untouched.

themes: soldiers' oral testimony vs official war record
surgeons' effort vs abandonment at death's certainty
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman recounts talking with wounded soldiers whose plain, unvarnished war stories he prizes over books, then describes visiting Armory-square hospital where a young Wisconsin lieutenant bleeds to death from an unstopped hemorrhage while ward life goes on indifferently around him, reflecting on how surgeons fight hard for the living but yield quietly once death is certain, closing with a footnoted quote from Garfield on Union soldiers, including Black soldiers, from rebel and border states.

themes: scale and organization of Civil War army hospitals
Washington's landscape dominated by hospital clusters
solitary nighttime ramble through the city
contrast between hospital suffering and calm moonlit sky
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: The narrator describes the vast network of Civil War army hospitals around Washington (Fairfax Seminary, the Convalescent camp, Finley, Campbell, Carver, Lincoln, Emory, and others), detailing their size, layout, and staffing, then recounts a solitary nighttime walk he took through Washington after leaving the hospital late one October night, finding calm in the moonlit sky and streets.

themes: solitude and quiet difference among comrades
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: Whitman describes meeting, among common soldiers in camp and hospital (often young Westerners), rare unworldly beings marked by innate spiritual sweetness and heroism who, despite little education, seem apart from their fellows, silent, odd, and given to solitary musing.

Whitman describes watching immense droves of cattle, up to a thousand head, driven through Washington's streets by mounted and foot drovers who call, whip, shout, and chase down escaping steers amid dust and noise.

themes: Civil War hospitals and wounded soldiers
literary tributes and criticism of poets
testi/whitman/atomized/complete_prose_wo.plot: This long composite unit (the file bundles far more than its "Hospital Perplexity" title, running through the rest of Specimen Days, Democratic Vistas, Collect, early poems, November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy) opens with Whitman describing the chaos of locating wounded soldiers in Civil War hospitals near Washington and at the front, then moves through wartime vignettes (bounty payments, deserters, army surgeons, the Grand Review, Lincoln's death and Sherman's army), into Whitman's nature and health-recovery journals, travel notes across the Mississippi Valley, Canada and the West, personal visits to Emerson and other literary figures, his essay on American democracy (Democratic Vistas), early poems and tales, and finally late-life reflections, tributes to poets (Burns, Tennyson, Shakespeare, Carlyle), and closing meditations on old age and death in Good-Bye My Fancy.

themes: neglect and cruelty toward the sick
physical and emotional suffering of wounded soldiers
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: The narrator describes the layout of Washington's hospital wards (including the Patent Office ward) and then tells the story of a young Massachusetts soldier, H., who nearly died from neglect and mistreatment during his transport from the front, until the narrator's visit and small acts of kindness restored his will to live.

themes: hospital visiting and care of sick soldiers
friendship and small gifts as healing
soldiers from many states bound by shared suffering
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: Narrator recounts nursing a patient ("H.") back from near-death through visits and gifts, reflects on his role as self-appointed hospital missionary amid thousands of sick and wounded men in Washington's fifty-odd hospitals, criticizes officious ward doctors and staff, describes the varied small items (jelly, tobacco, paper, letters) he distributes ward by ward, and highlights two Brooklyn soldiers, John Lowery and Amos H. Vliet of the Fifty-first New York, and their praised physician Dr. Frank Hinkle.

themes: ministering to the wounded and dying
Brooklyn soldiers as improvised community far from home
incompetence and petty tyranny among hospital officials vs. dedicated doctors
small gifts and letters as acts of comfort
war's carnage witnessed firsthand (amputations, graves, crowded wards)
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: Whitman catalogues Brooklyn soldiers and staff he has met across various Washington hospitals (Snyder, Dean, King, Lally, Hennessy, and others), contrasts the petty tyranny of some hospital officials (like "Red Stripe" and Dr. Hall at Judiciary-square) with the dedication of doctors like Bliss, Baxter, and Bowen, then shifts into a diary-style "Hospital Visits" account of his rounds from December 1862 through January 1863 — visiting Fredericksburg-area field hospitals, Falmouth, and Washington hospitals (Campbell, Armory-square) — where he writes letters home for the sick, distributes small sums of money, food, and reading matter, and attends to specific cases such as D. F. Russell and Charles Miller, before the text breaks off mid-sentence.

themes: ministry to the wounded and sick
hospital conditions and neglect after battle
charity, small gifts, and personal affection as healing
death and dying soldiers far from home
letters as link between soldiers and family
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: Whitman narrates years of visiting Washington-area army hospitals (1862-64)-tending, feeding, and writing letters for wounded and sick soldiers such as Oscar Wilber, John Mahay, William Cone, and the Rebel Irving, describing hospital layout and abuses-and includes his own letters home recounting his journey to find his wounded brother George near Fredericksburg and his subsequent hospital visits and lodging in Washington.

themes: hospital ministry and care for wounded soldiers
anxiety, waiting, and uncertain news from the front
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: A sequence of Walt Whitman's letters to his mother (and family) from Washington during 1863, recounting his daily hospital visits tending wounded and dying Civil War soldiers, interwoven with family news, worry over brother George's regiment and brother Andrew's illness, money and small gifts sent home, and reflections on the war (Vicksburg, Gettysburg, the New York draft riots, sightings of Lincoln).

themes: loyalty of Southern Unionist soldiers amid Confederate persecution
hospital caregiving and attachment to wounded soldiers
family correspondence and domestic worry (Andrew's illness, Jeff's wages)
daily life and war news in wartime Washington
faith in Union cause and Lincoln
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: In this run of letters to his mother (and one to friend Abby), Whitman praises Tennessee Unionist soldier John "Jack" Barker's suffering and steadfast loyalty, describes his own hospital-visiting routine and deep bonds with wounded soldiers (including Lewis Brown), reports Washington war news (Burnside, Rosecrans, Meade, Kilpatrick, Lincoln) and his confidence in eventual Union victory, and relays family matters back home—Andrew's declining health and death, Jeff's pay cut, and greetings to Mat, George, Mannahatta, and little California—while noting his own moves, meals, and daily circumstances.

In a run of letters to his mother from Washington (and briefly Culpepper/the front), Walt describes tending wounded and sick soldiers—especially Lewis Brown after his leg amputation—witnessing deaths, deprivation, and callous treatment, mixing in family news requests and a skeptical visit to the spirit medium Foster.

themes: war news and rumor vs. fact
anxious waiting for brother George's safety
Civil War campaign movements (Grant, Lee, Burnside)
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: In a run of dated letters to his mother from Washington (spanning April–May 1864), Walt Whitman reports on Congress, war rumors and troop movements (Burnside's, Grant's, and Lee's armies), sightings of his brother George's regiment and news of the wounded, his own hospital visits and tending of dying/recovering soldiers like Oscar Cunningham, and repeated reassurances of his own good health.

themes: Whitman's own declining health from hospital work
testi/whitman/atomized/the_wound_dresser.plot: In a run of Washington letters to his mother and brother Jeff, Whitman reports on incoming wounded, war news about Grant's advance on Richmond, news of brother George, the decline and deaths of soldiers Charles Cutter and Oscar Cunningham, and his own worsening health from prolonged hospital exposure, closing with an editorial note (dated the letters run to June 17, 1864) on how the hospital work eventually broke Whitman's health, followed by a short elegiac verse to his mother and the Gutenberg end-of-text footnotes.

testi/wilde/atomized/009_the_picture_of_.plot: Wilde's Preface declares his aesthetic manifesto: art exists solely to create beauty, has no moral purpose, and all art is quite useless.

Basil confesses to Lord Henry his obsessive artistic idolatry of Dorian Gray and refuses to exhibit the portrait because it exposes his soul; despite Basil's reluctance to introduce them, Dorian arrives at the studio as the chapter ends.

While Basil completes Dorian's portrait, Lord Henry mesmerizes Dorian with his philosophy of hedonism and the brevity of youth; upon seeing the finished painting, Dorian wishes his soul away so the picture ages in his place, speaking the fatal wish that sets the novel's central curse in motion.

Lord Henry visits his uncle to uncover Dorian's tragic family history, then dazzles guests at a society lunch where Dorian is present, while privately resolving to dominate the young man's soul as Basil's portrait dominates his image.
Dorian tells Lord Henry of his passionate love for actress Sibyl Vane, discovered performing Shakespeare in a dingy theatre; the chapter ends with Dorian's telegram announcing he is engaged to her.

Sibyl Vane declares her love for the mysterious Prince Charming (Dorian Gray) to her mother and departing brother James, who distrusts the gentleman; when Dorian passes them briefly in the park, James swears to kill him if he wrongs Sibyl, then wrings from their mother the admission that he is illegitimate.

At a private dinner, Dorian announces his engagement to actress Sibyl Vane; Basil worries about the mismatch while Lord Henry philosophizes on marriage, pleasure, and morality, and the three men then head to the theatre to watch Sibyl perform.

Dorian brings Basil and Lord Henry to watch Sibyl Vane perform Juliet, but she acts badly because real love has eclipsed art for her; Dorian cruelly rejects her, and returning home notices the portrait has taken on a cruel expression — the first sign his wish is taking effect.

Dorian learns from Lord Henry that Sibyl Vane has died; after brief guilt he examines the altered portrait and resolves to let it bear the burden of his sins while he pursues a life of eternal youth and pleasure.

Morning after Sibyl's death: Basil confronts Dorian's shocking coldness, confesses his obsessive idolisation of Dorian as the soul of his art, and Dorian — having kept Basil from seeing the portrait — resolves to hide it permanently.

Dorian has the portrait secretly moved to his locked childhood schoolroom, reads the decadent "yellow book" sent by Lord Henry with fascination, and coldly dismisses the newspaper inquest report announcing Sibyl Vane's death before meeting Lord Henry at the club.

Dorian Gray, consumed by the yellow book Lord Henry gave him, spends years obsessively pursuing aesthetic experiences — perfumes, exotic music, jewels, embroideries, vestments — while his youth stays intact and the hidden portrait silently bears the corruption of his dissolute secret life.
Basil confronts Dorian with rumors of moral ruin and ruined associates; Dorian, stung, seizes a lamp and leads him upstairs to see the portrait itself as his answer.
Dorian reveals the corrupted portrait to Basil, then in a sudden rage stabs him to death and calmly engineers an alibi through his valet.
Dorian, haunted by Basil Hallward's corpse, summons scientist Alan Campbell and blackmails him into chemically destroying the body with nitric acid, eliminating all evidence of the murder.

Dorian performs social normality at Lady Narborough's dinner with Lord Henry, then returns home to burn Basil Hallward's remaining belongings, and finally yields to opium craving and sneaks out toward the river den.

Dorian flees to an opium den to blot out guilt; James Vane corners him at gunpoint to avenge Sibyl's death, but Dorian's unchangingly youthful face convinces him he has the wrong man — until a woman confirms the terrible truth that Dorian has not aged in eighteen years.

At Selby Royal, Dorian and Lord Henry engage in sparkling wit with the Duchess of Monmouth, but Dorian collapses in a faint when he glimpses James Vane's face pressed against the conservatory window, watching him.
Dorian, consumed by terror that James Vane is hunting him, discovers after a shooting accident that the sailor killed in the hunt is Vane himself, and rides home with tears of relief at being safe.

Dorian dines with Lord Henry and declares intent to reform, while they debate Basil's mysterious disappearance; Dorian obliquely confesses to killing Basil (dismissed as posturing by Lord Henry), and their exchange circles around the soul, corruption, and the secret behind Dorian's unchanging youth.

Tormented by guilt and the worsening portrait, Dorian resolves to destroy it — stabbing it with Basil's murder knife — and is found dead, aged and hideous, while the portrait reverts to its youthful beauty.

testi/sayers/atomized/the_mind_of_the_ma.plot: Sayers clarifies her book is not apologetics but a factual commentary on the creeds' claims about God the Creator; lamenting widespread illiterate reading, she argues the mind's Trinitarian creative structure mirrors God.

Distinguishing arbitrary human 'law', codes resting on consent, from 'laws' stating unalterable fact about the universe, Sayers argues a universal natural moral law exists; defying it brings catastrophic 'judgments of God.'

The 'image of God' in man is the desire and ability to make things; since all language about God is analogical, we should read the creeds through the creative artist's experience of making something from nothing.

Every creative act is threefold, Idea (Father), Energy or Activity that works in time (Word), and Power responding in the soul (Spirit), three distinct yet consubstantial, an earthly trinity mirroring the heavenly.
The writer is both immanent in and transcendent of his work: each character externalizes part of his mind, yet the mind exceeds the sum of works; genuine creation needs diversity within unity.

Truly created characters possess a real free will the author defies at his peril; forcing plot by arbitrary 'miracle' is bad art, whereas letting nature run free reconciles free will and predestination through grace.

Incarnation is analogous to a writer entering his own story as a character with a double, divine-and-human nature: a true but partial self-revelation whose sincerity is infallibly tested by artistic truth.

Sayers analyses evil as Not-Being contingent on the Good: by creating Hamlet the poet creates Not-Hamlet, so God's Good necessarily begets evil, which self-will actualises at the Fall and only creative redemption can transmute.

The Power (Holy Ghost) is the book-as-read: once incarnate, the Idea works in readers' minds, gathering accumulated verbal power across writers, mirroring the writer's Trinity of Idea, Energy and Power in the reader.

Creative love is jealous yet not possessive nor sentimental: it grants the creature independence, embraces sacrifice, and demands co-operation, reconciling predestination with free will; Imagination is distinguished as the outward-driving opposite of self-absorbed Fantasy.

Every artist's trinity is imperfect, or scalene: writers become father-ridden, son-ridden, or ghost-ridden, and their failures parallel the Christological heresies, since a weak Idea, Energy, or Power distorts the work like original sin.

The modern habit of framing life as detective-style problems with final solutions falsifies reality; unlike soluble puzzles, death, war and work must be met creatively, made into something new rather than solved.

Industrialism and unemployment cannot be solved economically alone: work must be seen as a sacrament of creative energy, done with love and integrity for its own worth, distinguishing exacting love from indifferent kindness.

The appendix reproduces the relevant portions of the Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian (Quicunque Vult) Creeds affirming Trinity-in-Unity and the Incarnation, followed by the book's collected footnotes and source references.

themes: peace and storms of married life
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/a_duet/chapte.plot: In a closing dedicatory letter, the author addresses Maude Crosse directly, comparing young marriage to a small boat's voyage through calm and storm, and wishes her and Frank a happy life together.
Frank and Maude exchange a comic series of love letters repeatedly changing their proposed wedding date to accommodate relatives, finally settling on the 30th of June.

Frank writes an anguished letter wondering whether he is wrong to ask Maude to give up her comfortable life for his modest income, and after her passionate letters of reassurance he rushes by train to see her and the crisis passes.

In further letters Maude describes her clumsy first attempt at cooking and the wedding presents arriving, while Frank confesses his mounting bills and reveals he has become financial surety for a colleague, Farintosh, and describes their new house, The Lindens.

Frank waits nervously at Charing Cross for Maude, gives her an engagement ring in the station waiting-room, and the couple then stroll through London discussing the Eleanor Cross, Whitehall, and Charles I before going to lunch.
Frank and Maude spend a rainy afternoon touring Westminster Abbey, viewing the tombs of poets, statesmen and monarchs, and reflect on love, mortality and their own foreordained marriage.

On his wedding morning Frank frets at the hotel with his best man Rupton Hale and Maude's brother Jack Selby; despite a fumbled search for the ring and wedding fee, the ceremony at St Monica's Church proceeds and the newlyweds depart for Brighton.

On honeymoon at Brighton, Frank and Maude clumsily try to pass themselves off as an old married couple to the hotel staff, but a newspaper announcement of their wedding exposes the ruse to their amusement.

Arriving two days early at their new home The Lindens, Frank and Maude find it dark and empty, break in through a window, cook their own supper, and discover the new cook passed out drunk in the kitchen, who is later removed by the police.
Frank proposes that he and Maude jointly draft a set of household maxims for their marriage, and together they debate and compile twenty rules covering temper, freedom, money and mutual respect.

Frank confesses to numerous past infatuations before meeting Maude, provoking her mock jealousy, until she retaliates by claiming to have kissed and sat on a man's knee, revealed as a joke to have happened when she was three years old.

Frank discovers Maude crying over Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management because she cannot master it, reassures her that her efforts already make him happy, and the two mock the book's pompous advice together.

On a winter evening Frank reads Maude passages from Samuel Pepys's diary, explaining its cipher and candid confessions and discussing Pepys's marriage, until he grows distracted admiring Maude instead of the book.

Following a cryptic telegram, Frank and Maude meet in the City and visit St Olave's church to see Pepys's memorial and grave, hearing the old clerk's account of the exhumed remains, before finishing the day with buttered toast and a play.

Frank discovers his surety for the dishonest agent Farintosh has left him liable for a mounting debt to the Hotspur Insurance Company, and despite mixed legal opinions he and Maude brace for a lawsuit as the case heads toward trial.

Without Frank's knowledge, Maude enlists her father's money and her brother Jack's blunt bargaining to negotiate a much-reduced settlement with the insurance company, then presents Frank with the cancelled bond as a birthday gift.

Three Woking wives form a 'Browning Society' to improve their minds, but their meeting repeatedly wanders into gossip about servants, recipes and fancy-dress costumes, and their baffled attempt to read Browning's 'Caliban upon Setebos' causes the society to collapse after a single meeting.

Frank misreads a share-price listing and unwittingly commits to buying nearly a thousand pounds of gold-mine shares instead of fifty, but a lucky market rise lets him sell at a profit, and the couple use the windfall to buy a new piano.

Frank receives a letter from a former flame, Violet Wright, threatening to visit his wife unless he meets her; at a private restaurant he resists her advances and firmly ends their old relationship, provoking her anger.

Violet Wright unexpectedly calls on Maude at The Lindens, and after a tense start the two women form an unlikely bond, with Violet giving Maude heartfelt advice on keeping her husband's love before leaving without betraying Frank's secret.

Inspired by reading Carlyle's biography and letters, Frank and Maude visit the Carlyles' house at Cheyne Row, touring the rooms and relics while debating whether the great writer neglected his wife, and conclude that their own love matters more than fame.

As Maude's confinement approaches, Frank refuses to leave despite her attempts to spare him the ordeal, and when their son is born he is overcome with relief and joy, realising their marriage has now become a family trio.
In a closing letter to 'the Author,' Maude joyfully describes a typical day with her new baby, marvelling at his expressions and personality, ending the novel on a note of domestic happiness.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/a_study_in_sc.plot: Wounded army doctor John Watson, newly returned from Afghanistan, is introduced by his old acquaintance Stamford to the eccentric Sherlock Holmes, who astonishes him by instantly deducing he has been in Afghanistan; the two agree to share lodgings at Baker Street.

Living together at Baker Street, Watson catalogues Holmes's strange gaps and depths of knowledge, and Holmes reveals he is the world's only 'consulting detective,' demonstrating his method by explaining exactly how he deduced Watson had come from Afghanistan.

Holmes and Watson investigate the murder of Enoch Drebber, found dead without a wound in an empty house with the word 'RACHE' written in blood on the wall, and Holmes deduces details about the unknown murderer from footprints and evidence at the scene.

Holmes explains to Watson how he deduced the murderer's height, age and habits from the crime scene, then the pair interview constable John Rance, who reveals he unwittingly encountered and released the very suspect they seek.

Holmes places a newspaper advertisement about the found wedding ring to lure the murderer, but the elderly woman who answers it proves to be a disguised accomplice who slips away from his pursuit by leaping from a moving cab.

Gregson proudly reports he has arrested Arthur Charpentier for Drebber's murder after uncovering the Charpentier family's dramatic confrontation with Drebber, but Lestrade then arrives with shocking news that Drebber's secretary Stangerson has also been murdered.

Lestrade describes finding Stangerson stabbed to death with the same bloody 'RACHE' message nearby; Holmes tests two mysterious pills on a dying dog to confirm one is poison, then dramatically has the disguised cabman Jefferson Hope arrested as the murderer of both Drebber and Stangerson.
A one-line divider announcing Part II, "The Country of the Saints," which shifts the novel's action back to the American desert decades earlier.

Dying of thirst in the Utah desert, wanderer John Ferrier and the orphaned child Lucy are found by a passing Mormon caravan; Ferrier adopts Lucy as his daughter and agrees to join the Mormons under Brigham Young in order to survive.

John Ferrier becomes the richest farmer in the settlement while stubbornly refusing to take multiple wives; his adopted daughter Lucy grows into a beautiful young woman and falls in love with the hunter Jefferson Hope, who promises to return and marry her.

Brigham Young visits John Ferrier and decrees that Lucy must marry one of the Elders' sons within a month; Ferrier secretly resolves to defy the Church and flee Utah with his daughter rather than let her be forced into the marriage.

After Ferrier throws out the two young Mormon suitors, ominous daily countdown warnings appear around his house; Jefferson Hope returns secretly and helps Ferrier and Lucy flee through the mountains by night, slipping past armed Mormon sentinels using a stolen countersign.

The Mormon Avenging Angels overtake the fugitives, kill John Ferrier and drag Lucy back to be forcibly married to Drebber; she dies of grief within a month, and the vengeful Jefferson Hope spends years tracking Drebber and Stangerson across two continents to London.

Dying of an aneurysm, the captured Jefferson Hope confesses in full to the police and Holmes how he tracked Drebber and Stangerson to London and killed each in turn, using a poison-pill ordeal on Drebber and a knife on Stangerson, to avenge Lucy and John Ferrier.

Jefferson Hope dies in his cell before trial; Holmes explains to Watson the full chain of deductions by which he solved the case, while the newspapers give all the credit for the capture to Scotland Yard's Gregson and Lestrade instead of him.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/a_visit_to_th.plot: Conan Doyle explains that Italian authorities invited him to observe their lines in 1916, that he first visited the British and French fronts for comparison, and that he wrote this account to counter enemy propaganda and misunderstanding among the Allies.

Conan Doyle tours British front-line trenches near Ypres, watches an artillery observation post ('Mother') destroy a German outpost, attends a medal ceremony for wounded soldiers, and surveys the ruined city of Ypres and the eerie lights of the Salient at night.

Conan Doyle tours the Italian front along the Isonzo and in the Carnic Alps and Trentino, narrowly survives an Austrian artillery ambush on the road to Monfalcone, and praises the courage of Italian soldiers and the leadership of General Cadorna.

Conan Doyle visits French trenches at Soissons and in the Argonne forest, meets vivid French generals and the politician Clemenceau, and describes the discipline, dandyism, and grim resolve of French soldiers amid the ruins of war, before closing with an account of the earlier Boer War veldt.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/beyond_the_ci.plot: Two prim elderly sisters spy from their window as their flamboyant, physically formidable new neighbour Mrs. Westmacott moves into the villa opposite with her nephew Charles, shocking them by manhandling a rude cabman.

The Williams sisters pay a nervous call on Mrs. Westmacott, are terrified by her pet snake Eliza, and are subjected to her passionate speech on women's rights and her plan to found a local suffrage guild.

The chapter introduces the Walker and Hay Denver households in detail via the shared tennis lawn, and the Admiral and his wife notice that their son Harold seems distracted and possibly in love with one of the Walker sisters.

Charles Westmacott clumsily asks Clara Walker for career advice and lets slip that his aunt might remarry; that night Clara suspects her sister Ida and Harold Denver have an understanding, but playful Ida refuses to confide the secret.

Mrs. Westmacott persistently argues for women's suffrage and professional opportunity with the skeptical Admiral, winning him over point by point with her arguments and her own sailing adventures, until he agrees to join her platform.

Mrs. Westmacott hints to Clara that her nephew Charles wants to marry Ida; that same evening Harold Denver proposes to Clara herself, and she accepts, guiltily aware of a flicker of relief that Ida remains free for Charles.
Charles Westmacott takes Ida Walker on his tandem tricycle and haltingly proposes that she join him ranching in Texas; she gives no firm answer but leaves him hopeful by not withdrawing her hand.

Clara becomes convinced her father intends to marry Mrs. Westmacott and, fearing it would make him miserable, joins Ida in hatching a scheme to feign enthusiastic devotion to Mrs. Westmacott's emancipated ideas in order to put him off the match.

Clara and Ida begin their prank in earnest, disrupting the household with smelly chemistry experiments, smoking, and Clara's absurd plan to become a ship's pilot, all to disillusion their father with Mrs. Westmacott's philosophy.

The sisters' campaign peaks with unruly pets, a divided skirt, and a scandalous late-night 'supper' with cigarettes and champagne attended by their fiancés; the horrified Doctor finally renounces Mrs. Westmacott's influence, and the girls confess it was all to save him.

Mrs. Westmacott warns the Admiral that her disreputable brother Jeremiah Pearson, Harold's business partner, cannot be trusted; soon after, Pearson absconds having embezzled the firm's funds, leaving Harold bankrupt and dishonoured, though Clara refuses to break their engagement.

Clara persuades her father to secretly advance money to help save Harold from ruin, while the Admiral, unwilling to accept charity, privately resolves to raise funds of his own, even considering returning to sea, to save his son's honour.

The Admiral tries to raise money by mortgaging his naval pension through the moneylender Reuben Metaxa, whose crooked scheme, aided by a fake doctor's grim diagnosis, is exposed when the suspicious Charles Westmacott persuades him to walk away.

The honest lawyer McAdam arranges a legitimate sale of the Admiral's pension to a genuine investor, after which the undaunted Admiral seeks work as a ship's officer at a shipping company and is treated with sudden respect once his true identity and record are revealed.

Harold learns his debts are smaller than feared and that his parents have raised enough money to cover them, but on discovering his father sold his naval pension to do so, he refuses to touch the money and rushes off determined to undo the sacrifice.

The Williams sisters watch a man secretly climb into Mrs. Westmacott's house at night and strike her down; the alarmed neighbours rush over and find her stunned but alive, with no clue yet as to her assailant's identity.

Mrs. Westmacott reveals her estranged brother Jeremiah Pearson attacked her when she refused to give him money she had held in trust, and she uses that same money to restore the Admiral's pension and clear Harold's debts, clearing the way for the joint wedding of Clara to Harold and Ida to Charles.

themes: national pride and vengeance against Britain
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/danger_and_ot.plot: The fictional Captain John Sirius narrates how his small nation's flotilla of eight submarines systematically sinks British merchant shipping, starving Britain into a humiliating peace despite her vast conventional navy.

themes: poetic justice against a swindling financier
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/danger_and_ot.plot: Country magistrate Sir Henry Hailworthy, masked as a highwayman, robs three motorists on a Sussex road one Sunday night — his friend Ronald Barker, two actresses, and financier Sir George Wilde who had ruined him in a bank collapse — and next morning, unmasked by Barker's sharp eye, explains it was revenge on Wilde with the other robberies as cover, having already arranged to return everything he took from the innocent victims.

An American journalist who mocked an English footman's obsequious manner in a published article is confronted first at the country house and later in London by the footman, Henry Harding, who defends the honor and self-respect of good service and threatens violence until the journalist admits he misjudged him.

To win a thousand pounds from his uncle, the dandy Sir Charles Tregellis, young rake Vereker Tregellis stages a public ambush at Vauxhall Gardens in which two disguised women provoke Sir Charles's despised rival Lord Barrymore and his hired bully Hooper into a brawl, leaving them beaten and humiliated before the whole of fashionable London.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/his_last_bow/.plot: Holmes investigates the murder of young Spaniard Aloysius Garcia and uncovers that his household were conspirators plotting to assassinate the fugitive Central American tyrant Don Murillo, hiding as Henderson at High Gable, and rescues Murillo's drugged captive-governess Miss Burnet before the tyrant and his secretary flee England, only to be killed abroad months later.

Holmes deduces from a pair of severed ears mistakenly posted to Miss Cushing that her jealous, drink-ruined brother-in-law Jim Browner murdered his wife Mary and her lover Alec Fairbairn after Mary's meddling sister Sarah had poisoned the marriage with jealousy.

Holmes unravels the mystery of a landlady's silent, reclusive lodger and discovers an Italian couple, Gennaro and Emilia Lucca, hiding from the murderous Red Circle enforcer Giuseppe Gorgiano, who is found stabbed to death after Gennaro kills him to protect his wife.

Called in by his brother Mycroft, Holmes investigates the theft of the Bruce-Partington submarine plans and the death of clerk Cadogan West, discovering that Sir James Walter's brother Colonel Valentine Walter sold the plans to foreign agent Hugo Oberstein, who killed West when he intervened, and Holmes lures Oberstein back to England to be arrested.

Holmes fakes a fatal tropical disease to lure the vindictive planter Culverton Smith, who had murdered his own nephew with a poisoned spring-trap box, into gloating confession while Watson and a hidden Inspector Morton listen, after which Smith is arrested.

themes: predatory con artists preying on lonely women
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/his_last_bow/.plot: Watson and then Holmes trace the vanished Lady Frances Carfax across the Continent and back to London, discovering she has been drugged and imprisoned by the con artist Henry Peters and his wife, and Holmes saves her at the last minute from being buried alive inside a coffin built to conceal her alongside another woman's corpse.

Holmes investigates a Cornish horror in which one sister dies of fright and two brothers are driven mad, uncovering that their lodger cousin Mortimer Tregennis poisoned them with African devil's-foot root for money, and that explorer Dr Leon Sterndale then secretly executed Tregennis in revenge for the death of Brenda, the woman he had loved in secret for years.

themes: patriotism on the eve of war
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/his_last_bow/.plot: Posing for two years as the Irish-American spy Altamont, Holmes infiltrates German master-spy Von Bork's operation, drugs and captures him on the eve of WWI, and recovers his stolen naval-signal papers with Watson's help.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: In this brief preface Doyle surveys his own eventful life of sport, medicine, war service and travel, and announces that his final years have been devoted to spreading the results of his decades-long study of the occult.

Doyle recounts his Anglo-Irish artistic family background, his parents' hard-pressed household in Edinburgh, boyhood fistfights and a glimpse of Fenian unrest in Ireland, and his precocious early appetite for reading and writing stories.

Doyle describes his harsh schooling at Hodder and Stonyhurst under the Jesuits, including severe punishment and his discovery of a talent for verse, followed by a happier year at Feldkirch in Austria and a penniless visit to his eccentric great-uncle Michael Conan in Paris.

themes: origin of Sherlock Holmes's deductive method
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle studies medicine at Edinburgh, observes his teacher Dr Joseph Bell's astonishing diagnostic deductions (the model for Holmes), works as an assistant doctor to earn money, and describes his father's decline and his own drift from Catholic faith into agnosticism.

themes: danger and endurance in the Arctic
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: As ship's surgeon aboard the whaler Hope, twenty-year-old Doyle spends seven months in the Arctic hunting seals and whales, nearly drowning several times, and returns physically transformed and toughened by the voyage.

themes: disease and death in colonial Africa
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: As ship's surgeon on the steamer Mayumba, Doyle sails down the West African coast, nearly dies of fever at Lagos, witnesses the deadly toll of the climate on colonists, resolves to give up wandering and drink, and survives a shipboard fire on the voyage home.

themes: starting a medical practice from nothing
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle recounts his volatile friendship with the eccentric, genius-quack doctor Cullingworth, who lures him into a chaotic Plymouth practice, then turns on him out of jealous suspicion, forcing Doyle to strike out alone and found his own practice in Portsmouth with almost no money.

themes: mortality and faith in medical practice
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Living almost penniless in his first house at Southsea, Doyle slowly builds a meagre medical practice, is joined by his young brother Innes, endures the death of a patient under his own roof, and marries Louisa Hawkins in 1885.

Doyle describes his slow literary rise through short stories, the creation of Sherlock Holmes (modelled on Joseph Bell) and the hard road to publishing 'A Study in Scarlet', the acceptance of 'Micah Clarke' after many rejections, and a memorable dinner with Oscar Wilde that led to 'The Sign of Four' and 'The Picture of Dorian Gray'.

themes: literary and political life in Portsmouth
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle recounts his growing interest in psychic research and telepathy in Southsea, his impulsive trip to Berlin to witness Koch's tuberculosis-cure demonstration (and rebuff by Bergmann), and his political and literary activities in Portsmouth before leaving for London in 1890.

themes: birth of the Sherlock Holmes stories
killing off Holmes at Reichenbach Falls
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle studies ophthalmology in Vienna and opens an oculist practice in London that attracts no patients while his Sherlock Holmes stories in The Strand bring fame; after nearly dying of influenza he resolves to live by his pen alone, moves to Norwood, and eventually kills off Holmes at the Reichenbach Falls, provoking a huge public outcry.

themes: stage and film dramatizations of Holmes
Holmes perceived as a real person
curious fan letters and real deductions
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle discusses stage and film adaptations of Sherlock Holmes (Gillette's play, The Speckled Band), Barrie's comic parody written after their failed opera collaboration, how illustrators shaped Holmes's image, and recounts curious letters, hoaxes, and real puzzles the public sent him hoping Holmes could solve.

themes: retreat to Davos for her health
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle recounts joining literary London (Jerome K. Jerome's circle, selling 'A Straggler of '15' to Henry Irving), the devastating diagnosis of his wife's tuberculosis, their retreat to Davos and Maloja for her health, and his 1894 lecture tour of America with his brother Innes under agent Major Pond.

themes: seeking a cure abroad for consumption
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle takes his wife and sister to Cairo for the winter of 1895-96, mixes with the British officials rebuilding Egypt (Cromer, Kitchener, Slatin), tours the Nile and a remote Coptic monastery with Colonel Lewis after getting lost overnight in the desert, and the chapter ends as news arrives that war has been declared against the Dervishes in the Sudan.

Doyle becomes honorary war correspondent for the Westminster Gazette and travels up the Nile to the Sudan frontier with fellow journalists, camel-riding through the desert to Wady Halfa and Sarras and dining with Kitchener, before being recalled home without seeing actual fighting.

themes: shadow of the coming Boer War
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Settled at Undershaw, Doyle writes several novels, deepens his psychic research including investigating a haunted house at Charmouth and a strange encounter with a secret occult society, while sensing the approaching shadow of war with the Boers in South Africa.

themes: volunteering after the Black Week disasters
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: After Britain's disastrous Black Week, Doyle joins John Langman's volunteer field hospital as unofficial medical supervisor, sails for South Africa, and on arrival at Bloemfontein the hospital is overwhelmed by a devastating typhoid epidemic caused by the Boers cutting the town's water supply.

themes: skirmishes and artillery fire at Brandfort
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle rides with the advancing British army as it takes Brandfort and pushes toward the Vet River, witnessing artillery duels, the looting of a Boer farm, and wounded and dead soldiers including an abandoned Australian trooper, before returning to hospital duty at Bloemfontein.

themes: military rivalries between Roberts and Buller factions
quelling a mutiny among hospital staff
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle recounts military feuds between Roberts and Buller supporters, personally defusing a mutiny among his hospital's orderlies, traveling to newly captured Pretoria where he meets Lord Roberts and witnesses a remarkable spinal operation on a wounded Boer officer, before sailing home to England in July 1900.

themes: propaganda and public opinion in wartime
translation as a tool of persuasion
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle conceives and writes in a week a pamphlet defending British conduct in the Boer War, raises thousands of pounds by public subscription, and organizes its translation and free distribution in some twenty languages across Europe and beyond.

Doyle recounts his two unsuccessful runs for Parliament: Central Edinburgh in 1900, lost after a last-minute smear branding him a secret Roman Catholic, and the Border Burghs in 1905 on a Tariff Reform platform against Tommy Shaw, concluding that politics was never his true calling.

After South Africa, Doyle is knighted, writes his history of the Boer War, loses his first wife in 1906, and then campaigns to overturn the wrongful convictions of George Edalji and Oscar Slater, exposing failures of the police and Home Office.

Doyle describes travels to Constantinople and Greece, his staging of boxing and adventure dramas at the Adelphi, his reporting on the 1908 Olympic Dorando marathon, his Congo reform campaign with Casement and Morel, and a catalogue of his often ruinous business speculations.

themes: portraits of the great and famous
the private character behind public reputation
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle offers a gallery of personal reminiscences of statesmen and writers he has known, including Roosevelt's blunt vitality, Balfour's golf and psychic silence, Meredith's pride, Barrie's collaboration on 'The Admirable Crichton', and Kipling's Vermont hospitality.

themes: cricket and golf as lifelong passions
the thrill and danger of new pursuits (motoring, skiing, ballooning)
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle surveys a lifetime of sport, questioning the morality of hunting and racing, celebrating boxing and cricket (including bowling out W. G. Grace), and recounting narrow escapes in early motoring, ballooning, and pioneering skiing in Switzerland.

themes: the promise and vastness of Canada
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: In spring 1914 Doyle and his wife tour North America, from New York's prisons and baseball to Parkman's historic battlefields, then across the Canadian prairies to Jasper Park in the Rockies, reflecting on Canada's future within the Empire just before war breaks out.

themes: Britain's blindness to the German threat
the submarine and the Channel Tunnel debate
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle describes how a pre-war German motor race and Bernhardi's writings convinced him war was coming, details his published warnings about submarine blockade and the need for a Channel Tunnel, and recounts a sharp cross-examination by General Henry Wilson on Britain's readiness.

themes: secret communication with prisoners of war
grief for a family devastated by the war
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle founds a village Volunteer force that grows nationwide, serves as a private for the war's duration, smuggles coded news to British prisoners at Magdeburg, meets figures like Empress Eugenie, and recounts the deaths of many relatives including his son Kingsley and brother Innes.

themes: a civilian's first sight of the front
the discipline and confidence of the British Army
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Granted a pass to the front in 1916, Doyle crosses with General Robertson, tours trenches near Bethune and the Ypres Salient, watches an artillery duel involving the gun 'Mother', meets Field Marshal Haig at GHQ, and briefly reunites with his son Kingsley just before the Somme offensive.

themes: mountain warfare and the Alpine front
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle visits the Italian front at Udine, narrowly survives an Austrian shrapnel barrage on the road to Monfalcone, tours the Alpini positions in the Carnic Alps and Trentino, and later recalls a psychic premonition of the word 'Piave' that presaged Italy's decisive 1918 victory there.

themes: desecration of sacred and cultural sites
vivid character portraits of French officers
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: Doyle visits French sectors near Soissons and in the Argonne, meets Clemenceau and colourful commanders like the fierce General Henneque and a colonel nicknamed 'Cyrano', tours front-line trenches, and narrowly avoids an artillery shell that had been laid in wait for his returning car.

themes: the joy and chaos of Armistice
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/memories_and_.plot: After breakfasting with Prime Minister Lloyd George, Doyle later joins the Australian forces in September 1918, watches from a tank the breaching of the Hindenburg Line near Bellicourt, witnesses grim battlefield scenes and columns of prisoners, and finally describes the outbreak of Armistice celebrations in London.

In his closing chapter Doyle declares Spiritualism the central purpose of his life, describes years of global lecture tours with his wife, recounts personal evidence of contact with his dead mother, son, and brother, and predicts that psychic knowledge will transform religion and science.

themes: family tension between Nonconformity and the Church
narrating history to the next generation
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Aged narrator Micah Clarke begins his memoir for his grandchildren by describing his stern Ironside father Joseph Clarke, a former Cromwellian officer turned tanner, whose violent fits of religious fervour (including an apocalyptic false alarm) shaped Micah's Hampshire childhood.

themes: the value of reading and self-education
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Micah describes the era's anti-Catholic anxiety over a Catholic succession, his schooling under Mr Chillingfoot at Petersfield, and his expulsion after sawing through a footbridge that dunks the pompous Vicar Pinfold into a stream, ending with his growing eagerness to leave the village.

themes: the romance of a sailor's traveller's tales
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Micah introduces two formative mentors of his boyhood: the learned, gentle carpenter-philosopher Zachary Palmer, who reassures him about religion and virtue, and the tattooed old sailor Solomon Sprent, whose vivid tales of naval battles and foreign lands stir Micah's appetite for adventure.

themes: muster and drilling of raw troops
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Saxon organizes the Wiltshire volunteers into disciplined companies in Taunton's market-square as Mayor Timewell reviews the assembled rebel forces and reads a proclamation declaring Monmouth king, along with a list of the town's recent dead.

The four companions inspect the town's arms depot and dine at Mayor Timewell's crowded household, where Sir Gervas courts Timewell's granddaughter Ruth and the old soldiers swap war stories, until the Mayor reveals that Argyle's rising in Scotland has failed and invites the men to lodge with him.

Reuben fights off masked attackers at night to rescue a cloaked woman who turns out to be Ruth Timewell, and Micah realizes his friend has fallen in love with her; the next morning word comes that Monmouth's army is about to make its triumphant entry into Taunton.

Monmouth enters Taunton in triumph, knights Mayor Timewell on the spot, and the assembled regional regiments of fishermen, clothworkers, and peasants march past in review while Reuben confides to Micah his hopeless-seeming love for Ruth.

themes: council of war and rivalry of factions
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: At Monmouth's council in the castle hall, Micah wins a hand-grip and sword-strength contest against the German mercenary Buyse, delivers a gold ingot and a cryptic prophetic verse to Monmouth, and then volunteers to carry a secret message to the wavering Duke of Beaufort.

themes: homesickness on the eve of a mission
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Micah and Sir Gervas receive letters from home; Micah reads aloud a philosophical letter from the old carpenter Zachariah Palmer and a comic nautical one from the sailor Solomon Sprent, while Sir Gervas rages at his uncle's betrayal of his old nurse and reflects on his ruined fortune.

Riding alone by night toward Badminton with Monmouth's letter, Micah is swept from his horse by a rope trap and captured by a gang of smugglers who nearly execute him as a suspected exciseman before his true identity is confirmed, after which they agree to carry him and his horse onward by lugger toward Bristol.

The smugglers' lugger dodges a King's warship in dense fog and lands Micah near Bristol; guided to Badminton by the talkative Farmer Brown, Micah forces a public audience with the Duke of Beaufort and delivers Monmouth's letter, provoking the Duke's furious denunciation and Micah's immediate arrest.

Condemned to hang, Micah is held in the reputedly haunted Boteler dungeon at Badminton, where Farmer Brown visits him through a window and, that night, the Duke of Beaufort himself secretly frees him through a hidden trapdoor, giving a private conciliatory message for Monmouth before Micah rides off and is joyfully reunited with Reuben and Sir Gervas.

Micah reports the results of his mission to Monmouth's council, which nearly erupts into violence between Puritan zealots and courtiers before the King restores order and the army resolves to march on toward Bristol the next morning.

The rebel army marches miserably through mud toward Bristol while Reuben laments his stalled courtship of Ruth; Micah and Reuben capture the Royalist officer Major Ogilvy near Keynsham Bridge, and Monmouth's council, finding the enemy too strong across the Avon, decides to turn toward Bath instead of attacking Bristol.

At Wells, a mob of fanatic soldiers sacks the cathedral until Micah's group and reinforcements suppress the riot in bloody hand-to-hand fighting at the altar rail, after which the exhausted, storm-battered army is reviewed before falling back toward Bridgewater.

themes: reminiscence of city pleasures versus rural life
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: On a night foraging raid from Bridgewater to gather supplies, Micah and Sir Gervas talk of London life and the war's hopelessness before defying Major Hooker's orders and riding off alone toward a lonely farmhouse after hearing a woman's terrified scream.

themes: a highwayman's rough code of honor
treachery punished on the eve of battle
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Micah and Sir Gervas save a farmer from torturing dragoons with the help of the highwayman Hector Marot, gather supplies from grateful villagers and return safely to camp; that night Monmouth's council resolves on a surprise attack, and Micah and Reuben intercept the traitor John Derrick, who fatally stabs Reuben before drowning in the marsh, while a small girl guarding a lonely cottage shelters the wounded men.

Monmouth's army marches by night to surprise the Royalist camp at Sedgemoor, but the attack falters at an unseen ditch, the Bussex Rhine; after fierce close-quarter fighting Monmouth abandons the field, the rebel line is broken by cavalry and cannon, and Sir Gervas is left to die with his company as Micah and Saxon narrowly escape.

Fleeing the rout at Sedgemoor, Micah hides in a windmill with the cowardly Taunton clerk Tetheridge, who secretly betrays him to a Royalist patrol; nearly hanged on the spot, Micah is spared when his name is recognized as connected to Major Ogilvy, and Sergeant Gredder escorts him as a prisoner toward Gommatch.

Imprisoned first at Gommatch church and then at Bridgewater and Taunton, Micah learns of Monmouth's capture and the cruelty of the Bloody Assizes; the old sailor Solomon Sprent visits with news from home and wild rescue schemes, and the chapter closes with the arrival in Taunton of the dreaded Judge Jeffreys.

themes: the Bloody Assizes and judicial cruelty
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/micah_clarke/.plot: Judge Jeffreys presides over a sham trial that condemns the Taunton prisoners to be sold as slaves; aboard the prison ship at Poole, squabbling gentry claim captives for profit, until Decimus Saxon secretly buys Micah's freedom and reveals that the highwayman Hector Marot, posing as crew, will free the other prisoners once the ship is at sea.

The novel closes as Micah recounts the later fates of his companions - Reuben's marriage to Ruth Timewell, Saxon's career fighting Indians in Virginia, old Solomon Sprent's peaceful death, and the unknown fate of Hector Marot's freed prisoner-ship - as the aged narrator ends his memoir to his grandchildren.

themes: moral reform as a con trick
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: A quiet stranger calling himself the Reverend Elias B. Hopkins reforms the lawless gold-mining camp of Jackman's Gulch through relentless Bible readings and a Sunday service, then reveals himself as the bushranger Conky Jim, holding the congregation at gunpoint while his gang murders the gold-keeper and robs the camp's stored treasure.

themes: endless pursuit by vigilantes and police
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: A prison doctor draws out the life story of convict Wolf Tone Maloney, a former bushranger who saved his own neck by turning Queen's evidence against his gang and was hounded across continents by vigilantes and detectives ever since; months later the doctor witnesses Maloney's fatal shootout with his old enemy Tattooed Tom.

A reclusive Scottish hermit rescues a young Russian woman from a shipwreck on his desolate coast and then refuses to surrender her to the desperate sailor who claims her as his abducted love; the sailor finally steals her away by boat during a storm, and both are found drowned on the beach, locked together in death.

A nervous, imaginative passenger on a transatlantic steamer becomes convinced that two fellow passengers are dynamiters carrying a bomb set to go off at ten o'clock, and after an agony of dread finally confronts them at the fatal hour, only to discover the 'infernal machine' is a trap releasing two racing carrier pigeons for a betting match.

themes: a carnivorous plant as instrument of fate
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: An American storyteller relates how, in a Montana mining camp, a mild Englishman named Tom Scott faced down the murderous bully Alabama Joe, who then ambushed him at night but was instead killed when a giant man-eating flytrap closed on him as he lay in wait, sparing Scott from a lynch mob's rope.

themes: an April Fool's prank turned dangerous
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: In a rowdy gold-mining camp the simple, gigantic miner Abe 'Bones' Durton falls for the assayer's daughter Carrie Sinclair; a prank love-letter meant as an April Fool's joke lures him to her house on the very night a gang of bushrangers led by her rejected suitor Black Tom Ferguson attacks it, and Bones and his partner defend the home until the camp arrives to rout the rangers, after which Bones and Carrie eventually marry.

themes: a ghost legend explained by ingenuity
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: Two down-on-their-luck friends in the Cape Colony bush investigate a local legend of a glowing 'demon's eye' haunting Sasassa Valley and, using a rigged sighting-stick, locate and extract a valuable diamond from the cliff face, securing their fortune.

themes: a wager settled by a horse race
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: Home from India, Lieutenant Jack Hawthorne and shy cousin Sol Barker both fall for young Nelly Montague and agree to let a Derby sweepstakes wager decide who should court her, but while they are absorbed in horse-racing news Nelly quietly falls for a third suitor, Nicholas Cronin, and eventually marries him instead.

themes: a drugged vision of stock ghost-types
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/my_friend_the.plot: A wealthy self-made man obsessed with acquiring a resident ghost for his newly bought manor hires a supposed spirit-broker who drugs him with chloral, producing a vivid hallucinated parade of stock apparitions before robbing the house of its silver plate, leaving the narrator cured of his taste for the supernatural.

themes: historical sources for a Regency novel
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: This unit is Conan Doyle's preface to Rodney Stone, in which he lists the historical works he consulted and thanks two friends for information on prize-fighting; it contains no story action or characters.

themes: nostalgic narration of a vanished Regency England
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: The elderly narrator Rodney Stone opens his memoir with his family's naval history and his boyhood in the village of Friar's Oak near Brighton, introducing his sailor father, his fashionable uncle Sir Charles Tregellis, and his friendship with Boy Jim, nephew of the retired champion boxer turned blacksmith Harrison, closing with an anecdote of Harrison facing down a young aristocrat's insult with his fists.

Driven by pride, Boy Jim persuades the reluctant Rodney to break into the haunted Cliffe Royal at night to see the ghost of the murdered Captain Barrington; they glimpse a shadowy figure on the stairs and flee in terror, only to be found on the road by Champion Harrison, who is himself on a secret errand.

Rodney and Jim visit the reclusive, hard-drinking Miss Hinton, a former Haymarket actress living at Anstey Cross; her dazzling theatrical performances win the boys over, and Jim's gentle insistence that she give up drink begins a lasting, redemptive friendship.

Rodney's father, Lieutenant Anson Stone, returns home from years at sea with a wounded leg during the Peace of Amiens, and the family's joy is complicated by a letter announcing an impending visit from the wealthy, fashionable Sir Charles Tregellis.

themes: class contrast between country and town
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: The flamboyant Sir Charles Tregellis arrives at Friar's Oak, dazzles the household with his wit and manner, and agrees to take Rodney to London with him, while a chance meeting with Champion Harrison stirs old memories tied to the Cliffe Royal tragedy.

On the eve of departure Rodney's mother tearfully showers him with advice for London life, and the next day he sets off with his uncle Sir Charles, watched by the whole village and by an envious Boy Jim, who longs for his own chance to escape Friar's Oak.

Rodney travels to Brighton with his uncle, is presented to the Prince of Wales at the Pavilion amid gossip and political banter, and witnesses the fashionable world's obsession with prize-fighting as his uncle arranges a boxing wager.

themes: danger and daring on the road
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: Sir Charles races his curricle against Sir John Lade's four-in-hand from Brighton to London, narrowly avoiding a deadly collision when Lady Lade tries to force them off a bridge, and delivers Rodney safely to his new London home.

Rodney is introduced to London's fashionable clubs, watches Sir Charles verbally spar with the rising dandy Brummell, and overhears the sinister Sir Lothian Hume claim he may soon inherit the title of the long-vanished, presumed-murderer Lord Avon.
At a boisterous supper for the boxing Fancy hosted by Sir Charles, with the Prince secretly present, a mysterious stranger downstairs sends up his hat as a challenge to fight any man in the room.

The mysterious challenger is revealed to be Boy Jim, who defeats the drunken bruiser Joe Berks in a bare-knuckle bout staged in a coach-house, winning Sir Charles's offer to be his champion against Crab Wilson of Gloucester.

At Fladong's, the sailors' London haunt, Rodney listens to veteran naval officers debate prize-money, ship quality, and French seamanship, until thrilling news arrives that war has broken out again and the whole fleet is being mobilized.

themes: contrast between public glory and private frailty
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: Rodney and his father visit Admiral Nelson, who promises Anson a ship and Rodney a naval berth, and they witness Nelson's odd devotion to the theatrical Lady Hamilton just before his urgent orders to sail arrive.

themes: uncle-nephew tension over class and worth
loyalty to friends over social rank
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/rodney_stone/.plot: As the great prize-fight nears, Sir Charles frets over Rodney's friendship with the low-born Jim, until the prizefighter Bill Warr warns them of a plot by Joe Berks and hired thugs to cripple Jim before the match, sending them racing to Crawley.

Arriving at Crawley the night before the fight, the party discovers Jim has vanished from his locked room, apparently lured out through the window by a mysterious woman, and finds a bloodstain and a bludgeon lying on the nearby road.

With Jim still missing and the fight about to be forfeited, Sir Charles bitterly accuses Sir Lothian Hume of conspiracy before thirty thousand spectators, and at the very last second a substitute champion's hat is thrown into the ring to save the match.

The substitute champion proves to be the retired Champion Harrison, come out of retirement with his wife's grudging blessing, and after a magistrate halts the match on legal grounds the whole crowd stampedes across the county line to restart it.

Harrison and Wilson fight a long, brutal battle in driving rain, Harrison rallying with age and grit, until a mob incited by Sir Lothian's hired roughs breaks into the ring and forces the referee to declare the contest a draw.

Summoned mysteriously to Cliffe Royal, Rodney and Sir Charles learn that Miss Hinton is in fact Jim's mother and that the fugitive Lord Avon, believed for eighteen years to be his brother's murderer, is Jim's father, alive and hiding in the house.

Lord Avon explains to his old friend Sir Charles how he discovered his brother Captain Barrington's marked-card cheating and confronted him on the fatal night, using the pricked cards themselves to prove his own innocence at last.

The valet Ambrose confesses that he killed Captain Barrington in revenge for seducing his fiancee, clearing Lord Avon of murder, who is nonetheless placed under a friendly magistrate's custody pending formal trial.

Sir Lothian Hume is arrested for debt and disgraced, the vindicated Lord Avon and his family live out happier days, and Rodney departs to serve under Nelson as the narrator reflects, decades later, on the fates of everyone he has known.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_fir.plot: A young man is found shot dead alone in a locked express-train compartment with six watches in his pockets; years later a confessional letter reveals he was his brother's card-sharping partner, accidentally killed by that partner during a struggle when his elder brother tried to save him.

A respected doctor is apparently found murdered and his fiancee's brother stands trial for it, but at the trial it emerges the doctor faked his own death after his estranged twin brother died of heart failure in his study, and the doctor himself appears to testify and save the innocent man.

A priceless jeweled breastplate in a museum is mysteriously tampered with each night; the culprit turns out to be the former curator, secretly restoring the true stones his daughter's reformed criminal fiance had earlier stolen and replaced with fakes.

A chartered special train and its passengers vanish without trace between two stations; a condemned criminal's confession years later reveals it was diverted onto a disused branch line and driven straight into an abandoned mineshaft to silence a witness against corrupt French financiers.

A young man is summoned to his estranged uncle's remote moorland house, which is besieged that night by a vengeful ex-convict sea captain and his sailors seeking stolen diamonds; the uncle dies falling from a window, and the diamonds are found hidden inside his hollow clubfoot boot.

themes: protecting a dying wife from shock
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_fir.plot: A young heir is forbidden to enter a sealed room in his house until his twenty-first birthday; when it is finally opened, it reveals his father's mummified body, dead by suicide years earlier to avoid disgracing his family while sparing his fragile wife the shock of ruin.

A penniless young man visits his wealthy cousin hoping for financial help, but is treacherously locked in a den with a savage pet Brazilian cat meant to kill him; he narrowly survives, and it is instead his murderous cousin who is killed by the beast once it has tasted blood.

themes: the healing power of bedside manner
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A young, modern-trained physician recalls his old-fashioned family doctor, whose outdated methods are quietly mocked by his up-to-date rivals, until an influenza epidemic strikes and even the narrator, falling ill, instinctively sends for the old man rather than his scientific young colleague.

themes: initiation and fear in medical training
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A terrified first-year medical student is led into the operating theatre to watch his first surgery and faints dead away from dread during the surgeon's preparations, only to be told afterward that the operation never took place at all and he had merely fainted during a lecture.

themes: the last survivor of a vanished regiment
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: An aged, failing veteran of Waterloo, cared for by his young grandniece Norah, is visited and honoured by a young sergeant and the colonel of his old regiment; reliving the battle in his mind, he dies crying the old battle-cry as if once more on the field.

themes: the sins of the father visited on the son
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A young baronet consults a specialist and learns he has inherited his grandfather's venereal disease, making his imminent marriage impossible; unable to face breaking his engagement, he is killed the same night in a street accident that may be suicide.

themes: chance and fortune in a career
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A penniless new doctor, after humiliating false starts with a gas inspector and a gypsy patient, is summoned by mistake to treat a wealthy man's wife, refuses to breach etiquette or flatter his patron, and his integrity ultimately wins him a prosperous partnership.

themes: fear and helplessness of the expectant father
the callousness of routine to the medical professional
birth and the renewal of ordinary life
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A commonplace shopkeeper endures a night of terror while his wife undergoes a difficult, dangerous labour attended by two doctors; after agonising hours the child is safely born and Johnson finds himself transformed by the experience.

themes: enduring marital love in old age
idealisation versus reality of the beloved
the wearying yet renewing routine of practice
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A country doctor observes an elderly gentleman on a seaside bench decline daily while separated from his wife, then rejuvenate on the morning of her return, revealing the depth of a fifty-year marriage when the plain, aging woman finally arrives.

themes: hidden feeling beneath a mask of detachment
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A rigidly rationalist physiology professor marries a widow who turns out to be the supposedly-drowned first wife of his own former student and protégé; on discovering the truth he nobly relinquishes her to her true husband and, though outwardly unmoved, wastes away and dies of what his colleagues privately call a broken heart.

A brilliant but reckless surgeon, lured by a disguised Lord Sannox posing as a Turkish merchant, is tricked into mutilating the drugged face of his own mistress, Lady Sannox, as the wronged husband's calculated revenge, driving Stone to madness.

themes: the complicity of doctor, wife and prime minister
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: While the gout-ridden Foreign Minister frets over state affairs, his wife Lady Clara skilfully manoeuvres the Prime Minister, the family doctor, and finally her husband himself into approving their daughter's marriage to the impoverished but well-born Lord Arthur, securing him the post at Tangier so the couple may wed and go together.

themes: the desensitising effect of medical practice
shocking and macabre cases from real life versus fiction
human courage in the face of illness and death
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: After a medical dinner, three doctors trade unsettling anecdotes from their careers—madness, gruesome surgeries, and stoic patients facing death—while a young layman secretly transcribes their talk for a magazine article.

themes: friendship and moral courage against evil
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: Oxford student Abercrombie Smith comes to suspect that his sinister neighbour Bellingham has learned to reanimate an ancient mummy and is using it to attack his enemies; after the creature nearly kills him, Smith forces Bellingham at gunpoint to destroy the mummy and his occult papyrus.

themes: dark comedy of a botched execution
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A committee overloads a condemned murderer with massive electric current intending instant death, but the shock instead renders him indestructible—surviving electrocution, hanging and shooting—leaving the authorities with an immortal criminal on their hands.

themes: professional rivalry turning to respect and love
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A complacent country doctor is professionally outclassed and personally transformed by a brilliant new rival who turns out to be a woman physician; he falls in love and proposes, but she refuses marriage to devote herself entirely to a scientific career, leaving him changed and alone.

themes: irony of dying from one's own specialty
comedy and tragedy intermingled in medical life
compassion and tact toward the dying and their families
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/round_the_red.plot: A veteran surgeon recounts to a young colleague a string of memorable cases—including a neurologist who diagnoses his own fatal disease mid-lecture and a chloroform mishap that costs a colleague his ear—reflecting on the blend of courage, tragedy and dark comedy in medical practice.

testi/conan_doyle/atomized/sir_nigel/sto.plot: In a prefatory note, Conan Doyle explains his research and choices in reconstructing fourteenth-century England for the novel, defending small historical liberties and the depiction of period cruelty as necessary to authenticity.

themes: the Black Death and social upheaval
decline of the old feudal nobility
a young man's suppressed longing for glory
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/sir_nigel/sto.plot: After the Black Death ravages England and breaks the old feudal order, the impoverished, ancient house of Loring survives only in Nigel and his fierce grandmother, who keeps him at home at Tilford despite his eagerness for a soldier's life.

themes: superstition and rumor of the supernatural
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/sir_nigel/sto.plot: The Abbot of Waverley and his grasping sacrist discuss squeezing the impoverished Loring family through legal claims, provoked by Nigel's prank of putting pike in the abbey's fishpond, when a monk bursts in reporting that 'the Devil' has attacked brethren in a field.

themes: taming of a wild spirit through courage and skill
a young knight's first feat of prowess
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/sir_nigel/sto.plot: The 'devil' proves to be a savage, untamable horse the abbey has acquired; Nigel saves a servant from it, is mockingly given the horse by the sacrist, and after a wild, punishing ride across the countryside breaks it to his will, winning the magnificent steed Pommers.

themes: legal persecution of the powerless by the Church
testi/conan_doyle/atomized/sir_nigel/sto.plot: After a quiet evening of song and reminiscence at Tilford, armed men led by the Abbey's summoner and sacrist storm the manor by night, arrest Nigel on trumped-up charges over his defiance of the Abbey's claims, and Lady Ermyntrude furiously curses Waverley Abbey as they drag him away.

The Basilisk carries Nigel and Knolles's men through a Channel fog past an unseen Spanish armada, fights off a boarding party from a Spanish galley, and then joins the English fleet's pitched battle with the Spaniards off Winchelsea, where Nigel and Knolles help save the Black Prince aboard a captured carack.
